title: Qué tienen en común los países que sí han logrado reducir el suicidio
content: Países como Noruega, Finlandia, Dinamarca y Alemania ha conseguido disminuir las tasas de suicidio en las últimas décadas; sus planes se caracterizan por ser a largo plazo, con objetivos realistas y estructuras de gobernanza capaces de sostener las intervenciones España registra 10 suicidios al día: “La prevención no cabe en una sala de consulta” La adopción de estrategias nacionales de prevención del suicidio se ha convertido en una prioridad internacional, impulsada por el reconocimiento del suicidio como un problema de salud pública global y por la evidencia que demuestra que las intervenciones aisladas no son suficientes para revertir las tendencias de mortalidad. Sin embargo, aunque más de 40 países han implementado iniciativas nacionales, entre ellos España, con su Plan de Acción para la Prevención del Suicidio (2025-27), los resultados son marcadamente desiguales. Mientras países como Finlandia, Noruega o Dinamarca han mostrado avances importantes, otros contextos con planes igualmente ambiciosos han observado un impacto limitado o inconsistente. Aunque más de 40 países han implementado iniciativas nacionales, los resultados son marcadamente desiguales Esta heterogeneidad obliga a analizar no solo el contenido técnico de las estrategias, sino los procesos que determinan su aplicabilidad, coherencia, sostenibilidad y capacidad de adaptación a contextos socioculturales diversos. Los elementos que explican la eficacia Los países que han logrado mayores avances tienen en común algo fundamental: cuentan con estrategias que actúan a varios niveles y que combinan intervenciones universales, selectivas e indicadas, junto con acciones de postvención tras intentos y muertes por suicidio, dentro de un marco de coordinación y gestión coherente. Las medidas más sólidas incluyen sistemas de vigilancia epidemiológica capaces de integrar información procedente de múltiples fuentes, la restricción del acceso a medios letales y campañas de comunicación que abordan explícitamente el estigma, utilizando enfoques culturalmente adecuados. Estas acciones no actúan de manera aislada, sino que operan sobre determinantes amplios y modifican actitudes de la población, al tiempo que reducen las barreras estructurales para la búsqueda de ayuda. Las estrategias más efectivas han priorizado intervenciones dirigidas a grupos específicos –adolescentes, migrantes, minorías étnicas, personas mayores aisladas, comunidades LGBTQ+ o población penitenciaria Las estrategias más efectivas han priorizado intervenciones dirigidas a grupos específicos –adolescentes, migrantes, minorías étnicas, personas mayores aisladas, comunidades LGBTQ+ o población penitenciaria– mediante modelos comunitarios, redes de apoyo y programas adaptados cultural y lingüísticamente. La evidencia muestra que la sensibilidad cultural y la adecuación contextual no son elementos accesorios, sino determinantes de la eficacia, especialmente en poblaciones históricamente excluidas de los sistemas o circuitos de ayuda. Las acciones dirigidas a personas con riesgo elevado o con intentos previos constituyen un punto crítico. Los estudios coinciden en que el seguimiento intensivo tras un intento de suicidio y la incorporación de protocolos estructurados en atención primaria son dos de los mecanismos de mayor impacto. Asimismo, la formación de gatekeepers –personas clave capaces de identificar señales tempranas de riesgo y activar los recursos asistenciales adecuados– en entornos educativos, comunitarios y sanitarios facilita la detección precoz y la activación de circuitos asistenciales eficaces. El análisis comparado evidencia que la mera existencia de un plan nacional, incluso cuando está basado en recomendaciones internacionales, no garantiza resultados. La diferencia entre estrategias efectivas y estrategias nominales radica en la forma de ponerlas en marcha. La clave está en una buena coordinación La coordinación de varios sectores es especialmente determinante: allí donde salud, educación, servicios sociales, justicia y medios operan de manera aislada, las intervenciones pierden coherencia y capacidad de impacto. Por el contrario, los países que han avanzado –como Noruega o Alemania– han desarrollado estructuras estables de gobernanza, con responsabilidades bien definidas, mecanismos de coordinación y sistemas de seguimiento integrados. La disponibilidad de recursos humanos y financieros es otra variable crítica. Países como India, que aprobó hace pocos años su estrategia nacional, han debido reorientar su plan hacia un modelo de salud mental comunitaria debido a la escasez estructural de profesionales especializados. Este tipo de adaptación, lejos de debilitar la estrategia, la hace más realista y sostenible en contextos de recursos limitados. La obtención de datos fiables permite evaluar con precisión el impacto de las intervenciones y orientar decisiones de política pública A ello se suma la importancia de los sistemas de vigilancia. La obtención de datos fiables –que pueden incluir certificación forense rigurosa; registros multiagencia, es decir, sistemas en los que varias instituciones u organismos comparten y cruzan información sobre un mismo problema, o autopsias psicológicas– permite evaluar con precisión el impacto de las intervenciones y orientar decisiones de política pública. Las desigualdades territoriales, la fragmentación institucional y el estigma cultural siguen actuando como barreras transversales. En Groenlandia, por ejemplo, la estrategia nacional ha situado la equidad territorial como eje central, reconociendo las distancias geográficas como una barrera estructural para el acceso a la atención. Canadá, con su Plan Nacional de Acción 2024–2027, ha explicitado por primera vez mecanismos formales de colaboración multisectorial para corregir déficits de coordinación acumulados durante años. Estas experiencias muestran que las barreras no se superan únicamente con prescripciones técnicas: requieren transformaciones estructurales. Lo fundamental: cómo medir el impacto real Uno de los desafíos más persistentes en la prevención del suicidio es la dificultad para atribuir descensos de la mortalidad directamente a la implementación de estrategias nacionales. La conducta suicida está influida por muchos factores –cambios sociales, fluctuaciones económicas, reformas sanitarias, dinámicas culturales o variaciones en la disponibilidad de recursos–, lo que complica el aislamiento del efecto específico de un plan [nacional]. Precisamente por ello, los planes más maduros, como los de Suecia, Noruega, Finlandia y Australia, han incorporado sistemas de evaluación continua que permiten monitorear cambios antes de que se observen variaciones en la mortalidad. Estos sistemas incluyen indicadores intermedios como tiempos de acceso a servicios, continuidad asistencial, registro de intentos y medidas poblacionales de estigma. Este enfoque reconoce que la reducción de muertes es un objetivo a largo plazo, y que los indicadores de proceso permiten detectar si la estrategia está modificando los factores que, previsiblemente, acabarán influyendo en la mortalidad. No existe un modelo único, pero sí un conjunto de fundamentos que comparten las estrategias más robustas La capacidad de un país para revisar, ajustar y corregir su estrategia a partir de estos datos constituye un elemento central de efectividad. De hecho, las estrategias más exitosas no son las que acumulan más acciones, sino aquellas que establecen mecanismos explícitos de aprendizaje, retroalimentación y mejora continua, integrando datos procedentes de vigilancia epidemiológica, evaluaciones externas y análisis de desempeño. No existe un modelo único, pero sí un conjunto de fundamentos que comparten las estrategias más robustas. En cuanto a experiencias con resultados positivos, destacan los casos de Noruega, que ha logrado reducciones significativas mediante estrategias sostenidas desde 1995; Finlandia y Dinamarca, que combinaron restricciones de medios letales con expansión de servicios; Alemania, cuyo programa NAAD permitió reducir un 24 % los actos suicidas, y Países Bajos, que implementó el modelo SUPRANET Community, articulando gobernanza local y coordinación multisectorial. Estas experiencias evidencian que la reducción de la mortalidad depende de planes a largo plazo, con objetivos realistas y estructuras de gobernanza capaces de sostener las intervenciones. Cuando estos elementos se integran –calidad del diseño, coherencia en la implementación, gobernanza estable y evaluación continua–, la reducción del suicidio se convierte en una posibilidad concreta. En un fenómeno tan complejo, la consistencia estratégica y la planificación basada en datos son tan esenciales como las intervenciones específicas orientadas al riesgo. La experiencia internacional deja, por tanto, una lección clara: prevenir el suicidio no consiste simplemente en acumular intervenciones. Requiere construir sistemas capaces de coordinarlas, sostenerlas, evaluarlas y adaptarlas en el tiempo. Elizabeth Suárez Soto es doctora en Psicología y Psicóloga Clínica Infanto Juvenil de la Universidad Internacional de Valencia Este artículo fue publicado originalmente en The Conversation. Puedes leerlo aquí.

title: Um desafio pessoal levou esse biólogo a criar um aplicativo que apoia pacientes com câncer
content:
César Filho, WeCancer (Fonte: WeCancer | Reprodução)
Redatora
Publicado em 9 de setembro de 2026 às 05h01.
Uma experiência dolorosa ao lado da mãe em tratamento contra o câncer despertou em César Filho uma missão: transformar o cuidado oncológico por meio da tecnologia.
O que nasceu de uma dor virou inovação na saúde, com o app WeCancer impactando mais de 10 mil pacientes.
“A gente só entende o sistema de saúde de verdade quando alguém que a gente ama precisa dele.” Foi assim que César Filho, biólogo de formação, descobriu uma vocação que mudaria sua vida — e a de milhares de pacientes.
Era para ser só mais uma consulta. Mas o que viu ao acompanhar sua mãe em um tratamento contra o câncer foi uma sucessão de falhas no acompanhamento, falta de comunicação entre profissionais e a solidão do paciente diante de um sistema fragmentado.
Ao invés de se conformar, César decidiu agir.Foi o início da WeCancer, um aplicativo que conecta pacientes com câncer a uma equipe de saúde digital, oferecendo apoio, orientação e escuta no dia a dia da jornada oncológica.
Hoje, o aplicativo já impactou milhares de vidas e trabalha em parceria com grandes hospitais e operadoras de saúde. Mas o caminho até aqui foi repleto de desafios — e aprendizados.
A ideia de empreender na área da saúde surgiu de um momento profundamente pessoal: o tratamento da mãe de César. Ele percebeu que, mesmo com acesso a bons profissionais, o processo era solitário e confuso.
Com esse propósito claro, César começou a desenhar a ideia da WeCancer, mesmo sem experiência anterior com startups ou tecnologia. O que ele tinha era o desejo de resolver um problema real.
A virada de chave aconteceu quando César foi selecionado para participar do Programa de Liderança do Na Prática. Foi ali que ele deu o “salto”: deixou a teoria de lado e mergulhou em um ambiente de aprendizado mão na massa.
Durante a experiência, César teve contato com metodologias ágeis, acesso a uma rede de mentores e apoio para criar o primeiro protótipo da WeCancer.
O programa também reforçou em sua trajetória a importância da escuta ativa, da colaboração e da ação rápida — pilares que ele carrega até hoje como empreendedor.
Mas o maior desafio ainda estava por vir: levantar recursos para levar o projeto para uma imersão nos EUA. Sem investidores e sem capital próprio, César lançou uma campanha de financiamento coletivo.
Essa experiência não só garantiu a ida aos Estados Unidos, como também se transformou num símbolo da garra que moveu o projeto desde o começo. Persistência e criatividade marcaram o início da WeCancer.
Hoje, a WeCancer é uma tecnologia consolidada, que já atendeu mais de 10 mil pacientes e coleciona prêmios e reconhecimentos no setor. Mas, para César, o mais importante é ver que aquela dor inicial deu origem a uma solução real.
E o apoio do Na Prática, segundo ele, foi uma das peças-chave nessa virada: “Eles me ensinaram a me mover mesmo com poucos recursos — a testar, ouvir e melhorar. Foi ali que eu aprendi a empreender com propósito.”
Quando perguntado sobre qual conselho daria para outros jovens com uma ideia na cabeça, César não hesita:
“Tira do papel. Mas antes, escuta de verdade quem vive o problema. É essa escuta que vai te dar clareza para seguir.”
“A gente acha que precisa estar pronto pra começar. Mas, na real, a gente começa e vai se tornando pronto.” Essa é a mentalidade que guiou César — e que pode inspirar outros a fazerem o próprio salto.

title: Ethiopia Writes a New Chapter in Global Environmental History With 56.8 Billion Planted Tree Seedlings
content:
Ethiopia Writes a New Chapter in Global Environmental History With 56.8 Billion Planted Tree Seedlings
Addis Ababa, September 10, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia has planted 56.8 billion tree seedlings over eight years through its Green Legacy Initiative, surpassing its initial 50-billion-seedling target and marking what the country describes as a new chapter in global environmental history.
Launched in 2019 at the initiative of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, Green Legacy was conceived as a national response to land degradation, deforestation, biodiversity loss and the degradation of water resources, while linking environmental restoration with sustainable development.
The scale of the undertaking has grown far beyond a conventional tree-planting campaign. More than 3 billion seedlings have been planted in a single day during the initiative’s years of implementation, while more than 25 million citizens have been mobilized annually to take part in the nationwide effort.
The initiative has also been designed around the productive value of trees. About 60 percent of the seedlings planted are agroforestry species, including fruit trees, coffee and fodder varieties, while the remainder consists of forest trees.
The approach connects landscape restoration with food production, household livelihoods and the strengthening of rural economic security.
According to the reported outcomes of the initiative, annual deforestation has declined from 92,000 hectares to 27,000 hectares, while soil erosion on agricultural land has fallen from 130 tonnes per hectare annually to 54 tonnes.
The amount of sediment entering water bodies has likewise declined from 1.9 billion tonnes to 208 million tonnes annually.
The environmental campaign has also generated an economic and social dividend, with nearly 2.6 million jobs created for young people and women.
Fruit and forest clusters emerging across different parts of the country are further creating new opportunities for farmers while strengthening the productive value of restored landscapes.
At the heart of Green Legacy has been mass public participation, coordinated through government structures from the federal level to local communities.
The initiative has consequently developed into a nationwide movement in which environmental restoration is tied to civic participation, youth engagement and a broader sense of collective responsibility for the country’s natural resources.
For Ethiopia, the transformation represents more than the number of seedlings planted. It demonstrates an effort to confront environmental degradation at national scale while using restoration to advance livelihoods, food security, climate resilience and sustainable development.
The achievement was highlighted as Ethiopia concluded its 2026 Green Legacy tree-planting campaign on Thursday under the theme “Let Us Plant Hope.”
The completion of this year’s campaign gives added significance to the cumulative 56.8-billion figure, placing the latest milestone within an eight-year national environmental journey.
Through Green Legacy, Ethiopia is also presenting a different position in the global climate conversation: not only as a country confronting the consequences of climate change and desertification, but as one seeking to contribute actively to their solution through large-scale restoration and collective action.

title: Governo Federal demarca 668 mil hectares para conservação
content:
Governo Federal demarca 668 mil hectares para conservação
Quatro novas Reservas de Desenvolvimento Sustentável vão proteger a floresta amazônica e beneficiar 1,2 mil famílias da região
Quatro novas Reservas de Desenvolvimento Sustentável vão proteger a floresta amazônica e beneficiar 1,2 mil famílias da região
Boas notícias para a Amazônia: no dia 8 de agosto, o Governo Federal anunciou a criação de quatro novas RDS (Reservas de Desenvolvimento Sustentável) no Amazonas, ampliando em mais de 668 mil hectares a área protegida no Estado e fortalecendo a produção sustentável na região. Ao todo, as quatro áreas beneficiarão mais de 1,2 mil famílias, que poderão utilizar os territórios para a produção e a coleta sustentável de alimentos, atividades permitidas nesse tipo de Unidade de Conservação.
“O que fizemos foi criar áreas protegidas e, com isso, não beneficiamos apenas a Amazônia, mas também o Brasil, que precisa da chuva produzida nessa região, e a humanidade, que precisa do carbono nela estocado”, celebra André Guimarães, diretor executivo do IPAM (Instituto de Pesquisa Ambiental da Amazônia) e enviado especial da Sociedade Civil para a COP30, que participou da celebração.
Para o presidente da República, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), a criação das Reservas de Desenvolvimento Sustentável contribui para a resolução dos embates sobre o desenvolvimento e a conservação da região no entorno da BR-319 e reforça o caminho para que a floresta seja vista também como um ativo econômico capaz de proteger a cultura local, fomentar o turismo e gerar renda para as comunidades.
“A questão ambiental é também uma questão econômica. Embora muitos economistas não tenham aprendido na faculdade sobre a bioeconomia, os povos da floresta, os ribeirinhos, os agricultores, eles criaram essa economia. Cabe a nós, governantes, portanto, dar a eles as condições para que ela se torne uma economia alternativa. Só teremos uma conservação total da Amazônia quando a sociedade brasileira entender que a floresta em pé é mais rentável que uma floresta deitada e queimada”, destacou o presidente.
Com a criação das novas unidades, o Amazonas passa a contar com mais quatro RDS na região da BR-319, que liga Manaus a Porto Velho, alcançando uma área protegida que abrange mais de 65% do Estado, segundo dados do Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima apresentados no evento. No Piauí, outro decreto ampliou o Parque Nacional de Sete Cidades, nos municípios de Brasileira e Piracuruca, aumentando em mais de 7 mil hectares a área protegida no Estado.
“Há três dias, a humanidade falhou ao constatar que ultrapassaremos o aumento de 1,5°C na temperatura média global, mas hoje enfrentamos esse cenário e colocamos, mais uma vez, o Brasil na liderança da agenda climática. É uma comemoração do Dia da Amazônia que reforça o compromisso do Brasil com o desenvolvimento sustentável da região”, ressalta Guimarães.
A cerimônia também marcou a assinatura de contratos do BNDES (Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social), que destinarão R$ 50 milhões do Fundo Amazônia ao projeto Naturezas Quilombolas, voltado ao apoio à gestão ambiental em mais de 16 territórios por meio da Fundação Guamá, e a homologação de contratos de R$ 70 milhões para a ativação dos primeiros Núcleos de Desenvolvimento da Sociobioeconomia na Amazônia.
Ambos os projetos têm como objetivo incentivar o desenvolvimento sustentável da região e fortalecer a proteção dos serviços ambientais essenciais desempenhados pela floresta. Para o ministro João Paulo Capobianco, do Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima, a proteção dos recursos amazônicos deve ser analisada também como investimento em infraestrutura e soberania nacional.
“Separados por apenas dois dias no calendário, o Dia da Amazônia e a Independência do Brasil estão unidos. Nosso destino como nação soberana está ligado à conservação da floresta, à dignidade de seus povos e à prosperidade de toda a sociedade brasileira. A Amazônia integra a infraestrutura natural que mantém o Brasil pulsando, e os serviços prestados pela floresta podem ser menos visíveis que as grandes obras de engenharia, mas sustentam nossa segurança hídrica, energética e alimentar”, salientou o presidente.

title: “El servicio educativo tendrá éxito en la medida en que sea comunitario”
content:
Por segunda vez, encabeza esta noble institución
Teólogo y filósofo, habla con La Jornada de la ciencia-arte de la tutoría, un modelo de aprendizaje que se aplica en las comunidades donde llega el organismo creado en 1971, y de los pensadores que influyeron en su visión pedagógica
Lunes 7 de septiembre de 2026, p. 7
“En el Consejo Nacional de Fomento Educativo (Conafe) hemos comprendido que nuestro mayor logro es entender que el servicio educativo tendrá éxito en la medida que sea comunitario. Hemos logrado ser menos burocracia y más comunidad. Es asimilar la diferencia entre educación y escolarización”, afirma su director general, Gabriel Cámara y Cervera.
Pionero en el desarrollo de las redes de tutoría, un modelo pedagógico que pone en el centro una enseñanza en diálogo con el otro, donde el cuidado de su dignidad y el respeto a su propio proceso de aprendizaje es vital, señala en entrevista con La Jornada que la “relación educativa es más ética que técnica. No es tanto lo que yo sé o lo que el otro quiere saber, sino cómo y desde dónde lo quiere hacer”.
Rodeado de libros, en una oficina austera del edificio sede de la Secretaría de Educación Pública, que está ubicado en avenida Universidad 1200, narra su paso por el Conafe, que fue fundado hace 55 años por decreto presidencial el 11 de septiembre de 1971, y a donde llegó, por primera ocasión, en 1996 para diseñar la secundaria, que todavía no existía en el organismo.
Filósofo formado en el Instituto Libre de Estudios Superiores, con una licenciatura en Teología por el Woodstock College y doctor en Planeación Educativa por la Universidad de Harvard, Cámara y Cervera afirma: “Donde hay aprendizaje de excelencia, hay comunidad”.
Y reconoce en su proyecto la influencia de pensadores como es el caso del filósofo Iván Illich, quien pugnó por “recuperar la autonomía individual y los saberes comunitarios en los que nos hemos cultivado como personas”.
Fue en su experiencia con las comunidades cuando enfrentó el desafío de atender a niños y jóvenes en condiciones de pobreza, quienes no podían dedicar los mismos años de estudio que otros niños de contextos urbanos para ir a la escuela y concluir su formación.
“Y fue ahí donde pudimos vivir, en la práctica, lo que señalaban los filósofos Illich y (Thomas) Reid: que uno aprende por interés, no lo que le manda a aprender un maestro”, señala.
Aclara que “no es que los profesores lo hagan mal, pero el gran desafío del sistema educativo es cómo ofrecemos esto que proponemos como lo mejor. Cómo hacemos que la Nueva Escuela Mexicana (NEM) u otro proyecto corresponda con el interés del aprendiz. Porque si no corresponde, es letra muerta”.
La práctica docente en muchas escuelas urbanas, explica, implica “hacer muchas cosas que la NEM no contempla directamente, como atender el orden, la disciplina, tienen que entretener, y la relación de aprendizaje propiamente se disuelve. Y nosotros nos concentramos en el aprendizaje; no tenemos que entretener niños”.
Más de 320 mil alumnos
El Conafe abrió un campo nuevo, afirma, “donde lo que ofrecemos responde al interés de cada aprendiz”. Y con el apoyo de 44 mil 596 educadores comunitarios, actualmente atiende a 320 mil alumnos: 155 mil 920 de prescolar; 100 mil 777 de primaria y 63 mil 801 de secundaria.
Su paso por el organismo público, reconoce, ha estado sujeto a los vaivenes de las administraciones federales y de los “vientos políticos”.
Por ejemplo, entre 1997 y 2003 logró consolidar el proyecto de la posprimaria, que centraba el aprendizaje en los intereses de cada persona e incluía una atención personalizada basada en el diálogo, denominada relación tutora. El modelo, pese a demostrar su éxito, no logró permear en todo el país debido a un cambio de gobierno.
Luego de su salida del organismo, comenzó un intenso trabajo en telesecundarias incompletas, unitarias y bidocentes (con uno o dos maestros por plantel para impartir los tres grados escolares).
“Y ahí los maestros se dieron cuenta de que esto que ofrecíamos era lo que necesitaban, porque si el aprendizaje no es interpersonal, de maestros y estudiantes, y de docentes entre sí, de capacitadores y capacitados, si no hay esta relación interpersonal, no hay cambio”, explica el funcionario.
Retorno al Conafe, por invitación de AMLO
Fue sólo hasta 2016 cuando, gracias a un equipo de especialistas formados con este enfoque, la relación tutora regresa al Conafe, pero fue años después, en el gobierno del ex presidente Andrés Manuel López Obrador, que Cámara y Cervera volvió al organismo.
En 2021, recuerda, luego del paso por Conafe de una administración que calificó de “talibanes” a quienes defendían la propuesta de impulsar la relación tutora como motor del aprendizaje, el experto en educación fue convocado por el ex mandatario federal.
“Me propone que me quede en Conafe, y le digo: ‘Andrés Manuel, tengo 91 años, estoy achacoso y sordo’. Y me responde: ‘no importa’, y me tuve que aventar”, narra.
Gracias a esa oportunidad, afirma, “pude volver a recoger lo que estaba disperso y traer a Conafe al equipo que impulsó la relación tutora. Y ahora estamos en una situación diferente a otras instituciones, porque aquí buscamos crear comunidad”.
Y lo hacen, asegura, por medio de acciones como la creación del seminario Confesión y Proclama, que todos las mañanas encabeza el doctor Cámara y Cervera como un espacio en el que los tutores, sin importar su jerarquía, exponen su práctica y reciben retroalimentación para mejorar.
Con su regreso al consejo nació en 2022 el Modelo de Educación Comunitaria para el Bienestar, basado en tres principios: la autogestión educativa de la comunidad, la inclusión de todos sus miembros en los procesos de aprendizaje y la búsqueda del bienestar comunitario por medio de la educación.
Con este esfuerzo se consolidan las comunidades de aprendizaje, –abiertas a niñas, niños, jóvenes y adultos–, las cuales, reconoce, no han estado exentas de obstáculos, pues al no seguir la pauta que marcan los años de escolarización para un aprendiz, se tuvieron que establecer criterios científicos para saber qué habilidades adquieren los estudiantes.
Por ello, en colaboración con la Secretaría de Ciencia, Humanidades, Tecnología e Innovación, el Conafe encabezó en 2023 un estudio sobre la relación tutora, que ha demostrado que “no se tienen que pasar muchos años (en el sistema escolarizado) para lograr lo que la educación básica te ofrece como derecho. Hemos demostrado que hay una ciencia-arte de la tutoría al margen de los años escolares”.
Y ese logro ahora se ve reflejado en los 10 mil jóvenes que a partir del ciclo escolar 2026-2027 son atendidos en el nivel bachillerato en 140 comunidades.
“Ahí también seguimos haciendo lo mismo, aprendiendo en comunidad, sólo que con temas más complejos, pero integrados, no con asignaturas separadas. Abordamos conceptos como la ecocivilización, con lo que buscamos hacerlos reflexionar sobre el cambio civilizatorio y los desafíos que enfrentamos para la sobrevivencia del planeta”, concluye.

title: From Leaking Roofs to Bright Learning Walls: How a Crumbling Govt School Became a Space Kids Love
content: “Earlier, when it rained, water used to fall from the roof. Now there is no such tension, and we can concentrate on our studies.” For years, rainy days at school meant something very different for Aastha Kohle and Yogeshwari Chamat. At Gardiner High School in Nagpur’s Civil Lines, the girls had watched rainwater seep through their classroom roof. Tiles had fallen, plaster had come off the walls, and parts of the building had grown unsafe. The school had stood there since 1933, and its age was beginning to show in ways that affected the children studying inside it. Then came the summer break. When Aastha and Yogeshwari returned to school in July 2026, the difference was impossible to miss. The roof had been repaired. The classrooms were brighter. Colourful illustrations from their syllabus covered the walls, and spaces that had once felt neglected had been thoughtfully redesigned. There was also a science lab, which soon became one of their favourite places in school. “Our walls look beautiful, and there are pretty paintings in our classrooms,” they say. From science concepts to mathematical formulae, the walls now turn everyday classroom spaces into extensions of the lesson. For the girls, the change has shaped how they feel at school too. Their confidence has grown, they say, and the lessons they once encountered only in books now surround them in their classrooms. Science concepts and mathematical formulae appear on the walls, turning the school itself into part of how they learn. That idea, of creating a school environment that supports children as they learn, is central to Zero Gravity’s work. It began with a girl erasing her notebook Zero Gravity is a youth-led initiative working under the Dr Shrikant Jichkar Foundation, founded by Maitri Jichkar in memory of her late father. Started in Nagpur in 2008, the organisation works across education, healthcare and rural development, with education at the heart of its work. Maitri’s decision to focus on school infrastructure grew out of a moment she witnessed years ago. Around 2010-11, while visiting a government school where her organisation was supporting students with stationery, she walked into a classroom with a leaking roof. Children had crowded into the part of the room where it was not raining. There was little furniture, and some students did not even have school bags. Then she noticed a girl carefully erasing something from her notebook. When Maitri asked her why, the girl replied that if she did not erase what she had written that day, she would have nothing to write on the next day. Maitri Jichkar’s journey with school transformation began with a girl erasing her notebook because she had no pages left to write on. “That just stuck with me,” Maitri recalls. “I realised the vast gap between opportunities.” For her, the question was also one of dignity. “Just because a child comes from an underprivileged family doesn't mean that our system has to offer him something that he thinks he deserves,” she says. “No child should have to live or learn this way.” The experience eventually led to the Happy School Project, which began around 2013 with a simple goal: transform government schools into places where children could learn with a sense of pride and belonging. What if the walls could help children learn? In its early years, Zero Gravity depended largely on volunteers who would pick up paintbrushes and work with local communities to brighten schools. But Maitri soon realised that painting walls addressed only one part of a school’s needs. Today, the organisation’s team of architects and designers looks at everything from lighting, ventilation, toilets and furniture to teaching aids, playgrounds and learning spaces. The building itself also becomes a teaching tool. Through what Zero Gravity calls ‘Building as a Learning Aid’, the team maps concepts from the school curriculum and incorporates them into the physical environment. A science concept might appear on a classroom wall. Mathematical formulae can become part of the design. Writing surfaces and interactive spaces are created so that teachers can use the building while teaching. For Zero Gravity, repairing a school is only the beginning — the team also rethinks lighting, ventilation, furniture, learning spaces and how children experience them. “The core is to integrate and increase the educational value of the school building,” Maitri explains. The process begins with a needs assessment, followed by a detailed study of the building, budgeting and design. Architects create drawings and 3D models, while the team works on curriculum integration, artwork and space optimisation. Artists, labourers, local vendors and volunteers then help bring those plans to life, with Zero Gravity supervising the work. The small volunteer-led effort now works alongside municipal corporations, Zilla Parishads, district administrations and CSR partners. The organisation has transformed more than 150 schools so far and currently has a waiting list of nearly 1,000 schools. Transformation began with a falling brick At Gardiner High School, the government school in Nagpur where Aastha and Yogeshwari study, the first challenge was safety. The 1933 structure had deteriorated to a point where two classrooms were no longer being used because the roof was considered unsafe. The principal, Mrs Shveta Dhalwale, remembers the school before the transformation as a place where leaking roofs, falling tiles, damaged plaster and waterlogged areas had become part of everyday life. In fact, one incident made the need for intervention even more urgent. A brick once fell from a ventilator in the last room of the building while children were playing outside. Thankfully, no one was hurt. Principal Dhalwale shares, “Whenever I go to that room, I thank God that nothing happened that day.” When Zero Gravity first came in May 2026, the school did not expect a transformation of this scale. “We thought they would fix the tiles and plaster a few rooms,” Dhalwale says. “But this is beyond our expectations.” The team first had to address the basics, including the roof and other structural repairs. Even seemingly simple work such as electrical wiring had to be carefully planned because the old walls could not safely be drilled into. At Gardiner High School, years of leaking roofs, falling tiles and damaged plaster gave way to classrooms designed with children and learning in mind. With the structure made safe, the team turned to the spaces where children would learn. Classrooms were redesigned with colourful, curriculum-linked artwork. Science concepts appeared on walls, along with visuals such as the solar system and the Arabian desert. The science lab and other learning spaces were also redesigned. The children joined in, too. They painted, created artwork and helped make the new spaces their own. ‘We have to preserve it for the next classes’ For Dhalwale, one of the most heartening changes has been the way students now interact with their surroundings. Earlier, children would sometimes draw on the walls. Today, they see those same walls as part of their learning space, and something worth protecting. “They know we have to preserve it for the next classes,” she says. She has noticed other changes too. Attendance has improved, and students have started bringing their friends to the school to seek admission. The difference is visible inside the classroom as well. Dhalwale says the transformed spaces have made teaching more joyful for teachers and students alike. The Building as a Learning Aid approach brings the curriculum into the classroom itself, turning walls and everyday spaces into teaching tools. “It is a happy teaching and learning place, both for the students and teachers,” says Dhalwale. “We enjoy teaching with a joyful atmosphere around.” And the transformation has continued beyond the renovation itself. Zero Gravity now works closely with the school, responding to its evolving needs. After spending about a month revamping the school space, the team is now developing a library, with plans to eventually use storytelling as a way to open conversations around healthcare and mental wellbeing with the children. ‘Create a space where children can explore’ For Samiran Ghodmare, a counselling psychologist and Zero Gravity volunteer, the work has changed how he looks at education. When he first joined the Happy School Project, he wondered how much changing a physical space could really mean to a child. His work had centred on children’s mental health, but Zero Gravity made him realise that the basics come first. “Before even working on anyone’s mental health, the basic needs should first be fulfilled,” he says. He began to see a school as both a place of learning and, for many children, their first comfortable space outside home. If that space feels neglected or unsafe, it becomes harder for them to be curious, creative or even open up. The children now see their walls differently — not as surfaces to draw on, but as learning spaces they want to protect for those who come after them. Samiran has also seen how change inspires people to contribute. Volunteers who arrive for a few days often stay on, taking responsibility for more schools, connecting donors or offering their professional skills. “You want the children to be more interactive with the space,” Samiran says. “We need to create a space where it gives them an opportunity to explore their mind, their creativity and their world.” That same thinking is shaping Gardiner’s next learning space. As Zero Gravity continues working with the school, Samiran is helping develop a library where storytelling can eventually open conversations around mental and physical health. When the neighbourhood started showing up The transformation at Gardiner also changed how the neighbourhood saw the school. As the work progressed, people began contributing in their own ways — from stationery and computers to furniture. A private school even donated its old furniture, which was still in good condition. Maitri has seen this ripple effect across other projects too. The transformation has also brought the neighbourhood closer, with people contributing stationery, computers and furniture to the school. At one government school, teachers had pooled money to buy scholarship-exam books, while children sometimes tore one textbook into three parts so they could share it. After Zero Gravity built and stocked a library, more students began preparing for scholarship exams, with several eventually earning scholarships. The space also became a study centre for young people in the community. In another village, a community hall that had remained unused for 15 years was repaired and painted. Soon, residents began organising cleanliness drives, while the administration decided to develop a library and study centre there. For Maitri, these moments show how a physical transformation can change what a community believes is possible. “We are just raising the standard of how these places should look,” she says. “So that becomes a minimum standard.” A place that tells a child: you matter Today, children at Gardiner High School walk into classrooms where the roof no longer leaks, lessons continue on the walls, and a library is being built for them. For Zero Gravity, a school is more than a building — it is a child’s first reminder that their learning, safety and dreams matter. Maitri believes that giving children the right opportunities today can shape generations to come. For her, the larger purpose of Zero Gravity is to create spaces that show children they are worthy of care. “I just want children to feel that the system, and society in general, knows how to care for them,” she says. “I want them to know that they matter. All images courtesy Zero Gravity

title: Alfonso Durazo rompe récord educativo en Sonora con más de 736 mil becas entregadas
content:
Sonora registra una inversión y cobertura sin precedentes en apoyo a estudiantes. Durante los cinco años de la administración del gobernador Alfonso Durazo Montaño se han entregado más de 736 mil becas, en una entidad que cuenta con alrededor de 805 mil estudiantes.
La cifra permite dimensionar el alcance de la estrategia: el número de becas entregadas equivale a más de nueve apoyos por cada 10 estudiantes que integran la comunidad estudiantil sonorense.
Para alcanzar esta cobertura, el Gobierno de Sonora ha destinado más de 3 mil 700 millones de pesos exclusivamente a becas, una inversión que supera por más del doble lo ejercido durante los tres sexenios anteriores juntos, es decir, los 18 años previos.
Por primera vez en la entidad, los apoyos abarcan todos los niveles educativos, desde educación básica hasta nivel superior, a través de Becas Sonora de Oportunidades, el programa de becas más grande en la historia del estado.
La estrategia impulsada por Durazo no se limita al apoyo económico. En cinco años se han entregado 2 millones 230 mil paquetes de uniformes escolares gratuitos, reduciendo gastos para las familias y garantizando mejores condiciones para que niñas, niños y jóvenes continúen sus estudios.
Para el ciclo escolar actual, con el apoyo del Gobierno de México, Sonora fue el primer estado del país en la distribución de más de 3 millones de libros de texto gratuitos, mientras que 94 mil 800 estudiantes son beneficiarios de desayunos escolares, como parte de una política que busca atender las condiciones que inciden directamente en la permanencia y el aprendizaje.
En infraestructura, el Gobierno de Sonora ha invertido 3 mil 364 millones de pesos en construcción, rehabilitación y mejoramiento de planteles educativos, con obras para dignificar los espacios donde se forman las nuevas generaciones.
Los resultados colocan a la educación como uno de los principales ejes de la administración estatal: más de 736 mil becas entregadas, 2 millones 230 mil paquetes de uniformes, más de 3 millones de libros de texto gratuitos en el presente ciclo, alimentación para cerca de 195 mil estudiantes y más de 3 mil 300 millones de pesos destinados a infraestructura educativa.
Para el gobernador Alfonso Durazo, la apuesta es que el origen o la condición económica de una familia no determinen hasta dónde puede llegar un estudiante.
En Sonora, la diferencia frente al pasado se refleja en la inversión: en solo cinco años se han destinado a becas más del doble de recursos que en los 18 años anteriores, convirtiendo a la educación en una de las principales herramientas para ampliar oportunidades y transformar el futuro de una generación.

title: La tasa de analfabetismo en el país es la más baja en la historia
content:
La Unesco reconoce que 96% de los mexicanos saben leer y escribir
Miércoles 9 de septiembre de 2026, p. 9
San Juan Chamula, Chis., En el marco del Congreso Mundial por el 60 aniversario del Día Internacional de la Alfabetización 2026, la Organización de Naciones Unidas para la Educación, la Ciencia y la Cultura (Unesco) felicitó a México por sus progresos en materia de alfabetización, al ser un país que “avanza en esta materia”.
Lo anterior, luego de que el país alcanzara la tasa de analfabetismo más baja de su historia: del total de la población de 15 años y más, quienes no saben leer ni escribir representan 3.8 por ciento; es decir, más de 96 por ciento son alfabetizados.
Lidia Arthur Brito, subdirectora general de la Unesco, quien encabezó la ceremonia oficial en esta comunidad, en el corazón de los Altos de Chiapas, destacó la conducción de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo en dichos progresos.
“Quiero reconocer el liderazgo de la Presidenta, quien es la primera mujer en llegar a este cargo en México, y es además, una gran científica. Sabemos que ella, con todo su equipo, con todo el pueblo mexicano, continúan el sueño de Benito Juárez, de Justo Sierra, de José Vasconcelos, y claro, de Jaime Torres Bodet, el segundo director general de la Unesco, y dos veces titular de la Secretaría de Educación Pública, quienes ponen a México en la ruta de un país completamente alfabetizado”, afirmó en la Plaza de la Paz de esta comunidad, ante miles de indígenas de todas las etnias del estado.
Afirmó que los avances de nuestro país y, en particular, de comunidades indígenas como San Juan Chamula, “demuestra que la alfabetización no consiste únicamente en adquirir competencias de lectura y escritura, sino también en fortalecer la identidad, preservar las lenguas y ampliar las oportunidades de desarrollo para todas las personas”.
Chiapas, declaró, es un ejemplo de diversidad que distingue a México. Sus pueblos han mantenido vivas las tradiciones, conocimientos y formas de organización, que “constituyen un patrimonio invaluable para la humanidad”.
Acompañada del titular de la SEP, Mario Delgado Carrillo y del gobernador de Chiapas, Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar, Brito destacó que la educación “es más poderosa cuando dialoga con las culturas, las lenguas y los saberes”.
Antes de la entrega de los Premios Internacionales de Alfabetización Unesco 2026, que en esta edición reconocieron a seis proyectos innovadores en México, Líbano, Nigeria, Colombia, Países Bajos y Tailandia, entre ellos el Programa de Alfabetización Chiapas Puede, la subdirectora general de la Unesco admitió que, pese a los avances alcanzados en las décadas recientes, pues la tasa de jóvenes alfabetizados en el mundo pasó de 75 a 93 por ciento entre 1975 y 2024, “tenemos que reflexionar sobre lo que realmente significa la alfabetización en el siglo XXI”.
Admitió que la alfabetización “va más allá de la escritura y la lectura, porque abarca los conocimientos, las competencias y las capacidades necesarias para desenvolverse plenamente en la sociedades actuales, y navegar por un mundo muy complejo”.

title: Global fund aims to end FGM, New York sees safest summer ever, Bhutan ends dog-transmitted human rabies
content:
Photo: Jessica Lea/DFID via Flickr (CC BY 2.0)
In today’s edition: a new fund has been launched with the aim of ending the practice of female genital mutilation, violent crime in New York City hits a historic low between June and August, and Bhutan has become the first country in South-East Asia to officially eliminate human rabies transmitted by dogs.
The aim of Her Horizon Fund is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending female genital mutilation within a generation. Advocates warn that while international recognition of FGM as a human rights violation has grown, and countries such as Burkina Faso, the Gambia and Kenya have criminalised the practice, progress remains fragile.
Source: The Guardian
Between June and August, New York City saw 195 shooting incidents, 249 shooting victims and 66 murders – the fewest in recorded history for each category. Major crime dropped by 6.6% citywide in August, with The Bronx leading the decline.
Source: CBS News
The WHO has validated Bhutan’s elimination of canine-transmitted rabies as a public health problem in the region. Rabies is a viral disease that is almost always fatal once clinical symptoms appear, but deaths can be prevented by vaccinating dogs to curb the disease at its source. Additionally, the use of post exposure prophylaxis stops the virus from reaching the central nervous system after a bite.
Source: WHO
Tim Andrews received a kidney transplanted from a pig in January 2025, sparing him months of needing to go to hospital to have his blood filtered by a dialysis machine. The kidney continued to function until it was removed in October that year. Tim then needed dialysis for 82 days until he had an organ from a donor in January of this year. That organ has been working well.
Source: BBC News
Despite the Trump administration’s vocal opposition to renewable energy, the overwhelming majority of new solar power generation is taking place in conservative US states. Texas and Florida, the two largest Trump-supporting states by population, are in fact leading the way in the country’s adoption of solar.
Source: Grist
The laws, signed by the Democratic California governor on Thursday, bars social media companies from using infinite scroll and autoplay for users under 16. “This is about actually addressing the problem, the scrolling, the algorithms. This is about addressing the substantive issue around the engineering,” Gaving Newsom said at a news conference.
Source: The Guardian
Apple and Google will be forced to block explicit images on children’s smartphones by law in the UK after talks failed to produce a breakthrough, the government has said. The legislation comes a few months after the government announced a social media ban for under-16s.
Source: The Guardian
How much exercise do you need per week? A new study suggests that the type of activity could make an unexpectedly big difference: according to research, just three minutes of intense sprinting reportedly trigger more measurable changes in the body than 90 minutes of moderate cycling.
Source: Science Daily
US farmers are increasingly turning to perennial grains which can withstand extreme weather and drought. Researchers at The Land Institute in Kansas are developing perennial versions of annual crops which can be planted once every couple of seasons, improving soil health and storing carbon.
Source: AP News
Family-run Al-Qarara Seed Bank is striving to help Palestinians gain sovereignty over their food security. The project has two main aims. One is to collect and preserve the seeds of local plants that may thrive better in this landscape; the other is to create a node for seed distribution for farmers who need to save every possible penny.
Source: The Guardian
Dear readers, if you’re looking for even more positivity, we’d like to introduce you to Honeyletter. It’s a daily good news email from New York bringing you five verified stories every weekday morning. Three minutes, no doom. They also built the honeymap, a world map of every good thing they have ever reported.
Source: Honeyletter

title: From Nutrition to Knowledge, Knowledge to Transformation: Ethiopia’s School Feeding Journey
content:
From Nutrition to Knowledge, Knowledge to Transformation: Ethiopia’s School Feeding Journey
Addis Ababa, September 10, 2026 (FMC) — Every generation inherits a country, but it is what that generation learns, creates and builds that determines what it leaves behind. In Ethiopia, that future is increasingly being shaped in classrooms where a school meal represents far more than food: it is an investment in healthier bodies, sharper minds, stronger learning, greater opportunity and the human capabilities on which national transformation ultimately depends.
For children, hunger is not simply an empty stomach. It can follow them into the classroom, affecting concentration, participation, attendance and their ability to make the most of an education. By placing nutrition alongside teaching and learning, Ethiopia’s expanding school feeding programme is addressing one of the most basic conditions for a child to learn, grow and remain engaged in school.
The significance therefore reaches from the physical to the intellectual. A balanced meal can help support children’s health and wellbeing while reducing short-term hunger during the school day.
Better nourishment, in turn, creates a stronger foundation for concentration, classroom participation and educational performance.
Evidence from school feeding programmes in Addis Ababa has pointed to gains in attendance, enrolment and academic performance, while educators and families have reported improvements in concentration and reductions in dropout.
The experience underscores a simple but consequential reality: the quality of education cannot be separated from the condition of the child receiving it.
This understanding has increasingly placed school feeding within Ethiopia’s wider education and development agenda. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has highlighted the expansion of school feeding among notable achievements in the education sector.
In 2022, he said 1.7 million students were receiving meals twice a day, reflecting the scale the programme had reached at that stage.
School feeding was subsequently incorporated into the government’s broader education reform priorities, while the Prime Minister has continued to emphasize that development must ultimately be measured by improvements in people’s everyday lives.
The scale has since grown substantially.
Ethiopia’s 2024/25 education data put the number of pre-primary, primary and middle-level students reached through school feeding at more than 8 million.
All regions and city administrations are implementing school feeding in different forms, while about 17 billion birr was invested in the programme during the year, with government and communities providing more than 90 percent of the resources.
Behind those figures lies a much larger question: what kind of generation can a country build when children are given a stronger chance to learn?
The answer extends well beyond examination results.
Education is the pathway through which children acquire knowledge, but sustained learning can also develop the skills needed to navigate an increasingly complex economy.
The foundations of future productivity, entrepreneurship, scientific thinking, technology and innovation are laid long before a young person enters the workforce.
In that sense, school feeding belongs to the earliest stage of a much longer national investment.
Nutrition supports learning; learning builds capabilities; capabilities create skills; and skills open the door to innovation and productivity.
The journey begins with the child, but its destination is national development.
The programme also reaches beyond the school gates by connecting education with agriculture and local economies.
Under home-grown approaches, food can move from Ethiopian farms through local markets and supply chains into school kitchens, where mothers and other community members prepare meals for pupils.
That creates an unusual development chain.
A farmer produces. A local market connects. A mother earns and participates. A school delivers. A child eats and learns.
What appears to be a simple meal can therefore activate several layers of the economy and society at once.
For farming communities, school feeding can create institutional demand for agricultural produce. For women involved in meal preparation, it can create income and a more direct role in the local economy.
For families, school meals can ease part of the daily cost of feeding children. And for schools, they can help create an environment in which pupils are better prepared to learn.
The programme consequently brings together areas of development that are often treated separately: nutrition, education, agriculture, livelihoods, social protection and human-capital formation.
Its social significance is equally profound.
Ethiopia’s diversity is one of the defining features of the country. Building a strong and cohesive nation therefore requires institutions capable of bringing citizens together across differences while allowing those differences to flourish.
Schools are among the most important of those institutions.
The food that reaches a school can originate with farmers; it can be prepared by mothers; it can be served by school communities; and it reaches children who, regardless of their background, are being prepared to become the future custodians of the country.
The chain is shared even when the people within it are different.
In that sense, school feeding offers a practical expression of collective nation-building. It demonstrates how citizens can contribute to a common future in different ways, with the child at the centre of the effort.
This is also why Ethiopia’s experience resonates beyond the question of how many meals are served.
Across Africa, governments are increasingly recognizing school meals as an investment in education, nutrition, social protection and local economic development rather than merely as a safety-net intervention.
Ethiopia’s expanding national programme forms part of that wider continental movement toward treating school feeding as a long-term public investment.
The country’s own trajectory is particularly significant because the programme has evolved from addressing immediate barriers to school attendance and hunger toward a broader development instrument connecting the classroom to the farm, the household and the economy.
Prime Minister Abiy’s more recent emphasis on improving citizens’ everyday lives has placed this logic within the wider philosophy of national development: economic progress matters most when it translates into tangible improvements in people’s lives and expands their opportunities.
For a child, that opportunity can begin with something as fundamental as having enough to eat before opening a textbook.
From there, the effects can accumulate—better physical wellbeing, greater concentration, stronger participation, improved educational performance, continued schooling, acquisition of knowledge and skills, and eventually the capacity to contribute to an economy increasingly shaped by technology, creativity and innovation.
That is the larger story unfolding behind Ethiopia’s school feeding programme.
It is not simply about what children receive at lunchtime. It is about what a country makes possible when it nourishes the body so the mind can learn, equips the mind so skills can grow, and develops skills so a generation can create, innovate and build.
A school meal lasts a day.
The knowledge it helps a child gain can last a lifetime.
And the capabilities of millions of such children can help determine the future of a nation.

title: Víctor M. Quintana S.: La lucha lagunera abre vía para defender el agua
content:
uienes más defienden el agua en este país –y en casi todo el planeta– no son los estados, sino muy diversas organizaciones y movimientos de base. No es extraño: quienes más sufren de la escasez o de la contaminación del vital líquido son las comunidades rurales, los usuarios urbanos, los pueblos indígenas y los pequeños y medianos agricultores.
En toda nuestra geografía bullen los movimientos en defensa del agua: en la Huasteca, comunidades indígenas y mestizas, así como organizaciones del noreste del país, se oponen al fracking y exigen un blindaje presidencial, porque reducirá y contaminará el agua de todas y de todos; el colectivo Tierra Mestiza lucha contra la apropiación del agua por parte de embotelladoras y empresas privadas en la región de Cholula, Puebla; las y los ciudadanos de la zona metropolitana de Guadalajara luchan contra la privatización del líquido y por tener agua verdaderamente potable; en Ascensión, Chihuahua, las y los ejidatarios se oponen a los pozos clandestinos y al tendido de líneas que los electrifican, porque están abatiendo sus acuíferos y los niveles freáticos se contaminan de metales pesados. En varias lenguas indígenas, en castellano, con acentos del sur, del centro y del norte del país, el grito es el mismo: “Agua para todas y para todos, agua para la vida”.
Para todos ellos ha abierto una brecha importante el triunfo esculpido a pulso por las organizaciones ciudadanas de la Comarca Lagunera. La Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación (SCJN) acaba de rechazar el intento de la Comisión Nacional del Agua (Conagua) y la Consejería Jurídica de la Presidencia por modificar la sentencia número 543 que protege el acuífero principal de la Comarca Lagunera. La ejecutoria del amparo en revisión 543/2022 ordenó cesar las acciones que agravan la sobrexplotación del acuífero mencionado, y al dejar sin materia el recurso de Conagua y la Consejería Jurídica, la Corte determina que la resolución del amparo sigue vigente, firme y con plena fuerza ejecutoria.
Ya habíamos relatado en estas mismas páginas la saga de las organizaciones sociales de la comarca: Prodefensa del Nazas, Encuentro Ciudadano Lagunero y Desarrollo Cardenista para el Campo Lagunero, que en 2019 interpusieron un amparo contra la Secretaría de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (Semarnat) y la Conagua, porque sus acciones y omisiones incidían en la sobrexplotación del acuífero y no garantizaban el derecho humano al agua de la población. Cuatro años después, el 1º de marzo de 2023, la primera sala de la SCJN emitió la sentencia 543, en la que aprueba por unanimidad otorgar el amparo de la justicia federal contra la sobrexplotación del acuífero Principal Región Lagunera y ordena a la Conagua, la Semarnat y al organismo Cuencas Centrales del Norte que paren de dar concesiones de nuevos pozos y que hagan programas que reparen el nivel del acuífero.
A la lentitud por parte de las tres dependencias para poner en marcha el acuerdo judicial se sumó el recurso legal interpuesto por 29 concesionarios del agua subterránea, sobre todo lecheros, para anular la sentencia 543. Las organizaciones se manifestaron y lograron que el 12 de marzo pasado, un tribunal colegiado rechazara el recurso de los concesionarios.
El conflicto escaló, pero también la terquedad ciudadana lagunera: ante la presión de las empresas concesionarias, hizo que la Consejería Jurídica de la Presidencia, en representación expresa, presentó ante la Corte el oficio 100.CJEF.06053, pidiendo delimitar y modificar los alcances de la sentencia, estableciendo que no podía limitarse la actuación de la Conagua en materia de derechos de los concesionarios sobre el agua subterránea, incluidas las prórrogas de concesión. Las organizaciones laguneras denunciaron públicamente este hecho como injerencia del Ejecutivo en el Judicial de poderes, y con toda la argumentación jurídica en la mano, hablaron con el presidente de la SCJN y la ministra ponente, la licenciada Lenia Batres Guaderrama. Así lograron que la Corte declare firme y vigente la sentencia 543, que protege el acuífero principal de la Comarca Lagunera.
El triunfo de la ciudadanía se logró con base en la continua denuncia e información al público, una sólida defensa jurídica llevada a cabo por abogados jóvenes y competentes y una inquebrantable voluntad de lucha. Gracias a eso se logró preservar el derecho humano al agua para más de un millón de habitantes de la comarca, se impidió una violación a la división de poderes, se acotaron las atribuciones de la Conagua y la Semarnat y se ponen límites muy claros a la concentración de concesiones y sobrexplotación de los acuíferos por unas cuantas empresas.
Pero tal vez lo más importante es que la lucha de estas organizaciones laguneras (que, por cierto, aún tienen algunas batallas legales por delante), como todos los movimientos sociales, abre un inédito viable, es decir, muestra que es posible hacer uso de las instancias e instrumentos legales, sobre todo del juicio de amparo, para proteger los bienes comunes y derechos de todas y de todos.
Eso les agradecen todas las comunidades, personas y organizaciones que luchan por el agua y el territorio en nuestro México.

title: How Indigenous Protected Areas became a vital way to protect nature in Australia
content:
When you think of conservation in Australia, chances are you'll think of a national park.
But there's another fast-growing way of conserving land: Indigenous Protected Areas (IPAs). These areas of land or sea Country are voluntarily dedicated by Traditional Owners to protect nature and cultural values and responsibilities.
Once dedicated, an IPA becomes part of Australia's National Reserve System—our network of protected areas. To protect the area, Indigenous rangers tackle invasive species and undertake cultural burning and many other tasks.
In 2022, the Australian government signed up to an international pledge to protect 30% of lands and waters by 2030. This is one reason why IPAs have grown so rapidly in recent years.
In July, 4.7 million hectares (11.6 million acres) of the Simpson Desert was dedicated as the newest protected area—the Pmere Atherre Antenterreme IPA.
Maintaining the success of Indigenous Protected Areas will require long-term funding, strong Indigenous governance and complementary conservation elsewhere.
How does this work?
While national parks are established and managed by governments, IPAs are Indigenous-led.
After deciding to establish an IPA, Traditional Owners develop a management plan and determine how Country is to be cared for, drawing on Indigenous knowledge and contemporary conservation science.
Caring for Country means looking after plants, animals, water, fire, sacred places and cultural practices as part of an interconnected whole.
Declaring an IPA doesn't change existing tenure arrangements. For example, an IPA can cover freehold Indigenous land, land granted under land-rights legislation, Indigenous-held leasehold or pastoral land, Crown land and marine areas.
From pilot program to over half of Australia's reserve system
In 1998, Nantawarrina became Australia's first Indigenous Protected Area. The former pastoral station in South Australia's Flinders Ranges was heavily degraded. Over the following decades, the Nipapanha people worked to restore the land and its biodiversity.
There are now 96 IPAs across Australia, spanning 113 million hectares (279 million acres). That's almost 15% of the continent. Marine IPAs cover a smaller portion of Australian waters—9.3 million hectares (23 million acres), or about 1.1% of our marine estate.
The growth of IPAs has far outstripped the growth of other types of conservation land. IPAs now make up more than 55% of lands protected in Australia's National Reserve System.
Across all types of protection—both government and non-government—25% of Australia's land is now protected, and 24% of seas are highly protected "no-take" areas where fishing is banned.
The largest IPAs lie in Australia's deserts, some of the world's largest uncleared arid ecosystems. They form part of a vast, culturally connected landscape shaped by Indigenous stewardship over tens of thousands of years.
People who care for Country
At the heart of Indigenous Protected Areas are Indigenous rangers, who combine cultural practice and traditional knowledge with contemporary conservation practices.
Ranger teams began growing in number from 2007, when dedicated federal funding became available. The program is now called the Indigenous Rangers Program.
No two Indigenous ranger programs are alike—each is locally led and grounded in Traditional Owner priorities. The program of work can include burning to prevent large wildfires or maintain cultural practices and care for Country.
Rangers look after cultural sites and culturally important species, and protect threatened species by managing threats, monitoring how populations are faring and undertaking surveys and research to find out more about them.
Rangers and researchers have worked together to combine Indigenous knowledge with new technologies such as drones, satellite imagery and environmental DNA to better understand how Country is changing and inform its care.
Ranger programs also create local jobs, stronger community governance and opportunities for Elders to pass on language, cultural knowledge and practical skills to younger generations. These programs show that caring for Country can deliver environmental, cultural and social benefits.
Many Indigenous Protected Areas welcome visitors, offering cultural and nature-based tourism, walking, camping, fishing and guided experiences. Access rules vary. Some have restricted access at certain times or require permission to enter. These arrangements reflect Indigenous ownership and management.
How are these areas funded?
Like many other protected areas, IPAs are publicly funded. The Australian government gives funds to declare and manage new IPAs through protected area and Indigenous ranger programs. Some state governments provide extra support to ranger teams.
However, these funds usually cover only a fraction of the costs of managing Country in this way. IPAs with ranger programs receive just over A$1 per hectare from government funding. By comparison, national park funding varies from around $16 per hectare in Queensland to $58 per hectare in NSW. State governments largely fund national parks.
Many Indigenous organizations try to augment funding with income from carbon projects, philanthropic grants, research partnerships and environmental management contracts. This financial uncertainty creates a large administrative workload.
Can we make these areas even stronger?
As this approach to conservation matures, our growing reliance on IPAs as a key conservation approach should be matched by increased funding and capability support.
It also makes sense to invest more in monitoring and reporting to track environmental, cultural and social benefits, and to pinpoint any areas to strengthen. Better data will also help policymakers know how Australia is tracking toward our commitments to the Global Biodiversity Framework.
Indigenous Protected Areas are working well. But they're not the answer to every conservation challenge. They complement but do not replace other protected areas. The complex land tenures of the more heavily cleared and densely populated areas on Australia's east coast make it more challenging to declare new IPAs here, for instance.
As Australia works toward its conservation goals, it will rely more and more on Indigenous Protected Areas. But we believe the success of these areas speaks to something much deeper—the fact that Australia's oldest systems of caring for Country are still among the most effective ways to conserve nature.

title: Meet 4 people who got the HIV prevention jab
content:
By Mia Malan and Ida Jooste
Almost 55,000 people in South Africa have already had a shot that protects them against HIV for six months at a time, the health department says. Lenacapavir, or LEN, has been available through the health department since June. The injection gives near-perfect protection against HIV and, because it lasts for six months, people only need to return to a clinic twice a year.
For now, LEN is available at 360 government clinics — about one in 10 — across six provinces. The Free State, Limpopo and the Northern Cape don’t yet have it. That should start to change when cheaper generic versions become available in 2027.
The health department plans to use some of its own budget, along with a grant from the Children’s Investment Fund Foundation through the Global Fund, to buy more LEN and expand the number of clinics that offer it. And South Africa needs to scale up fast. Modelling shows that between one-million and two-million people would need to use LEN each year between now and 2043 for the injection to make a big enough dent in new HIV infections to help end Aids as a public health threat.
For now, the health department is focusing particularly on people who have a higher chance of getting HIV: teenage girls and young women aged 15–24, sex workers, transgender women, gay and bisexual men and other men who have sex with men, and pregnant and breastfeeding women. People who use government clinics and want HIV prevention medicine can choose between a daily prevention pill and the six-monthly injection. Both are free.
Getting LEN involves a little more than just one jab. At the first appointment, a health worker gives two injections, either in the stomach or buttocks. The person also takes two LEN tablets that day and another two the next day. If they return for their next injections on time — 24 to 28 weeks after the previous injection — they don’t need to take the tablets again.
But what is it actually like to use LEN — and why are people choosing it over a daily pill?
We spoke to four people from groups the roll-out is particularly trying to reach: a sex worker, a student, a pregnant woman and a transgender woman. Here, in their own words, they explain why they chose LEN, what getting the injections felt like and whether they’ll be back for their next shots.
Precious Mafanga
I’m 39, a mother of four, a wife and a sex worker.
I live at Ikhwezi Hostel in Langa. I’m also a peer educator with Tholwana e Molemo, where I help other sex workers with their health and other needs.
In our work, time is money. We rent rooms for R500 a day, so sometimes we’re chasing minutes. On a good day, it’s one client after another. As soon as he leaves, it’s “next!” You can easily make more than R1,500.
But on a bad day, you might not even make enough to pay the rent. Then there’s pressure to agree when a client offers you more money for sex without a condom. You pay the rent and start all over again the next day.
I got my LEN injections at Delft Community Health Centre near Cape Town in June and spent a few hours at the clinic.
While I was waiting, my phone kept ringing. Clients were calling and I wanted to leave to see them. But I stayed and got my injections.
Before LEN, I took the daily HIV prevention pill for four or five years. It wasn’t easy. You have to remember to take it every day.
With LEN, I don’t have that worry. The medicine stays in my body for six months, so I only have to go to the clinic twice a year.
As a peer educator, I help link other sex workers to clinics where they can get HIV prevention medicine without being judged. When US funding cuts disrupted outreach services, many of our sisters stopped taking their daily prevention pills. Some later tested positive for HIV.
That’s why LEN is so important for us.
But we still hand out condoms because LEN doesn’t prevent pregnancy or other sexually transmitted infections.
I’ve sent my eldest child’s partner to get LEN. And now that I know younger people can get it too, I’m sending my 17-year-old.
I wish people understood our work as sex workers. We’re not selling our bodies. We’re selling a service. We’re exchanging sex for money.
Because if I sold my body to a client, I wouldn’t have a body anymore.
Siviwe Gaika
I’m 24 and live in New Brighton, a township in Gqeberha. I’m studying towards a law degree at Nelson Mandela University. It’s my second degree; I already have one in social sciences from Rhodes University. I also run the social media accounts for Advocates for the Prevention of HIV and Aids.
Before LEN, I wasn’t using HIV prevention medicine because the only option I knew about was a daily pill. My life is busy: if I’m not in lectures, I’m studying or working. Taking a pill every day would have been one more thing on an already long to-do list.
So when I heard about LEN, I thought, ‘If I only have to go to the clinic and deal with the nurses twice a year, I can do that."
I got my shot at Kwazakhele Community Health Centre in Gqeberha, about 20 minutes from where I live. But it took three visits.
The first time I went, in June, I was told there wasn’t a nurse trained to give LEN. The second time, staff said the clinic didn’t have a certificate to prescribe it.
I went back in early July and finally got my shot. I had to wait about four hours, partly because I didn’t have a clinic file and they had to open one for me. There wasn’t a separate queue for LEN either, so I had to wait in the general queue.
The nurse who gave me the injection was patient. She explained how LEN works, that I could choose between the daily pill and LEN, and what side effects I might have.
She also got me to set a reminder on my phone to take the two LEN pills I needed the next day.
I deliberately took the pills in public because I wanted someone to ask me what I was taking. I was in the library when my alarm went off. One person came over and asked about the pills, so my plan worked.
I also recorded myself taking them and posted the video on TikTok. I told people what I was taking and how long it had taken me to get LEN — because four hours is a long time to wait.
I told them about the two bumps I got under my skin where I was injected too. I couldn’t wear jeans for about two weeks and took a break from the gym. But the bumps gradually got smaller, and they don’t bother me anymore.
That’s been my journey.
Lindiwe Mqatazana
I’m 25 and a waste picker, working on contract for the City of Cape Town.
In July, I suspected I was pregnant, so I went to Vuyani Clinic in Gugulethu for a test. When it came back positive, I decided there and then that I wanted to start LEN.
There’s an unborn child now, so I have to stay safe for him or her.
The nurse explained that LEN is safe for me and my baby. After I tested negative for HIV, she told me I could choose between the six-monthly LEN injection and the daily HIV prevention pill. I chose LEN.
I had used the daily pill before, but it made me feel nauseous. I also travel home to the Eastern Cape often. When you’re on the road, it’s easy to forget your tablets.
Getting LEN was easy. I went to the clinic early in the morning, so they could see me straight away. From walking in to walking out it took about an hour-and-a-half.
The nurses used ice to numb the injection sites for about 10 minutes. My friends are scared of LEN because they think it has to be injected into your stomach. But because I’m pregnant, the nurses injected it into my buttocks. You can choose.
I can feel a small bump under the skin on my left buttock, but I haven’t had headaches or other side effects.
As young women, we often don’t use condoms. We date. But everything has changed for me now that I’m pregnant.
I think I’ll tell people at work about LEN too, because some of them are in danger.
Dimpho Tsotetsi
I’m Dimpho Divine Tsotetsi. I’m a trans woman and work as a peer educator. I used to work at a donor-funded transgender clinic, but it closed after US President Donald Trump cut funding for such facilities in 2025.
I got my LEN shot on July 1 at Chiawelo Community Health Centre in Soweto. I arrived at 9.15am and got the injections at 10.45am.
First, I had to join the general queue to get tested for HIV. Once I tested negative, I could move to a special LEN queue.
The nurse gave me two LEN tablets. About 30 minutes later, I got two injections, one on each side of my tummy. I have a small bump under my skin at each injection site. [LEN forms a depot under the skin, which slowly releases the medicine over six months.]
The bumps bothered me at first. I normally wear a waist trainer, but it was uncomfortable for about a month. Now I wear it only sometimes and choose looser, flowy clothes. I can still feel the bumps when I wear tight clothes.
Before LEN, I took the daily HIV prevention pill for nine years. I struggled to take it consistently. You get pill fatigue. You also have to remember to take your pills with you when you go out or travel.
So I’m definitely going back for my second LEN shot after six months. The bumps caused some discomfort, but that’s nothing compared with the burden of taking a pill every day.
There’s another advantage for trans people. In our community, some people associate taking HIV prevention medicine with being promiscuous. A partner can find your pills. They can’t find an injection you got at a clinic.
LEN makes my life simpler.
This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism. Sign up for the newsletter.
