title: Low-cost phone lessons keep children learning during emergency school closures across five countries
content:
The COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns forced people to find ways to get things done remotely. Companies developed systems that made working from home run smoothly. Educators also had to shift to mobile phones and group video calls to get their lessons across and make sure students didn't lose out on their progress. This exposed the need for education systems to be more resilient and adaptive to local and global disruptions.
A recent Nature study explored how low-tech mobile phone programs could keep children learning when schools close because of major emergencies such as disease outbreaks, extreme weather or natural disasters.
Across India, Kenya, Nepal, the Philippines and Uganda, researchers conducted large-scale randomized trials to test remote-learning methods delivered through simple mobile phones.
Adding a weekly, one-on-one, 20-minute phone-call tutorial to text messages led to significant gains in basic math skills across all five countries. Students learned roughly three times more when they received phone calls tailored to their learning level.
The combined phone-call and SMS tutorial program cost just $11 per child. For every $100 spent, it generated 3.6 years of high-quality schooling, putting it among the top 10 most cost-effective education interventions ever evaluated, out of 150 studies worldwide.
Learning must go on
Nearly 25% of the world's population lives in countries where education is at risk of disruption because of political, medical or climate emergencies. A recent report estimated that around 222 million children face regular disruptions to their education, losing precious opportunities to learn and worsening the existing global learning crisis, in which fewer than half of primary-school-age children in low- and middle-income countries can read a simple story or do basic arithmetic.
When schools shut down, education systems need fast, low-cost and flexible ways to keep kids learning. However, rigorous evidence on what actually works during emergencies is rare.
Mobile phones have permeated into most nooks and crannies of the world where humans reside, leading researchers to explore them as a tool for reaching primary school children during emergencies. Wherever there are mobile phones, people can connect via text messages and phone calls, which might feel less efficient than the internet, but more than 70% of households in low-income countries have the former and only 15% have the latter.
Hello, it's math
To find out whether a single mobile-phone-based emergency education strategy could work in different parts of the world, researchers needed a coordinated, multicountry trial. Between December 2020 and July 2022, more than 16,000 households with primary school students from the five countries participated in the remote-learning experiment. Researchers randomly assigned students to different groups to compare levels of remote support.
Students in the control group received no remote tutoring during the trial period. Families in the SMS-only group received weekly text messages containing basic math problems and practice reminders. This group was not tested in India. Students in the phone call and SMS group received the weekly text messages plus a 20-minute, one-on-one phone tutoring session each week for 8–12 weeks.
The phone calls were built around targeted teaching. Each week, instructors used a short assessment during the call to determine what the child could do, then designed the math lesson around those specific needs instead of simply following the grade-level curriculum. At the end of the trial, researchers tested progress using the standard Annual Status of Education Report tool.
Economic yet effective
They found that weekly live tutoring calls paired with text messages delivered large learning gains in basic math across all five countries. On average, students in the phone tutoring program gained 0.321 standard deviations in learning, meaning their gains were three times larger than those of the median education intervention evaluated globally.
The combined phone-call and SMS program led to a 92% jump in the number of students who could correctly solve division problems. Students also improved on more advanced skills, including fractions, where performance increased by 6.4 percentage points.
Uganda and the Philippines saw the biggest improvements, where long school closures left children with few opportunities to continue learning. In Uganda, phone tutoring helped fourth graders make up all the learning they had lost during the pandemic and even outperform fifth graders who did not receive the program.
The researchers found that the approach worked just as well when delivered by government teachers as by nongovernmental organizations, giving them confidence that it can be scaled through public education systems.
The results show that by deploying a low-cost mobile-based intervention strategy, education systems can maintain learning amid disruptions across diverse settings. The approach is now moving into classrooms across Karnataka, India, supporting learning during the school year and keeping children connected when monsoon closures shut schools.

title: ‘A single wrong step’: Women deminers reach where men cannot to protect children in Syria
content:
In a dry field in Syria’s Idlib countryside, Lama Haj Kaddour holds a detonator, steady and practised.
She and her all-female team have spent hours locating and safely approaching a buried landmine. A short distance away, the rest of the team waits, still and silent.
When the blast goes off, a column of smoke rises from where the mine had been.
Kaddour wears a protective vest over her clothes. Like her colleagues, she dresses fully in black with only her eyes visible, in line with social norms in Idlib.
Fourteen years of civil war have left Syria littered with landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW). The threat has followed families back to the villages they fled, even after the end of a conflict that killed hundreds of thousands, displaced millions and devastated the economy.
Kaddour is one of 31 women now working in operational roles in Idlib’s demining effort, according to The HALO Trust, an international NGO involved in Syria’s demining work.
They clear landmines, survey contaminated ground and teach communities how to recognise the dangers left behind by the civil war.
Kaddour, a 33-year-old mother of three, left the Hama countryside for Idlib in 2019. She first worked with relief organisations before joining The HALO Trust.
In a conservative region like Idlib, being a woman can carry a particular advantage in demining work.
“A woman working in this field can enter local households and speak directly with women and children in ways her male colleagues often cannot, giving her direct access to a part of the community that is otherwise hard to reach in a conservative context,” Emma Pomfret, Global Media Manager for The HALO Trust, tells TRT World.
Women remain a minority in demining worldwide.
A 2019 survey of a dozen mine action operators published by the Journal of Conventional Weapons Destruction found that women made up only around 20 percent of mine action staff globally, with clearance roles particularly male-dominated.
According to Pomfret, however, more women are entering the field in Syria.
The fall of the Assad regime in late 2024 removed severe operational restrictions that had constrained HALO’s work, she says, allowing the organisation to expand training and clearance into areas including Daraa and the northwest and recruit from a much larger pool of people.
“When the Assad regime fell in December 2024, HALO opened recruitment and training to women, as we do on all of our programmes globally,” she says.
Supporting landmine survivors
In training hubs such as Daraa, women now make up about 20 percent of new demining trainees — eight out of a recent class of 40, according to Pomfret. As HALO expands beyond 250 staff nationwide, women are increasingly working as manual deminers, team supervisors, paramedics and community educators.
The shift is not only about new opportunities. Some of the women joining HALO were widowed during the war and are now the main breadwinners for their families, Pomfret says.
Kaddour's own path into demining began earlier. She started by supporting landmine survivors before training for fieldwork in 2022 and taking on the work of clearing unexploded ordnance herself.
“I could never live with the idea that a single wrong step by my children could set off a landmine that ends their lives, or takes one of their limbs,” Kaddour tells TRT World.
More than three million displaced people have returned to areas badly damaged by the conflict. Many find their homes still standing, but the roads leading to them contaminated.
Raed al-Hassoun, director of clearance operations at Syria’s National Mine Action Centre, tells TRT World that 49 landmine incidents were recorded across the country between the start of 2026 and the end of August, killing 24 people and injuring 61.
On August 31, an unexploded object detonated in the village of Faydat Ibn Muwaina in the Deir Ezzor countryside as children were handling it. Four children were killed and one was injured, according to SANA.
The Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR) says at least 3,799 civilians — including 1,000 children and 377 women — have been killed by landmines and cluster munition remnants across Syria since March 2011, with 329 of those deaths recorded since December 2024.
The highest tolls were recorded in Aleppo, with 814 deaths, followed by Raqqa with 676 and Deir Ezzor with 645. Hama, Daraa and Idlib were also among the worst affected.
According to SNHR, the Assad regime, Russian forces and terror groups have planted landmines across Syrian territory since 2011, often without marking or recording their locations.
Siba Abdul Karim, a 36-year-old mother of two who heads the non-technical survey department at The HALO Trust, says floods and heavy rains can expose or move buried mines and other war remnants.
“The danger isn’t necessarily fixed where the war left it,” she tells TRT World
“Floodwater, like what we saw in late August, can reshape the land and carry buried explosive objects with it, rendering old maps insufficient. Ground that seemed safe yesterday can become a fresh hazard after a flood or landslide.”
Abdul Karim and her colleagues have chosen to confront that danger directly.
The women say years of war have made them less afraid of the risks involved in their work.
“Every morning, I say goodbye to my children before leaving for the field. Every evening, when I walk back through the door, I give thanks that I made it home unharmed,” Abdul Karim tells TRT World.
She recalls once calming a child who had found an explosive device, reassuring him before explaining the danger of what he had found.
Also working in the field is Mariam al Asaad, 26, who is married and has an eight-year-old daughter.
For nearly four years, al Asaad has volunteered with the Syrian Civil Defence, also known as the White Helmets, conducting non-technical surveys and risk education and helping map contaminated areas. In 2022, she received specialised training in survey and munitions classification, becoming one of the first women to join Syria’s ERW teams.
Every morning, al Asaad kisses her daughter goodbye before leaving for the field. When she returns home, she faces the challenge of balancing a dangerous job with motherhood.
“I worry all the time about the balance between my daughter and this job,” she tells TRT World.
For al Asaad, the work is also personal. Her father owned land east of Idlib that was contaminated with landmines the family did not know were there.
In 2017, as fighting around Idlib eased, he returned to tend to the family’s olive grove, taking al Asaad’s younger brother, then nine years old, with him.
“A landmine exploded when my brother threw a stone at the ground. It tore into his left foot,” she says.
With no way of knowing how many more mines lay buried there, the family abandoned the land.
“My father spent his final years watching the trees go wild, and the little fruit that still fell just rotted on the ground,” she says. “We ended up buying olive oil every season, even though we had a grove that used to give us our own.”
Al Asaad believes the grief of losing access to the land took a heavy toll on her father’s health.
Waiting for the land back
In the village of Dadikh in the Idlib countryside, Abu Mohammad al Ali, 62, owns land that was once his family’s sole source of livelihood. The war has turned it into a place he can no longer enter.
He grew olive and fruit trees there, relying on the harvest to support his family, before mines and other war remnants contaminated the land.
“We used to come here at first light, plough, plant, and tend to the trees,” al Ali tells TRT World.
“Today I’m afraid to take a single step onto my own land. The trees we worked so hard to grow have died because we can no longer reach them to water them and care for them.”
According to al Ali, his land was the scene of clashes and aerial bombardment during the war.
Assad regime forces, backed by Russian air support, attempted to advance towards the edges of the village but were unable to take the area from local forces.
His land lay along the front line.
Months of fighting left the land heavily contaminated with mines and other remnants of war, making it inaccessible even after the fighting stopped.
“Fear is part of daily life for my family and everyone in the village,” he says.
He recalls an incident in 2025 when a mine exploded on his land while a child was nearby.
Since then, he has struggled with the thought that land that once fed his family could instead kill a child.
“Farmers in Dadikh live between leaving their land and losing their livelihood, or returning to it with the possibility that the next step could be their last,” he says.
“The hardest part is that when I look at my land, I still see it as it used to be. I see the trees, and I remember the seasons we used to wait for. But today I can't get close to it.”
“We just want the mines removed, and to know the land is safe before we send our children there or go back to farming it ourselves,” he adds.
Alongside clearance efforts, UNICEF and its partners are teaching children and families to recognise mine risks before demining teams can reach contaminated areas.
Fouad Mansour, a project manager at UNICEF, tells TRT World that the agency and its partners reached roughly 850,000 children, parents and caregivers with mine-risk education in 2025 and trained around 400 specialists.
“We use pictures, stories, games and visual material to turn a frightening fact into a behaviour a child can remember: don’t touch the strange object, move away from it, and tell an adult or the relevant authority,” he says.
Mansour says UNICEF works with 38 partners across mine clearance, victim assistance, risk education and advocacy.
It has also supported the development of a national risk-education framework integrated into the curriculum in coordination with Syria’s Ministry of Education.
A national effort to bring order
At the national level, Syria’s National Mine Action Centre is coordinating efforts by international and local organisations.
“We are currently developing the national standards that will govern the work of organisations in this field,” Raed al Hassoun says.
“We are also building a national information management system to collect the data that will underpin a roadmap for addressing landmine and ERW risk according to national priorities.”
Among the centre’s priorities is completing a national non-technical survey to determine the location, type and scale of contamination, amid what al Hassoun describes as limited capacity to address the problem's scale.
“Our own figures are still incomplete,” he says, adding that the national survey under way is intended to close that gap.
Military engineering teams from the Ministry of Defence and dedicated units from the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management also take part in clearance operations, he says.
“The reconstruction of Syria’s battered infrastructure depends first and foremost on resolving the mine issue,” al Hassoun says, pointing to the Jobar district of Damascus as an example.
At the request of the Damascus governorate, the centre established an operations room that brought together the HALO Trust, the International Committee of the Red Cross, teams from the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management, and Red Crescent non-technical survey teams.
Together, they cleared Jobar’s main and side roads, allowing reconstruction work to begin.
This article is published in collaboration with Egab.

title: Pitching in: Leukemia survivor offers lifeline to young people coping with cancer
content:
The organizer: Geoff Eaton
The pitch: Founding Young Adult Cancer Canada
Geoff Eaton had barely graduated from Memorial University in St. John’s in 1998 when he was diagnosed with Leukemia. He was 22 years old and at one point doctors said he had less than a 2-per-cent chance of surviving.
After months of chemotherapy and a bone marrow transplant from his father, Mr. Eaton’s health improved. At the time he was searching for an organization that offered support to young people coping with cancer. “We didn’t find anybody,” he recalled. “Young adult cancer is pretty new on the radar, and it wasn’t at all on the radar in the 2000s.”
That led Mr. Eaton to launch Young Adult Cancer Canada in 2000. The St. John’s-based charity provides a range of services to people between the ages of 15 and 39 who are living with cancer. YACC’s programs include chat groups, annual conferences, a four-day retreat and social connections. “We set out to be this national resource for these young adults,” said Mr. Eaton.
His own battle with cancer was far from over. In 2001 his Leukemia returned and he had another bone marrow transplant from his father. The transplant and treatments were a success and Mr. Eaton, now 50, is enjoying a full life with his wife and three children.
“There’s no question in my mind that I’m the luckiest person you’ve ever talked to in your life,” he said. “I’ve got a collection of miracles stacked up in my life, and I am very mindful of that.”
He’s continued to lead YACC as executive director and the charity supports nearly 8,000 young people across Canada. “Everything we do is centred on this notion of community,” he said.
YACC relies on donations, grants and sponsorships for its funding. This summer it received a major boost from the charitable arm of Spencer’s Gifts, a U.S.-based retailer with 50 outlets in Canada. Each of the Canadian stores is raising money for YACC from Aug. 20 to Sept. 13. “It’s a huge partnership for us,” said Mr. Eaton.
Mr. Eaton said his struggles with cancer have taught him that “there are good things in all of life’s challenges.”
“I really believe every win in our life is a team win, and that means at work and at home,” he added. “And YACC is a beautiful example of a team win.”

title: Desde 2025, Chiapas ha alfabetizado a 250 mil personas
content:
Viernes 11 de septiembre de 2026, p. 13
San Cristóbal de Las Casas, Chis., Galardonado con el Premio Internacional de Alfabetización Confusio de la Organización de Naciones Unidas para la Educación, la Ciencia y la Cultura (Unesco) 2026, el programa estatal Chiapas Puede ha logrado enseñar a leer y escribir a 250 mil personas en los 124 municipios de la entidad, en su mayoría indígenas, de 2025 a la fecha, informó Flor Marina Bermúdez, coordinadora del proyecto.
En entrevista con La Jornada, la funcionaria destacó que en promedio se destinan cada año 850 millones de pesos a la entrega de la beca Rosario Castellanos, con la que se garantizan 4 mil pesos a cada beneficiario que logra aprender a leer y escribir. Este apoyo, dijo, “es una de las acciones más efectivas para lograr que quienes no han tenido la oportunidad de escolarizarse puedan alfabetizarse”.
Indicó que por medio de un “modelo propio e innovador” de alfabetización desarrollado por el programa, que incluye la elaboración de los materiales didácticos a partir de las lenguas maternas de los alfabetizados, “hemos logrado una elevada tasa de éxito”. Enfatizó que actualmente se atiende a miles de indígenas de los cincos principales grupos lingüísticos en el estado: tseltal, tsotsil, chol, zoque y tojolabal.
Luego de ser reconocido por la Unesco como uno de los seis proyectos de alfabetización más innovadores del mundo, Bermúdez señaló que se buscó recuperar las mejores prácticas de alfabetización en América Latina para los pueblos indígenas y afrodescendientes, y “de la mano de alfabetizadores indígenas y con la visión de las etnopedagogías, coincidimos en hacer algo innovador: elaborar primero los materiales en lenguas indígenas y luego en español”.
Por ello, dijo, los libros que se usan en las comunidades no son traducciones, sino “textos auténticamente hechos por autores indígenas, que parten de la cosmovisión de los pueblos originarios, utilizando ejemplos que son comunes a éstos y las gramáticas del lenguaje, que hacen que los educandos puedan aprender primero en su lengua y luego en español”.
Se beneficiaron 165 mil mujeres
Agregó que este modelo de alfabetización ya impactó a 165 mil mujeres, en su mayoría indígenas, quienes representan 80 por ciento del total de la población que se ha logrado alfabetizar en la administración del gobernador Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar.
Precisó que en el estado se tenían detectadas entre 340 y 380 mil personas no alfabetizadas, por lo que para el año próximo se tiene la meta de alcanzar a otros 100 mil habitantes.

title: 8 mn adolescent girls given hpv vaccine in past six months: Govt
content:
HPV vaccine administered to 8 million adolescent girls in past 6 months: Govt
India has vaccinated 8 million adolescent girls in the past six months against the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) under the National HPV Vaccination Campaign.
India has vaccinated 8 million adolescent girls in the past six months against the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) under the National HPV Vaccination Campaign, aimed at preventing cervical cancer, Union ministry of health and family welfare announced on Friday.
“The milestone marks the expanding reach of HPV vaccination through the public health system and reinforces India’s commitment to strengthening preventive healthcare for adolescent girls,” said health ministry in a statement.
Also Read | Bengal health dept probes five accused of practising medicine with fake degrees
Five states —Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Mizoram— have achieved 100% cover of their respective identified target populations. Whereas, Bihar Andhra Pradesh and Assam have crossed 90% coverage, Karnataka achieved 85%, Chhattisgarh, Sikkim, Kerala, Telangana and Odisha crossed 60% coverage, the ministry said. Among States, Uttar Pradesh has recorded the highest number of vaccinations, with more than 2.2 million adolescent girls vaccinated under the campaign.
“The progress reflects coordinated implementation by States and Union Territories, sustained community mobilisation and active engagement of district-level health teams. States have adopted context-specific approaches to reach eligible adolescent girls through the public health delivery network, including in rural, urban, remote and geographically challenging areas,” read the health ministry statement.
Also Read | Addressing the adolescent health crisis through school-based action
With 123,000 new diagnoses annually, India accounts for approximately one-fifth of all cervical cancer cases globally and one-quarter of all cervical cancer deaths, and it is the second most common cancer among Indian women.
In a study published in The Lancet in June, it was shown that high HPV vaccination coverage was associated with a substantial reduction in cervical cancer deaths.
The vaccination campaign was launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on February 28 this year. Under the campaign, 14-year-old girls are provided voluntary and free-of-cost single-dose HPV vaccination, with parental consent, at government health facilities.
As per Registrar General of India (RGI) 2021 estimates, approximately 12 million girls constitute the annual cohort of 14-year-olds who are expected to benefit from the initiative each year.
“The campaign has placed strong emphasis on community engagement and credible information, with parents, healthcare providers, teachers and frontline health workers being actively engaged to address concerns and counter misinformation relating to HPV vaccination.”
Healthcare providers, including paediatricians, gynaecologists and experts from institutions such as AIIMS, along with teachers and frontline health workers including ASHAs and ANMs, have supported awareness and mobilisation efforts across States and districts.
“The campaign has also leveraged India’s digital health infrastructure through the U-WIN platform, enabling programme managers to monitor vaccination coverage at the district level, identify coverage gaps and missed beneficiaries, and support more effective programme planning and resource allocation. The national campaign builds on extensive global experience with HPV vaccination.,” said health ministry.
According to estimates, at least 800 million doses of HPV vaccines have been distributed globally, providing substantial real-world experience on their use and safety.
HPV vaccination, initially adopted predominantly by high-income countries, has progressively expanded into national immunisation programmes across countries at different income levels. At present, 87% of upper-middle-income countries, 78% of lower-middle-income countries and 54% of low-income countries have adopted HPV vaccines in their National Immunization Programmes.
Also Read | HPV vaccines for girls aged over 14, consent to use of personal info mandatory for Delhi Lakshmi Yojana
In a 2024 study, published in The Lancet, it was mentioned that there was emerging evidence suggesting one dose of HPV vaccine was as effective in preventing HPV infection and cervical precancerous lesions as a multidose regimen, and in 2022, The World Health Organisation (WHO) endorsed a single-dose HPV vaccination schedule in females aged 9–20 years.
“The growing adoption of HPV vaccination across diverse income settings reflects its increasing role as an important component of national strategies for cervical cancer prevention. All vaccination sessions under the campaign are conducted under the supervision of trained medical officers at government health facilities,” said the health ministry.
It added that government health facilities were also linked with 24×7 healthcare facilities for appropriate management of rare Adverse Events Following Immunization (AEFI), to ensure timely assessment, monitoring and management of any vaccination-related adverse event.
“With the campaign progressing towards its final phase, the focus remains on reaching the remaining eligible beneficiaries and ensuring that no eligible girl is left behind. The health ministry continues to work closely with States and Union Territories, healthcare professionals, frontline health workers and communities to strengthen awareness, facilitate access and support effective implementation of the HPV Vaccination Campaign,” read the statement.
- ABOUT THE AUTHORRhythma KaulRhythma Kaul is the national health editor of the Hindustan Times. She has been reporting on public health, medicine, and medical research, with a particular focus on how government decisions and health system reforms shape people’s lives. Rhythma has over 25 years of journalistic experience. She joined Hindustan Times in 2008, and has since covered everything from pandemics and infectious diseases to cutting‑edge medical research and climate‑related health challenges. Her stories routinely track the work of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, department of pharmaceuticals, and key national health programmes, making complex medical science and policy accessible to a wide audience. One of her prominent news breaks has been the 2012 Baby Falak case: A two-year-old brutally battered baby girl was admitted to AIIMS-Delhi with severe head injuries, multiple fractures, human bite marks, and burns. The police investigation revealed this to be a case of multi-state human-trafficking racket. She was profiled by The Wall Street Journal for breaking this story. Rhythma holds a Master’s degree from Jawaharlal Nehru University, Delhi. Prior to Hindustan Times, she worked with the India Today Group. Rhythma can be contacted at rhythma.kaul@hindustantimes.com. title: Can Community Programs Reduce Gun Violence?
content: A new study by researchers at UC Berkeley’s Center for Global Healthy Cities published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Network Open found that the California city of Richmond’s Office of Neighborhood Safety (ONS) was responsible for a 61% reduction in that city’s firearm homicides and injury shootings over the last 14 years. This is one of the only studies in the country to document the sustained impacts of a community violence intervention program on city-wide firearm violence over more than 10 years. According to lead author Alice Bruno, a doctoral student in epidemiology at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health, “we leveraged data from dozens of comparable cities across the United States to estimate what firearm violence would have looked like in Richmond without the ONS, Peacemaker Fellowship. We found that the Fellowship contributed to long-term reductions in violence, and that the declines only grew as the program operated.” Other UC Berkeley coauthors include Jason Corburn; Mahasin Mujahid, chair of the Division of Epidemiology; Sean Darling-Hammond; and Juan Cabrera. Sam Vaughn, director of ONS, said, “The statistics back up what we have seen in the streets: fewer shootings, fewer deaths, and a healthier community overall.” Homicide rates are down across the country; the FBI recently released data showing murder rates are down a record 18.1% nationally. However, Richmond has consistently outperformed national declines for over a decade, suggesting the results are due to that city’s innovative, street-outreach interventions and their mentorship of active firearm offenders, a program called Operation Peacemaker Fellowship, which was instituted in 2010. The Fellowship uses a public health approach to preventing gun violence. According to James Houston, the program manager of the ONS who oversees the day-to-day implementation of the Peacemaker Fellowship, including managing 14 street-outreach workers who currently serve 123 participants, “the credit goes to the young people making better decisions and the team that gives them support, mentorship, and encouragement every day to make a change.” According to Shasa Curl, Richmond city manager, Richmond had over 300 police officer full-time equivalent in 2014 and 180 in 2020, but was down to 121 active sworn officers by 2024. Yet during this time, the ONS, through continued city support and grants, was able to expand its staff and increase the number of fellows and participants. Even during the COVID-19 period, the study shows Richmond did not have as significant a spike in firearm violence as most cities did across the Bay Area and nationally. According to the ONS, the health impacts are lives saved, safer streets, and community members with a renewed positive life outlook. One former Peacemaker Fellowship participant said, “Before the ONS came to me, I didn’t care if I survived past 19, as long as I had a name in the streets. After my experience with the ONS, with my mentor coming at me every day, I got support for my stress, got a job, paying my bills, and have a kid now. I’m no longer terrorizing my community.” The paper notes the cascading health benefits for entire communities when gun violence reductions are sustained, such as the case in Richmond. Further research will explore how unique aspects of the ONS might be contributing to declines in gun violence, including that the program is a city government agency, independent from the police department, has had consistent funding, has trained and retained many of the same outreach workers for over a decade (these city staff are well paid with benefits), and delivers individualized supports to each participant based on their needs, such as food and housing assistance, cognitive behavioral therapy, addiction and anger management counseling, and other social services aimed at both reducing gun violence risk and addressing trauma. This article was originally published on Berkeley Public Health News. Read the original article.

title: Pedro Miguel: Analfabetismo: porcentaje agridulce
content:
l martes pasado, el secretario de Educación Pública, Mario Delgado, anunció en San Juan Chamula, Chiapas, una reducción histórica del analfabetismo, que cifró en 3.8 por ciento de la población de 15 años y más (https://tinyurl.com/ymnbsm2c). Es un avance significativo en apenas dos años, pues en 2024 esa proporción era de 4.1 por ciento; muy notable en los seis últimos años, en comparación con 4.7 por ciento de 2020, y mucho más, en relación con 9.5 por ciento de comienzos de este siglo. Más allá de las estadísticas, como lo señaló el funcionario, “la alfabetización es uno de los actos de justicia, equidad y amor más profundos que se puedan realizar” y una aplicación de la consigna “Por el bien de todos, primero los pobres” (https://tinyurl.com/32tkh2cv).
En efecto, el analfabetismo afecta principalmente a mujeres pobres y a las entidades con mayores rezagos sociales del país: Chiapas, Guerrero y Oaxaca, y combatirlo significa una acción concreta de combate a la pobreza, la marginación y la desigualdad. De manera que alcanzar ese mínimo de 3.8 por ciento informado por el titular de la SEP es un logro nacional al que no debe escatimarse el mérito.
Pero, al mismo tiempo, los números esconden una realidad dolorosa e ina-ceptable. México tiene una población total de unos 134 millones 400 mil habitantes, de los cuales 101 millones tienen 15 años o más. El 3.8 por ciento de esa cifra significa que más de 3 millones 800 mil adolescentes y adultos en el país carecen de habilidades mínimas de lectoescritura y que, en consecuencia, ven reducidas sus capacidades de expresión, de comprensión del mundo, de pensamiento crítico y de participación política, social y económica. Desde esta perspectiva, el anuncio del secretario de Educación Pública es una noticia agridulce que debiera llevar a la reflexión y, sobre todo, a una acción radical, no para reducir, sino para erradicar el analfabetismo remanente.
No sería, desde luego, una tarea fácil, toda vez que la población afectada tiene un alto grado de dispersión, es rural en su gran mayoría y requiere de estrategias regionales diferentes; no es lo mismo abatir 1.4 por ciento de analfabetismo en la capital del país que enfrentar 13 por ciento en Chiapas. Incluso en entidades contiguas esos índices pueden brincar en forma significativa; así, son de 5.9 en Puebla y de 2.8 en Tlaxcala, o de 3.4 en Zacatecas y de 2 en Aguascalientes, o de 5.1 en Hidalgo y de 2.6 en el estado de México, lo que denota la existencia de realidades sociales particulares y de la necesidad de pensar en estrategias diferentes para cada localidad.
Por otra parte, eliminar el analfabetismo no se ha formulado como un objetivo explícito de los planes de gobierno, para los cuales este propósito se encuentra implícito en los compromisos del Plan Nacional de Desarrollo y en la política social de combate a la pobreza, superación de las brechas de género, fortalecimiento del sistema de educación pública y planes de justicia para el agro y las comunidades indígenas.
Sin embargo, la individualización de este problema podría permitir la definición de un objetivo nacional concreto: incorporar a casi 4 millones de personas al mundo del lenguaje escrito –y aquí uno debería preguntarse qué lenguaje o lenguajes en particular, porque el español no es el único de México–, lo que significaría un acto contundente de dignificación, es decir, de creación de condiciones para el ejercicio pleno de todos sus derechos, para su incorporación en circunstancias menos desfavorables a la economía y a la política.
Hace 65 años, en 1961, a Cuba le tomó un año alfabetizar a casi un millón de personas. No sería descabellado, entonces, pensar que en México podría lograrse la erradicación del analfabetismo, que numéricamente es cuatro veces mayor, en los más de cuatro años que le restan a este sexenio. Sería una obra social mucho más barata que cualquier gran proyecto de infraestructura y que la mayoría de los programas sociales, aunque tan benéfica como ellos, y sería además un objetivo difícilmente cuestionable en el terreno político (por más que las oposiciones ayunas de programa y los loros mediáticos inventaran algo que objetarle) y capaz de generar un amplio consenso social.
Se necesitaría, eso sí, una inequívoca voluntad política y un vasto esfuerzo de coordinación institucional de la propia SEP –por medio del INEA y el Conafe, por ejemplo– con las secretarías del Bienestar –para involucrar a los Servidores de la Nación–, del Trabajo –Jóvenes Construyendo el Futuro–, de Cultura, Ciencia, Humanidades, Tecnología e Innovación, Defensa y Marina –por la logística– y Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural; por añadidura, habría que sumar esfuerzos con los gobiernos de los estados y municipales, y convocar a voluntarias y voluntarios de todas las edades, clases y condiciones sociales.
Pero valdría la pena. Llegar a 2030 sin analfabetismo sería un logro social magnífico para el Segundo Piso de la Cuarta Transformación.

title: A Belgian professor and 20 years of pediatric liver transplants in Vietnam
content:
Raymond Reding, MD, PhD, is a Belgian specialist in pediatric liver transplantation at Saint-Luc University Clinics in Brussels, where he has been involved in the development of one of Europe's established pediatric liver transplant programs.
His connection with Vietnam dates back to the late 1990s, when a university cooperation program began training doctors from Children's Hospital 2 in pediatric gastrointestinal and liver transplant care.
A connection that changed everything
Reding's connection with Vietnam began in 1995, when he read an article about the successful separation of the Vietnamese-German conjoined twins.
Impressed by the surgery, he contacted Professor Tran Dong A, who had led the operation, and proposed collaborating on pediatric gastrointestinal and liver care, including liver transplantation.
Reding initially came to Vietnam with a more modest goal: to share his knowledge and experience in treating pediatric gastrointestinal diseases.
But his visits soon took a different direction.
Hospital leaders wanted to go beyond knowledge-sharing and build a pediatric organ transplant program, a completely new and highly challenging field in Vietnam at the time.
Reding was asked to help turn that ambition into reality, beginning a collaboration that would eventually make pediatric liver transplantation a lasting capability at Children's Hospital 2.
Reding recalled Tran Dong A, then head of surgery at Children's Hospital 2, telling him that the hospital truly wanted to perform organ transplants, but that realizing the goal would require extensive preparation.
The two sides therefore started with the fundamentals, working toward the first pediatric liver transplant in southern Vietnam.
On December 5, 2005, that operation was successfully performed at Children's Hospital 2, opening a new chapter for pediatric liver transplantation in the region.
The first transplant would not happen overnight.
Reding and the hospital team spent five years preparing for the operation, working on everything from specialized equipment and infrastructure to comprehensive protocols for running an entire transplant program.
But Reding said the most critical factor was the people.
The team focused on training doctors and medical staff who were not only technically skilled, but also able to understand one another's every move, coordinate seamlessly and remain ready to face unprecedented challenges.
Building a self-sustaining program
Since the first transplant in 2005, Children's Hospital 2's program has continued to grow.
A total of 74 liver transplants have now been performed at the hospital. During Reding's most recent visit, he and the hospital team carried out four living-donor liver transplants in just one week.
The journey has also been marked by difficult and tense moments.
Reding still remembers a surgical complication that occurred on the very first day of the hospital's first liver transplant, when pediatric patient Xuan Quy had to undergo an immediate second operation. Working together, the team managed to save the transplanted liver.
The program's ability to stand on its own was tested even further during the COVID-19 pandemic.
With international flights grounded and travel severely restricted, Reding could no longer be there to work alongside the doctors at Children's Hospital 2.
For about two years, however, the team continued performing liver transplants and maintained and developed the program without his direct support.
When Reding returned after the pandemic, he was impressed by how much the team had advanced, progress that motivated him to keep returning to Vietnam and working alongside them.
Today, Reding sees clear progress in both the number of transplants the hospital can perform and, more importantly, the quality of its care.
"The number of transplants the hospital can perform has increased, but what is much more important, in my view, is the quality," Reding said.
He said the team's medical expertise has improved significantly and now meets international standards, putting Children's Hospital 2 among the leading pediatric transplant centers in Vietnam and Southeast Asia.
More importantly, the team has become strong enough to operate independently and continue developing the program.
For Reding, the progress also points to a larger ambition for pediatric transplantation in Vietnam.
He estimates that the country could have around 100 pediatric transplant cases a year and hopes Children's Hospital 2 can eventually perform most of them, including for children from northern Vietnam.
He believes Vietnam has the potential to develop transplant centers that serve as regional referral centers, not only for Vietnamese patients but also for children from neighboring countries.
In his view, Children's Hospital 2 has the potential to become a trusted regional center for pediatric transplantation as its expertise and capacity continue to grow.
The doctor who gave children a second chance at life
For the doctors and families who have worked with Reding, he is more than a doctor. He is a lifeline for children with severe liver disease, giving them a second chance at life when they are on the brink of death.
Professor Tran Dong A, who first brought Reding into collaboration with Children's Hospital 2, said their relationship has grown far beyond medicine. "Professor Raymond Reding and I have become very close friends," Tran Dong A said.
For Dr. Pham Ngoc Thach, deputy director of Children's Hospital 2, Reding's greatest contribution has been helping the hospital build a strong transplant program that allows more children with severe liver disease to receive treatment in Vietnam.
"The greatest contribution of Professor Raymond Reding is helping turn a highly complex technique into a strong medical capability for the hospital," Thach said.
Dr. Tran Thanh Tri, head of the hospital's liver, biliary and pancreatic surgery and liver transplant department, was among the Vietnamese doctors sent to Belgium for liver transplant training in 2002.
He said Reding's influence extends beyond technical knowledge. "I have learned so much from Professor Reding. He is not only my mentor, but also the person who shaped the way I practice my profession," Tri said.
But for the families whose children have received a new liver, Reding's contribution is measured in something much more personal: the chance to keep their children alive and watch them grow up.
N.T.B. was diagnosed with F4 cirrhosis and received a liver transplant from his mother at just 22 months old, with Reding and the Children's Hospital 2 team performing the procedure. Now five, he is healthy and in his second year of school.
His mother, Vu Anh Nguyen, still remembers meeting Reding before the operation. "Our family was extremely happy and felt very fortunate when Professor Raymond Reding agreed to perform the transplant with the Children's Hospital 2 team," Nguyen said.
"We met him the day before the surgery and were deeply impressed by how gentle, cheerful and approachable he was."
"He is not only a foreign surgeon, but also the person who gave our child a chance at life and gave us back our family life. Our family will always remember and be grateful to Professor Reding," Nguyen said.
For the families of children once on the brink of death, Reding's legacy is not measured in surgical techniques or the number of procedures performed. It is measured in children who survived, families who stayed together and ordinary childhoods that became possible.

title: Brasil registra a menor taxa de analfabetismo da história: menos de 5%
content:
Brasil registra a menor taxa de analfabetismo da história: menos de 5%
O Brasil conseguiu derrubar a taxa de analfabetismo para menos de 5% pela primeira vez na série histórica da PNAD Contínua. A taxa caiu de 5,3% no ano anterior para 4,9% dos brasileiros em 2025. Isso em relação a jovens com 15 anos ou mais que não sabiam ler nem escrever. Isso significa quase 600 mil analfabetos a menos.
O resultado é o menor desde 2016, quando começou a série atual da Pesquisa Nacional por Amostra de Domicílios Contínua, do IBGE. Naquele primeiro levantamento, o índice era de 6,7%.
Nesta semana, o Ministério da Educação voltou a destacar o avanço e divulgou novos dados sobre a Educação de Jovens e Adultos, a EJA. Em 2025, mais de 2,25 milhões de estudantes estavam matriculados nessa modalidade em quase 30 mil escolas brasileiras. O número é ótimo, mas o desafio ainda é grande.
Nordeste concentra maior número
A queda, porém, não ocorreu de maneira uniforme no país. O Nordeste ainda concentrava 4,8 milhões das pessoas analfabetas em 2025, mais da metade do total brasileiro. A taxa na região era de 10,6%. No Norte, o índice ficou em 5,7%. Depois aparecem Centro-Oeste, com 3,3%, Sul, com 2,4%, e Sudeste, com 2,3%.
A idade também pesa bastante no resultado. Dos 8,4 milhões de brasileiros que não sabiam ler nem escrever, 4,9 milhões tinham 60 anos ou mais. Isso representa 58% do total de pessoas analfabetas do país.
Entre os brasileiros com 60 anos ou mais, a taxa de analfabetismo chegou a 13,8%. Se forem consideradas apenas as pessoas de 15 a 59 anos, o índice nacional cai para 2,6%.
Leia mais notícia boa sobre Educação
- Aluna da EJA tira 10 na prova e comemora: “Posso mandar para o meu neto?”; vídeo
- Mãe de três filhos da Cidade de Deus se forma na UERJ aos 45 anos e conta história em livro
- Professor adotou três irmãos para mantê-los juntos e 3 anos depois, eles são os melhores alunos
Quem é considerado analfabeto?
Pelo critério utilizado pelo IBGE, é considerada analfabeta a pessoa que não consegue ler e escrever um bilhete simples.
A taxa nacional saiu de 6,7% em 2016 para 4,9% em 2025. O dado de 2025 é o mais recente disponível e foi divulgado originalmente pelo IBGE em junho. A pesquisa passou por reponderação com base nos resultados do Censo 2022.
O MEC atribui parte do avanço dos indicadores à ampliação das políticas de alfabetização e da EJA. O Pacto também reúne ações do Programa Brasil Alfabetizado, formação de professores e expansão da educação profissional para jovens e adultos.
Mais de 2 milhões voltaram a estudar
Um dos caminhos para reduzir esses números é a Educação de Jovens e Adultos. Dados divulgados pelo MEC nesta quinta-feira, 10, mostram que 2.252.069 estudantes estavam matriculados na EJA em 2025. Eles estavam distribuídos por 29.696 escolas públicas e privadas.
A rede pública concentra a grande maioria: 2.084.947 matrículas em 28.204 escolas.
O Nordeste também possui a maior rede de atendimento da modalidade. Foram 1,2 milhão de matrículas em 2025. O Sudeste registrou 493,6 mil; o Norte, 255 mil; o Sul, 192,9 mil; e o Centro-Oeste, 105,2 mil.
Como voltar a estudar
Para quem deixou a escola e quer retomar os estudos, o governo federal criou o CadEJA, plataforma que registra o interesse por uma vaga na Educação de Jovens e Adultos.
Pessoas a partir dos 15 anos podem procurar uma oportunidade para concluir o ensino fundamental. Para o ensino médio, a idade mínima é de 18 anos.
No CadEJA, o interessado seleciona a opção “Quero voltar a estudar”, preenche os dados solicitados e aguarda o contato de um operador, que orienta sobre as oportunidades de matrícula disponíveis na região.
O sistema foi instituído pela Portaria nº 275 de 2026 e faz parte das ações do Pacto Nacional pela Superação do Analfabetismo e Qualificação da Educação de Jovens e Adultos.

title: Meals, transit, and trust helped one California school end chronic absence for unhoused students
content:
At Scholarship Prep South Bay in Wilmington, Calif., school leaders say an attendance strategy centered on basic needs, trust, and community care helped ensure that no student experiencing homelessness at the charter school was chronically absent — an unusual result in a state where unstable housing often contributes to repeated missed school days.
Here's what to know
The school served 421 students, including 54 who were experiencing homelessness, according to the Los Angeles Times. Scholarship Prep South Bay spans transitional kindergarten through eighth grade, and nearly 93% of its students come from low-income families.
Support at the school extends well beyond academics. Students receive meals, before- and after-school care, uniforms, hygiene supplies, on-campus health and wellness services, and access to washers and dryers. Families can also get weekly food boxes, grocery assistance, hotel help, and Metro GoPass TAP cards for transportation.
Scholarship Prep chief executive and co-founder Jason Watts said the model is both simple and far-reaching, per the Times: "We create a school where everyone is welcome, cares about students and families, has incredible wraparound services, gives students what they need — and they stay."
California data show a sharp difference in absenteeism rates. About 35% of students experiencing homelessness are chronically absent statewide, compared with 19% of students overall. Studies from the UCLA Center for the Transformation of Schools found that the number of homeless students in Los Angeles County increased from 47,689 in the 2022-23 school year to 61,249 in 2023-24.
More background
Trauma-informed support is part of the school's everyday approach. Staff members are trained to help children who have experienced trauma, and social and emotional learning is built into daily classroom lessons.
Kristen Crowe, the school's chief community officer, said that approach begins with dignity.
"We lead with love and respect," Crowe said, per the Times, describing a family resource center focused on belonging rather than judgment.
Each classroom has a "rainbow cart" stocked with basics such as deodorant, toothbrushes, toothpaste, hair care products, and school supplies. The school also starts the day with a morning meeting so teachers can check in and get a sense of how students are doing.
According to the Times, Jace, a 14-year-old eighth grader, said, "My favorite thing about being here is that the teachers are very friendly, and you get to connect with them. They're very helpful also, no matter if you need support with a specific subject, whether it's outside of school or not."
What's being done?
To keep the support system in place, Scholarship Prep South Bay says it works with more than 50 community partners. Those partnerships help supply food, school materials, hygiene kits, counseling, and other services meant to reduce the barriers that can keep children out of class.
Students also have access to calming corners in their classrooms, stocked with breathing exercise instructions, fidgets, stress balls, and noise-canceling headphones. If they need more time to reset, they can spend 10 minutes in a mental health room to decompress.
Spring 2025 state test results show the school still has areas to improve, especially in math. The paper noted that those comparisons may not fully reflect the school's circumstances, given its high share of low-income and homeless students and the challenges of frequent student mobility.
"Loving the whole child includes the family," said Principal Allison Vann, the Times reported.
Jennifer Friend, CEO of Project Hope Alliance, added, "Our greatest impact is by investing in today's students experiencing homelessness. Every day I get to watch our youth show up powerfully, and that is an investment well placed," per the Times.
Where can I learn more?
Supporting student engagement usually starts with addressing basic necessities, such as reliable transit and nutrition, while fostering an encouraging environment on campus. Across different communities, schools are enriching student experiences through accessible meals, eco-friendly transportation, and interactive initiatives that build strong connections.
• Teachers and parents organized food collections, put out for families after school.
• In Oakland, the district made a groundbreaking decision to electrify buses for cleaner rides.
• Teachers harnessed children's curiosity to help inspire school composting and cut cafeteria waste.
By fostering a welcoming environment and simplifying daily routines, schools create the foundation students need to attend consistently. Scholarship Prep South Bay's impressive attendance progress reflects the power of this dedicated approach.

title: Mario Delgado destaca avances clave y becas universales en la política educativa nacional
content:
Mario Delgado destaca avances clave y becas universales en la política educativa nacional
Subrayó que los proyectos desplegados en educación básica, media superior y superior consolidan el derecho constitucional a las aulas.
En el marco de la gira institucional "Honestidad y resultados", encabezada por la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, el secretario de Educación Pública, Mario Delgado Carrillo, presentó una amplia evaluación de la política educativa nacional. El funcionario subrayó que los proyectos desplegados en Educación Básica, Media Superior y Superior consolidan el derecho constitucional a las aulas, con el objetivo firme de evitar la deserción escolar por limitaciones económicas.
Mario Delgado enfatizó que la Beca Universal de Educación Básica "Rita Cetina" se ha constituido como una pilar central de justicia social. La estrategia ejerció un presupuesto de 87 mil 393 millones de pesos, beneficiando directamente a 15 millones de alumnas y alumnos de niveles inicial, preescolar, primaria y secundaria, con una cobertura que alcanzó a 11.1 millones de familias en el territorio nacional.
En materia de infraestructura escolar, el titular de la SEP resaltó las aportaciones directas otorgadas a través del programa "La Escuela es Nuestra". Tan sólo en el primer semestre de 2026, la iniciativa canalizó 18 mil 406.1 millones de pesos a 65 mil 745 comunidades de educación básica. Paralelamente, en el nivel medio superior se asignaron 4 mil 288.8 millones de pesos para beneficiar a 5 mil 737 planteles.
El funcionario federal puso especial énfasis en la revalorización del magisterio. Delgado Carrillo informó que más de 23 mil docentes de educación básica accedieron al programa de promoción horizontal durante el ciclo 2025-2026, obteniendo incentivos salariales directos. Asimismo, detalló que el gobierno avanza hacia la edificación de un nuevo sistema transparente de admisión, promoción y cambios de adscripción que sustituirá de manera definitiva a la Usicamm, erradicando prácticas de corrupción.
Respecto a la expansión de la matrícula pública en Educación Superior, el secretario anunció la apertura de 13 nuevas sedes de la Universidad Nacional Rosario Castellanos con capacidad para 119 mil 280 estudiantes, así como el crecimiento de las Universidades para el Bienestar Benito Juárez García, que alcanzarán 239 sedes. Estos esfuerzos permitirán integrar a cerca de un cuarto de millón de jóvenes que anteriormente no encontraban opciones en el sistema universitario público.
Finalmente, el titular de la Secretaría de Educación Pública abordó las políticas de salud integral en el entorno escolar. Destacó el impacto del programa "Vive saludable, vive feliz", mediante el cual se evaluó el estado físico, bucal y visual de 10.9 millones de estudiantes de primaria, logrando además erradicar la venta de comida chatarra en más del 86 por ciento de las escuelas públicas.
En el ámbito normativo, Delgado reveló que 17 entidades federativas ya han promulgado leyes para regular el uso de dispositivos móviles y teléfonos inteligentes dentro de las aulas de clase.

title: Abiodun And The Women Agenda: Empowering Women, Strengthening Families, Securing Ogun
content:
Latest Headlines
Abiodun And The Women Agenda: Empowering Women, Strengthening Families, Securing Ogun
By Kayode Akinmade
A government’s commitment to women is best judged not by the number of empowerment programmes it announces, but by whether it creates lasting pathways for women to earn, lead and shape society. By that measure, Governor Dapo Abiodun’s record in Ogun State presents a clear and deliberate women’s agenda.
Under Abiodun, women’s development has moved beyond episodic assistance to become part of the State’s broader economic and social strategy. From productive capital and livelihood support to skills acquisition, financial inclusion, enterprise development and leadership opportunities, the administration has pursued a simple proposition: Ogun’s development cannot be complete when its women are economically constrained or excluded from decision-making.
The scale of the intervention reinforces that proposition. Under his leadership, Ogun State, in partnership with the World Bank-supported Nigeria for Women Project, has directly empowered about 100,000 women. Official figures also indicate the establishment of 8,759 Women Affinity Groups involving 247,273 women across the State’s 20 Local Government Areas. These figures represent different dimensions of the programme and should not be conflated.
The substance of the policy, however, is the opportunity created for women to build sustainable livelihoods. Oko’wo Dapo illustrates this approach. Relaunched in 2022, the programme initially provided livelihood grants to 2,094 women. By January 2026, Governor Abiodun reported that more than ₦5 billion had been invested in women-focused livelihood programmes over six years—about ₦3 billion through the World Bank-supported initiative and another ₦2 billion from Ogun State. Oko’wo Dapo had, by then, reportedly empowered about 55,000 women.
These figures should not be added mechanically because programme categories and beneficiaries may overlap. Their significance lies in the scale and continuity of public investment.
The Governor’s proposal to institutionalise Oko’wo Dapo as a statewide Women’s Trust Fund could provide a more durable framework for this intervention, provided it is backed by strong governance, transparency and measurable outcomes.
His commitment has also been reinforced through strategic collaboration. During the recent visit of First Lady Senator Oluremi Tinubu to Ogun State, Governor Abiodun provided institutional support and ensured the cooperation of the State Government, strengthening the alignment between Ogun’s women-focused programmes and the First Lady’s national initiatives on women’s economic empowerment and social inclusion.
The wider significance of this agenda is that women’s economic advancement is also an investment in household and community stability. Women play critical roles in household welfare, agriculture, commerce and local economies. Strengthening their livelihoods can help families withstand economic shocks and reduce vulnerabilities to exploitation, trafficking and other social pressures.
This is not an argument that poverty produces criminality. It is an acknowledgement that expanding legitimate economic opportunities is part of preventive development and human security.
That thinking fits naturally into the Governor’s ISEYA agenda—Infrastructure, Social Welfare and Wellbeing, Education, Youth Development and Agriculture and Food Security—where women are central participants and beneficiaries.
The commitment also predates the current scale of the Nigeria for Women Project. The administration’s 2020 Budget Speech reported that Ogun’s participation in Federal Government social-investment programmes had provided direct employment and empowerment opportunities for more than 3,090 women. Women and young people were also identified as priority beneficiaries of agricultural and livelihood interventions, including the FADAMA Graduate Unemployed Youths and Women Scheme.
This continuity is important. It shows that the women agenda is not an isolated intervention but part of a broader governing philosophy that seeks to expand women’s economic opportunities and strengthen their contribution to the State’s development.
But for Governor Abiodun, advancement cannot end with economics. Women must also have a place where decisions are made.
His administration has created opportunities for women to serve in the State Executive Council, State House of Assembly, National Assembly, boards, agencies and parastatals. These appointments represent more than representation; they provide women with authority, visibility and platforms to influence policy and public affairs.
This combination of economic opportunity and institutional inclusion gives the women agenda greater depth. It recognises women not merely as beneficiaries of government programmes, but as entrepreneurs, professionals, policymakers, community leaders and partners in governance.
The real measure of the policy should therefore be its lasting impact: stronger enterprises, improved incomes, greater financial inclusion, more secure households and increased participation by women in public life.
The proposed Women’s Trust Fund could help consolidate these gains and provide a sustainable institutional foundation for the next phase.
Taken together, the record points to a clear philosophy: give women the economic foundation to prosper and the institutional space to lead.
That is the essence of the Abiodun women agenda—a deliberate investment in women as economic actors, community builders and leaders, and ultimately in the strength of families, the stability of communities and the prosperity of Ogun State.
*Akinmade writes from Abeokuta

title: WHO validates Chile as first South American country to eliminate dog-transmitted rabies
content:
Chile has become the first country in South America to eliminate dog-transmitted rabies to humans, following more than five decades of public health "prevention and surveillance," the World Health Organization said Monday.
The WHO said the last reported case of dog-to-human rabies occurred in 1972.
"This validation reflects decades of commitment to protecting communities from rabies and demonstrates the impact of sustained investment in public health," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a statement. "Chile's success offers valuable lessons for countries working to end human deaths caused by this preventable disease."
Rabies spreads through the saliva of an infected animal, usually through a bite. However, the virus can also infect someone if saliva enters the eyes, nose or mouth, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Rabies is almost always fatal once the initial symptoms appear, but it can be prevented through vaccination, effective surveillance and prompt access to post-exposure prophylaxis.
Chile has long maintained a public health policy focused on prevention and surveillance to combat the disease. Efforts include extensive vaccination campaigns for pets and vaccines for people who may have been exposed to the virus, WHO said. "These actions were complemented by door-to-door dog vaccination campaigns, specific measures for managing the dog population, and community awareness and education initiatives," it added.
Celebrating the milestone in Santiago, Chilean Health Minister May Chomali praised the " joint efforts " that led to the achievement.
"The public policy on rabies eradication has yielded the results we desired as a community and as a country," she said, highlighting the work inside communities and municipalities. "They are the ones on the ground, where education, vaccination, and pet control take place."
Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Director Jarbas Barbosa praised Chile for its role in demonstrating "what can be achieved" when countries invest in "vaccination, surveillance, and access to care."
Human cases of dog-transmitted rabies in the Americas have dropped by more than 98% since 1983, with only a few cases reported annually nowadays. That progress contrasts with the nearly 60,000 people killed by the virus every year, most bitten by dogs, according to WHO.

title: Casi medio millón de niños y adolescentes tienen ya gafas y lentillas gratis
content:
Casi medio millón de niños y adolescentes tienen ya gafas y lentillas gratis
Campaña con Manolito Gafotas
Sánchez presenta la nueva edición del Plan Veo, dotado con 73 millones de euros y en el que participan el 75% de las ópticas del país
Manolito Gafotas, nacido de una familia trabajadora de Carabanchel, lleva gafas desde los 5 años. Él, un niño curioso que todo lo mira y lo quiere saber, está orgulloso de sus lentes, porque con ellas puede ver bien el mundo que le rodea. ¿El problema? Que cuando se le rompían, sus padres debían esperar “unos meses” para disponer de ese dinero para pagarlas. “Me ponían celo y a correr”, relata este personaje de la escritora Elvira Lindo. Ahora las tiene gratis, gracias al Plan Veo, puesto en marcha en diciembre del año pasado para menores de 16 años: 100 euros al año para la compra de gafas y lentillas infantiles. La ayuda estará disponible hasta el 31 de diciembre.
Esta es la campaña que han presentado esta mañana el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, y la ministra de Sanidad, Mónica García, quienes han reconocido que los beneficiarios han superado las previsiones, por lo que se ha tenido que ampliar el presupuesto a 73 millones de euros.
Según los datos facilitados por García, casi medio millón de niños y adolescentes se han acogido a este programa (en marcha desde el 17 de diciembre del 2025), que ha llegado a todos los rincones de España gracias a la colaboración de unas 7.800 ópticas (casi el 75% de las existentes) y 13.000 profesionales.
“Gracias a este plan, miles de niños y adolescentes pueden jugar sin miedo, dejar de heredar las gafas de otros, ponérselas cuando les corresponde y no meses después o ir con los cristales rayados o con niebla”, señala García, quien recuerda que esta prestación se ha incorporado a la sanidad pública de manera universal (sin distinción de la situación económica de la familia), porque “los derechos son universales”.
Estas medidas, añade, son las mejores armas contra la desigualdad. “Las gafas de Manolito ya no son un problema”, dice García, quien, emulando a este personaje, señala: “Que ningún niño vea peor porque en su casa no hay dinero mola un pegote”.
Sánchez ha defendido este plan, que apuntala los derechos y la sanidad pública. El presidente del Gobierno ha recordado que más de 700.000 de los niños sufren pobreza visual y que uno de cada tres estudiantes con malos resultados académicos podría tener un problema visual no diagnosticado. Para paliar esto, nació el Plan VEO, indica.
Sánchez ha aprovechado el acto para recordar cómo su Gobierno ha reforzado el Estado del bienestar aumentando en 145.000 millones la inversión destinada a las prestaciones sociales y ha ampliado derechos, incorporando, entre otros, nuevos cribados neonatales y ampliando las edades de los programas de detección precoz del cáncer.
“No vamos a dejar que ese sistema se debilite, se desmantele. Y no vamos a aceptar que aquello que pertenece a todos los españoles, singularmente la sanidad pública, termine dependiendo del bolsillo de cada uno, o acabe en el bolsillo de unos pocos”, ha finalizado.

title: Following Timor-Leste’s Triumph, All of Southeast Asia Has Eliminated Trachoma
content:
The World Health Organization (WHO) recently announced it has certified Timor-Leste as having eliminated trachoma as a public health problem.
The leading infectious cause of blindness, the achievement on the island nation now means that the entire Southeast Asian region, as defined by the WHO, is trachoma-free.
It means over 2 billion people now live with minimal risk of contracting trachoma bacteria, and with access to medical services capable of detecting and quickly treating it should it occur.
“The elimination of trachoma from the South-East Asia Region is a significant step towards our global target of eliminating trachoma worldwide by 2030,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “I congratulate Timor-Leste on this important achievement.”
Caused by the bacteria Chlamydia trachomatis, repeated infections can lead to scarring of the inner eyelid, causing the eyelashes to turn inward (trichiasis), which can ultimately result in blindness.
The disease is strongly associated with poverty and inequities in access to basic resources, including water, sanitation, hygiene products, and medical services.
WHO’s validation follows a rigorous, multi-year process to determine whether trachoma poses a public health problem in the country and to document the medical system’s capacity to detect, investigate, and manage cases that occur in the future.
A series of investigations between 2015 and 2017 saw the examination of children on the country’s Atauro Island, the screening of patients attending eye clinics across the country, and a series of specific house-to-house searches. No trace of trachoma was found.
MEDICAL ADVANCEMENTS: African Continent Gains 10 Years of Life Expectancy Since 2000 Despite Wars, Famine, and Instability
Timor-Leste subsequently generated further evidence through various studies. In a 2025 survey, 4,949 samples from children aged 1–5 years were analyzed covering all 13 municipalities. Testing found no evidence of transmission at a level requiring trachoma-specific public health intervention.
“Timor-Leste has once again demonstrated that strong national leadership, high-quality evidence and integrated health services can deliver lasting public health gains,” said Dr. Nilesh Buddha, Officer-in-Charge at WHO Southeast Asia Regional Office.
SOUTHEAST ASIA: Southeast Asia Nears Malaria Elimination, Down Two-Thirds Since 2010
“The country’s approach also shows the value of integrating surveillance across diseases so that limited resources produce the greatest possible benefit for communities.”
Laos DPR achieved elimination in 2017, followed by Nepal a year later, Myanmar in 2020, and India in 2024. Vietnam, Cambodia, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Maldives, Bhutan, and Thailand had all eliminated it as well.

title: Inside India’s first transwomen rescue squad, trained in Kolhapur
content:
In the last week of August, a group of people gathered at Rajaram Lake, pulled on orange life jackets, checked their ropes, and spent 10 days practising rescue drills in the water. It looked like routine disaster-response training – until you learned who they were. This is India’s first transgender disaster management and rescue team, and for its members, the life jacket has come to mean something far bigger than safety gear.
The Kolhapur District Disaster Management Authority has trained over 2,500 volunteers in the last decade. In 2019, it created the state’s first all-women rescue unit, the ‘Aapda Sakhi’ team, which now counts more than 500 trained volunteers. But ahead of this year’s monsoon, officials decided to try something unique.
“We thought, why not train a transwomen team,” said Prasad Sankpal, District Disaster Management Officer, Kolhapur. “So a first-of-its-kind transgender disaster management and rescue team initiative was begun in the country.”
The first batch of 10 transwomen, all associated with the Kolhapur-based Maitri NGO, went through their inaugural training module from May 26 to 28. Since then, the district has trained 15 transwomen in total, with fresh rounds of practice held every three months – the most recent a 10-day exercise at Rajaram Lake in the last week of August.
Recruits learned rescue swimming, how to operate an inflatable rescue boat, dry and wet lifesaving techniques, motorboat handling and maintenance, and First Aid and CPR.
“So far the results are excellent,” Sankpal said. “The institutional strengthening is already visible – the volunteers now help victims of road accidents without any instructions.”
For the women themselves, the initiative is about something the training manual doesn’t cover.
“Even today, people see us as sex workers or beggars,” said Mayuri Alvekar, founder of Maitri NGO, who brought the other volunteers on board. “I believe that such opportunities of working with the administration would help promote inclusivity and give us space in mainstream society, while changing the perspective towards us. We have been helping people during disasters or rescue needs but faced discrimination. However, now we are getting recognition and, most importantly, an identity.”
“To take the initiative further, I have also created a similar volunteer team in Dhule and Parbhani,” Alvekar added.
Suhasini Devmane, another team member and Maharashtra’s first transgender tourist guide, spent eight years as an ayurvedic panchakarma expert while hiding who she was.
“Despite a desire to contribute to society, many of us had previously been unable to participate in social initiatives due to a lack of opportunities,” she said. “For over eight years, I had to hide my identity – else I would have lost my job, and my financial situation didn’t allow for that risk then. I believe this training will not only change society’s perspective towards transgender people but also boost the self-confidence of individuals within the community.”
Shivani Gajabar, who is currently pursuing a Master of Social Work degree at Shivaji University, Kolhapur, says the acceptance hasn’t fully arrived yet.
“Even today, transgender community members feel alienated from mainstream society,” she said. “Though giving us a platform in the disaster management rescue team is a welcome step and would help bring inclusivity – and we all would give our best while saving lives – I feel there is a long way ahead to fill the gap. Even when I go regularly to attend classes, no one sits on my bench. I’m all alone.”
Her family cut off contact when she left home in Class 7. “They used to think I could not do any considerable work,” she said. “However, now, being part of the disaster management rescue team, my family members have started communicating with me again.”
The administration isn’t stopping at floods and drowning rescues. “There are around 30 categories of man-made and natural disasters, including wildlife rescues involving snakes and crocodiles in Kolhapur, and the transwomen volunteers will gradually be trained for these as well,” Sankpal said.
One gap the authorities want to close: money. The volunteers currently work for free. “We are also planning to deploy them for crowd management during upcoming festivals such as Navaratri, Anant Chaturdashi, and the Jyotiba Yatra among others. Also, efforts are underway to grant home guard status to the transwomen volunteers, which would come with an honorarium,” Sankpal told The Indian Express.

title: India's Kerala gets nearly 40 snake rescue calls a day, and 2,952 volunteers charge nothing
content:
Kerala, India, handles around 40 snake rescues a day, free of charge.
Here's what to know
Kerala faces an astonishing volume of human-wildlife encounters, with nearly 40 snake rescues every day, according to The New Indian Express.
Across Kerala, many of those calls are handled by volunteers who do the work for free, removing snakes from yards, vehicles, kitchens, storerooms, and other ordinary places while trying to protect both residents and the animals.
Kerala now uses its Snake Awareness, Rescue and Protection Application (SARPA), as a key part of its response to snake sightings to give people access to a trained rescuer who can capture it and release it back into its habitat.
Since the program began in August 2020, forest department figures show 105,696 sighting reports and 87,708 rescues. Some of the snakes handled through the program are protected under Schedule I and II of the Wildlife Protection Act.
Mission SARPA nodal officer Muhammad Anvar Yunus said, "Keralam's dense settlements and proximity to natural habitats mean encounters with snakes are common. A snake inside a house or compound can trigger fear, leading to attempts to kill it. Instead, (via SARPA) residents alert the rescue network, following which a certified volunteer reaches the spot, captures the snake and relocates it to a suitable habitat. The system has helped shift focus from eliminating snakes to managing encounters with them safely."
More background
The New Indian Express reported that SARPA's statewide network of 2,952 certified volunteers helps the system respond quickly when snake sightings trigger panic. They go to places they may not know, sometimes deal with venomous species, and pay their own travel costs, all while offering the service free to the public.
What's being done?
Forest department officials say the state is considering added support for rescuers, including a travel allowance to offset the cost of reaching rescue sites and an insurance scheme that reflects the risks of the work.
A volunteer from Palakkad told The New Indian Express, "We are taught to rescue a snake scientifically and without risk. However, there is still some risk involved while dealing with venomous snakes. We also request providing snake catching kits to all certified volunteers."
Where can I learn more?
Similar encounters are playing out elsewhere, from cobra removals inside Indian homes to growing concern over snakebites as temperatures climb. They also highlight the overlap between rescue work and conservation when dangerous animals need to be moved carefully and returned to the wild.
• In Telangana, India, an Indian cobra relocation turned a frightening home encounter into a safe release.
• Across India, rising temperatures and snakebites are raising fears of a worsening public health crisis.
• In the Philippines, rescuers freed an injured python and a water monitor after earlier captivity.
• In Louisiana, conservationists released rare pine snake hatchlings to rebuild a species under pressure.
Each case points to the same basic lesson: when people and snakes share space, trained rescue, safe relocation, and long-term conservation all matter.
