title: Com megaoperação, Brasil acumula 70 mil resgatados da escravidão desde 1995
content:
Uma megaoperação resgatou 479 pessoas de condições análogas às de escravo em 231 ações de fiscalização em todo o país. Dessas, 13 eram crianças e adolescentes, 75 mulheres, nove trabalhadoras domésticas e 68 migrantes oriundos da Argentina, Uruguai, Paraguai, Bolívia, Venezuela, Burkina Faso, Senegal e Guiné-Bissau.
Com isso, o Brasil ultrapassou a marca de 70 mil pessoas resgatadas desde que o Estado brasileiro reconheceu, diante das Nações Unidas, a persistência de formas contemporâneas de escravidão em seu território e criou, em maio de 1995, o sistema de fiscalização para combatê-lo. A reportagem pediu à Inspeção do Trabalho do governo federal uma totalização de resgatados: são, neste momento, 70.271 (o número está em constante atualização porque há sempre uma operação em curso).
Entre as vítimas, duas trabalhadoras domésticas negras, de 90 e 65 anos, permaneceram 75 e 58 anos, respectivamente, vinculadas a uma mesma família em Belo Horizonte. De acordo com a fiscalização, elas foram transferidas de uma geração para outra de empregadores.
A Operação Resgate 6, realizada entre 1 e 31 de agosto, foi um esforço concentrado de auditores fiscais do Ministério do Trabalho e Emprego, procuradores do Ministério Público do Trabalho e do Ministério Público Federal, agentes da Polícia Federal e defensores da Defensoria Pública da União.
Realizada anualmente, ela tem sido uma das maiores ferramentas de combate a esse crime, não pelo número de resgatados (em 2007, 1.064 foram libertados em uma só fiscalização em uma fazenda de cana e usina em Ulianópolis, no Pará), mas pela estrutura envolvida, quantidade de ações fiscais simultâneas e diversidade de atuação.
Vale ressaltar que operações de fiscalização guiadas por denúncias de trabalho escravo são realizadas semanalmente no Brasil desde maio de 1995. Quando constatam o crime, elas resgatam os trabalhadores e obrigam o pagamento dos valores atrasados, além de buscar indenizações e a condenação criminal dos envolvidos.
Nessa edição da Operação Resgate, as ações no meio rural corresponderam a 57,5% do total e registraram 292 resgatados, enquanto as no meio urbano representaram 36,5%, com 178 resgatados. A região Sudeste concentrou o maior número de trabalhadores, com 267, dos quais 208 apenas em Minas Gerais.
No total, foram pagos mais de R$ 1,4 milhão em verbas trabalhistas e rescisórias. Cada vítima foi inscrita no seguro-desemprego especial para resgatados e receberá seis parcelas de um salário-mínimo cada.
Doméstica de 90 anos permaneceu 75 anos com a mesma família
Os patrões das trabalhadoras domésticas tentaram convencer as autoridades de que as duas eram membros da família, mas a fiscalização apontou que elas, na verdade, prestavam serviços. Limpavam a casa, faziam as compras, preparavam as refeições, entre outras tarefas, não tendo descanso nem aos domingos, não contando com direitos trabalhistas e enfrentando restrições à vida social.
Além disso, ao contrário de outros membros da família, elas não tiveram as mesmas oportunidades de educação (não chegaram à quinta série do ensino fundamental) ou de construção de projetos de vida. Também não tiveram garantidos direitos patrimoniais e sucessórios.
Após o resgate, ambas foram encaminhadas para acolhimento em uma instituição governamental de assistência a mulheres vítimas de violência e passaram a ser acompanhadas por uma rede de proteção.
Como evidência do vínculo estabelecido, ainda se referem à antiga empregadora como “a patroa”. Segundo a fiscalização, uma das vítimas demonstrava, inclusive, insistência em realizar tarefas domésticas no local de acolhimento, como lavar louças e ajudar na limpeza.
Café, batata, cebola
Ainda em Minas Gerais, três ações com resgates ocorreram na colheita manual do café. A primeira, em Santa Rosa da Serra, retirou oito trabalhadores migrantes oriundos do interior do estado da Bahia. No segundo caso, em Turvolândia, foram resgatados dois migrantes de Campo Formoso (BA) e Florianópolis (SC) que exerciam atividades na colheita sem registro formal e em condições degradantes de trabalho.
Na terceira ação, mais nove trabalhadores submetidos a condições análogas às de escravo em uma propriedade produtora de café localizada na zona rural de Campos Altos, recrutados na região de Bonito (BA).
Entre as irregularidades: ausência de água potável nas frentes de trabalho, inexistência de instalações sanitárias, falta de local adequado para refeições e descanso, ausência de equipamentos de proteção individual, falta de camas, utilização da cozinha como dormitório, condições inadequadas de higiene e instalações elétricas precárias.
Em Estrela do Sul (MG), foram resgatados 44 trabalhadores que atuavam no cultivo de batata, dos quais 21 brasileiros vindos do Nordeste, 17 senegaleses, cinco de Burkina Faso e um de Guiné-Bissau.
De acordo com a fiscalização, a situação atingia de maneira grave três mulheres que integravam o grupo, pois, sem instalações que lhes assegurassem privacidade e condições mínimas de higiene, elas recorriam a embalagens vazias utilizadas na atividade agrícola para tentar esconder o corpo enquanto urinavam ou defecavam no campo.
Já em Matias Cardoso, foram flagrados dois empregadores explorando trabalhadores na colheita de mudas de batata para plantio, envolvendo 38 vítimas. Um empregador foi flagrado escravizando 36 vítimas, sendo 20 mulheres e cinco adolescentes. Um outro empregador escravizava dois adolescentes na colheita das mudas. De acordo com os auditores fiscais, no início da ação, houve tentativa de fuga das vítimas por orientação dos encarregados da atividade.
E, em uma ação em Araxá (MG), foram resgatados 47 no cultivo da cebola. Durante a fiscalização, foram constatadas graves irregularidades relacionadas à saúde, à segurança e à dignidade das vítimas. Entre os resgatados, quatro adolescentes, incluindo uma trabalhadora de 15 anos. A equipe identificou ainda que a maioria realizava as atividades descalça e sem qualquer proteção em área em que houve aplicação de agrotóxicos.
Um ano e meio sem receber salário
Em Roraima, as operações resgataram seis trabalhadores de condições análogas às de escravo em Boa Vista. Em um sítio em Bom Intento, um trabalhador estava há um ano e meio sem registro e sem recebimento de salário e trabalhava na construção de cercas, na estrutura e criação de aves e porcos.
Em uma carvoaria no Distrito Industrial, cinco venezuelanos trabalhavam na produção de carvão e residiam no próprio local de trabalho em estruturas improvisadas e estavam expostos a todo tipo de poeira e sujidade.
“A vulnerabilidade dos trabalhadores foi decisiva para que fossem reduzidos à condição análoga à escravidão sob o falso pretexto de ajuda humanitária. Os proprietários das terras se aproveitaram dessa fragilidade para negar direitos básicos”, afirma o coordenador dessa operação, o auditor fiscal do trabalho Maurício Krepsky.
Os locais usados como alojamento estavam em condições precárias, com superlotação, calor excessivo, ausência de privacidade, deficiência de instalações sanitárias, instalações elétricas improvisadas e ausência de local para refeições.
A fiscalização identificou, ainda, dois adolescentes, de 15 e 16 anos, em situação de trabalho infantil no cultivo de maracujá em uma fazenda em Bonfim (RR).
Tarifaço de Trump
O governo Trump aplicou uma tarifa de 12,5% sobre produtos de dezenas de países (Brasil, China, Índia, mas também aliados fiéis como Argentina, Israel e Japão) sob o pretexto de que esses países seriam incapazes de barrar mercadorias feitas com trabalho forçado. Outros seis, como Canadá, México e União Europeia, levaram 10%. Isso vem depois do tarifaço de 25% contra o Brasil, motivado por outras razões (Pix, big techs, busca de privilégios a setores dos EUA, eleições brasileiras).
Ironicamente, o modelo brasileiro de enfrentamento a esse crime, que atua, inclusive, para punir de forma cirúrgica empregadores em cadeias produtivas, é visto como mais eficiente até do que as políticas implementadas pelo governo dos EUA. A Casa Branca, aliás, reconhecia os esforços do Brasil nessa área e vinha apoiando o nosso sistema de combate à escravidão até o retorno de Trump ao poder.
Os Estados Unidos são o país com maior número de pessoas escravizadas no continente americano, com quase 1,1 milhão de pessoas nessas condições, de acordo com o Global Slavery Index (GSI), calculado pela Walk Free, em parceria com a Organização Internacional do Trabalho. Não só isso, como ainda lideram o mundo em termos de importações de produtos em risco de terem sido feitos com trabalho escravo, batendo quase 170 bilhões de dólares.
Trabalho escravo no Brasil
A Lei Áurea aboliu a escravidão formal em maio de 1888, o que significou que o Estado brasileiro não mais reconhece que alguém seja dono de outra pessoa. Persistiram, contudo, situações que transformam pessoas em instrumentos descartáveis de trabalho, negando a elas sua liberdade e dignidade.
Desde a década de 1940, a legislação brasileira prevê a punição para esse crime. A essas formas dá-se o nome de trabalho escravo contemporâneo, escravidão contemporânea, condições análogas às de escravo.
De acordo com o artigo 149 do Código Penal, quatro elementos podem definir escravidão contemporânea: trabalho forçado (que envolve cerceamento do direito de ir e vir), servidão por dívida (um cativeiro atrelado a dívidas, muitas vezes fraudulentas), condições degradantes (trabalho que nega a dignidade humana, colocando em risco a saúde e a vida) ou jornada exaustiva (levar o trabalhador ao completo esgotamento, dada a intensidade da exploração, também colocando em risco sua saúde e vida).
Mais de 70 mil trabalhadores resgatados estavam em fazendas de gado, soja, algodão, café, frutas, erva-mate, batatas, cebola, sisal, na derrubada de mata nativa, na produção de carvão para a siderurgia, na extração de caulim e de minérios, na construção civil, em oficinas de costura, em bordéis, entre outras atividades, como o trabalho doméstico.
No total, a pecuária bovina é a principal atividade econômica flagrada desde 1995. Denúncias podem ser feitas de forma anônima pela Plataforma Ipê ou pelo Disque 100.

title: Kottayam to King's College: UK nurse shares journey of winning Aster Guardians Award
content:
Kottayam to King's College: UK nurse shares journey of winning Aster Guardians Award
Dr Agimol Pradeep co-founded Upahaar, which registered over 10,000 organ and stem cell donors. She now plans to invest half her prize in the initiative
- PUBLISHED: Sat 12 Sept 2026, 9:23 PM
Nurse Dr Agimol Pradeep was on duty the day a young woman in her late 20s with liver failure was brought in, close to death. A transplant was her only hope. By chance, or by the Almighty’s grace, Dr Agimol was the on-call transplant coordinator when a match was found.
She escorted the girl to theatre, then cared for her through recovery. he girl survived and made a choice that would shape Dr Agimol's career. "She then decided to be my patient advocate when we go out in the community to promote organ donation," Dr Agimol recalled, speaking to Khaleej Times from the southern Indian state of Kerala. "She will always be with me in the journey, reminding me why I do this job."
Dr Agimol, a Senior Transplant Coordinator at King's College Hospital, was sharing her experience just moments after being named winner of the Aster Guardians Global Nursing Award 2026 in a grand ceremony that took place in the metropolitan city of Kochi. "Winning an award, representing my home country, India, in my birth land, Kerala, is beyond any imagination," she said.
Stay up to date with the latest news. Follow KT on WhatsApp Channels.
Since its launch in 2021, the Aster Guardians Global Nursing Award has grown into a global platform that celebrates nurses who are advancing the profession and creating meaningful change. This year drew over 134,000 registrations from 214 countries, bringing forward stories of nurses working across different healthcare settings, communities and disciplines.
Dedicating her work
That moment with the young woman was a turning point in Dr Agimol’s life. It was the start of her career built on noticing what others overlook. Early in her work, she saw that South Asian patients were dying while waiting for transplants, because too few donors shared their ethnicity.
She pursued a PhD examining the cultural, religious and social barriers stopping Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi families from donating. She didn't stop at research. She worked directly with religious leaders and community groups, and co-founded Upahaar, a volunteer initiative that has registered over 10,000 organ and stem cell donors.
Throughout her career, she has dedicated her work to addressing inequities in healthcare and strengthening access to care. Her work has also contributed to regulatory change enabling internationally trained nurses to re-enter the UK workforce, helping address critical workforce shortages. Her contributions to patient access, community engagement and healthcare capacity have earned her recognition including the British Empire Medal.
True calling
Born and raised in the city of Kottayam, Dr Agimol knew early that nursing was her path and her decision. "I could see that I could make a large change with this career," she said.
She now plans to invest half her $250,000 prize in Upahaar and the rest in nursing education. "It's about empowering more nurses to become advocates and changemakers," she said.
She described her profession as a true calling. “The message I have for others who are considering nursing as a career is that it is a true calling,” she said. “It comes with the responsibility of being there for people when they are possibly at one of the lowest points of their lives. It requires true passion.”

title: Therapeutic Family Camps Bring Healing and Hope to Aboriginal Children in Remote Australia
content:
In one of the most remote corners of Australia, a quiet revolution in child health is unfolding around campfires, swimming holes and shared meals. A new qualitative study published in The Lancet Regional Health – Western Pacific describes how a week-long therapeutic family camp, co-led by Aboriginal women and non-Indigenous clinicians, is transforming the way children with complex neurodevelopmental needs and early life trauma are supported in the Fitzroy Valley of Western Australia. The research, led by Anita Pickard of the University of Sydney together with colleagues from the Marninwarntikura Women’s Resource Centre and Royal Far West, offers one of the first detailed accounts of how culturally governed, recreation-based camps can deliver measurable benefits for families who have long struggled to access mainstream services.
The Fitzroy Valley is home to roughly 3,500 people spread across 32 communities, about 400 kilometres from the nearest regional centre of Broome. Around 80 per cent of residents identify as Aboriginal and belong to five predominant language groups: Bunuba, Gooniyandi, Walmajarri, Wangkatjungka and Nyikina. The region has earned international recognition for its community-led response to foetal alcohol spectrum disorder, spearheaded by senior women whose authority flows from kinship and Country. Yet families there have consistently reported limited access to health and disability services, and children with developmental delays or social-emotional difficulties face elevated risks of mental illness and other comorbidities later in life without early support.
That gap prompted the Marninwarntikura Women’s Resource Centre, an Aboriginal community-controlled organisation based in Fitzroy Crossing, to form the Marurra-U partnership with Royal Far West, a New South Wales-based specialist developmental health service. The partnership operates a two-way governance model in which Aboriginal knowledge and clinical expertise meet on equal ground, delivering a wraparound model of care that includes telehealth therapy, capacity building for local teachers, and the family camp that formed the focus of the new study. The camp itself is held at the Broome Camp School, the closest facility to the Fitzroy Valley offering accommodation, meals and activities in a single location, and was run twice, in April 2024 and April 2025.
Each camp brought together occupational therapists, speech pathologists and a social worker alongside Aboriginal family support workers from the Fitzroy Valley. Children aged between one and eighteen years attended with their parents and siblings, participating in music sessions, sports, arts and crafts, low-ropes courses, swimming and raft building. Behind the playful surface lay deliberate therapeutic aims: building vocabulary, speech fluency, oral motor skills, listening and memory, social and expressive language, and emotion regulation through play-based activity. The camp also deliberately incorporated risky play, activities that require children to assess their own capabilities, test limits and manage risk, which developmental research links to confidence and personal growth.
Crucially, parents were not bystanders. While children played, parents attended workshops grounded in the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander social and emotional wellbeing model, working on personal artwork while learning about child brain development, grief and loss, intergenerational trauma and practical strategies for supporting children with complex needs. Workshop topics were chosen by the Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal Marurra-U team based on priorities identified through the centre’s research, advocacy and community work. Local language and knowledge were woven throughout: parents and children taught the group songs in Gooniyandi and Walmajarri, traditional instruments featured in music sessions, and parents showed the team how to make damper. One Aboriginal family support worker observed that the clinicians’ approach made families feel good because there was no judgement and no guilt.
To capture what worked, the research team used an Aboriginal Participatory Action Research approach with a strengths-based lens, treating lived experience as expert knowledge rather than deficit. Researchers lived at the camp for five days, participating in every activity and recording daily debriefs, an approach they describe as ethnographic observation paired with relational engagement, in which knowledge emerges through collaboration rather than detached observation. Their observations were validated by Aboriginal co-researchers during debriefs and on subsequent visits to Fitzroy Crossing. On the last day of each camp, an Aboriginal researcher and MWRC staff member invited parents to yarning sessions, conducted in English with Kimberley Kriol translation where needed. All seven parents at the 2024 camp and at least one parent from six of nine families in 2025 took part, with findings fed back to the community in person for validation.
The results paint a striking picture of change. Parents described their children as more confident, more independent and calmer, with one reporting that her son slept better and his behaviour was much improved, and another saying camp helped her find ways to make him calmer. Shy children made friends, sometimes for the first time, and siblings shared experiences that brought families closer together. One mother recounted that her son made her toast the morning after camp, a small domestic gesture she read as a genuine shift in their relationship. In one family of a child with epilepsy, parents perceived a reduction in night-time seizures during the activity-filled week, though the researchers caution this was not verified by a health professional and the cause remains unclear.
Parents themselves emerged as powerful agents of the camp’s success. They arrived seeking help with behaviour, speech, emotion regulation and social skills, and left with concrete strategies framed within kinship values and collective care rather than deficit models. Many said the knowledge about brain development helped them understand their children and parent more effectively, and some wanted to carry that knowledge back to schools so teachers could better support their children. Respite proved to be a strategic outcome in its own right: held away from the Fitzroy Valley, the camp freed parents from kinship obligations and daily pressures, allowing them to sit, yarn and connect in ways they said were impossible at home. One parent described arriving and feeling her body simply go loose and relaxed. Fathers, whose engagement in parenting programs is uncommon in the region, actively joined workshops and sports, an outcome both staff and parents celebrated, though the team noted the absence of male staff in 2025 and plans to involve more fathers and young men in future.
The study’s fourth theme may be its most consequential finding: two-way teams work. Parents repeatedly emphasised that the combination of an Aboriginal staff member who speaks the local language and understands the community with a non-Indigenous clinician who is professional at what she does made a big difference, because the message came from an Aboriginal woman too. Aboriginal team members connected clinical knowledge about brain development, trauma and communication to families’ histories and experiences, and explained how colonisation and intergenerational trauma continue to shape parenting and family structures in the valley. Trust built through prior contact with Marurra-U services proved decisive; one mother said she does not leave her children with anybody, but the camp team’s kindness made her feel her kids were safe. The 2025 camp even employed Aboriginal parents who had attended the previous year, which the team credited with deepening trust and boosting engagement.
The authors are careful about the limits of their evidence. Yarning sessions included only parents and carers, so children’s voices are absent, participant numbers were small, and no quantitative measures or formal assessments of language or motor skills were used, consistent with the Indigenous research methodology. Longitudinal data and culturally appropriate evaluation tools co-designed with families are needed to capture specific therapeutic outcomes and effects on education. Still, the study concludes that family-centred therapeutic camps, delivered through two-way teams with trauma-informed practice and local Aboriginal women’s leadership, show genuine promise for improving emotion regulation, social skills, confidence and behaviour in children while empowering parents. Set within a broader wraparound model that includes telehealth and service-provider training, the Marurra-U camp suggests a replicable blueprint: when clinical expertise is woven together with cultural authority, community leadership and relationship, healing follows, and the researchers ask what health systems might look like if every program were built this way.

title: How Afghan Women Are Rebuilding Reproductive Health Care
content:
In Helmand province in southern Afghanistan, Ram Bibi, a 30-year-old mother now pregnant with her sixth child, counts herself as one of the lucky ones. She gets regular prenatal checkups at the Qari Safed family health house not far from her home. Here, midwife Marzia screens her for anemia, provides supplements and vaccinations, and has taught her to recognize danger signs in pregnancy. When her time comes, Bibi plans to deliver her baby at the family health house.
In another remote village in northwestern Afghanistan, when 40-year-old Manawara began bleeding in her 38th week of pregnancy, she was able to access immediate care at the nearby family health house. The attending midwife found that her baby was in breech position. Medication and emergency protocols helped stabilize Manawara and she delivered a healthy baby.
Such care may not seem extraordinary, but in Afghanistan, considered one of the most dangerous places in the world to be a mother, baby or child, Bibi and Manawara are outliers. In 2024, a study logged how many Afghans accessed health care services and found that thanks to a deteriorating public health system and severe restrictions on women’s movement, less than one-third are able to access health care. In fact, Bibi’s previous children were all born at home without skilled assistance, and both she and her newborns suffered infections.
Bibi and Manawara were able to get safe care through their local family health houses (FHHs), known in the local language Dari as Ashiana-e-Sehi. Part of a program initiated by the United Nations Population Fund UNFPA in 2009, over 450 of these friendly community clinics have become crucial access points for essential maternal and newborn care.
Globally, community medicine has often been used to improve health care access, especially in low-income countries. For example, Bangladesh has over 13,000 community clinics to deliver primary health care to people’s doorsteps, not just for women and children, but serving the entire community. Maternity waiting homes in Malawi, Zambia, Kenya and other African countries allow women from remote areas to stay near a hospital during the final weeks of pregnancy, avoiding the dangerous journey when labor begins. A 2025 review found that maternity waiting homes were linked with more facility-based deliveries and better chances of survival for both mothers and infants.
When the community steps in
“Most of our FHHs are in what we call ‘white areas,’ where health access is particularly difficult,” says Najeebullah Afghan, health and nutrition specialist at UNFPA. Places classified as white areas are at least 10 kilometers (or a three-hour walk) from the nearest basic health facility. Built on community-owned land, each FHH serves about 1,500 to 4,000 people living nearby and has a trained community midwife recruited from the local population who provides reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health services. With basic medical equipment and 35 medical and non-medical items necessary for maternal health care provided by UNFPA, these community clinics are often the only health care facilities available to women like Bibi and Manawara.
For example, the Arkalik FHH in northern Afghanistan’s Farhan province is an hour’s drive from the nearest hospital. It is run by midwife Laila Amini, who sees up to 70 patients a day, even though the FHH was originally built to service 300 patients a month. “Several years ago, a young girl died of pregnancy-related complications because her family couldn’t get her to the hospital in time,” she says. “Since then, I have been monitoring the health of all the women and children in the FHH.”
Similarly, at the Masyam FHH in Herat province, western Afghanistan, midwife Monika Rahmati caters to the needs of dozens of women every day. For any health emergencies, patients need to travel over 80 miles on mountainous roads to Herat City. “That’s why our FHH serves a very important role in the community,” she says.

An assessment of the usage of FHHs in six provinces by the International Planned Parenthood Federation found that nearly three-quarters of women surveyed lived within one kilometer of their local FHH, and 82 percent could walk to it.
Many FHHs have had a far-reaching impact on the villages they service. Amini says proudly that they have not seen a single pregnancy-related death in the last seven years. The IPPF assessment found that 88.7 percent of respondents rated FHHs as “very important” for accessing sexual, reproductive, maternal and child health services.
However, in a country where two-thirds of women have no access to health care, UNFPA’s 450 FHHs can only do so much. Bringing a midwife closer to home removes one major barrier to care, but it cannot fix a health system in crisis.
A health system in crisis
Patient loads are often untenably high. The Arkalik FHH, for example, sees more patients in a week than it was designed to treat in a month. In the IPPF assessment, many midwives describe seeing 20 to 60 clients a day and keeping long hours. It also finds that there are periodic shortages of medicines, and 55.7 percent of the people surveyed said they wanted FHHs to provide additional services such as vaccination, laboratory testing and treatment for minor illnesses.
The shortage of trained staff is another challenge, and something community health centers are often criticized for. In Bangladesh, for example, the perceived quality of care received in community clinics is often poor as they sometimes lack qualified staff.
In Afghanistan, since the December 2024 ban on women’s medical education, ongoing training and support of midwives has become even more challenging. Najeebullah says that digital learning has been their only viable option. In 2023, UNFPA and the Maternity Foundation launched the Safe Delivery App in the local language Dari (the version in Pashto will be launched later this year). The app provides step-by-step guidance, instructional videos and evidence-based protocols for emergencies including postpartum hemorrhage, neonatal resuscitation, infection prevention and Kangaroo Mother Care. It also works during power outages and can be downloaded for use without internet access.
The app has been downloaded 5,127 times by midwives in Afghanistan in 2026, and Najeebulah says it has been used to train and support around 1,200 midwives. Research on the use of this app in other countries indicates that health worker knowledge and self-confidence in basic emergency obstetric and newborn care increased significantly three months after it was introduced, compared with health workers who did not use it.
Nasima Niazi, reproductive health manager at UNFPA’s local partner, Agency for Assistance and Development of Afghanistan, has trained 171 midwives, including Rahmati, to use the Safe Delivery App. “It is easy to use the app, but I wish they would add more content in the local languages Dari and Pashto,” she says.
Even so, UNFPA claims that it has had a life-saving impact. “In Kandahar, midwife Freshta used the app to support her before and during a high-risk delivery, successfully preventing a life-threatening complication. And in Kapisa, midwife Parween used [the app] to convince a family to transfer a premature newborn (1.1 kilograms) to hospital, and the baby survived and thrived,” Najeebullah says.
Amini and Rahmati find themselves using the app every day, and say it has proved especially useful in dealing with labor complications. They also access UNFPA’s free helpline, staffed around the clock by gynecologists, midwives and a psychosocial counselor.
Many cultural obstacles to women seeking or delivering health care remain. The rule that women can’t leave home without a Mahram (male family member who acts as an escort) applies to health seekers as well as health workers, Najeebullah says. FHHs have adapted by providing midwives with accommodation at the facility, allowing them to remain available around the clock. Where possible, UNFPA also employs their mahrams as drivers or cleaners.
Rahmati and Amini say that however close the FHH, family attitudes will determine whether a woman seeks care at all. “The older women, especially mothers-in-law, say, ‘We gave birth at home, why should the daughter-in-law go to hospital now?’” Rahmati adds.
Although the European Union, Japan and other countries funded this program after the recent USAID cuts, the biggest challenge to the long-term sustainability of the FHH model is its heavy dependence on external donor funding. A significant change could be underway. Afghanistan’s National Health Policy for 2025 to 2030 puts primary health care and community-level services at the center of its ambition for universal health coverage. Although the policy does not specifically mention FHHs, Najeebullah hopes that this could give them a much-needed boost.
Meanwhile, the UNFPA and Maternity Foundation are working on a Pashto version of the Safe Delivery App and aim to train over 3,000 more midwives by 2027. And despite all the constraints on their work, Amini and Rahmati say they are motivated to go to work every morning.
“Zero maternal deaths in my village in seven years represents the success of my work,” Amini says.
“Every time I’m able to deliver a healthy infant, it makes me happy,” Rahmati says. “Even though things are difficult right now, a new, healthy life always brings hope and joy.”

human_wellbeing_impact.evidence: Medication and emergency protocols helped stabilize Manawara and she delivered a healthy baby.

social_cohesion_impact.evidence: has a trained community midwife recruited from the local population who provides reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health services

justice_rights_impact.evidence: thanks to a deteriorating public health system and severe restrictions on women’s movement, less than one-third are able to access health care

evidence_level.evidence: “Zero maternal deaths in my village in seven years represents the success of my work,” Amini says.

benefit_distribution.evidence: each FHH serves about 1,500 to 4,000 people living nearby

change_durability.evidence: the biggest challenge to the long-term sustainability of the FHH model is its heavy dependence on external donor funding

title: Mexico cuts homicides by 51%, India hits gender parity in higher education, supermarket grows food on its roof
content:
Photo: Jakob Owens/Unsplash (CC0)
In today’s edition: Mexico has cut its daily homicide rate by 51% under the presidency of Claudia Sheinbaum, India has reached gender parity in higher education for the first time, and a Berlin supermarket is turning unused urban space into productive land.
Mexico is seeing a sustained decline in homicides, with July marking the lowest monthly average in more than a decade. Daily killings fell to 42.5, continuing a broader downward trend in violent crime, and the January-July average also dropped to its lowest level for that period since 2015.
Source: Mexico News Daily
The Health House by House programme is bringing basic care directly to communities, with 22.8 million home visits carried out between July 2025 and June 2026. More than 21,000 workers are checking vital signs, updating vaccinations and connecting people to specialist care, while the programme builds the health data infrastructure needed for a planned universal health service in 2027.
Source: Mexico Business
Women’s participation in India’s higher education system has grown faster than overall enrollment, helping the country reach gender parity for the first time. Additionally, over the past decade, expanding universities and colleges alongside stronger access for underserved groups has resulted in 31.5% increase in enrollment.
Source: DD India
JR Nagar in the south of India made rainwater harvesting pits mandatory for every building in 2010. Residents say the approach has kept groundwater levels stable and eliminated the need for water tankers, whilst advocates say the community offers a practical model for reducing water shortages and improving local water security.
Source: The Hindu
Hull 096, the world’s largest battery-electric ferry, has been delivered to its new home. Its 100% electric propulsion replaces diesel on the vessel, and points to a future in which battery power can be used at a much larger scale in passenger shipping.
Source: ABC News
New school food standards in England prohibit deep-fried items and set tighter rules for the food served to pupils. The changes aim to make healthier meals the default and improve children’s diets at school.
Source: BBC News
At 2,760 square metres, the Lankwitz REWE is now Germany’s largest rooftop farm. The farm makes use of hydroponic technologies: the lettuce varieties are grown with very little soil. The whole growing process takes a little over three weeks. Once cut, the greens go straight downstairs to be packaged and sold, both on site and in other stores in the city and region.
Source: The Guardian
Two UK solutions are using pictures to help people with disabilities communicate and understand information: Books Beyond Words uses wordless picture books to help people with learning disabilities share and discuss stories. TapSOS lets people who cannot easily speak on the phone contact emergency services through a smartphone app.
Source: BBC News
Farmers in Zimbabwe are using solar-powered lights, mobile cattle enclosures and beekeeping to keep lions away from livestock. The approach reduces attacks on cattle whilst giving communities practical ways to protect their livelihoods and coexist with wildlife.
Source: IPS News
Two years after four dams were removed, about 20,000 fall-run Chinook salmon have returned to the Klamath River in California and Oregon. The comeback points to the real-world impact of restoring river habitat, though drought, water use and remaining barriers still threaten long-term recovery.
Source: Inside Climate News

title: La capa de ozono se recuperará en 40 años gracias al Protocolo de Montreal, según expertos
content:
La capa de ozono, el manto natural que protege la Tierra de la radiación ultravioleta, se está recuperando lentamente y la ciencia estima en unos cuarenta años el tiempo aproximado para completar ese proceso, según subraya Naciones Unidas en el Día Internacional de la Preservación de la Capa de Ozono, el 16 de septiembre.
La protección de la capa de ozono se acordó en el marco del Convenio de Viena (1985) y posteriormente, con el Protocolo de Montreal (1987), se establecieron las obligaciones para la eliminación de las sustancias que destruyen ese manto natural, los gases clorofluorocarbonados (CFC).
En 2016, con la firma de la Enmienda de Kigali, se acordó además la reducción gradual de la producción y consumo de gases hidrofluorocarbonos (HFC), utilizados en la refrigeración y para el aire acondicionado.
Ahora el Día Mundial del Ozono conmemora los 10 años de la Enmienda de Kigali, acordada dentro del Protocolo de Montreal, y hace hincapié en la relación entre protección del ozono y salvaguarda del clima.
Fueron dos científicos, el ingeniero químico mexicano Mario Molina-Pasquel Henríquez y el químico estadounidense Frank Sherwood Rowland, los que descubrieron en los años setenta que los gases CFC destruían la capa de ozono.
Ambos fueron galardonados con el Premio Nobel de Química en 1995, junto al químico neerlandés Paul Jozef Crutzen, quien también estudió la formación y descomposición del ozono.
Gracias a sus estudios, la comunidad internacional se puso de acuerdo para la firma del Protocolo de Montreal y agilizar la prohibición de CFC, gases muy utilizados en sistemas de refrigeración, aerosoles (lacas de peluquería, desodorantes, insecticidas o pinturas), espumas aislantes o disolventes industriales, que aún persisten en la atmósfera.
En 1985, los científicos Joe Farman, Brian Gardiner y Jonathan Shanklin, del Instituto Antártico Británico, detectaron un gran agujero en la capa de ozono sobre la Antártida que se abre y se cierra de forma cíclica todos los años.
Menor agujero y evidencia científica
Según un informe de la Organización Meteorológica Mundial (OMM) de septiembre de 2025, la capa de ozono va “camino de recuperarse” y en 2024 el agujero “fue menor” que en años precedentes.
La OMM asegura, no obstante, que es un proceso que “aún tardará varios decenios”, un periodo que científicos de la NASA y de la Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica (NOAA, por sus siglas en inglés) fijan en 40 años.
Según explica a EFE el investigador del Centro Atmosférico de Izaña de la Agencia Estatal de Meteorología (Aemet) de España, Alberto Redondas Marrero, “la capa de ozono se está recuperando y tenemos evidencias claras de que el Protocolo de Montreal está funcionando”.
El también responsable del Centro de calibración de ozono y la red de observación de ozono (EuBrewnet) indica que los resultados preliminares del estudio Ozone Assessment que forman parte de la evaluación científica de 2026 —que se publicará a finales de año— “muestran una recuperación clara del ozono en la alta estratosfera entre 2000 y 2024 y prácticamente en todas las latitudes”.
Explica que los resultados del estudio se presentaron en un “reciente congreso en Davos celebrando los primeros 100 años de la medida de ozono” y subraya que “el balance conjunto es muy significativo”.
Redondas asegura que el Protocolo de Montreal “está permitiendo recuperar la capa de ozono y, al mismo tiempo, ha evitado una cantidad importante de calentamiento global”, mientras que la Enmienda de Kigali “completa ese éxito reduciendo ahora el impacto climático de los gases que sustituyeron a las sustancias destructoras del ozono”.
Por eso, afirma, “10 años después de Kigali, el Día Mundial del Ozono de 2026 pone especialmente de relieve que proteger la capa de ozono y proteger el clima son objetivos distintos, pero estrechamente relacionados”.
No obstante, recuerda que “la recuperación es mucho más lenta que su destrucción” y, para que la recuperación sea completa, se necesita tiempo “porque los CFC permanecen en la atmósfera durante muchas décadas”.
Las proyecciones indican que “podríamos volver aproximadamente a los niveles de 1980 hacia 2040 para el promedio global, mientras que en la Antártida tendremos que esperar hasta la década de 2060”, sostiene el experto, según reportó EFE.

social_cohesion_impact.evidence: la comunidad internacional se puso de acuerdo para la firma del Protocolo de Montreal y agilizar la prohibición de CFC

justice_rights_impact.evidence: No evidence in article

title: Gunayala: A Living Model of Autonomy and Self-government
content: Gunayala: A Living Model of Autonomy and Self-government tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 11:14 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe Gunayala is a leading example of Indigenous autonomy and self-government in Abya Yala. The Guna Peoples have been defending their territory, their identity, and their own form of governance long before international instruments such as the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples formally recognized the rights to self-determination, autonomy, and self-government. Our Peoples have been practicing their own forms of organization and decision-making for centuries, and today we continue to live and exercise these internationally recognized rights in Gunayala. The ancestral territory of Gunayala Comarca is located on the Caribbean coast of Panama and extends to the Colombian border, comprising mainland, forests, rivers, mangroves, coastlines, the sea, and numerous islands where our communities are located. It is the home of our Guna ancestors, and is where we continue to live and pass on our knowledge and our way of understanding the world. Its coastline is approximately 315 kilometers long and includes more than 400 small islands and islets; we often describe our communities as seaside villages. Our people traverse this territory from the mountain ranges, down its rivers, through the forests, mangroves, and beaches until we reach the sea, the islands, the coral reefs, and the white sands—places that are not only part of our geography, but also our memory, our spirituality, and our struggles. Our autonomy did not originate from a State law, and our form of self-governance existed long before its formal legal recognition. Law 16, enacted on February 19, 1953, legally organized what was then called the Comarca of San Blas, now Gunayala. Subsequently, other laws and judicial decisions have recognized our organization and autonomy. Fully understanding our autonomy also requires remembering an event that profoundly marked our history: the Dule Revolution of 1925. The Dule, or People’s, Revolution was a decisive moment in the defense of our rights, our territory, our culture, and our way of life against the Panamanian government’s policies that sought to “civilize the Indians of San Blas,” as our people were then known. In truth, we already had our own civilization, with authorities, norms, knowledge, spirituality, and a worldview that guided our lives long before the Republic of Panama existed. The Revolution did not create our autonomy, but rather defended and reaffirmed it. This year, as we commemorate 101 years since that feat, it continues to hold profound meaning for us. The autonomy that our ancestors defended more than a century ago does not belong only to the past; it endures and is exercised every day in our communities. One of the spaces where our form of self-governance comes to life is the Onmagged Nega, the House of Congress, where the community gathers to listen, dialogue, and reflect on the issues that affect us, and to make collective decisions. There, our Sagla (traditional authorities) guide us through their songs, which transmit the memory, knowledge, and teachings of our ancestors, while the Argar help interpret that knowledge and relate it to the situations the community experiences in the present. Murals in Gunayala reflect the Guna way of life, which bridges land and sea. Photo by Julien Defourny. For us, song is not separate from governance. In our worldview, governing means not only managing resources, approving laws, or exercising authority, but also guiding, listening, advising, transmitting knowledge, and assuming responsibility toward the community. From each of our communities, a broader collective structure is built that connects the 49 communities of Gunayala through the Guna General Congress, where our people have organized to govern themselves collectively. The Congress is our highest political and administrative body and addresses matters related to territory, natural resources, education, and other issues that affect the lives of our communities, as well as maintaining relations with the State and other institutions. Alongside it is the General Congress of Guna Culture, responsible for strengthening our Traditional Knowledge, spirituality, songs, language, and other cultural expressions that form our identity. This relationship between the two institutions demonstrates a fundamental tenet of our model: governance, culture, spirituality, knowledge, and territory are not separate, but interconnected. Decisions in Gunayala are made collectively, guided by our customary law, norms, and worldview. The Igardummadwala, our Fundamental Law—together with the statutes, regulations, and resolutions from our Congresses, as well as community norms—forms our unique system and expresses our right to govern ourselves according to our own rules and institutions. This takes on special importance in the face of external projects or interests, because self-government cannot be reduced to mere recognition written in a law. It only becomes real in practice when a Peoples can make decisions about matters that transform their territory and way of life. Maraca with a Naa Ukuryaa. This symbol has been part of Guna culture for centuries, representing the octopus that created the universe, the four cardinal points, and the origin point of humanity. Photo by Julien Defourny. Over time, our autonomy has been tested by various interests in our territory and resources, and in recent years, by proposals for development megaprojects such as the Central America Electrical Interconnection System. In the face of these situations, our authorities, assemblies, resolutions, and internal norms serve as tools for exercising our autonomy. Governing ourselves means having the ability to say no, to set conditions, and to decide what is compatible with our vision for our territory. To see Gunayala as a model of self-government does not imply it is a perfect system, or one frozen in time. Our self-government is a living system that must continue to adapt to the challenges of today. Some of our practices and forms of knowledge have weakened over time, and many of our young people live outside the territory. Our communities are undergoing social, economic, cultural, and environmental transformations, while climate change increasingly impacts our coasts, islands, and ecosystems. Maintaining our autonomy entails acknowledging these realities and continuing to strengthen our heritage so that our language, knowledge, norms, and unique forms of organization remain meaningful for future generations. I am proud to note that in 2017, I helped found what is now known as the General Congress of Guna Youth—a space dedicated to strengthening our people’s leadership, conservation efforts, and values in Gunayala. We also cannot overlook the young people living outside the territory who maintain ties to their communities and return to visit their families, participate in traditional ceremonies, celebrate community anniversaries, or commemorate the Guna Revolution. This relationship with new generations is fundamental to ensuring that our culture, knowledge, and self-governance continue to strengthen over time. Women also play a vital role in this continuity, as they participate in passing on our language, knowledge, and cultural practices, and in shaping new generations. Likewise, our relationship with the land is expressed through knowledge systems like Nainu, our traditional agricultural practice. Passed down through generations and rooted in an understanding of cycles, crops, and land management, it reminds us that our way of governing ourselves is deeply intertwined with how we care for life. In the face of biodiversity loss and climate change, Gunayala’s experience has much to offer—not because we hold all the answers, but because over generations, we have learned that there can be no autonomy without territory, no territory without knowledge, and no knowledge without community. Our experience demonstrates that recognizing the rights of Indigenous Peoples means more than simply outlining a territory on a map. It requires respecting their authorities, institutions, knowledge systems, and norms, and, above all, their capacity to make collective decisions about their present and future. Our autonomy is not merely a right recognized by laws or international instruments. It is a practice we continue to exercise, defend, and strengthen through the Onmagged Nega, our Congresses, our norms, the transmission of our knowledge, and the defense of the territory inherited from our ancestors. Perhaps one of the greatest contributions Gunayala can share with other Indigenous Peoples and the world is demonstrating that self-governance is not a relic of the past, but a living expression of our self-determination and a collective commitment to safeguarding who we are, our territory, and the legacy we will leave to future generations. --Iniquilipi Chiari-Lombardo (Guna) is Deputy Secretary of the Guna General Congress. May Pérez (Guna) is Cultural Survival Panama Advocacy Coordinator. Top photo: Uggubseni community in the Gunayala Comarca in Panama. Photo by Iniquilipi Chiari-Lombardo/TV Indígena. Main Image

title: 10 iniciativas indígenas de retomada do território
content:
Em diferentes regiões do Brasil, povos indígenas têm recuperado terras transformadas em pastagens, degradadas pelo garimpo ou usadas como depósito de lixo, assumindo também o trabalho de restaurar a vegetação e restabelecer as condições para viver nesses lugares. São comunidades que avançam na direção contrária à das frentes de destruição: em vez de se limitarem a defender o que resta, passaram a lutar para retomar aquilo que foi perdido.
Destacamos aqui 10 reportagens publicadas pela Mongabay sobre como diversos povos indígenas do país, aliando tecnologia e saberes ancestrais, estão transformando seus territórios em lugares melhores para se viver.
Por que os Maxakali estão convocando os espíritos para recuperar a Mata Atlântica
Confinados em pequenas terras indígenas tomadas por pastagens no nordeste de Minas Gerais, os Tikmũ’ũn/Maxakali estão recuperando áreas de Mata Atlântica e implantando quintais agroflorestais por meio do projeto Hãmhi. Iniciada em 2023, a iniciativa forma e remunera agentes agroflorestais e viveiristas indígenas. O trabalho busca enfrentar a fome e recompor a vegetação necessária à vida cultural e religiosa do povo. A floresta é o lugar onde vivem os yãmĩyxop, povos-espíritos cujos cantos preservam o conhecimento sobre uma Mata Atlântica que já quase desapareceu na região.
Povo Xokleng restaura araucárias sagradas em terra indígena de Santa Catarina
Zág é como os Laklãnõ/Xokleng chamam a araucária — árvore para eles sagrada, cujas florestas hoje se reduzem a menos de 3% da área original. Vendo sua identidade desaparecer junto com esse ecossistema característico do Sul brasileiro, uma família da Terra Indígena Ibirama-Laklãnõ, em Santa Catarina, iniciou um projeto de restauração das araucárias. Desde então, a iniciativa já produziu mais de 140 mil mudas e reflorestou cerca de mil hectares. A iniciativa é uma resposta a um longo histórico de confinamento territorial dos Laklãnõ/Xokleng — da expulsão do Vale do Itajaí à construção da Barragem Norte.
Abolir as cercas, libertar a vida: povo Akroá Gamella retoma território ancestral e desativa lixão a céu aberto
Por mais de uma década, seringas, fraldas usadas e até tumores foram despejados dentro da Terra Indígena Taquaritiua, no Maranhão — sobre as nascentes de onde a aldeia Tabarelzinho bebia água. Em agosto de 2024, os Akroá Gamella decidiram que aquilo tinha ido longe demais: expulsaram à força o grileiro que ocupava a área havia quatro décadas e desligaram dois lixões municipais que funcionavam dentro de uma zona úmida protegida internacionalmente. As retomadas hoje restauram o território com práticas agroecológicas, reflorestamento de espécies nativas e recuperação de nascentes. Mas a violência continua.
Mulheres Krahô lideram guarda indígena para proteger território em Tocantins
Treze mulheres Krahô compõem o grupo de vigilância Mē Hoprê Catêjê para proteger os 303 mil hectares da Terra Indígena Kraolândia, no Tocantins, pressionada por madeireiros, caçadores, carvoarias e fazendas de soja e algodão. Durante quinze dias por mês, elas percorrem o território desarmadas, identificam sinais de invasão e encaminham as denúncias à Funai. A iniciativa nasceu da troca de experiências com outras guardiãs indígenas e segue protocolos baseados nos modos de vida Krahô. Além das ameaças externas, as integrantes enfrentam críticas dos homens de suas aldeias por deixarem temporariamente os cuidados domésticos para assumir funções de proteção territorial.
Kapinawás: meio século de luta pelo território sagrado no Vale do Catimbau
Até os anos 1970, ninguém no vale do Catimbau se dizia indígena — eram “caboclos”, sem nome nem terra reconhecida. Isso mudou em meio a uma guerra com grileiros, ocasião em que os moradores dessa área do agreste pernambucano encontraram uma escritura imperial na qual constava a doação daquelas terras aos seus antepassados indígenas. Cinquenta anos depois, surgiu a Terra Indígena Kapinawá, mas agora com um novo conflito: a criação do Parque Nacional do Catimbau, sobreposto ao território e limitando o acesso aos locais sagrados. Hoje, enquanto lutam para recuperar seus santuários, os Kapinawá desenvolvem um laboratório de recuperação da Caatinga, cultivando viveiros e plantando mudas por todo o território.
Jovens Yanomami recorrem a drones para vigiar seu território amazônico
Como vigiar, a pé e de canoa, um território do tamanho de Portugal? Foi essa pergunta que levou a Hutukara Associação Yanomami, em 2022, a apostar em algo inédito: ensinar jovens Yanomami e Ye’kwana a pilotar drones. A urgência decorria de uma invasão de 20 mil garimpeiros em 2019, durante o governo de Jair Bolsonaro, que desencadeou uma crise humanitária. Poucos anos depois, a combinação do monitoramento por drones com operações de desintrusão empreendidas pelo governo Lula reduziu em 91% as áreas de extração de ouro na Terra Indígena Yanomami.
Como mulheres Bakairi revolucionaram o combate aos incêndios no Cerrado
O som lembrava chuva chegando — só que era fogo. Foi assim que os Bakairi descreveram o incêndio de 2018 que devastou parte de seu território em Mato Grosso, enquanto aguardavam socorro. Da tragédia nasceu uma brigada voluntária hoje formada, em sua maioria, por mulheres — de adolescentes a avós —, treinada por um bombeiro aposentado. O resultado: quatro anos seguidos sem grandes incêndios na Terra Indígena Santana. A poucos quilômetros dali, outro povo sem essa mesma estrutura viveu o oposto — prova de que, no Cerrado, ter ou não uma brigada pode ser uma questão de sobrevivência.
Povo Pataxó restaura áreas degradadas para formar corredor ecológico no sul da Bahia
No litoral onde os portugueses avistaram o Brasil pela primeira vez, uma cooperativa Pataxó passou quatro anos replantando o pau-brasil e mais uma centena de espécies endêmicas da Mata Atlântica. Foram 210 hectares recuperados no sul da Bahia, em áreas da Terra Indígena Barra Velha do Monte Pascoal, metade deles com financiamento inédito do BNDES para sistemas agroflorestais — um raro caso de dinheiro público chegando a um projeto pequeno e indígena. Por trás desse avanço, porém, há uma luta: dos 50 mil hectares já demarcados para os Pataxó ali, apenas 9 mil estão, de fato, em suas mãos.
Guerreiras da Amazônia mostram que igualdade de gênero e conservação da floresta andam de mãos dadas
Na Terra Indígena Caru, no Maranhão, as Guerreiras da Floresta combinam patrulhas com mapas e drones com um trabalho de educação nas escolas e nos povoados vizinhos, buscando reduzir as invasões e a exploração ilegal de madeira. Formado em 2014 por mulheres Guajajara, o grupo complementa a atuação dos Guardiões da Floresta num território de 173 mil hectares que abriga também os Awá-Guajá e conserva um dos últimos trechos contínuos de floresta amazônica no estado. Os números comprovam seu esforço: o desmatamento na Terra Indígena Caru caiu de 2 mil para 63 hectares em apenas dois anos.
Projeto de gestão indígena pode ajudar a conservar a onça-pintada
Lançado em 2025, o projeto Ywy Ipuranguete prevê apoio à gestão de quinze terras indígenas, abrangendo cerca de 6 milhões de hectares em cinco biomas brasileiros. A iniciativa reúne monitoramento territorial, restauração e atividades produtivas, com potencial para beneficiar a onça-pintada ao proteger seus habitats e presas. Na Terra Indígena Caramuru-Paraguassu, na Bahia, lar do povo Pataxó Hã-Hã-Hãe, lideranças relatam que o maior felino das Américas voltou a aparecer após a retomada de antigas fazendas e a regeneração da vegetação.
Imagem do banner: Joalson Maxakali, agente florestal do projeto Hãmhi na Terra Indígena Maxakali (MG). Foto: Xavier Bartaburu.

title: El maestro que hizo de Iberoamérica y Europa una casa común
content:
El maestro que hizo de Iberoamérica y Europa una casa común
Tras ocho años al frente de la Organización de Estados Iberoamericanos (OEI), el educador español Mariano Jabonero deja este diciembre una institución convertida en una red de cooperación “muy americana”, con 23 países integrantes, más de 600 proyectos anuales, millones de beneficiarios y reconocida con el Premio Princesa de Asturias. Su última batalla es también una idea política: América Latina no es la periferia de Occidente, sino una de sus partes esenciales
En El Salvador, país que por entonces lloraba las 80.000 almas que se había tragado su guerra civil, se le acercó un día un campesino:
—Gracias por enseñarme a usar el ordenador.
Mariano Jabonero (San Martín de Valdeiglesias, Madrid, 1953), que llevaba desde 1984 asistiendo al Gobierno en tareas de cooperación con Latinoamérica, había recibido el encargo de capitanear un proyecto de cooperación con apoyo español en el plan de paz y reconstrucción institucional allí. Extrañado, miró al hombre que tenía a su frente y le respondió:
—Disculpe, pero no hemos entregado ordenadores.
—Este es mi portátil —indicó el campesino, sacando del bolsillo un bolígrafo— Ahora sé escribir y contar. Ya no volverán a engañarme.
La anécdota es de 1992, pero la moraleja sigue igual de vigente: “En los países con alta alfabetización, los ingresos per cápita se duplican. Es el primer paso para una sociedad libre”, explica Jabonero, sentado en la sala de reuniones de la sede de la Organización de Estados Iberoamericanos (OEI) de Madrid, ahora que se despide, tras ocho años, de su cargo de secretario general. Lo que sigue es el balance de lo logrado en ese período por parte de quien, antes que ninguna otra cosa, se reclama “maestro”. Resuena con gravedad el sustantivo cuando lo pronuncia, acarrea su voz el orgullo del verdadero sentimiento de pertenencia. Porque en cuarenta años no ha cambiado su convencimiento de que es en el aula, entre pupitres y pizarras, donde se construye ciudadanía; de que el diálogo y la democracia se aprenden.
Un repaso a la labor de ocho años
Acción siempre sobre el terreno
La Organización de Estados Iberoamericanos (OEI) es la mayor red multilateral de cooperación en la región, con 23 Estados miembro. En la imagen, una actividad de la Noche Iberoamericana de l@s Investigador@s, celebrada en Montevideo (Uruguay) en 2023
Fotos: Cedidas por OEI
Trabajando por el futuro
Uno de sus principales ámbitos de actuación es la educación, entendida también como la formación que dará futuro y empleo a los beneficiarios de estos programas. En la imagen, una alumna de la Escuela Taller de Asunción (Paraguay), impulsada por la OEI en colaboración con la Agencia Española de Cooperación Internacional para el Desarrollo (AECID)
Más científicas iberoamericanas
La igualdad de oportunidades y la inclusión de la mujer en el ámbito de la investigación y la ciencia es uno de los grandes retos regionales en Iberoamérica, y como tal tratan de afrontarlo los proyectos de la OEI. En la fotografía, un instante del programa Mujeres en ciencia celebrada en 2023 en Montevideo (Uruguay)
Energía limpia (y justa)
La sostenibilidad y la suficiencia energética son un desafío de presente y futuro, como señala Jabonero. Con financiación europea, la OEI desarrolló el proyecto Energytran para impulsar una transición justa y limpia entre Europa y América Latina. La imagen corresponde a una instalación de placas fotovoltaicas en Ciudad de México, en 2024
COP30 (Brasil)
Uno de los grandes hitos recientes fue la organización por parte de la OEI, en colaboración con el Gobierno de Brasil, de la COP30, la cumbre anual de Naciones Unidas sobre el cambio climático, celebrada en noviembre de 2025 en Belém (Brasil), en la que se adoptaron 56 decisiones consensuadas, incluida una hoja de ruta para el abandono del uso de los combustibles fósiles. Reunió a más de 300.000 asistentes: el mayor proyecto organizado en la Amazonia
Alfabetización, la base
Los tres ejes principales de actuación de los proyectos de la OEI son la educación, la ciencia y la cultura. Pero, para todos, el primer paso fue el lograr que Iberoamérica sea una región con un 98% de alfabetización. En Honduras (en la imagen), la OEI contribuyó a la declaración del país como “Territorio libre de analfabetismo” en 2025
Un balance inmaculado
Durante los último ocho años, el periodo durante el que el pedagogo Mariano Jabonero ha estado al frente de la secretaría general de la OEI, la institución ha puesto en marcha 2.500 proyectos en los 23 países integrantes, que han impactado en la vida de un total de 22 millones de personas. “Nuestro equipo está formado por excelentes profesionales, actuamos con transparencia y autonomía. Tenemos un enorme arraigo y, sobre todo, logramos que la cooperación suceda, lo que hace que todos los países y beneficiarios confíen en nosotros”, explica Jabonero
Este diciembre deja Jabonero una OEI que, alejada del papel asistencial y burocrático que pudo tener en sus comienzos (se creó en 1949), se ha convertido en un bien público regional de utilidad indiscutida, que, bajo su gestión, ha impulsado más de 600 proyectos anuales en educación, ciencia, cultura y educación en derechos humanos y democracia para más de 22 millones de beneficiarios, una organización de gestión transparente (“podemos rastrear en directo adónde ha ido el dinero de una factura pagada en Honduras”) que trabaja sobre el terreno en los 23 países que la integran; una OEI, remarca Jabonero, “muy americana, pero sin injerencia ni un solo dólar de EE UU”. “Al principio la financiación procedía sobre todo de España. Ahora el porcentaje de aporte español es mínimo. Hemos logrado que se entienda como un invento de la región y para la región”.
Un profesor filósofo forjado en la Transición
Jabonero nació en un pueblo del suroeste de Madrid y su juventud es la de quien, frente a los estertores represivos y violentos de la dictadura de Franco, anhelaba “la llegada de un régimen de libertades y tolerancia”. Fue su conciencia social la que, en un tiempo tan efervescente, lo condujo hacia los estudios de Filosofía y Ciencias de la Educación.
“Recuerdo la publicación del primer número de EL PAÍS, en mayo de 1976. Lo compré en un quiosco en Campamento [barrio del distrito La Latina de Madrid donde se asentaban cuarteles de militares y guardias civiles]. Mi primer destino como maestro fue allí cerca, en un colegio público de Aluche”. Para entonces, Jabonero ya había viajado a Francia, y a su regreso la mitad de la carga clandestina de su mochila eran libros aquí prohibidos: “La poesía española censurada o a pensadores como Paulo Freire los leí en panfletos ciclostilados”.
Repite una cita célebre, atribuida a uno de los padres de esta Europa nuestra, Jean Monnet: “Si tuviera que volver a empezar [a construir la Unión Europea, se refiere], empezaría por la cultura”. Pedagogía, educación y sociología son para Jabonero caras del mismo cubo. A finales de los años 70, obtuvo, frente a 850 candidatos, una de las 18 plazas a inspector de Educación, momento en que descubrió lo que realmente entrañaba el derecho a la educación, la enorme responsabilidad sobre sus hombros: “el sistema, las políticas públicas, tienen que lograr que el alumnado pueda sentarse en el aula y aprender lengua o matemáticas en condiciones óptimas; y eso incluye desde la rehabilitación de escuelas rurales que no tenían ni baños ni agua corriente en aquel tiempo hasta la garantía de que esos niños y niñas hubieran podido desayunar en casa antes de venir al colegio”.
No podemos perder de vista el valor de la Educación como elemento corrector de las desigualdades de cuna, esa fe democrática que hoy Jabonero observa a su alrededor “tristemente cansada, agotada”, expresa, tomando las palabras del filósofo germano-coreano Byung-Chul Han. Los siguientes pasos, como en un destino inexorable, fueron los que modelaron al pedagogo indispensable que Jabonero es hoy: pasó por el Ministerio de Educación, llegaron El Salvador, Argentina, Colombia y la cooperación —la literatura del bum fue su llave hacia eso que a Martín Caparrós le gusta llamar Ñamérica—, dio clase en la Complutense, trabajó para Unesco, dirigió la Fundación Santillana, ejerció de consultor para gobiernos de todo el continente… hasta que en 2018 y por unanimidad fue elegido, durante dos mandatos, secretario general de la OEI.
Sentirse en casa: por qué Iberoamérica es Occidente
Cola de un cine. En París o en Berlín. Si, entre el tumulto de voces, Jabonero oye la suave cadencia del colombiano o el marcado deje del español caribeño dice que no puede evitar girarse y trabar conversación. “He vivido en muchos países de Iberoamérica y siempre me he sentido en casa”. Le apena la concepción errada que todavía, dice, se tiene en España de los vecinos del otro lado del Atlántico: “Respecto de la tierra de dictaduras, guerras y pobreza que pervive en cierto imaginario, el cambio ha sido brutal: 98% de alfabetización, es la zona donde más ha crecido la matriculación en estudios superiores, 33 millones de estudiantes, en el 70% de los casos de familias donde los progenitores no pasaron por la universidad”.
Todavía pesan la inequidad o sus economías, demasiado dependientes de la venta de materias primas: “El litio boliviano está en manos de empresas chinas; el cobre se produce en Chile y Perú, pero se cotiza en Estados Unidos; las flores ecuatorianas se venden en Ámsterdam”. Pero están, cuenta, “a un salto de constituirse en verdaderas sociedades de conocimiento, como lo son las más competitivas”.
Entre los hablantes de español y portugués —esta última, la lengua cuyo uso más crece en África— sumamos 850 millones de personas en el mundo. Se trata de un potencial incontestable, que motiva el alegato que quiere lanzar “sin caer en demasiada retórica”: por lengua, por historia, por derecho, por cultura, por religión “América Latina no es la periferia de Occidente, sino una parte más de su núcleo”.
Reputación y futuro
¿Qué méritos motivan un galardón como el Princesa de Asturias de Cooperación Internacional de 2024 o el premio Anna Frank del pasado marzo? ¿Cómo navega la OEI para que gobiernos de todos los colores la valoren por igual en sus 77 años de acción? “Hemos sabido estar a la altura de las circunstancias”, responde Jabonero. Y enumera algunos ejemplos de por qué sus proyectos de cooperación han generado un inmensurable impacto en la zona: fue, por ejemplo, un costarricense becado por la OEI para doctorarse en la Universidad de Sevilla quien redactó la Ley de Cuidados de su país.
Durante la pandemia, unos 180 millones de estudiantes latinoamericanos quedaron excluidos de las aulas y aproximadamente la mitad no tenía una conexión a internet suficiente. La OEI produjo entonces cientos de contenidos digitales, ayudó a los sistemas educativos nacionales a mantener la actividad y concedió miles de becas para formar a profesores universitarios que hasta entonces trabajaban casi exclusivamente con cuaderno y tiza. En una de las escenas más insólitas de aquel periodo, programas educativos de televisión mexicanos llegaron a emitirse en Guinea Ecuatorial.
Si la democracia se tambalea, hará falta más democracia y más consenso. Eso defiende a capa y espada Jabonero para un futuro en el que identifica varios desafíos que no admiten complacencia: la transición digital —una tecnología al servicio de todos—, la transición verde —nuevas y sostenibles fuentes de energía que no subyuguen a los habitantes del Sur Global— y, sobre todo, una transición justa, sin perdedores, imposible si no se recupera esa vieja e inquebrantable fe en la Educación. Cómo no va a creer en su poder este maestro que vio cómo un campesino podía cambiar su mundo con un boli.

title: Barcelona, una ciudad que educa más allá del aula
content:
CIUDAD EDUCADORA
Barcelona, una ciudad que
educa más allá del aula
La capital catalana consolida un modelo de Ciudad Educadora que extiende el aprendizaje a los barrios e implica equipamientos, entidades y ciudadanía en la construcción de una Barcelona más equitativa, sostenible y cohesionada
Un sábado por la mañana, un patio escolar abierto se transforma en un espacio de juego y encuentro. Familias que no se conocían comparten espacio, criaturas que no van a la misma escuela juegan juntas y el barrio gana un punto de convivencia. En otro rincón de la ciudad, niños, niñas y adolescentes participan en actividades culturales, artísticas o deportivas fuera del horario lectivo. Son escenas que responden a una misma idea: en Barcelona, educar va mucho más allá de la escuela.
La ciudad trabaja con esta mirada desde 1990, cuando firmó la Carta de Ciudades Educadoras. Más de tres décadas después, el modelo afronta una etapa de consolidación y actualización. "La educación es una tarea compartida por toda la ciudad", explica Pilar Lleonart, responsable de Ciudad Educadora. Calles, plazas, equipamientos culturales y deportivos, entidades y vecindario tienen, desde esta perspectiva, una función educativa.
De la idea al barrio
El reto es convertir estos principios en actuaciones tangibles. Una de las más visibles es Transformem els Patis, que convierte los espacios escolares en entornos más verdes, inclusivos, coeducativos y abiertos al barrio. Actualmente se han realizado 79 transformaciones, 48 de las cuales cumplen los requisitos de refugio climático.
La transformación no es solo física. Infancia, profesorado, familias, entidades y vecindario participan en el proceso de definición de los espacios. La misma concepción hay detrás del programa Patis Oberts, que pone los espacios escolares a disposición de la ciudadanía los fines de semana y durante periodos de vacaciones. La ciudad dispone actualmente de 66 patios abiertos distribuidos por los diez distritos. La escuela deja así de ser un recinto que cierra cuando acaba el horario lectivo y se convierte en un equipamiento del barrio.
Los programas, en cifras
Que el código postal no marque
La equidad es otro gran eje del modelo. El programa Tardes Educatives nació después de detectar que las oportunidades fuera del horario escolar variaban mucho según el territorio. En algunos barrios predominaban actividades como el refuerzo escolar o el fútbol, mientras que el acceso a propuestas artísticas, culturales o científicas era menor. El programa busca ampliar esta oferta y eliminar barreras económicas. Los últimos datos sitúan la actividad en 2.035 propuestas con 222 entidades participantes, acompañadas de ayudas y becas. "Lo que queremos es que el código postal no implique que puedas hacer unas determinadas actividades y dejes de hacer otras", explica Lleonart.
La Xarxa Educació i Ciutat, que articula la colaboración entre administración, centros educativos y entidades, amplía todavía más este ecosistema: el curso pasado ofreció 2.260 propuestas educativas y 42.970 plazas de equidad (gratuitas), con la participación de 146 entidades. Las actividades pasan, además, por una evaluación de calidad pedagógica. "La ciudad educa si todo el mundo facilita recursos que lleguen a todos", remarca.
La mirada abarca todas las edades. Por ejemplo, el Espai de Joc 0-99, que ofrece propuestas lúdicas y educativas para todas las edades, ha recibido durante el curso 2025-2026 más de 35.000 usuarios y promueve el juego intergeneracional, mientras que la Escola Municipal de Segones Oportunitats acompaña a jóvenes que han quedado fuera de los itinerarios formativos ordinarios para que puedan retomar su recorrido educativo y laboral.
Una estrategia de ciudad
Barcelona Ciudad Educadora no es una política exclusiva de la Direcció d'Educació ni de una única institución. Es una estrategia de ciudad compartida que implica al conjunto de las administraciones y agentes educativos, con un papel destacado del Consorci d'Educació de Barcelona, y también de los ámbitos de urbanismo, cultura, deportes, salud, derechos sociales y movilidad.
Esta mirada se hace especialmente visible ante la emergencia climática con programas como el Pla Clima Escola Barcelona, que en 2029 habrá climatizado con energía renovable 170 escuelas, o Transformem els Patis, con más árboles, sombra, agua o biodiversidad para mejorar el confort, pero también para educar en sostenibilidad.
Los programas, en cifras
"El gran reto hoy es pasar de una idea inspiradora a una estrategia operativa, capaz de traducir sus principios en acciones concretas y visibles en los barrios. En definitiva, se trata de hacer de la educación un proyecto colectivo de ciudad que la ciudadanía pueda reconocer, vivir y sentir como propio", resume Pilar Lleonart.
"La 'escola bressol' no es solo cuidar: es educación desde el primer día"
Barcelona consolida un modelo de Ciudad Educadora que extiende el aprendizaje a los barrios e implica equipamientos, entidades y ciudadanía en la construcción de una Barcelona más equitativa, sostenible y cohesionada
La capital catalana continúa ampliando la red de escoles bressol municipales. Este curso, la ciudad cuenta con 106 centros y unas 9.000 plazas de 0 a 3 años, después de la apertura de la EBM Tramuntana, en Sant Andreu de Palomar, y de la ampliación de la EBM La Mar, en la Barceloneta, con dos nuevos grupos. Además, hay diversos proyectos que se encuentran en diferentes fases de desarrollo.
Crear más plazas es solo una parte del reto. La otra es decidir dónde hacen más falta. Para planificar la ampliación de la red, el Ayuntamiento, a través del Instituto Municipal de Educación (IMEB), analiza la situación de los 73 barrios de la ciudad a partir de indicadores como: número de niños empadronados, demanda no atendida, nuevas promociones de vivienda, oferta privada, niveles de renta o vulnerabilidad de las familias. "Esto nos permite ordenar los 73 barrios y definir cuál es la prioridad de necesidad de escuela infantil", explica Alícia Aguilera, gerente del Instituto Municipal de Educación de Barcelona (IMEB).
Nuevas 'escoles bressol' y ampliaciones

El modelo conecta directamente con la idea de Barcelona Ciudad Educadora. La escuela infantil no funciona de manera aislada, sino en relación con los servicios sociales, culturales y de salud y con el conjunto del barrio. Las familias también tienen un papel central. Participan en las asociaciones de familias o el consejo educativo de la escuela, y se pueden organizar también para hacer uso del patio una vez acabada la jornada (Pati en família); lo hacen un 75% de las escuelas. "Se promueve que las familias formen parte de los espacios participativos donde se toman decisiones en el ámbito comunitario y también se organicen para hacer actividades con sus hijos e hijas después del horario escolar", indica Aguilera.
Igualdad de oportunidades
Dos aspectos muy presentes en la red son la inclusión y la igualdad de oportunidades. En este sentido, las escuelas infantiles disponen de plazas reservadas para niños con necesidades educativas específicas y también para los que se encuentran en situación de vulnerabilidad y/o exclusión social. La red dispone de un equipo de educación inclusiva y trabaja con servicios sociales y servicios especializados.
La red de escoles bressol municipales de Barcelona afronta los próximos años con tres prioridades alineadas con la Garantía Infantil Europea: garantizar la equidad, reforzar la calidad educativa y ampliar la accesibilidad. También es prioritario avanzar en la ampliación de plazas públicas para que todas las familias que las necesiten puedan acceder a ellas. Para el IMEB, el papel de las escoles bressol y de los espacios familiares es clave para el bienestar de la infancia y la igualdad de oportunidades.
