title: De la sabiduría lunar al Whatsapp: la información climática que salvó las cosechas de los agricultores ecuatorianos
content:
- En Ecuador, más de 15 000 agricultores usan los boletines climáticos didácticos para planificar sus siembras y sus cosechas.
- Entre 2022 y 2025, el Instituto Nacional de Meteorología e Hidrología del Ecuador (Inamhi) pasó de emitir 51 advertencias climáticas a 70, confirmando que los cambios en el clima van en aumento.
- La información climática permite prevenir y gestionar el riesgo de desastres y tomar mejores decisiones en agricultura para garantizar la seguridad alimentaria.
- Nuna, un chatbot, ha abierto las opciones de compartir con agricultores de la provincia de Imbabura información climática más allá de las predicciones meteorológicas.
El domingo, Evita Tupiza, la señora que tiene las vacas, la que hace el queso y lo vende el domingo en el mercado de San Blas, en la provincia de Imbabura, le dijo a Gladys Flores que el boletín meteorológico que recibe por WhatsApp la está ayudando a decidir si ordeña o no en las madrugadas. Este no es un asunto trivial para Tupiza: hacerlo bajo el sol fuerte, daña la leche y después no puede producir quesos. Saber con tiempo si va a llover o si habrá altas temperaturas, también le ayuda a prever lugares de sombra para dejar sus vacas en las mañanas.
Hasta hace diez años, quizá cinco, a Evita Tupiza le hubiese bastado con mirar a la luna. En San Blas, una parroquia rural de alrededor de 5000 personas, los agricultores se manejaban a través de “cabañuelas”, cálculos ancestrales en que, observando las variaciones atmosféricas de los primeros días del mes de enero, podían pronosticar el tiempo de los próximos doce meses. Los que sabían leer, acudirían al almanaque Bristol, ese famoso folleto naranja con el doctor Cyrenius Charles Bristol en la portada llevando un traje de hace casi dos siglos. Esta revista que se imprime ininterrumpidamente desde 1832, trae predicciones astronómicas, astrológicas, el calendario lunar y consejos para la siembra
Sin embargo, ahora ni las cabañuelas, ni el almanaque, ni la luna aciertan en sus predicciones del clima, según manifiestan con desconcierto los agricultores de San Blas.
Leer más |Santa Martha: una comunidad cacataibo de Perú cercada por el narcotráfico y el recorte territorial
Como Gaby Flores y Evita Tupiza, alrededor de 15 000 agricultores en Ecuador ―según un informe del Programa Mundial de Alimentos― han mejorado, potenciado o salvado sus cosechas, su tierra y sus animales, gracias a los boletines meteorológicos que líderes comunitarios, servidores públicos de las prefecturas y comuneros capacitados, comparten en los grupos de WhatsApp.
Como una especie de guardianes del clima, estas personas masifican informes que, de manera digerible, explican los datos que el Instituto Nacional de Meteorología e Hidrología del Ecuador (Inamhi) produce en tiempo real. Esto es un asunto vital para los ecuatorianos ya que en los últimos cinco años los eventos climáticos extremos han ido en aumento. Entre 2022 y 2025, el Inamhi pasó de emitir 51 advertencias climáticas a 70.
Información y buenas decisiones
La frontera de Ecuador y Colombia fue el punto de partida de un proyecto ambicioso de adaptación climática incentivado por el Programa Mundial de Alimentos (WFP por sus siglas en inglés) en coordinación con gobiernos locales y otras instituciones públicas. Inició en 2018 con el objetivo de fortalecer las capacidades adaptativas alrededor de las dos cuencas hidrográficas que cruzan y unen los dos países, la Mira-Mataje y la Guáitara-Carchi.
Estas zonas incluyen dos departamentos colombianos y cuatro provincias ecuatorianas con población mayoritariamente indígena y afrodescendiente asentadas en cinco ecosistemas frágiles: manglares, bosques secos, bosques tropicales húmedos, bosques nublados y matorrales; que ya venían sufriendo las variabilidades climáticas del calentamiento global.
Durante seis años se realizaron decenas de colaboraciones estratégicas. Formación a líderes comunitarios, especialmente mujeres, en procesos participativos de 97 comunidades afrodescendientes y 76 comunidades indígenas Awá. Se instalaron 30 equipos meteorológicos, se coordinaron encuentros binacionales, se realizaron rescates de saberes ancestrales, se documentaron más de 350 especies de plantas nativas o tradicionales con atributos nutricionales y nueve boletines climáticos comenzaron a circular entre las 24 000 personas que participaron en las capacitaciones sobre cambio climático. Pasaron una pandemia, el aumento de la violencia en Ecuador, la presencia de grupos armados en la frontera con Colombia y, sin embargo, desde 2024 se comenzaron a ver los frutos que parten de un empoderamiento social de los datos científicos.
“Si tú no tienes información, no vas a poder tomar buenas decisiones, vas a estar corriendo en círculos porque no sabes a qué te estás enfrentando, a qué amenaza y en qué nivel de exposición estás”, dice Diego Guzmán, oficial de cambio climático y sistemas agroalimentarios de WPF. La idea aplica a varios aspectos de la vida, pero Guzmán se refiere a los factores climáticos que perturban, en mayor medida, a comunidades no preparadas para asumir los nuevos escenarios ecológicos.
Esto lo corroboran dos técnicos sentados en una oficina austera de muros cremas del segundo piso del edificio de la prefectura de Imbabura.
Edison Marcial y Vinicio Fuentes asistieron a varias de las capacitaciones de sistemas de manejo de datos meteorológicos que dictaron especialistas del Inamhi. Les explicaron lo más complicado y teórico de los procesos científicos de la meteorología: qué satélites se usan, cómo hacen las agencias nacionales los pronósticos del tiempo, qué son los modelos matemáticos de predicción, las plataformas digitales en las que se procesan los datos, los mapas de color y el monitoreo en tiempo real en el Visor Hidrometeorológico Nacional.
“Es de acceso público toda la información”, dice Edison Marcial, mientras muestra una imagen en su teléfono celular: un mapa de la provincia de Imbabura con unos aros de colores, en la gama del verde al rojo. “El Inamhi te manda así, la imagen en bruto”.
El WPF hizo que personal del propio Inamhi capacitara a dos funcionarios de cada provincia en Ecuador y departamento en Colombia. El objetivo era que los técnicos locales entendieran los modelos de predicción oficiales y los tradujeran de tal manera que cualquier persona los pudiera interpretar. Fue así que la primera parte del proyecto de creación de boletines climáticos, en 2024, dio como resultado nueve boletines (entre semanales y diarios) que llegaron a compartirse entre 15 000 agricultores de los dos países.
Los primeros boletines salvaron las cosechas
En 2024, Ecuador rompió los récord de temperaturas altas con sequías extremas: más de 80 000 hectáreas quemadas y una grave crisis energética, según datos de la Secretaría Nacional de Riesgos. Ese mismo año, los boletines meteorológicos didácticos comenzaron a circular cada tres días, en las provincias de Carchi, Imbabura, Esmeraldas y Sucumbíos. Se trataba de una imagen con el mapa de la provincia y la intensidad de las lluvias. Una leyenda de seis colores que variaba desde el rojo (que significa lluvias intensas) y el verde en el medio (señal de lluvia moderada), hasta llegar al blanco que indica ausencia total de lluvia. A un costado se mostraban las temperaturas máximas y mínimas.
Esto evitó pérdidas en la zona del Valle del Chota y en la zona de Urcuquí, en la Provincia de Imbabura, donde está el terreno familiar de Gladys Flores, hija, nieta y bisnieta de campesinos.
“Cuando era pequeña, mi bisabuela me contaba que sus padres también fueron agricultores en este mismo terreno”, dice Flores mientras recorre sus sembríos, mostrándolos con orgullo. Es la quinta generación que trabaja esa tierra.
En su casa de ladrillos, madera y techo de Eternit, ella y su esposo, César Vinueza, comparten una limonada y sus experiencias en el campo. Cuentan que el agua que riega sus productos es muy limpia porque viene cinco kilómetros arriba del río Warmiyaku, dónde está la captación.
“Esa piscina de captación y la acequia [canal artificial a cielo abierto] es de antes de la venida de los españoles. Es muy antigua”, comenta Flores.“Mi papá sabía con exactitud cuándo venía el verano y la época seca. Ahora llueve cuando no es de llover. Encima, el caudal del río ha bajado bastante. Antes no podíamos controlar la fuerza del agua cuando nos tocaba el turno del riego. Ahora baja poquito. Toca estar yendo a ver qué pasa en la captación y que todo esté bien”.
Leer más | Día Internacional de los Primates: tres proyectos para salvarlos del tráfico y la pérdida de hábitat
Con menos agua de riego y más sequía, Flores, su esposo y todo el pueblo de San Blas están “cosechando agua”, es decir, llenan unos tanques enormes de plástico que recuperan el agua cuando llueve.
“En 2024 vino fuerte la sequía. Nos tocó hacer turnos con las demás compañeras. Cada 15 días recibimos el agua de la acequia para regar nuestros terrenos. Justo en ese tiempo llegaron los boletines y, viendo en las fotos que iba a estar seca la época que normalmente era de lluvia, atrasamos el cultivo del fréjol. Gracias a esas cartillas no perdimos tanto de nuestro trabajo”, recuerda Gladys Flores.
César Vinueza, el esposo de Gladys, cuenta que la casa en la que viven fue construida para un lugar frío, cerca a los páramos que es donde se asienta San Blas. Sin embargo, el calor actual es tan fuerte que el techo que tenía que guardar el calor, ahora lo acumula de tal manera que tienen que hacer ciertos cambios. “Estoy preocupado, nunca me imaginé que el Eternit fuera tan caliente. A la una de la tarde es insoportable, por eso voy a arreglar esas dos ventanas para que entre el aire directo, como casa de la costa”.
Todos ríen.
Flores y Vinueza se juntaron con otras mujeres agricultoras para crear la asociación agropecuaria “Frutos de mi Tierra”. Casi llegan a los 10 años llevando sus productos a la feria del pueblo los domingos y los miércoles en la Universidad Yachay.
Leer más | Eric Terena, el DJ indígena que denuncia el silenciamiento de la Amazonía | ENTREVISTA
“Nuestro principal orgullo es que hemos eliminado a los intermediarios, de aquí salen los productos directo a los compradores”, dice Vinueza.
Gladys Flores administra el grupo de WhatsApp de la asociación y es la encargada de compartir, cada tres días, el boletín climático que la prefectura de Imbabura le envía a ella.
Desde que se dieron cuenta que con esa información pudieron evitar una siembra de fréjol que se perdería por la sequía inesperada de 2024, las mujeres de Frutos de mi Tierra son acérrimas usuarias del boletín que, en dos años, tuvo una cadena de innovaciones que superó las expectativas de los propios organismos estatales y de cooperación internacional que iniciaron el proyecto en 2018.
Flores cuenta que gracias a los videos que reciben con los pronósticos y las alertas climáticas, las mujeres campesinas que no saben leer y escribir ya no tienen que mostrar la infografía colorida a sus hijos o nietos para que confirmen lo que ellas ven en colores, sino que con el audio ya “entienden todito”. Y que esa información, como le dijo Evita Tupiza, le ha permitido planificar el ordeño de sus vacas para la producción de los quesos.
El aficionado al arte que prepara a los agricultores
Vinicio Fuentes es agrónomo y tiene un máster en sistemas de información geográfica, pero habla como productor de televisión o creador de contenidos.
Sentado frente a su computadora, busca emocionado los primeros videos que creó a partir de los pronósticos oficiales del Inamhi. Fuentes no se conformó con mandar el boletín de colores y fue más allá. Primero, le puso voz y animó la imagen. De inmediato se dio cuenta que los agricultores comenzaron a estar pendientes de la información.
“Lo que siempre estoy pensando es: ¿cómo hago digeribles todos estos datos? Por suerte han tenido la paciencia de permitirme la prueba y el error”, cuenta Fuentes con una sonrisa disimulada que muestra cómo disfruta de su trabajo.
Uno de los problemas más frecuentes que enfrentó en sus procesos de comunicación era que la persona que hacía las locuciones no estaba siempre disponible para cuando el boletín climático comenzó a ser un ritual. Entonces Fuentes probó con una voz de inteligencia artificial. Esto fue un éxito porque le permitió hacer más eficiente la producción de los boletines cada tres días. Con el tiempo, y con las pruebas, también se dio cuenta que los videos debían ser más cortos para que no fueran “tan pesados” y los usuarios pudieran abrirlos desde sus teléfonos.
“Lo que la gente necesita saber es si va a llover o no”, dice con la seguridad de la experiencia, Edison Marcial, quien fue parte del Programa Mundial de Alimentos antes de trabajar en la prefectura de Imbabura. Asegura ser testigo de cómo el interés de Vinicio Fuentes y sus ganas de mejorar los boletines hicieron que Imbabura fuera pionera de iniciativas mucho más ambiciosas como “Nuna”, el chatbot, o la Granja Digital, una plataforma con datos públicos y accesibles con los cuales los productores de Imbabura pueden consultar información sobre sus predios, la fertilidad de sus suelos y buenas prácticas agrícolas.
“Vimos que WhatsApp es uno de los medios masivos de comunicación entre las comunidades agrícolas”, comenta Fuentes mientras conecta su computadora a una pantalla gigante en la oficina de uno de sus jefes para mostrar cómo funciona el chatbot que creó.
Con un grupo de creativos dieron vida a un personaje que suma todas las características culturales de los diferentes pueblos de Imbabura. Se llama Nuna y significa “alma” o “energía vital” en kichwa. Tiene la máscara tradicional de diablo huma pero con plumas de los colibríes que existen en los diferentes cantones de la provincia.
“La idea fue tener un chat en el que puedes hacer consultas continuamente y ya no ser un usuario pasivo que recibe los boletines”, dice Fuentes con orgullo.
En la pantalla se abre la conversación. ¡Hola, soy Nuna, tu asistente virtual de la Prefectura de Imbabura, gracias por tu mensaje! Nuna abre una serie de opciones: Geoparque Imbabura, Clima, Ferias Productoras, Rutas Turísticas, Novedades, Smartfarm y Servicios Mecánicos.
“Aprovechamos que tenemos toda esta lógica de comunicación a partir del boletín climático, que fue el inicio de esto, para potenciar y difundir toda la información que tenemos como Prefectura”, explica Fuentes.
Al dar click a la opción “Clima”, Nuna comparte el video del boletín agroclimático de Imbabura, las advertencias meteorológicas nacionales del Inamhi (información adicional sobre eventos intensos de lluvias o sequías) y el calendario lunar, como una forma de incluir y respetar la diversidad cultural.
Desde el 1 de enero al 31 de mayo de 2026, el Inamhi había registrado 2026 eventos adversos como inundaciones, deslizamientos y aluviones.
Leer más | Antártida: cierran la pesquería de kril por sobrepesca y crece la alerta por sus impactos
El aprendizaje se aprovecha y se comparte en cadena
Esta nueva forma de entregar información climática está llegando a todo el país. El 4 de junio de 2026, PWF, Inamhi, Ministerio de Ambiente y Energía y representantes de las prefecturas de Imbabura y Manabí ―provincia ecuatoriana costera que sufre inundaciones continuas― se reunieron en la Capilla del Hombre, en Quito. Era el lanzamiento oficial de los boletines nacionales del Inamhi. “De la información climática a la acción territorial” se llamó el evento
Vinicio Fuentes, muy tímido, parado al fondo de la sala con los brazos echados para atrás, escuchaba las intervenciones de las autoridades, de los científicos y el testimonio de Juan De Mera Centeno, agricultor de la asociación Raíces Manabas que produce principalmente arroz, verduras, hortalizas y frutas en Manabí. “Al tener acceso a esta información optimizamos tiempo y recursos. Por ejemplo, para el trasplante de una semilla, si sabemos que va a llover, ponemos en pausa el trabajo porque inundado el suelo, todo se pierde”, dice el campesino de la costa ecuatoriana.
Manabí es la segunda provincia que hace los boletines meteorológicos con video para alrededor de 9000 agricultores.
“No fue fácil motivar a la prefectura de Manabí para que haga los boletines metereológicos”, confiesa Diego Guzmán de PWF. “Allá no creen, o no creían―Guzmán suelta una risa― en la cooperación internacional”.
Fue entonces cuando invitaron a Vinicio Fuentes a la Prefectura de la provincia costera. Él contó su experiencia a Jairo Moreira, su par, el encargado de compartir la información que recibe del Inamhi a las diferentes organizaciones de agricultores de Manabí.
“El PWF nos dio el equipamiento, un ordenador con un programa de edición de video. El Inamhi nos capacitó para interpretar los datos y los mapas que nos envían. El ingeniero Vinicio nos enseñó cómo ellos hacen los videos con palabras más sencillas. Así iniciamos la producción de los boletines aquí”, confirma Moreira.
Y pasó algo que no esperaba: los usuarios de Manabí tampoco se pierden un solo boletín. Al igual que en Imbabura, el video corto y didáctico ha hecho que sus agricultores usen esta información como parte de su trabajo. A partir de los boletines toman decisiones sobre sus tierras y sus productos.
Por ejemplo, si ven que va a llover, los productores de cacao no sacan a secar sus semillas. También les ayuda a planificar la época de siembra y de cosecha de productos de ciclo corto.
“Esto lo implementamos en diciembre de 2024 y el testimonio de los agricultores es que, con esta información hacen mucho mejor su trabajo porque pueden adaptarse a las variaciones climáticas”, dice Moreira y agrega que cuando se demoran y no envían el boletín a tiempo, los campesinos usuarios los llaman, los presionan y les preguntan qué pasó con el boletín. “Ha tenido muy buena aceptación. Ahora nos lo piden asociaciones que están fuera de los grupos de la Prefectura. También estudiantes de universidades y otras federaciones de campesinos”.
Ese 4 de junio en La Capilla del Hombre, uno de los complejos arquitectónicos y culturales más importantes de Quito, Matteo Perrone, representante de PWF para Ecuador, dijo a una sala llena que uno de los principales logros del proyecto de adaptación al cambio climático en Ecuador fue la descentralización del conocimiento.
Luego, pasaron un video hecho por los técnicos del Inhami. Tomando la idea de la prefectura de Imbabura, ahora los boletines nacionales también se harán en video con una voz en IA que cuenta lo que significan los colores en el mapa de calor.
Pocos entre la gente del evento saben que el hombre que está de pie al otro lado del escenario, con las manos echadas para atrás, que le gusta tocar guitarra, piano y editar los boletines climáticos en CapCut, es Vinicio Fuentes, quien, con su motivación, logró que se replique la forma de informar y dar herramientas a los agricultores que él inició hace algún tiempo desde Imbabura.

title: Appraising Uba Sani’s Bold Rescue of Kaduna’s Out-of-School Children
content:
Latest Headlines
Appraising Uba Sani’s Bold Rescue of Kaduna’s Out-of-School Children
Abdulkareem Kubau
The truest measure of an education policy is not the elegance of its declarations, but the number of children whose lives it changes. In Kaduna State, Governor Uba Sani has steadily moved education reform from aspiration to measurable action, confronting one of the gravest threats to the state’s future: the exclusion of children from school. His administration has treated the out-of-school crisis neither as an inherited misfortune nor as an insoluble feature of northern Nigeria, but as an emergency demanding money, evidence, competent management and sustained political will.
That seriousness is visible first in the state’s priorities. For three consecutive years, education has received the largest single share of Kaduna’s budget. The sector took 25 per cent in 2024, 26.14 per cent in 2025 and 25 per cent of the N985.9 billion 2026 budget. In a public culture where education is frequently celebrated in speeches but weakened in expenditure, this consistency matters. It has given institutional weight to the administration’s conviction that Kaduna cannot defeat poverty, insecurity, unemployment or social exclusion without first enlarging access to knowledge.
The investment supports a broader architecture of reform. Tuition fees in state-owned tertiary institutions were halved, contributing to an enrolment rise exceeding 200 per cent. The retirement age for teachers moved from 60 to 65, while the state committed to recruiting 2,000 primary school teachers annually. Across the 23 local government areas, thousands of classrooms have been built or renovated and essential facilities, furniture and learning materials provided. School feeding has strengthened retention, while extensive education data capture has improved planning.
Yet the defining strength of the Governor Sani approach is its recognition that improved schools alone cannot solve exclusion. A classroom may exist while the poorest child remains unable to enter it. Tuition may be free while uniforms, books, transport, levies and the loss of a child’s labour place education beyond a family’s means.
In Kaduna’s household mapping, economic constraints accounted for 58.5 per cent of exclusion, and lack of money dominated the reasons given within that category. “Free education” therefore describes a legal entitlement; it does not erase the real price borne by vulnerable households.
This understanding places the Reaching Out-of-School Children Project at the heart of the Governor Sani administration’s education agenda. ROOSC is not a ceremonial programme or isolated donor initiative. It expresses Governor Sani’s determination to find excluded children, understand why each is outside the classroom, remove the barrier and create a pathway into sustained learning. Valued at $62.8 million and operating across all 23 local government areas, the four-year intervention combines state funding with grants and technical support.
Its ambition is substantial. ROOSC aims to enrol 100,000 out-of-school children and benefit 1.2 million learners. It provides for 102 new schools and learning centres, 170 renovations and work on 2,304 classrooms. It will strengthen school-based management committees, train teachers and officers, improve learning outcomes and make schools safer and more inclusive. Civil works have commenced, but the project’s reach extends beyond buildings.
Children who cannot immediately return through conventional schooling are offered flexible routes. Accelerated basic education enables older learners to recover lost years. Integrated Qur’anic and Tsangaya education combines religious instruction with literacy, numeracy and life skills. Catch-up clubs prepare dropouts for re-entry, while radio lessons reach difficult terrain. Vulnerable learners receive materials, girls receive menstrual-health support, and children with disabilities receive assessment and assistive devices. This is reform shaped around the child, not a demand that every child fit one rigid system.
Early results justify the confidence now surrounding ROOSC. More than 26,000 out-of-school children have been enrolled cumulatively, with boys and girls represented in near-equal numbers. Thousands more have been reached through accelerated education, integrated learning, catch-up clubs and radio instruction. Over 1,600 catch-up learners have moved into formal schools, while the first accelerated-learning cohort recorded retention of nearly 85 per cent. Teachers, head teachers and quality-assurance officers have received structured professional development, with recorded competency gains. These are not abstract outputs; they are children restored to possibility and schools acquiring the capacity to keep them there.
The project’s most consequential achievement may be its replacement of estimates with evidence. A statewide enumeration visited 360,319 homes and identified 187,719 out-of-school children aged six to 17, including 106,353 boys and 81,366 girls. Enumerators used digital devices, geofencing and independent checks. The result was a name-and-location map showing where excluded children live and why they are missing school.
That distinction has transformed planning. When the household map is combined with the digital Annual School Census, government can see both sides of the problem: children outside the system and the schools, teachers and classrooms available within it. Kaduna can consequently decide where a new school is essential, where an existing one requires expansion, where teachers are scarce, and where feeding, transport, cash support, community engagement or a flexible calendar will achieve more than another building. Reform becomes precise rather than performative.
The map also dismantles comfortable generalisations. Kaduna North Senatorial Zone carries about half of the identified burden, but exclusion differs sharply among communities. Kubau’s problem is strongly connected to shortages within the education system. In Giwa, farm labour exerts a powerful pull on children. Makarfi requires stronger post-primary and vocational pathways. Soba demands deeper cultural and community engagement, while poverty and displacement weigh heavily in Igabi. A uniform remedy would waste resources; evidence permits the administration to match each barrier with an appropriate response.
Other findings are equally instructive. Nearly two-thirds of excluded children are of primary-school age, proving that intervention must begin at the point of first enrolment. More than 60 per cent have never attended school, while the remainder entered and later dropped out, often during the earliest primary years. These groups require different solutions: mobilisation and first-time access for one, recovery and accelerated re-entry for the other. More than 17,000 children have spent over two years outside education, increasing the urgency of catch-up programmes.
The data has also exposed a gender reversal that policy must not ignore. Boys constitute 56.7 per cent of the identified population, influenced significantly by farming, petty commerce and informal apprenticeships. Protecting girl-child education remains indispensable, but the evidence now requires an equally deliberate boy-child retention strategy. It is precisely this willingness to follow facts rather than stereotypes that gives the Kaduna model its national importance. The federal government’s decision to embrace the household-mapping approach as a framework for wider identification validates a notable subnational innovation: Kaduna is not merely responding to a national crisis; it is helping Nigeria rethink how that crisis should be measured.
The movement from an estimated out-of-school population of about 535,000 at the beginning of the Governor Sani administration to a directly enumerated 187,719 is profoundly encouraging, although the figures arise from different methods and age parameters and should not be treated as a strict statistical comparison.
The responsible conclusion is nevertheless compelling. Kaduna has moved from broad estimates exceeding half a million to a verified register of fewer than 200,000 children, while interventions have returned large numbers to learning. The achievement deserves celebration, but the remaining 187,719 children constitute an obligation, not a footnote.
Behind this machinery is the ROOSC Project Management Unit coordinated by Mr Ezra Angai. Under his leadership the Project has been a huge success. Angai’s background in banking, development work and public administration equips him for that demanding intersection. Under his stewardship, the unit has translated the governor’s policy direction into implementation, monitoring resources and results across communities while keeping the project centred on measurable outcomes.
His coordination has helped make ROOSC one of the administration’s most persuasive demonstrations of placing capable hands in critical positions. The project’s emerging success belongs to a wider chain of leadership: a governor who established the priority and defended the investment; education institutions that convert policy into service; partners that provide finance and expertise; teachers who animate classrooms; communities that release and support their children; and a management team that holds the parts together. Effective reform is rarely the work of one office, but it always requires leadership able to give many offices a common purpose.
Governor Sani’s education record is ultimately a statement about the kind of Kaduna he seeks to build. Every child returned to school is one life less exposed to illiteracy, exploitation, criminal recruitment, forced marriage and inherited poverty. Every competent teacher retained, classroom restored and meal served strengthens not only an education system but the social foundations of peace. The long-term value of ROOSC will therefore exceed its enrolment figures, because education enlarges productive citizenship and gives vulnerable communities a stake in stability.
The work is unfinished. Insecurity still closes schools and displaces families. Poverty still forces impossible choices. Teacher shortages, infrastructure gaps, early dropout and social resistance remain formidable. But Kaduna now possesses what serious reform requires: political commitment, remarkably improved security conditions across the state, substantial financing, household-level evidence, differentiated interventions and accountable coordination. It has moved beyond lamenting the out-of-school crisis to building an instrument capable of defeating it.
That is the significance of the Sani education story. It is the story of reform graduating into results, of public expenditure acquiring a human face, and of excluded children becoming visible to the state by name, location and need. Through ROOSC, ably coordinated by Ezra Angai, Kaduna has shown that the scourge of out-of-school children is neither inevitable nor beyond remedy. It can be reduced when compassion is organised, resources are protected and policy is governed by evidence.
The most fitting tribute to the Governor Sani administration is therefore found not in rhetoric, but in the growing number of Kaduna children walking back into classrooms; and towards futures once placed beyond their reach.
•Kubau, a freelance journalist, resides in Kurmin Mashi, Kaduna.

title: Beyond silence: Why sign language is a fundamental right, not a privilege
content:
Ammon News - A sudden midnight medical emergency inside a family home is a terrifying prospect for any parent. For a deaf mother or father, however, the crisis carries an added, invisible barrier: the agonizing race against time to call for help, explain precise symptoms, and understand urgent instructions when conventional communication channels fail.
In such critical moments, the breakdown rarely stems from sign language itself, but from an environment unprepared to listen. True accessibility means that emergency response networks, public institutions, and civic spaces are structured to receive, process, and act upon information from deaf citizens with the same speed and accuracy afforded to anyone else.
Marking the International Day of Sign Languages on September 23, this report explores how institutional innovation is transforming emergency access in the Kingdom, alongside the broader societal push to treat sign language not as a courtesy, but as an inherent right.
Recognizing that standard voice calls exclude the deaf community, the Public Security Directorate (PSD) operates a specialized, round-the-clock emergency dispatch service linked directly to the main 911 operations room.
The system functions through the dedicated "114 Deaf JO" mobile application, which routes video calls to operations officers fluent in sign language. When a call is placed, trained personnel assess the emergency–logging the caller's precise coordinates, the nature of the crisis, and whether active injuries or hazards exist – while dispatching the appropriate field units.
Crucially, the protocol bridges the critical window before paramedics arrive. Operations officers can guide callers through emergency first aid via live video sign language, maintaining continuous oversight through the OnCall management system until responders reach the scene. While requests span humanitarian aid and traffic accidents, the platform has also become a vital lifeline for reporting cybercrimes and securing specialized police intervention.
While technological interventions mark a major leap forward, international advocates argue that systemic integration must go much deeper. In a statement observing this year's global theme – "The Human Rights of Deaf People" – the international advocacy network "Communication Without Borders" stressed that legal recognition of sign language is merely a starting point.
Full civic inclusion requires unobstructed access to national sign languages across education, employment, and public services. Advocates emphasize that sign languages are complete, sophisticated linguistic systems rather than auxiliary gestures. Guaranteeing early childhood exposure to sign language and inclusive education is essential to cognitive development, while adhering to the core principle of disability advocacy: "nothing about us without us." For Rawan Abu Khuffash, the first hearing-impaired graduate of the Faculty of Sharia, accessible communication is synonymous with personal dignity and autonomy.
"When public and private institutions fail to provide accessible communication channels, they strip deaf citizens of their independence," Abu Khuffash said. Navigating legal, medical, or administrative transactions without an interpreter often forces individuals to rely on intermediaries, compromising personal privacy and increasing the risk of miscommunication.
As institutions prepare to mark the international day, Abu Khuffash urged a cultural and professional shift across Jordan's labor market – one that invests in staff training, digital accommodations, and barrier-free environments.
Ultimately, the national dialogue surrounding the deaf community converges on a singular truth: accessibility and communication are not optional amenities or charitable concessions. They are foundational pillars of a truly inclusive society where every citizen can navigate life on equal terms.
Petra

title: As climate disasters multiply, Indigenous governance offers a way forward
content: Indigenous lands from Canada to Ecuador to Nepal are increasingly being hit by catastrophic storms, fires, and floods. Worse, these climate disasters often come one after the other as overlapping crises rather than isolated incidents. Still, despite the ongoing destruction, Indigenous peoples continue to prove that they have the knowledge and skills to respond, if only global powers will let them. Even amid growing recognition by scientists and policymakers of the power of Indigenous expertise to respond to climate change, the key role that Indigenous governance plays in those knowledge systems has not received as much respect. That’s according to a new report from Land Is Life that highlights the global success of Indigenous climate adaptation and resilience amid escalating crises. The report also says supporting Indigenous governance through legal recognition, financing, and partnerships — none of which are occurring on a large scale — is the best way to reduce climate disaster risk worldwide. “We show that it’s not that they are only the most impacted, but they are already implementing effective solutions,” said Luisa Castañeda Quintana, the executive director of Land Is Life, a global nonprofit dedicated to Indigenous self-determination. “When it comes to adaptation, we don’t really need to create new structures or systems. We just need to see what is working.” The report adds to an expansive body of research showing that Indigenous self-determination, land stewardship, and cultural knowledge and practices are proven climate solutions. The report, released today, offers dozens of examples. In Kenya, Indigenous Endorois and Tugen women cultivated drought-resistant varieties of sorghum, millet, and other key foods that provided some of the region’s only harvests in years with severe drought. In Brazil, Coordination of Indigenous Organizations of the Brazilian Amazon — the nation’s largest regional Indigenous network — helps organize fire management and response. It also provides training and mobilizes response teams. The report is based on detailed case studies and more than 200 survey responses from 46 countries spanning six ecosystems: forests, mountains, drylands, freshwater systems, grasslands, and coastal. Castañeda Quintana said a broad global study was essential to show climate change and environmental disasters are not limited by national or even ecological boundaries, and responses to them must transcend borders. It also is essential to recognize that disasters do not arrive one at a time. More than 80 percent of survey respondents said that they face two or more at once, and over 90 percent reported rising frequency. For example, in 2019, the Kichwa People of Sarayaku in the Ecuadorian Amazon faced devastating floods along the Bobonaza River, destroying crops and homes. Daniel Santi, who is the president of the community, which numbers roughly 1,600 and inhabits more than 500 square miles, said that his people were able to respond effectively because of their strong governance structures that were already in place. In other words, self-determination and governance allowed them to decide how best to prepare for, and respond to, a crisis. “This organization makes it possible to confront any problem and any threat,” Santi said. The report argues that the combination of Indigenous governance and knowledge is what makes these adaptation strategies so effective. Knowledge rooted in the land can be put into action immediately. Sarayaku elders, for example, noticed rain and lightning patterns at the river’s headwaters that signaled possible flooding and were then able to warn the community. Sarayaku structure includes clear decision-making processes, mechanisms to address the most urgent needs like housing for families with destroyed homes, and dedicated representatives to communicate status updates and needs with external authorities. According to Santi, these responses are guided by minga, a Kichwa term for solidarity and collective responsibility. But many countries do not legally recognize Indigenous peoples or their governments, refuse to use Indigenous languages for emergency alerts, and continue to criminalize Indigenous culture. Those conditions can weaken the impact of Indigenous knowledge and governance. Read Next As climate change threatens their lands, Indigenous nations demand more power at the UN Dionne Phillips Santi believes Indigenous peoples have a lot to teach the world about adapting and responding to climate change, but communities like his need support as it continues to accelerate. He is calling for greater legal protections for Indigenous land and authority, as well as resources and partnerships that embrace Indigenous knowledge and decision-making. In Peru’s Ausangate Regional Conservation Area, Quechua communities joined a conservation organization to document environmental indicators, improve community monitoring, and pursue other efforts that combined Indigenous knowledge with Western research. According to the report, this is an example of how productive partnerships increase resilience. The report also found other shortcomings in many of the world’s mitigation and adaptation strategies. They include climate initiatives that focus on short-term benefits, rejecting Indigenous self-governance and imposing external authority on communities, and drawing on or celebrating Indigenous knowledge without supporting the people who provide it. Despite growing evidence that shows Indigenous land stewardship is effective and that providing Indigenous communities with direct financing helps with global climate adaptation, funding and legal security remain insufficient. “It’s always the lack of resources and the lack of access to funding that makes it so difficult for us to work, especially when climate change makes us the most vulnerable,” said Anisha Buda, who is from the Kaike Magar community and is a program officer at the national Indigenous Women Forum in Nepal. Rather than outlining a specific template for Indigenous governance, the report urges governments, philanthropists, and policymakers to foster the conditions that allow Indigenous communities to thrive. Flexible and direct funding is one of those key conditions. Land Is Life released the report during New York Climate Week specifically to call out the need for more direct financing for Indigenous communities. Despite billions of dollars pledged around the world, barely any of that money is earmarked for Indigenous peoples. And even when it is, Indigenous leaders say that they still don’t receive it. “It’s also so frustrating, right?” said Buda. “Because there are so many projects that are supposed to be for Indigenous peoples, but they are implemented by non-Indigenous organizations and non-Indigenous peoples.” With the U.S. and European countries pulling back billions of dollars from climate commitments in recent years and wars in Iran and Ukraine stretching global resources, Indigenous leaders worry they will be left even further behind. “We are in a moment where resources are scarce,” said Gisela Hurtado, the report’s author. “Where can we put the little money that we have? Where can we put it to make it much more effective? And for me, for the report, the idea is put it into what already is working.” As the climate continues to change and the world experiences escalating impacts, Hurtado says the Indigenous responses outlined in the report offer a way forward. “What they are seeing in the territories, we’re going to see it also in the future,” Hurtado said. “They are the ones that are much more connected with the Earth to know what is going to happen in the future.” This story was originally published by Grist with the headline As climate disasters multiply, Indigenous governance offers a way forward on Sep 23, 2026.

title: People Of Purpose: How Prerana Founder Priti Patkar Reached 19,883 Children From Red-Light Areas Across Maharashtra
content:
For Priti Patkar, social work began not with a predetermined career path, but with a question that emerged from witnessing the lives of children growing up in Mumbai’s red-light areas: how could children born into exploitation be given the opportunity to choose a different future.
Trained as a social worker at Nirmala Niketan and later at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, where she stood first in her specialisation, Priti’s understanding of child protection was shaped by her early exposure to Kamathipura. Her journey eventually led to the founding of Prerana, an organisation focused on protecting women and children from trafficking, commercial sexual exploitation and other forms of violence.
A Defining Encounter With Kamathipura
A visit to Kamathipura in 1986 became a turning point in Priti’s life. As a social-work student, she encountered children growing up amid circumstances where exploitation could continue across generations.
What stayed with her was three generations and the youngest of them being a child of women from the same family on the streets and bylanes of Kamathipura, soliciting for customers. The experience made her confront a difficult question: what could be done to ensure that children born into such circumstances were not automatically destined to inherit the same life?
At the time, children’s rights were receiving increasing attention globally, yet Priti saw how children in places like Kamathipura remained largely invisible while many of their basic rights were being violated.
That experience became part of the foundation for Prerana, which she began with her husband, Dr. Pravin Patkar, with support and guidance from Mrs. Farida Lambay and Dr. Hazel D’Lima.
From Rescue To Prevention
Priti’s early experiences also changed how she understood social intervention. She realised that protecting children could not simply mean removing them from immediate danger.
Children needed safe spaces, education, healthcare, counselling, family support and pathways towards a different future. This thinking led to the development of Prerana’s Night Care Centre programme, described in the interview as the first initiative of its kind.
The programme provided children born to women in prostitution with a safe place to stay during the night, away from the violence, exploitation and influences of the red-light area. But the intervention went beyond shelter. Children were supported with education, healthcare, nutrition and psychosocial care.
Prerana also worked with their mothers. The intention was not to separate mothers and children, but to protect children while recognising the importance of their relationships with their families.
For Priti, that distinction remains central. The goal was never to decide what a child should become. It was to create the conditions in which a child could eventually decide for themselves.
Challenging Stigma And Intergenerational Trafficking
The work was not without resistance. Priti recalls that there was widespread stigma surrounding children born to women in prostitution, including the assumption that they would inevitably enter the same trade as their mothers.
Prerana had to challenge both the circumstances surrounding these children and the assumptions society had made about their futures.
The organisation also encountered resistance from people benefiting from the sex trade, particularly when children were supported in making choices that could take them away from exploitation. Priti emphasises that rescue alone cannot protect a child from being trafficked again. Without safe environments, education, family and community support, rehabilitation and continued services, children can remain vulnerable to re-trafficking.
Its work with women similarly extended beyond immediate assistance. Prerana has supported access to alternative rehabilitation and livelihood opportunities, social-security entitlements, identity and protection documents, and government schemes and services.
The broader aim has been to strengthen people’s ability to make informed choices and become more independent.
Building Trust, Sharing Learning
For Priti, meaningful social change requires patience. Communities cannot simply be approached with an outside solution and expected to participate immediately. Trust has to be built over time.
Even in the early years, convincing mothers to send their children to Prerana’s Night Care Centres required demonstrating that the organisation was not trying to separate them from their children. It was creating a safe environment where children could be protected while their mothers worked.
Over time, Priti’s work also reinforced her belief that people closest to a problem must be part of its solution. Mothers, children and communities have shaped Prerana’s learning, while collaboration with government agencies, police, schools and other civil-society organisations has helped extend that learning.
She believes social change cannot belong to one organisation alone. Interventions need to be shared, documented and adapted so that successful approaches can reach more people.
Measuring Success Through Choices
For Priti, the success of an intervention cannot be reduced to the number of children reached.
Prerana looks at whether children remain safe, connected to education and supported in their health and psychosocial needs. It also follows individual journeys, including educational progress and barriers that can lead to children dropping out of school.
But there is another measure that matters deeply to her: whether a person’s choices have expanded.
The Night Care Centre, which has benefited thousands of children over the years, represents this philosophy. Some children have gone on to pursue higher education, find employment and build lives different from what society once assumed would be their destiny.
For Priti, that is the larger purpose of child protection. It is not simply about removing a child from a dangerous situation. It is about creating safety, support and opportunities so that the child can imagine and choose a future beyond the circumstances into which they were born.
The Logical Indian Perspective
Priti Patkar’s journey began with witnessing an uncomfortable reality in Kamathipura and asking what could be done differently. Her work with Prerana has since focused on a principle that runs through her approach to child protection: rescue can be only the beginning.
From creating safe spaces at night to supporting education, healthcare, rehabilitation and family relationships, the focus has remained on disrupting intergenerational exploitation without taking away a child’s agency.
Her experience also shows why lasting social change requires more than individual interventions. It demands trust, community participation, institutional collaboration and a willingness to learn from the people closest to the problem.
At the heart of Priti’s work is a simple idea: every child deserves safety, dignity and the freedom to decide what they want their life to become.

title: The racist email that made this doctor take on the establishment
content:
Trailblazing eye surgeon Kris Rallah-Baker took on the establishment and won
The moment an eye patch is removed after cataract surgery and a patient can see clearly again: that's the moment of fulfilment for eye surgeon Kris Rallah-Baker.
It's even more rewarding for Australia's first Indigenous ophthalmologist to experience that "patch off" moment in remote Indigenous areas because Kris knows he's not just helping the patient but an entire community.
"A lot of the people you are working on are elders and holders of cultural knowledge," Kris tells Australian Story. "When those people aren't able to get out on country, they're not able to transmit intergenerational knowledge that's been around for thousands and thousands of years.
"So, there's a broader picture and a deeper importance … you're allowing that intergenerational knowledge to be passed on."
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains images of people who have died.
Kris knows how losing connection to country can affect a family — much of his own history has been lost. Some of his mob were part of the Stolen Generations, taken away by white authorities and put in missions where their stories and language were forbidden.
One of those was his maternal great-grandmother, Lena Nora. She was the daughter of an Aboriginal woman, Mary Nora, who was a domestic servant on a north Queensland station. Lena's father was the Scandinavian station master.
For reasons unknown, Mary left, or was sent from, the station with Lena and a son, ending up in a "Black camp" in Bowen.
It's believed the camp was raided by authorities. The family was separated, with Lena taken to Barambah mission (now Cherbourg) almost 1,000km away before being sent further south to Myora mission, on Minjerribah, or North Stradbroke Island.
The trauma instilled in Lena a fear and distrust of white authorities.
So when Lena fell ill later in life, she refused to go to hospital.
"She was fearful of white institutions because they'd taken her away and they imprisoned her and they enslaved her," Kris says. "She stayed at home and became more and more unwell and then passed of pneumonia."
Lena's story and the need to try to bridge the cultural gap in healthcare delivery is one of the reasons Kris decided to study medicine and, ultimately, ophthalmology.
It wasn't an easy road. Kris says those in positions of power put barriers in his way because of his Aboriginality. After qualifying, he was subjected to racism by a fellow doctor, this time for not being Black enough.
But an uncle once told a young Kris that getting where you want to be in life is rarely achieved in a straight line.
It's been a zigzag journey, Kris says, to becoming Australia's first Indigenous ophthalmologist, with a private practice in Noosa and pop-up outreach clinics in remote Indigenous communities.
Now he's working to make the path less ragged for others.
Loading...'A life that means something'
On Kris's farm in the Noosa hinterland, there are cattle, sheep and a goat but also his carefully bred flock of rare heritage chickens. Inside is a collection of Georgian antique furniture, his piano, and some of his own paintings and handmade furniture.
He is, he says, "a complex character", with an eclectic range of hobbies.
"For me, a life that means something is a life that gives back to others, but also a life where I've gained as much as I possibly can have gained out of my own life," he says.
"Have I engaged in the depth of life?"
Being successful is part of that rich tapestry. "I have my private practice in Noosa, and I'm unashamed about that because my family has been held behind for generations now, and there's no reason why I can't be successful in this Western system," he says.
One of Kris's first experiences of racism was when he began school in Brisbane after moving with his family from Canberra. At kindergarten in Canberra, he'd been identified as a gifted child — in Brisbane, he was put in an English-as-a-second-language class, purely because of his skin colour.
His mother Raelene ended that as soon as she found out. "It was just this racist assumption about an Aboriginal child," she says. "It was just unacceptable."
Raelene, one of Queensland's first Indigenous health workers, is from the Warrungu mob of the Cardwell/Tully area of north Queensland, and Yuggera from around Brisbane. She also has Irish and Indian heritage. Kris's father, David, has Scottish and Jewish heritage and discovered later in life that he is also Wiradjuri, from NSW's Mudgee area.
"My life has been a life of contrasts," Kris says.
From year 5, Kris went to a private boys' school and excelled at humanities. For a while, he was keen on studying law as a stepping stone to entering politics, an ambition he still holds.
But then Raelene invited an Aboriginal doctor home to chat with a 16-year-old Kris about medicine. By the end of the meeting he set his sights on being a doctor.
He studied medicine at the University of Newcastle but after spending "a horrible year" as a junior house officer at a major Brisbane hospital, his zigzag route began.
"I concluded that I was not happy working in this huge institution," he says. "There was a lot of bullying and harassment across the board … and I thought, 'Nope, my life is worth more than this.'"
He took a lower paying job as a senior Indigenous health worker and "I found myself and I found my happiness".
It was through this work that he met ear, nose and throat (ENT) specialist Chris Perry, who recognised Kris's potential.
Says Dr Perry: "His ability to connect with the elders and Queensland Health bureaucracy was very, very good. He's very good with people and he works very hard."
Then Dr Perry asked Kris if he would be interested in a career as an ENT specialist. He wasn't. He told Dr Perry he was interested in ophthalmology.
Dr Perry wasn't offended — he got straight on the phone to eye surgeon colleagues, asking if they could meet with this young Aboriginal doctor.
One of them was Glen Gole who had worked with the late Fred Hollows, the legendary ophthalmologist who dedicated himself to restoring the sight of Indigenous people and those in developing countries.
Professor Gole saw in Kris a keen young doctor who was "worthy of support".
"That changed my entire career trajectory," Kris says. "It was the zigzag."
'Not full-blood, are you?'
Ophthalmology is a competitive specialty, with a rigorous and lengthy training and exam regime.
"I felt that a small number of consultants did not want me to finish because I'm Aboriginal", Kris says.
He says his experience of racism rattled his confidence, causing him to fail the exit exams. But by 2018 Kris graduated, and on receiving the news he "just burst into tears".
But Kris, by now the president of the Australian Indigenous Doctors' Association, wanted to ensure others following in his groundbreaking footsteps were not subjected to discrimination.
He wrote an article about the "direct and unashamed racism" he'd experienced.
It caused a stir but, in the wash-up, The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists (RANZCO) issued an apology for not replying sensitively to Kris's public criticisms and began a transformation of its processes.
"They have reformed the college internally to the point now where they actually are one of the most culturally safe spaces of any of the medical colleges," Kris says.
But racism persists.
Kris was in his Noosa rooms in July 2022, a fully fledged ophthalmologist with stints of outreach work in Alice Springs and Darwin, when an email arrived from an ACT general practitioner.
It read, in part: "You are not full-blood, are you? Half? Quarter? One eight? Like a watered down bottle of Grange. Not the real thing."
It sent Kris reeling.
"After everything I'd been through … I'm finally a consultant and I'm still getting this same crap, the same garbage," he says.
"You think, 'When will this stop?' But you just have to realise that the world is not a fair place and it doesn't matter how many letters you have after your name or how many titles you have, it's not gonna stop."
That didn't mean Kris would stay silent. He took the matter to the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency, which investigated and referred it to the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal.
The landmark case resulted in the sender of the email being deregistered for a year.
Kris had the option of keeping his complaint anonymous. He rejected that, ready to take criticism — which didn't come — because speaking out was the right thing to do.
"I do it because I care about the Australian health system," he says. "I do it because I want better for other people."
Building trust and restoring sight
At a recent clinic in Cape York's Weipa to perform cataract surgeries, Kris was accompanied by Indigenous medical student Aiden Wu, who knows the zigzag route Kris had to take to realise his dream.
"We're quite fortunate that he's done a lot of the hard yards already," Aiden says.
"If Kris wasn't so genuine and able to … connect me with the right people, I wouldn't be on this trip and I probably wouldn't even be interested in ophthalmology."
It's a busy clinic, with patients bussed in from around the cape for surgery. One of them, Albert Bond from New Mapoon, calls Aiden over. He recognises him. They are family.
The interaction quickly makes Albert more comfortable as they chat about relatives from the Torres Strait.
"If there's someone familiar or someone that you can relate to," Aiden says, "it makes everything a lot easier, a lot more calm."
That's the beauty of having Indigenous medical specialists in these remote areas, Kris says. Of course, non-Indigenous ophthalmologists can win the trust of patients and do good work, he says.
It's just that being Indigenous helps build that trust sooner.
"There's an understanding of a shared history," Kris says. "There's an understanding that they know that they're going to be understood and they're going to be safe.
"It's about trust, because we come from a long history of abuse."
Kris's history is forever tied to his great-grandmother Lena, whose fear of white authorities stopped her from seeking medical help, leading to her death.
But the future, he says, is looking good. It excites him that there are six Indigenous trainees in the RANZCO program at the moment, with the second Indigenous ophthalmologist due to graduate next year. Soon afterwards, the first Torres Strait Islander eye surgeon will graduate, who will also be the first female Indigenous ophthalmologist.
"We're seeing cultural safety being built into training," says Kris, who is proud of his leadership in the process. "We're seeing the rates of preventable blindness, although still high, come down year on year … I think we have a very, very bright future."
Watch Australian Story, Eyes on the Prize, on Monday at 8pm (AEST) on ABCTV and ABC iview.

title: Korean Drone Rescue Program Helps Mozambique Achieve Zero Fatalities During Worst Flood in Decades
content:
In January, a community in northern Mozambique experienced one of its worst floods in decades, yet the raging waters failed to claim a single life.
This miracle was made possible thanks to a small squadron of drones and their pilots tasked with informing search and rescue efforts in real time.
The story, shared by the African Development Bank, centers around Marracuene, a district just north of the capital, where the Incomáti River burst its banks after weeks of rainfall.
As it would happen, in April 2025, the Bank’s South Korea–Africa Economic Cooperation (KOAFEC) Trust Fund had launched a program to train 30 public sector experts from the meteorology, road mapping, water management, and disaster response agencies in the use of drones in emergency response.
Called the Drone-Based Disaster Management Project, January’s floods came halfway through the piloting course, where students were not only learning how to fly the drones, but also to operate sophisticated equipment like LiDAR instruments and data platforms that could transmit information about disaster areas in real time.
Marracuene and the Incomáti River became the equivalent of a final-year exam.
“Before this project, I had absolutely no experience with drones,” says Kátia Manjate, one of the new pilots.
Under Korean instructors, she learned to run the entire pipeline, “from data collection all the way to the final product… the processing and understanding what results we can draw from it all.”
That early expertise was vital as the Incomáti totally forgot where its banks were, and submerged hundreds of square miles beneath murky water. 8 months before their training was set to finish, the government ordered the project’s team to the district, where they got to work successfully “locating stranded families, mapping washed-out roads, and streaming live imagery to rescue teams who had no other way to see what the water had done.”
LiDAR imagery showed how deep each brown pool was, and could successfully guide rescue vehicles through door-high flood waters.
DRONES OR ANGELS:
- Drones are Saving Hundreds of Fawns From Mower Deaths in Germany (WATCH)
- ‘Cheaper, More Humane’ Drones Emerge as Key Weapon in Mosquito Control from Poland to Africa
- Buddhist Nations Team Up to Use Heavy Lifting Drones to Clear Everest Slopes of Trash
Their work ensured that not only were there no recorded fatalities among the population, but none among the rescuers as well.
In August, the 30 pilots graduated from the program, 10 of whom with licenses to train further drone operators. Local councilwoman Márcia Moiane noted that the significance extends well beyond this flood when she spoke with a press team from the African Dev. Bank.
“This project marks a major leap forward — not only in technology but also in how we respond to emergencies. It means we can act faster and smarter, saving more lives.”

title: 264,000 DoorDash drivers are getting money in a massive $131.5 million settlement. Here’s what happened
content: DoorDash has agreed to pay more than $115 million to more than 260,000 delivery workers in New York City who were underpaid as part of a $131.5 million settlement with the city. The worker settlement is being heralded as a historic win by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and his administration, who claim that it’s both the largest settlement in the city’s history and the largest involving food-delivery workers in the U.S. That said, the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection began a citywide investigation years before Mamdani took office after receiving complaints from dozens of DoorDash workers—aka “Dashers.” The settlement owed to workers works out to an average payment of about $442, but the amounts due will likely vary widely. Workers who weren’t paid at all or who weren’t paid on time by DoorDash will receive compensation calculated at approximately 200% of the amount they were underpaid. Mamdani said in a statement that the settlement demonstrates how the city ensures workers get what they’re owed, adding that his administration will keep fighting for working people. In a televised address, he went even further, blasting the company’s “greedy algorithm” for failing to count every hour worked. “This was not a rounding error or an accidental mistake,” Mamdani said. “Today, after years of corporate greed and impunity, we are holding DoorDash to account.” DOORDASH: “WE SCREWED UP” DoorDash didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment from Fast Company, but a spokesperson told The New York Times that while the San Francisco-based company believed its approach to calculating the appropriate pay for its workers was “fair, practical, and legal,” it will use the city’s method going forward. The company spokesperson said the median payment that will be returned to affected workers is about $48. But some workers could be owed checks in excess of $10,000, Samuel Levine, commissioner of New York’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, told the outlet. In a statement to Documented, Samantha Ramirez, a spokesperson for DoorDash, acknowledged that the company made errors and had failed to pay some workers. “Simply put, we screwed up,” she said. “Our mistakes meant some Dashers were underpaid or paid late. While these mistakes weren’t intentional, that doesn’t make them okay.” DELIVERY APPS UNDER SCRUTINY DoorDash is one of several food-delivery companies that’s been targeted by New York over the years regarding the treatment of its workers. In 2023, the city began enforcing a minimum pay rate for delivery workers, which now stands at $22.13 per hour—or the full-time annual equivalent of about $46,000. The city agency that conducted the investigation found DoorDash had violated this minimum pay rate by excluding “several categories of trip time and on-call time when calculating compensable time.” That meant that more than 260,000 workers were underpaid over a period of more than four years, from April 2022 until June 2026. Those workers who were underpaid will begin receiving notifications from settlement administrators about the amount they’re owed, and checks will be sent out beginning in late October. Another round of checks will go out in early 2027, after DoorDash finishes correcting the compensable-time calculation errors that caused the underpayments, according to the city. But the settlement is but a drop in the bucket for DoorDash, which reported more than $13.7 billion in annual revenue in 2025, a nearly 28% increase from the prior year. Shares of the company fell about 0.4% in midafternoon trading on Tuesday, extending a year-to-date sell-off of more than 12%.

title: Martha's Rule rolled out at every A&E department in England
content:
Martha's Rule rolled out at every A&E department in England
- Published
The NHS is expanding Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England to help patients and families challenge staff and seek a rapid review about their care if they want.
It is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 in 2021 after developing blood poisoning, or sepsis. Her family's concerns were not listened to, which later prompted her parents, Merope and Paul, to change that culture by creating the rule.
Patients, loved ones and staff in A&E units will be able to call a dedicated phone number to trigger an urgent review if a patient's condition is deteriorating and they are concerned this is not being listened to.
The nationwide expansion should be complete by March 2028, after a trial at seven trusts. It is already being rolled out in all inpatient wards.
Scotland is beginning to use Martha's Rule and Northern Ireland is considering using it, while Wales has a similar scheme called Call4Concern.
Martha's story
In 2022 a coroner ruled, external Martha would probably have survived if she had been transferred earlier to intensive care and given appropriate treatment.
She was in King's College Hospital in London after a cycling accident on a family holiday where she fell heavily onto the handlebars after skidding on some sand.
It left her with serious injuries to her pancreas.
After a few weeks, she developed an infection and then signs of sepsis - when the body's response to an infection is overwhelming and ends up injuring its own tissues and organs - but this was not managed properly.
Prof Aidan Fowler, national director of patient safety at NHS England, said the expansion of Martha's Rule would give families and NHS staff "a critical new lifeline" to help improve care and save more lives.
Prof Fowler told the BBC that a Martha's Rule call would mean a patient receives an "appropriate response", for example, a senior nurse or member of the critical care outreach team could conduct a review of the case.
Staff can themselves also ask for a review from a different team if they are concerned the appropriate action is not being taken.
During an eight-month pilot of the scheme at seven emergency departments, 69 calls were made to dedicated Martha's Rule phone numbers, including some calls relating to acute deterioration following an urgent clinical review. In some cases, it led to a patient having immediate surgery or being transferred to intensive care.
Prof Fowler told the BBC's Today programme that, while these numbers might seem relatively small, the decision to roll out Martha's Rule further "is on a background of very, very extensive experience in other settings".
This included in-patient wards, where Prof Fowler said his teams had received "nearly 20,000 calls"; three quarters of which came from families.
Prof Fowler said: "Early testing has shown that Martha's Rule can work well in busy A&Es and builds on the evidence from our adult and children's wards, where thousands of calls have been made by patients, families and staff to date, with many leading to changes in treatment and potentially life-saving interventions."
Questioned whether busy A&E staff might struggle with a sudden influx of calls, Prof Fowler told the BBC this had not played out in the recent tests.
"There was a concern we would receive an overwhelming number of calls, and that would be a distraction and actually divert staff from the important work they're doing," he said.
"But that hasn't been the case, actually people have used it very sensibly," he added. "We've tested it through winter and across this busy summer and therefore I am not concerned that when we roll this out we are going to be overwhelmed with calls."
Health minister Baroness Merron said the initiative was part of "wider efforts to put patient safety at the heart of the NHS."
Actor Jason Watkins, whose two-and-a-half-year-old daughter Maude died from sepsis in 2011, praised the rollout, saying Martha's rule "is making a difference on the wards".
"It enables a parent to have a voice and if there is an issue, that is addressed," he told BBC Breakfast, and urged parents: "if you're at all worried when you go into A&E, ask for a second opinion."
Watkins said the rollout of Martha's law could benefit medical professionals too, explaining: "Those extremely dedicated medical practitioners, nurses, doctors and consultants, it gives them a pause and a thought 'am I doing everything I can to assess this child accurately?'".
The phased rollout in England will be completed by March 2028.
Patients and their families can check with their local hospital or NHS trust where Martha's Rule is available by visiting the trust's website or asking hospital staff.

title: Mission Accomplished? Rehab in Scotland, Five Years On
content:
When I started working in addiction treatment to reliably access residential rehab in Scotland you had to live in the right area, be wealthy or just plain lucky. I heard it too often from patients and families who could see what was needed and, despite their best efforts, couldn’t get near it. When we argued for change, we’d hear the same weary rebuttal from the doubters: ‘there’s no evidence that rehab works’. (Ten years earlier, they were saying precisely the same thing about mutual aid.)
So, it was with some excitement that I read the final report of Public Health Scotland’s evaluation of the Scottish Government’s Residential Rehabilitation programme, published in September. Official evaluations are always careful things. They are cautious, and caveated, though if you look underneath the hedged language, the story this one tells is remarkable.
Headline: the target was passed.
Back in 2021, the Scottish Government committed £100M (about $135M) over five years to residential rehab and set two targets: 650 beds, and 1,000 people a year publicly funded to go through rehab. In 2025/26, 1,125 Scottish residents started a publicly funded placement – a comfortable overshoot. This is likely an underestimate, since not every provider was submitting data. Overall access for Scottish residents is up by around 60% since 2019/20, and publicly funded placements have more than doubled.
Capacity
Bed capacity grew by 35%, from 425 to 574. More to the point, the growth was aimed at the gaps so that capacity was directed to where it was most needed. Mums can now be treated alongside their children. Aberlour’s Discovery Grove in Dundee and the Burrow in Falkirk were simply not there when this journey started. Rae House brought new provision to the North East. Nevis House extends reach across the Highlands and Islands. These were aimed precisely at the unmet need we mapped in the Working Group’s earlier days.
Referrers have changed their minds.
Three-quarters of staff surveyed say they now discuss rehab more often with the people they support. Two-thirds report making more referrals. Referrers are now far more willing to consider a placement for someone who has been through rehab before – up from 45% to 66%. That’s a positive because of the cumulative effect. Anyone who works in this field knows recovery is rarely linear. To be offered a second or third chance should be routine, and now it increasingly is. Meanwhile, the proportion worried that rehab increases overdose risk has fallen sharply. As referrers get more experience, they get more confident.
For the first time, we know what happens to people.
When the Residential Rehabilitation Working Group reported in December 2020, one of our nine recommendations was straightforward: outcomes should be measured, published and monitored. At the time, nobody in Scotland (or to be honest, anywhere in the UK) could tell you who was going to rehab and what happened to them. Now we have a national individual-level dataset, built from scratch, with almost all providers across the private, third and NHS sectors signed up.
The first full year of data shows that 55% of people starting publicly funded rehab finish it with a positive status – substance free, or stabilised – rising to 70% for alcohol placements. This compares very favourably with international completion rates. Nine out of ten of those assessed on the validated Outcomes Star improved in at least one area of their life, and most in several. Deaths following rehab were rare: one drug-related death in the six months after placement among the subset of 146 individuals who were followed up. Given our grim record on drug deaths and the potential risks, that really matters.
What still needs fixing.
None of this means the job is done. The report has a shopping list of problems waiting to be addressed. Waiting times for detox remain a serious bottleneck. Bed capacity still falls short of the 650-bed target, and funding still trails demand. The post-rehab pathway: housing, mental health support and aftercare needs to be the next focus. People going from structured, supportive rehabilitation back into the same challenges that contributed to their problems is not recovery. The good news is that the new Alcohol and Drugs Strategic Plan 2026–2035 contains commitments addressing these gaps. The evaluation gives all of us fresh ammunition to hold everyone (myself included) to them.
So what?
Over five years a postcode lottery became much more of a national pathway. A treatment that was for the rich, the insured or the lucky became a right for anyone for whom it is deemed clinically appropriate. A sector that operated largely in the dark now has a dataset that, to my knowledge, is unique in Europe. Huge thanks are due to all of those who have contributed to the Working Group over the years and to Ministers for accepting and enacting our recommendations.
A personal note, and a full circle.
Twenty years ago, frustrated at watching patients and families bounce off the same walls I’ve described here, I helped set up a rehab service rooted in the NHS, along with council and third sector partners, based on the therapeutic community model. Plenty of people told us the NHS couldn’t run an effective rehab programme. The premise was simple: services to aid recovery from addiction should be available on the same basis as services for cancer, diabetes or broken bones – comprehensive and free at the point of delivery.
We learned early that if you build it, they will come. Demand was never the problem. Because we wanted to know whether it worked rather than just believe it might, we commissioned rigorous evaluation from the outset: one-year outcomes, four-year outcomes, independently followed up and then published in peer-reviewed journals. Almost half of our patients were abstinent at four years; among those who completed, more than 60%. Remarkable.
Those lessons – make it easy to access and free at the delivery end, evaluate honestly, expect demand, and treat addiction like any other condition – are precisely the ones now scaled up across Scotland. The principle behind the now-established national dataset came from the same frustration we felt in 2005 when I couldn’t find rehab outcome data anywhere in Scotland, so we had to create the means to collect our own. The Mother and Child Units, the prison-to-rehab pathway, the commissioning framework – all of it started life as a recommendation from people who had run out of patience with the lottery.
When I see the PHS data now, I see the lessons of one small NHS-based therapeutic community in Edinburgh, learned slowly and at a cost, becoming ordinary practice across a whole country. Of course we had learned from others and ‘stood on the shoulders of giants’ (thank you Providence Projects and others) to some extent, but there was much new learning from our unique service too.
There are good reasons to be positive, and plenty of evidence with which to challenge the naysayers. The future looks brighter, not just for rehab, but for recovery from substance use disorders generally. And if we keep our nerve, our data and our funding commitments, the next five years can build on the last because the lesson of LEAP, and of the national programme, is the same: set the bar high.
Now, let’s get on with the rest of the work.
