title: Μείωση 35% των θανάτων από καρκίνο στις ΗΠΑ
content:
Η πιο σημαντική ρουτίνα δεν είναι αυτή που οδηγεί στον ύπνο. Είναι εκείνη που κάνει ένα παιδί να νιώθει ασφαλές.
Μείωση 35% των θανάτων από καρκίνο στις ΗΠΑ


Μείωση 35% των θανάτων από καρκίνο στις ΗΠΑ
Για το σύνολο των καρκίνων, η πενταετής σχετική επιβίωση σε ασθενείς με απομακρυσμένη νόσο έχει υπερδιπλασιαστεί τις τελευταίες τρεις δεκαετίες, από 17% στα μέσα της δεκαετίας του 1990 σε 36% την περίοδο 2016-2022
Η έρευνα για τον καρκίνο εξελίσσεται με ταχύτατους ρυθμούς, μεταμορφώνοντας σταδιακά τον τρόπο με τον οποίο οι επιστήμονες προλαμβάνουν, διαγιγνώσκουν και αντιμετωπίζουν τη νόσο. Έλληνες γιατροί αναφέρουν ότι τα αποτελέσματα δεκαετιών έρευνας είναι πλέον μετρήσιμα και στις ΗΠΑ οι θάνατοι μειώθηκαν.
Την σημαντική πρόοδο αποτυπώνει το Cancer Progress Report 2026 της American Association for Cancer Research (AACR), η 16η ετήσια έκθεση που συγκεντρώνει τα νεότερα δεδομένα για την επίπτωση, τη θνησιμότητα και την επιβίωση από τον καρκίνο και αναδεικνύει τον καθοριστικό ρόλο της βασικής, μεταφραστικής και κλινικής έρευνας στη βελτίωση της φροντίδας των ασθενών. Παράλληλα, παρουσιάζει τις επιστημονικές εξελίξεις που αναμένεται να διαμορφώσουν το μέλλον της ογκολογίας, από την τεχνητή νοημοσύνη και την υγρή βιοψία έως τα αντικαρκινικά εμβόλια και τις νέες θεραπευτικές προσεγγίσεις που βασίζονται στο RNA.

Οι Ιατροί της Θεραπευτικής Κλινικής (Νοσοκομείο Αλεξάνδρα) της Ιατρικής Σχολής του ΕΚΠΑ Θεοδώρα Ψαλτοπούλου (Καθηγήτρια Θεραπευτικής - Επιδημιολογίας - Προληπτικής Ιατρικής, Παθολόγος), Δρ. Μαρία Καπαρέλου (Παθολόγος - Ογκολόγος) και Θάνος Δημόπουλος (Καθηγητής Θεραπευτικής - Ογκολογίας - Αιματολογίας, Διευθυντής Θεραπευτικής Κλινικής, Νοσοκομείο «Αλεξάνδρα», τ. Πρύτανης ΕΚΠΑ) αναφέρουν στο Αθηναϊκό/Μακεδονικό Πρακτορείο Ειδήσεων ότι τα αποτελέσματα δεκαετιών έρευνας είναι πλέον μετρήσιμα. Στις ΗΠΑ, το συνολικό ποσοστό θανάτων από καρκίνο μειώθηκε κατά 35% μεταξύ 1991 και 2024, γεγονός που αντιστοιχεί σε περίπου 4,8 εκατομμύρια λιγότερους θανάτους. Στην εξέλιξη αυτή έχουν συμβάλει η μείωση του καπνίσματος, η πρόοδος στην πρόληψη και την έγκαιρη διάγνωση, καθώς και οι αποτελεσματικότερες θεραπευτικές επιλογές.

Βελτίωση καταγράφεται και στους ασθενείς με προχωρημένη ή μεταστατική νόσο. Για το σύνολο των καρκίνων, η πενταετής σχετική επιβίωση σε ασθενείς με απομακρυσμένη νόσο έχει υπερδιπλασιαστεί τις τελευταίες τρεις δεκαετίες, από 17% στα μέσα της δεκαετίας του 1990 σε 36% την περίοδο 2016-2022.

Χρόνια συντονισμένης προσπάθειας και διεπιστημονικής συνεργασίας έχουν οδηγήσει σε σημαντικές θεραπευτικές εξελίξεις, αναφέρουν οι ειδικοί. Όπως καταγράφει το AACR Cancer Progress Report 2026, από την 1η Ιουλίου 2025 έως τις 30 Ιουνίου 2026 ο FDA ενέκρινε 11 νέες αντικαρκινικές θεραπείες. Ανάμεσά τους περιλαμβάνονται η πρώτη μοριακά στοχευμένη θεραπεία για έναν σπάνιο και επιθετικό όγκο του εγκεφάλου με συγκεκριμένη γενετική αλλοίωση, η πρώτη θεραπεία που βασίζεται στην τεχνολογία proteolysis-targeting chimera για ασθενείς με καρκίνο του μαστού, ο πρώτος αναστολέας σημείου ελέγχου για τον καρκίνο των ωοθηκών και η πρώτη CAR-T κυτταρική θεραπεία για ασθενείς με λέμφωμα οριακής ζώνης. Κατά την ίδια περίοδο, εγκρίθηκαν επίσης νέες ενδείξεις για πέντε ήδη διαθέσιμες αντικαρκινικές θεραπείες, μία μη επεμβατική φορητή συσκευή για τη θεραπεία του καρκίνου του παγκρέατος, ένα τεστ αυτοσυλλογής δείγματος για τον HPV που μπορεί να πραγματοποιείται στο σπίτι, καθώς και αρκετά εργαλεία βασισμένα στην τεχνητή νοημοσύνη με στόχο τη βελτίωση της έγκαιρης ανίχνευσης και διάγνωσης του καρκίνου.
Ιδιαίτερη θέση στην έκθεση καταλαμβάνει η τεχνητή νοημοσύνη. Οι εφαρμογές της επεκτείνονται από τη βασική έρευνα και την ανάπτυξη νέων φαρμάκων έως την απεικόνιση, την ψηφιακή παθολογία και τον σχεδιασμό κλινικών μελετών. Παράλληλα, μπορεί να συμβάλλει στη βελτίωση της έγκαιρης ανίχνευσης και διάγνωσης του καρκίνου, στην πρόβλεψη της έκβασης των ασθενών και στην περαιτέρω εξατομίκευση των θεραπευτικών επιλογών.
Νέα δυναμική αποκτούν και τα προληπτικά και θεραπευτικά αντικαρκινικά εμβόλια. Νέες τεχνολογίες επιτρέπουν καλύτερο σχεδιασμό των εμβολίων, αναγνώριση ειδικών στόχων του όγκου και συνδυασμούς με άλλες θεραπείες. Η έκθεση αναφέρει ενθαρρυντικά πρώιμα αποτελέσματα από εξατομικευμένες προσεγγίσεις στον καρκίνο του παγκρέατος, στο μελάνωμα και στον πρώιμο τριπλά αρνητικό καρκίνο του μαστού, καθώς και από εμβόλιο που μελετάται σε άτομα με σύνδρομο Lynch.
Παρά τις σημαντικές εξελίξεις, το φορτίο της νόσου παραμένει μεγάλο. Για το 2026 εκτιμάται ότι στις ΗΠΑ θα διαγνωστούν περισσότερα από 2,1 εκατομμύρια νέα περιστατικά καρκίνου και περισσότεροι από 626.000 άνθρωποι θα χάσουν τη ζωή τους από τη νόσο. Παράλληλα, ιδιαίτερη ανησυχία προκαλεί η αύξηση των καρκίνων πρώιμης έναρξης, δηλαδή εκείνων που διαγιγνώσκονται σε ηλικίες 18-49 ετών. Παγκοσμίως, η επίπτωσή τους αυξήθηκε κατά σχεδόν 80% μεταξύ 1990 και 2019, με ορισμένους καρκίνους του γαστρεντερικού συστήματος να συμβάλλουν δυσανάλογα σε αυτή την αύξηση.

Το AACR Cancer Progress Report 2026 αναδεικνύει με σαφήνεια πόσο έχει αλλάξει το τοπίο του καρκίνου μέσα από δεκαετίες επιστημονικής έρευνας, αλλά και πόσο σημαντικές προκλήσεις παραμένουν. Η πρόοδος στην πρόληψη και την έγκαιρη διάγνωση, η ανάπτυξη νέων θεραπευτικών προσεγγίσεων και η αξιοποίηση τεχνολογιών αιχμής δημιουργούν νέες δυνατότητες για τους ασθενείς. Η συνέχιση της επένδυσης στην έρευνα και η ταχύτερη μεταφορά των επιστημονικών ανακαλύψεων στην κλινική πράξη αποτελούν βασικές προϋποθέσεις ώστε η πρόοδος αυτή να συνεχιστεί και να μεταφράζεται σε μεγαλύτερη επιβίωση και καλύτερη ποιότητα ζωής για όλο και περισσότερους ανθρώπους με καρκίνο.

Για το 2026 εκτιμάται ότι στις ΗΠΑ θα διαγνωστούν περισσότερα από 2,1 εκατομμύρια νέα περιστατικά καρκίνου και περισσότεροι από 626.000 άνθρωποι θα χάσουν τη ζωή τους από τη νόσο. Παράλληλα, ιδιαίτερη ανησυχία προκαλεί η αύξηση των καρκίνων πρώιμης έναρξης, δηλαδή εκείνων που διαγιγνώσκονται σε ηλικίες 18-49 ετών. Παγκοσμίως, η επίπτωσή τους αυξήθηκε κατά σχεδόν 80% μεταξύ 1990 και 2019, με ορισμένους καρκίνους του γαστρεντερικού συστήματος να συμβάλλουν δυσανάλογα σε αυτή την αύξηση.Το AACR Cancer Progress Report 2026 αναδεικνύει με σαφήνεια πόσο έχει αλλάξει το τοπίο του καρκίνου μέσα από δεκαετίες επιστημονικής έρευνας, αλλά και πόσο σημαντικές προκλήσεις παραμένουν. Η πρόοδος στην πρόληψη και την έγκαιρη διάγνωση, η ανάπτυξη νέων θεραπευτικών προσεγγίσεων και η αξιοποίηση τεχνολογιών αιχμής δημιουργούν νέες δυνατότητες για τους ασθενείς. Η συνέχιση της επένδυσης στην έρευνα και η ταχύτερη μεταφορά των επιστημονικών ανακαλύψεων στην κλινική πράξη αποτελούν βασικές προϋποθέσεις ώστε η πρόοδος αυτή να συνεχιστεί και να μεταφράζεται σε μεγαλύτερη επιβίωση και καλύτερη ποιότητα ζωής για όλο και περισσότερους ανθρώπους με καρκίνο.

title: A Viral Songwriting Challenge Shines a Spotlight on the Tradition of Hip Hop in West Virginia
content:
When Leeshia Lee got the idea to challenge artists to write a lyrical love letter to West Virginia, she had no idea it would create so much buzz. This spring and summer, the Dear West V. challenge went viral on social media. Submissions came in from all across the state.
“Clarksburg, Huntington, Charleston, hollers and hills that I’ve never heard of,” Lee said. “It was just great to see so many people take pride.”
Lee is from Charleston and is the cultural reporter with Black By God: The West Virginian. Black By God is a community news organization that centers Black voices from across the Mountain State.
“It is a way for us to change the narrative on how our stories are told,” Lee said. “It highlights the culture of Black people in West Virginia.”
Lee is also a former radio host, and over the years, she’s developed relationships with rappers, producers, and DJs from across the state.
“I decided that I wanted to challenge the artists in West Virginia all to write their version of a love letter to the 35th state.”
For the Dear West V. challenge, Lee chose a hip hop beat and all of the artists wrote a song to that same beat.
“I wanted to showcase the talent that is in West Virginia, because I believe there are thoroughly a lot of hidden gems here,” Lee said. “And on a large scale, mainstream scale, West Virginia doesn’t get the recognition that it deserves.”
For the challenge, Lee enlisted the help of Myles Satterfield, who goes by the artist name Myles T. Myles T is a hip hop producer who grew up in Charleston. He remembers listening to Lee’s radio show as a kid.
“Some of the local rappers, they were on the radio. And I was like, ‘Man, that’s cool. How do you do that?’” Myles T said.
Myles T is also the son of Crystal Good, a renowned Affilachian poet, and the founder of Black By God.
“My mother was a poet as well, so I was like, ‘Okay, you gonna write poetry, I’m gonna write raps,’” Myles T said. “But then eventually I gravitated more towards production.”
As a self-described nerd, Myles T says producing allowed him to explore his fascination with computers. When he was in college studying cyber security, he kept honing his skills in music.
“That was how I was paying rent. I was selling beats online to pay rent in college.”
These days, he lives in Los Angeles, working in cyber security and in music. He’s produced beats for industry heavy hitters like Big Sean and Wiz Khalifa. When Lee got the idea for the challenge, she reached out to Myles T.
“I asked him for a beat. And he sent me a couple but I chose the one beat,” Lee said.
Word about the Dear West V. challenge spread on social media. Artists wrote verses to Myles T’s beat, recorded themselves performing their songs, then submitted them to Black By God. They received over 100 submissions. Lee says many of the love letters expressed a sense of appreciation.
“I think that [in] the majority of the love letters, people paid homage to the neighborhoods that raised them.”
As Duke Johnson out of Huntington rapped:
See, I was raised here, the son of a African and a gringo.
Held it down from Moneyton to Mingo.
I’ve been in the projects, the trailer parks, nice houses, and hollers.
Met a lot of good folks that do what they can for a dollar.
Kind to our neighbor, respect in our behavior,
and we finally realizing that the coal ain’t gonna save us.
“There were some really deep moments in there too, where people talked about a lot of the loss that they saw, or a lot of the judgment that they got from their area, or how they don’t feel seen, or they don’t feel heard,” Myles T said. “There was so much in some of these verses.”
“Some of them were really, really political, talking about the environmental issues, the pharmaceutical industries…incarcerations,” Lee said.
Like Monstalung of Morgantown:
Dear West V, we have to do better
Places like McDowell got me writing this letter
High cancer rates throughout the state
The water’s bad, you can tell by the taste
They are cutting funding and programs for the people
Caging us up and calling us illegal
Nothing new, we’ve seen this sequel
Flipping the words and saying it’s not equal
Yo, shaking my head at the audacity
Like we ain’t surviving floods and catastrophes
So tell your family, tell your squad
That more than ever we need Black By God
Josh Mei, aka Spike Yee, is another artist from Morgantown who submitted a song to the challenge. “He referred to himself as AppalAsian,” Lee said. “And his love letter was very eye opening.”
“Growing up Chinese American [in Morgantown] in the 90s, you know, wasn’t the best experience. It wasn’t terrible, but it wasn’t the best,” Spike Yee said. “I still had a lot of self-identity issues.”
As a self-described socially awkward kid growing up in a traditional Chinese household, Spike Yee found inspiration in how hip hop artists presented themselves.
“It was like the bravado, the confidence that you have to show. These are all things that I really wanted as a child,” Spike Yee said.
It wasn’t until he got to college in Athens, Ohio, that Spike Yee started rapping. He began attending a monthly freestyle rap battle. At first, he was nervous to take the stage. But eventually, he found his stride.
“That rush became addicting. And so I started going back every time and I would just…keep battling. And then I started winning.”
Spike Yee is back in Morgantown now and is a known quantity in the hip hop scene there. He heard about the Dear West V. challenge through social media.
“I thought the beat was super dope, and I wanted to contribute a verse to the concept of a love letter to West Virginia. Just for myself.”
For Spike Yee, it was a chance to explore his complicated relationship with the state.
Growing up, I used to hate it here.
Jaded by the state of conditions,
and it would lead me to evade it in my later years.
Amount of times I wanted out, without a shadow of a doubt.
I had a paddle, but I couldn’t find a route.
Everybody said to go, so now he’s out on the run.
Headed west and saw the truth. Felt like the prodigal son.
Headed east back to my roots. Feel like I’m one of the ones.
Now let me hold it down in Morgantown. I’m second to none.
“I left so many times, and you know, I always came back,” Spike Yee said.
I spent so many years fishing for the answers. Like, when will it bite?
Just need a chance to be myself and take control of my life.
I feel serenity now. Take a look at how you raised him.
Chinese kid in Appalachia. I am AppalAsian.
In the land of almost heaven, watch for the throne.
The state accepted me and made sure I ain’t stepping alone.
It’s kind of crazy, never realized just where I belong.
So here’s my gratitude for giving me a home, West Virginia.
Another artist who submitted to the challenge is Nicole Johnson, aka CoCo Nicole. Growing up in Huntington, CoCo Nicole started rapping when she was in high school.
“You kind of roast each other when you’re in high school, right? Like, you always have jokes with your friend group. So as a way of doing that with each other, we would kind of freestyle and rap,” CoCo Nicole said. “So I really took a liking to it back when I was in probably ninth, tenth grade. Just doing that with the girls.”
She quickly discovered that rapping was a way to vent her emotions and document her life. Then in college, some friends invited her to record her songs.
“I never tried to sing at first, I just always knew I wanted to rap…and it just kind of came naturally,” CoCo Nicole said. “When I started projecting and putting that on the microphone, I always loved the way my voice sounds.”
As her confidence grew and her skills sharpened, CoCo Nicole started releasing her recordings and performing live. In 2024, she hit a career high when she opened for rapper Rick Ross in Ashland, Kentucky. But soon after that, she fell into a creative dry spell.
“I was like fresh out of having my baby, and I was postpartum. I just wasn’t inspired, I had a mental block from music. And I just felt like I wasn’t ever going to do it again,” CoCo Nicole said.
But then, her brother—who’s also a rapper—told her about the Dear West V. challenge. After seeing his submission and hearing the beat, she decided to write her own love letter.
“I was like, I’m getting back out there. I was like, I want to write, I’m inspired.”
Dear West Virginia, my words to you for birthing me.
How could I not appreciate a state creatin’ queens?
The type of women with ambition climbin’ hills of dreams.
We found our way next to the river where the money streams.
“I wanted to give thanks and give my love to West Virginia for creating the type of women that I know and I’m around, and even the type of women that raised me,” CoCo Nicole said.
Childhood in a wild hood.
Parents used to sacrifice, so we be all good.
Taught us morals and respect that go a long way.
I’ll take a country queen from here over anything.
For CoCo Nicole, the Dear West V. challenge reignited her creativity. She’s since written and recorded a handful of new songs and has even performed live again. “The creative juices are flowing,” she said.
For Leeshia Lee and Myles T, the response to the challenge was overwhelming. People from other states were following along online. So were people who Myles T says aren’t your typical hip hop fans.
“We’ll be in the gas station, and people be like, ‘Oh, y’all the ones doing the contest.’ And it’ll be like an old lady that I was like, ‘I had no clue that you would even see this. How did this even get in your radar?’” Myles T said.
CoCo Nicole says that the viral challenge galvanized the hip hop community across the state.
“The Dear West Virginia challenge really woke people back up,” she said. “I feel like what Leeshia and Myles have done is kind of waking people up to wanting to have more events, you know, to do things.”
Spike Yee agreed.
“It kind of showed everybody…we all exist. And we’re all here doing something that we love,” he said. “This is such a uniting factor for a bunch of people from so many different walks of life.”
Because the challenge was so successful, Leeshia Lee, Myles T, and Black By God decided to host an awards show this summer in Charleston. Tickets sold out, and everyone came dressed to impress for the black tie affair. Artists from the challenge were presented with a variety of awards. The categories included Most Heartfelt, Most Historic, and Best Female Performance, which CoCo Nicole was nominated for. In fact, she won.
“I prepared a speech for just in case I won, but I got up there and I forgot all my words,” CoCo Nicole said. “I was like, ‘I hope I sound good!’ Oh my god, I was so nervous.”
For CoCo Nicole, she hopes West Virginia’s hip hop community will continue to build upon the momentum that’s been generated from the Dear West V. challenge. She wants to see the Mountain State recognized as a hub for rap and hip hop.
“We see it happen in so many other big cities. I mean, Atlanta, LA, Houston. You see it happen everywhere else, but I feel like we have enough talent here to where if we all just come together and start pushing each other, it could be big. It could be a great thing.”
Through Black By God, Leeshia Lee and Myles T have plans to keep supporting West Virginia’s hip hop artists, with another awards show taking place this winter.
This article is part of the Living Traditions project, featuring an assortment of stories and podcasts about folklife in central Appalachia.

title: The race to document Indigenous knowledge to protect Philippines’ birds
content:
In the forests of the Philippines’ Mindoro Island, an urgent effort is underway to record the vanishing ecological knowledge of the Indigenous Iraya Mangyan community.
As elders age and fewer young people learn beside then, and deforestation and infrastructure development threaten the island’s endemic wildlife, traditional knowledge holders are partnering with conservationists to document wildlife, medicinal plants, and culturally important places, reports contributor Keith Anthony Fabro for Mongabay.
The community’s roughly 40,000-hectare (100,000-acre) ancestral domain overlaps with the UNESCO-designated Puerto Galera Biosphere Reserve, a protected ecological region on the northern tip of the island. There, the Center for Conservation Innovations Philippines (CCIPH), an NGO, is helping record the community’s oral heritage under the Mindoro Forest and Biodiversity Programme.
The environmental information gathered from the community becomes part of the Iraya’s Ancestral Domain Sustainable Development and Protection Plan, said Rey Luna, CCIPH project management adviser and former provincial officer of the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples.
Among the knowledge being documented is how local birds guide the Iraya’s daily lives and forest protection. These include three endemic birds deemed culturally important by the CCIPH: the turis, or Mindoro racket-tail (Prioniturus mindorensis); the siruk, or Mindoro boobook (Ninox mindorensis); and the sulit, or Mindoro scops owl (Otus mindorensis). The IUCN Red List classifies the turis and siruk as vulnerable, and the sulit as near threatened.
These birds carry deep spiritual and practical significance for the community. For instance, the sulit is associated with departed relatives, while the siruk’s calls are said to warn of malevolent spirits.
The turis is said to be a storm forecaster. Bernito Pampilo, an Iraya forest patroller, recalled how a noisy gathering of these parrots in a single tree saved his family from a destructive typhoon when he was 9. “When I see them gather like that, I prepare,” he said.
Ronet Santos, senior program operations manager of the D’Aboville Foundation, a nonprofit environmental organization working in Mindoro, said the three birds are also indicators of forest health. “Long-term indigenous observations can complement scientific knowledge and conservation initiatives by providing a complete temporal picture of these species’ behavior,” Santos said.
“When the turis, siruk and sulit are still here, it means our forest is still beautiful,” Lenito Pampilo, an Iraya community leader and eco-trail guide, told Mongabay. “If they disappear, our forest will disappear with them.”

title: Exhibition Centre comes alive with tradition, talent and flavour of Guyana’s First Peoples
content:
Arts, craft and Indigenous cuisine are taking centre stage at the Amerindian Heritage Month exhibition at the Exhibition Centre Sophia, providing all Guyanese with an opportunity to experience and celebrate the rich traditions of the country’s First Peoples.
The exhibition is among a number of activities being held throughout September as Guyana observes Amerindian Heritage Month, creating a platform for Indigenous artisans, entrepreneurs and producers to showcase their talents, products and culture.
Among the exhibitors is Danesh Camacho of Hummingbird Products, who is offering a variety of locally produced sauces and other products, along with Indigenous-inspired cuisine.
Camacho said the celebrations provide an important opportunity for persons, particularly those living in Georgetown and other coastal communities, to gain a deeper understanding and appreciation of Indigenous heritage.
“When September comes around, a lot of the Georgetown population would have an opportunity to partake in Indigenous cuisines, buy the crafts and partake in Indigenous culture that they wouldn’t normally get access to,” he explained.
He noted that the exhibition also helps to stimulate Indigenous economies by creating markets for entrepreneurs and opening opportunities for business partnerships.
Meanwhile, Indigenous craftswoman Morna Ferreira is displaying a variety of handcrafted items made from tibisiri, including jewellery boxes, placemats and fruit bowls.
Ferreira, has been participating in exhibitions for about twenty years, she explained that her craft has played an important role in supporting her family.
As a single parent of five children, she said the income earned from producing and selling her crafts helped her to raise her children and provide for their needs.
She encouraged Guyanese to support Indigenous artisans and use the exhibition as an opportunity to learn more about Amerindian culture.
“Come out, you could see different things, you could learn from it as well,” Ferreira encouraged.
The exhibition is also providing opportunities for other Indigenous artisans to display their creativity.
Cheryl, an exhibitor from the Mouraikubai community, is showcasing a range of handmade items, including headdresses, earrings, outfits and other craft pieces.
She said she was happy to be part of the Heritage Month celebrations and encouraged Guyanese to support the exhibitors throughout the observance.
Another exhibitor, Don Calbert, is using the occasion to showcase traditional Indigenous items, including fish traps, baskets, jewellery and other handcrafted pieces.
He said the exhibition gives Indigenous peoples an opportunity to proudly display their culture and traditions while interacting with fellow Guyanese and members of Indigenous communities.
The Heritage Month activities are not only helping to preserve and promote Guyana’s Indigenous traditions but are also creating valuable economic opportunities for artisans, entrepreneurs and producers.
Through initiatives such as the exhibition, Guyanese are being encouraged to experience the country’s rich cultural diversity while supporting Indigenous businesses and the preservation of traditional knowledge and skills.
Amerindian Heritage Month celebrations will continue until September 30, with several activities planned, including an Amerindian Heritage Dinner, school tours and an Amerindian Heritage Safari.
The month-long observance continues to provide a platform for Guyana’s First Peoples to celebrate, preserve and showcase their unique culture, traditions, talents and significant contributions to national development.

title: After mother's death, Wyoming rancher vowed to protect 2,506 acres forever
content:
Eight years ago, David Ellsbury stood at his mother's deathbed. She only had one request. Her final wish was that their family ranch would never be developed. She didn’t want a developer to carve it up the way they had everywhere else. And that’s exactly what the Crook County rancher did. Earlier this year, all 2,506 acres of the Ellsbury Diamond E Ranch were locked into permanent protection through the Wyoming Stock Growers Land Trust. No developer can touch it. No subdivision can fragment it. For David Ellsbury, protecting the land and the family tradition was a word he gave to his dying mother. “It will never be developed,” Ellsbury told the Cowboy State Daily.
Protecting the last homestead
Pic credit: Wyoming Stock Growers Land Trust
Back in the 1880s, four of Ellsbury's great-grandfathers had staked homesteads in the area northeast of Sundance. “My great-grandfather was such a visionary, and he didn’t know it. What a brave man,” Ellsbury said.
Talking to the Sundance Times, he recalled, “I, along with my father and grandfather, invested our lifetimes working this ranch to provide for our livelihoods. With the threat of encroaching development looming across my fencelines, I felt the need to preserve and conserve my family’s legacy and heritage for our future generations.
I share the sentiment often credited to Chief Seattle, ‘We do not inherit the earth from our ancestors, we borrow it from our children’.”
One by one, those original properties vanished. At least one was swallowed by a housing development. Of all the homesteads his great-grandfathers claimed, Ellsbury's is the only one still undeveloped. In fact, he once tried to buy a neighbouring property before it was subdivided. But developers were faster than him. So he couldn’t protect it. He saw the homestead disappear. That was happening right outside his fence.
The land will never be developed
Pic credit: Wyoming Stock Growers Land Trust
In order to protect the ranch, Ellsbury had to trade something else. He cannot sell the land for development. He cannot subdivide it. What he can do is keep it working, keep cattle grazing, keep hay cut, and keep the rhythm of seasonal labour that has structured his family's lives since the 1880s.
But that’s exactly what he needs. The easement is irrevocable. It’s not temporary, or ‘for now’; it’s forever. His descendants inherit the land with the same constraints built into its title. They don't get to choose the easy path. They get to choose the one his family has chosen for five generations.
Passing tradition
Ellsbury has twelve grandchildren. The oldest, in junior high and high school, are old enough to work the land. He is teaching them what the place wants and what it offers in return. “I’ve got to do it for them,” he said. They are learning belonging, which is something beyond ranching. And he is seeing them take to the work with genuine interest, not out of obligation.
David Ellsbury, however, no longer owns livestock. He had to let it go after suffering a heart attack. “A heart attack makes you stop and think,” he said. He passed the livestock operation to his sons.
The ranch sits within wildlife corridors designated by the Wyoming Game and Fish Department. So it shouldn’t be a surprise to see elk move through it. Mule deer are a common sighting. U.S. Forest Service land borders more than two miles of the eastern parcel and surrounds the western section. So the landscape basically functions as one integrated system. Protect this piece, and you protect the whole.
Crook County is changing. Energy projects, mining, and residential subdivisions are fragmenting operations and destroying the agricultural character that made the place liveable.
Ellsbury knows this more than anyone else. But this easement is permanent. So all his descendants can do is work the land, improve it, and live from it. Christine Adams, the Wyoming Stock Growers Land Trust executive director, called the project one of the most meaningful she'd been part of. The family said no to money and instead chose to protect their land at all costs. “It’s a testament to (the Ellsbury family’s) persistence, stewardship and respect for the land,” she told the outlet.
The Land Trust now manages more than 327,000 protected acres across Wyoming.
And Ellsbury’s began with a promise to his mother. She saw the land around her disappear. That deeply disturbed her. She was upset, and “on the day she died, she told me she did not want what happened to that place to happen to this place,” Ellsbury said.
“I have followed her wishes. It is of utmost importance to me to keep it going in the family, for it to stay in the family name,” he added.
Ellsbury made the bet to honor his mother's wish. He's spending the rest of his life making sure it pays off.

title: Assentamento Terra Vista recebe primeira turma de Filosofia na história do Pronera
content:
A cerimônia de abertura do curso de Licenciatura em Filosofia da Terra foi realizada no dia 24 de agosto, no Assentamento Terra Vista, no município de Arataca, sul da Bahia. Esta é a primeira turma de graduação em Filosofia promovida pelo Programa Nacional de Educação na Reforma Agrária (Pronera) e conta com 50 estudantes, reunindo educadores populares, lideranças comunitárias e jovens originários de assentamentos, comunidades quilombolas e aldeias indígenas.
A formação é fruto de uma articulação construída desde o período pré-pandemia e reúne o Instituto Nacional de Colonização e Reforma Agrária (Incra), a Universidade Estadual de Santa Cruz (UESC), a Teia dos Povos e movimentos sociais do campo, como MST, CETA, CPT e MLT. Ao longo de quatro anos, as aulas e atividades de pesquisa serão desenvolvidas integralmente dentro do próprio assentamento.
A proposta pedagógica da Licenciatura em Filosofia da Terra parte da Pedagogia da Alternância e da práxis agroecológica, colocando no centro as cosmovisões dos povos originários e das comunidades tradicionais.
Cris Ayie, do Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST) no território Claudemiro Dias Lima, integra a turma e destaca que uma das missões do grupo é poder ocupar esse lugar de disputa de ideias. “É um espaço de debates, de trazer realidades e se aprimorar no conhecimento que a gente já vem praticando ao longo dos tempos em cada território. É um espaço de confluência e de partilha de saberes. Essa turma é muito diversa e traz um acúmulo grande de experiências”, afirma.
Para o vice-reitor da UESC, Maurício Santana Moreau, a presença da academia no território estabelece uma relação horizontal de aprendizado mútuo. “A expectativa é que a gente trabalhe os saberes deles junto com o conhecimento acadêmico dos professores da universidade, e que quem saia ganhando seja toda a comunidade. Estamos muito felizes com esse momento importante e histórico”, observa.
O coordenador do curso e docente da UESC, professor Josué Cândido, explica o recorte específico da matriz curricular. “Esse curso tem um diferencial porque é uma filosofia da terra, voltada para pensar a questão agroecológica, o planeta e fazer com que nossos alunos se tornem seres críticos e reflexivos para levar essa contribuição para a educação na região”, relata.
Retomada do Pronera e soberania territorial
O início das aulas formaliza também a reorganização das instâncias regionais do programa. De acordo com Paulo Coqueiro, membro do Colegiado Estadual do Pronera na Bahia, o curso carrega duplo valor. “Esse curso inaugura a nova composição do Colegiado Estadual do Pronera na Bahia. É de uma grande importância histórica, quer seja por estar sediado dentro de um assentamento, quer seja por ser o primeiro curso dessa retomada”.
Fabrício Dias, chefe da Divisão de Educação do Campo do Incra Nacional, setor que gere o Pronera em âmbito federal, aponta o pioneirismo do debate filosófico na modalidade. “Depois de 28 anos de execução dessa política pública, realizamos a aula inaugural do primeiro curso de Filosofia do Pronera no Brasil todo. Foi um momento muito emocionante de retomada do programa na Bahia, principalmente com a inovação de trazer a filosofia para dentro do debate da educação do campo. Nossa expectativa é que esses alunos construam um outro pensar filosófico, aliado às populações tradicionais de todo o país”, ressalta.
No Terra Vista, a chegada da graduação é celebrada como consolidação de uma trajetória de luta pela terra e pelo conhecimento. Joelson Ferreira, liderança do assentamento e da Teia dos Povos, reforça o papel estratégico da formação. “Acredito que vai ser um marco para restabelecer um programa de formação capaz de ser instrumento de transformação da juventude e do povo que está nas áreas de reforma agrária, quilombolas e indígenas, para que a gente possa evoluir esse pensamento e construir uma militância capaz de entender e transformar a realidade. Essa parceria entre Incra, Pronera e UESC é fundamental para nos fortalecer”, observa Joelson.
Para Solange Brito, assentada no Terra Vista e integrante da Rede de Mulheres da Teia dos Povos, o impacto atinge diretamente o cotidiano da comunidade. “É de fundamental importância avançar na perspectiva política. Os estudantes pesquisando e se formando geram avanço na consciência da educação, da produção, da cultura e do fortalecimento dessa região tão rica, que é o bioma Mata Atlântica. Para nós, receber todos aqui representa um acúmulo de muita força”.
Com o calendário acadêmico em andamento no assentamento, a Licenciatura em Filosofia da Terra projeta consolidar, até a conclusão da turma, uma rede de educadores e pesquisadores preparados para atuar tanto nas salas de aula quanto nas organizações comunitárias, articulando soberania alimentar, preservação ambiental e pensamento crítico no campo.

title: Έξι φορές λιγότεροι νεκροί όπου υπάρχει έγκαιρη προειδοποίηση
content:
Μερικά λεπτά ή λίγες ώρες προειδοποίησης μπορούν να κάνουν τη διαφορά ανάμεσα στη ζωή και τον θάνατο όταν πλησιάζει μια πλημμύρα, ένας κυκλώνας ή ένα άλλο ακραίο φυσικό φαινόμενο. Και πλέον υπάρχουν στοιχεία που δείχνουν πόσο μεγάλη μπορεί να είναι αυτή η διαφορά.
Στις χώρες που διαθέτουν ολοκληρωμένα συστήματα έγκαιρης προειδοποίησης για πολλαπλούς κινδύνους, η θνησιμότητα από καταστροφές είναι έξι φορές χαμηλότερη σε σύγκριση με τις χώρες που δεν διαθέτουν αντίστοιχους μηχανισμούς, σύμφωνα με νέα έκθεση του ΟΗΕ.
Τα στοιχεία παρουσιάστηκαν ενώ οι παγκόσμιοι ηγέτες βρίσκονται στη Νέα Υόρκη για τη Σύνοδο του ΟΗΕ για το Κλίμα και καταγράφουν την πρόοδο της πρωτοβουλίας Early Warnings for All – Έγκαιρη Προειδοποίηση για Όλους, η οποία ξεκίνησε το 2022.
Ο στόχος είναι εξαιρετικά φιλόδοξος: μέχρι το τέλος του 2027 κάθε άνθρωπος στον πλανήτη να προστατεύεται από κάποιο αποτελεσματικό σύστημα έγκαιρης προειδοποίησης.
Από 56 σε 136 χώρες
Η πρόοδος των τελευταίων ετών είναι σημαντική. Σήμερα 136 χώρες διαθέτουν δυνατότητες έγκαιρης προειδοποίησης για πολλαπλούς κινδύνους, αριθμός αυξημένος κατά 143% σε σχέση με το 2015.
Παράλληλα, περισσότερες από 160 χώρες λαμβάνουν άμεση υποστήριξη για να ενισχύσουν τα συστήματά τους.
Μόνο την περίοδο 2022-2025 κινητοποιήθηκαν περίπου 2 δισ. δολάρια, με στόχο τη βελτίωση της προετοιμασίας, την προστασία ευάλωτων πληθυσμών και την ενίσχυση της δυνατότητας των κρατών να προβλέπουν και να αντιμετωπίζουν έγκαιρα τις καταστροφές.
Τα συστήματα αυτά δεν περιορίζονται σε μια εφαρμογή στο κινητό ή σε μια σειρήνα συναγερμού. Απαιτούν μετεωρολογικά και υδρολογικά δεδομένα, δίκτυα παρατήρησης, αξιόπιστες προβλέψεις, τηλεπικοινωνιακές υποδομές και κυρίως έναν μηχανισμό που μετατρέπει την επιστημονική πληροφορία σε συγκεκριμένη προειδοποίηση προς τον πολίτη.
Γιατί μια ακριβής πρόγνωση που δεν φτάνει εγκαίρως σε όσους κινδυνεύουν έχει ελάχιστη πρακτική αξία.
Όταν η προειδοποίηση έρχεται πριν από την καταστροφή
Χαρακτηριστικό παράδειγμα αποτελεί η Κολομβία. Τον Ιούνιο του 2026, ο Ερυθρός Σταυρός της χώρας ενεργοποίησε πρωτόκολλο έγκαιρης δράσης για την ξηρασία, μόλις εμφανίστηκαν οι πρώτες ενδείξεις του Ελ Νίνιο και πριν οι συνθήκες φτάσουν σε κρίσιμο επίπεδο.
Αυτή είναι η φιλοσοφία του νέου μοντέλου: οι αρχές να μην περιμένουν να συμβεί η καταστροφή για να κινητοποιηθούν, αλλά να δρουν όταν υπάρχουν πλέον επαρκείς ενδείξεις ότι αυτή πλησιάζει.
Το 2025, τέτοιες προληπτικές δράσεις έφτασαν σε 9,6 εκατομμύρια ανθρώπους σε 54 χώρες, μέσα από 146 ενεργοποιήσεις προγραμμάτων που υποστηρίχθηκαν με σχεδόν 120 εκατ. δολάρια.
Το τραγικό παράδειγμα του Νεπάλ
Η άλλη πλευρά του προβλήματος φαίνεται όταν το σύστημα δεν υπάρχει ή δεν λειτουργεί.
Κατά τις καταστροφικές παγετωνικές πλημμύρες του Αυγούστου στο Νεπάλ, οι κοινότητες που βρίσκονταν κατάντη έλαβαν ελάχιστη ή καθόλου έγκαιρη προειδοποίηση. Ο χρόνος για εκκένωση ήταν σχεδόν ανύπαρκτος.
Ο απολογισμός ήταν δραματικός: περισσότεροι από 1.000 νεκροί, χιλιάδες αγνοούμενοι και πάνω από 10.000 εκτοπισμένοι, μαζί με τεράστιες καταστροφές σε κατοικίες και κρίσιμες υποδομές.
Η περίπτωση δείχνει γιατί η έγκαιρη προειδοποίηση δεν αποτελεί απλώς ένα ακόμη εργαλείο πολιτικής προστασίας, αλλά βασική υποδομή μιας χώρας που βρίσκεται αντιμέτωπη με ολοένα συχνότερα και εντονότερα ακραία φαινόμενα.
Τα μεγαλύτερα κενά στους πιο ευάλωτους
Το παράδοξο είναι ότι οι μεγαλύτερες ελλείψεις εντοπίζονται ακριβώς στις χώρες που είναι περισσότερο εκτεθειμένες.
Οι λιγότερο ανεπτυγμένες χώρες, τα μικρά αναπτυσσόμενα νησιωτικά κράτη και οι περιοχές που πλήττονται από συγκρούσεις εξακολουθούν να παρουσιάζουν σοβαρά κενά.
Αυτά αφορούν την καταγραφή και κατανόηση των κινδύνων, τις υποδομές παρατήρησης και πρόγνωσης, τις τηλεπικοινωνίες, την επιχειρησιακή ικανότητα των αρχών και την προετοιμασία των ίδιων των κοινωνιών.
Περίπου 50 χώρες συμμετέχουν πλέον ενεργά στην εφαρμογή της πρωτοβουλίας του ΟΗΕ, ενώ έχουν δημιουργηθεί 31 εθνικοί οδικοί χάρτες.
Το μήνυμα του Αντόνιο Γκουτέρες είναι ότι η πρόοδος δεν αρκεί. Εκατομμύρια άνθρωποι εξακολουθούν να μένουν απροστάτευτοι.
Σε έναν πλανήτη όπου οι ακραίες θερμοκρασίες, οι πλημμύρες, οι ξηρασίες και οι πυρκαγιές εντείνονται, η προσαρμογή στην κλιματική κρίση δεν αφορά μόνο μεγάλα έργα και δισεκατομμύρια επενδύσεων.
Μερικές φορές αρχίζει από κάτι πολύ πιο απλό: να γνωρίζει κάποιος εγκαίρως ότι ο κίνδυνος έρχεται.

title: Boy's football ground challenge for 'heart of gold' mum
content:
Boy's football ground challenge for 'heart of gold' mum
- Published
A 10-year-old Dundee boy is completing ten laps of every professional football pitch in Scotland in memory of his late mother.
Jacob McDonald is walking around the 42 grounds to raise money and awareness in honour of his mum Vivienne, who died of a rare lung disease aged 32, when Jacob was 18-months-old.
Jacob's Ground Journeys will see him and his father Kenny travel more than 6,000 miles (9,656km) from Ross County to Stranraer with all the stops in between.
The duo have completed 18 football grounds so far, including Celtic, Rangers, and St Mirren.
Kenny said Jacob was excited at the prospect of the challenge.
He told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast: "He likes to be adventurous, looking at different places, and being a typical 10-year-old boy as well, he loves the attention.
"It's just been phenomenal."
Jacob became an ambassador for the Pulmonary Fibrosis Trust when he was seven.
The condition is incurable and is progressive, and the general prognosis is between three and five years.
His ground journey challenge has raised about £6,500 so far.
Jacob said: "It's been so much fun so far.
"Some of the pitches are massive and my legs get really tired, but I just think about my mum and keep going.
"My favourite ground so far was East Kilbride because everyone was so supportive. Dad jokes I walk faster than him now."
Jacob has met players including Dundee's Simon Murray and former Celtic player Charlie Mulgrew and the Edinburgh City players applauded him on his final lap, which Kenny said was "a lovely touch."
Kenny said clubs and businesses across the country had been "incredibly generous".
Jacob has sensory issues, finding bright light and noise difficult to be around, and wears ear defenders, with Kenny accompanying him at all times.
Kenny said Vivienne, who was diagnosed with the disease when she was 28, had a "heart of gold".
He said Vivienne became pregnant despite being told she could never have children.
"It was quite difficult, knowing Vivienne was going to pass and I was going to be left with Jacob," he said.
"And to be fair, the whole time that Vivienne was carrying Jacob we never spoke about her mortality.
"We just got on with it, she was happy, I was happy."
Kenny said that after Vivienne's funeral he had been sorting her belongings.
He said: "Unbeknownst to me, she'd left all these letters for myself and Jacob around the house that she knew we would find, for us to read.
"She's written letters for Jacob's milestones for his 16th, 18th, his 21st birthday.
"Other letters he's got, I'm going to wait until he starts high school, then I'm going to let him open them and have a proper read, so he understands more."

title: Just like an Italian piazza, this community garden has grown a community
content:
feel good
Just like an Italian piazza, Highbury garden celebrates 30 years of community
Thirty years ago, Mario Minuzzo looked at an overgrown patch of land behind his suburban Adelaide home and saw something special.
"In amongst all of that was vermin and snakes," Mr Minuzzo said.
"The critical thing that started me was when a red-bellied black snake ended up in our house amongst the children on Christmas morning."
Mr Minuzzo sought and was given permission to mow and maintain the land on Aqueduct Reserve at Highbury.
Growing interest from neighbours led to the establishment of the community garden in 1996.
Today, the 88-year-old is celebrating the legacy of the Pioneer Court Community Garden — a place where generations have grown together.
"I recall standing on the mound thirty years ago and thinking this would make a great community garden," Mr Minuzzo said.
"My heritage is Italian and in Italy, local people often meet in the piazza.
"They gather, walk, share stories, and connect, so my original vision for the garden was to create a sense of community and place — just like a piazza."
The community garden is home to more than 40 plots, 75 members and almost 400 fruit and nut trees and vines — from pomegranates and bananas, to grapes and macadamias.
It is on just under one hectare of land leased from the Department for Environment and Water and is one of the larger community gardens scattered across the state.
The garden's 'secret power'
Mr Minuzzo wanted the garden to be somewhere people could meet, share stories and connect.
"Australia in my view is one of the best multicultural examples in the world," he said.
Their membership spans generations, cultures and gardening experience, with long-term members sharing their knowledge with people just starting out.
Chairperson Marina Birch, who took over the reins from Mr Minuzzo in 2022, said she was proud of the garden.
"The secret power of our garden is actually the retired community," she said.
"They keep it going and without them we wouldn't be anywhere.
"But we do have a mix of families with young children, people not quite yet at retirement and a good variety of people from different countries as well."
Laura Fleming is the garden's youngest member.
"It has been so nice to meet local residents and learn from them and grow things I've never grown before," she said.
"It's clearly a huge legacy for Mario and all the people that have been involved.
"It's not been without a lot of hard work and I'm really grateful that they've put this effort in."
A helping hand
The garden's impact also extended beyond its boundaries.
Members grow produce specifically for charity and donate surplus fruit and vegetables to Pathway Community Centre, which partners with OzHarvest to help feed families in need.
The garden members has also been recognised for its contribution to the community, including winning the 2022 City of Tea Tree Gully Australia Day Award for Outstanding Community Group of the Year.
There are already plans for the next chapter, including a proposed native nursery to help restore areas affected by the giant pine scale infestation.

title: Tamil Nadu's 70-YO Palmyra Tree Climbers Find New Income Through a Professor's Tourism Trails
content: As the sun rises over the dry stretches of southern Tamil Nadu, silhouettes begin appearing against rows of towering palm trees. Some carry ropes coiled around their shoulders. Others carry sickles and woven baskets. For generations, these climbers have scaled palmyra trees before dawn, tapping sap, harvesting fruit, and collecting leaves that would eventually become everything from jaggery and handicrafts to sweets and roof coverings. Today, many of them are in their seventies. And that worries Dr Preethi Hari Babu. “Without community support, the tree cannot be protected. That is the charm of the palmyra — the community and the tree survive together,” says the 30-year-old tourism researcher and assistant professor from Chennai, whose doctoral research has focused on understanding how Tamil Nadu’s state tree can be revived through tourism and community engagement. “When I understood the benefits of the tree and saw communities trying to revive it, I realised there was so much more to explore,” Dr Preethi says. “I have hosted three tours. In each tour, nearly 20 to 30 people participated. Most of them did not know about the community and their livelihoods. They were overwhelmed to learn about them, purchased the products, and even saved their contacts to place orders in the future,” shares Dr Preethi. A journey that began in a classroom For Preethi, the journey into the world of palmyra did not begin in forests or farms. It began in classrooms. After completing her bachelor’s degree at Ethiraj College and later pursuing an MBA in Tourism, she entered the tourism sector, believing that every place has something unique that shapes its identity. While working with a nature conservation NGO in 2019, she joined a trail focused on palmyra landscapes. That changed everything. “When I understood the benefits of the tree and saw communities trying to revive it, I realised there was so much more to explore,” she says. Eventually, while pursuing her PhD in Tourism from Mizoram University, which she completed in 2025, she turned the palmyra tree into the centre of her research. The idea stayed with her long after the trail ended. Eventually, while pursuing her PhD in Tourism from Mizoram University, which she completed in 2025, she turned the palmyra tree into the centre of her research — not just as a species, but as an ecosystem connecting livelihoods, ecology, culture, and identity. More than just a tree Across Tamil Nadu, palmyra trees stand along roadsides, fields, and coastal landscapes. But according to Preethi, reducing them to scenery misses their significance. Large communities depend on the tree directly for income. “There are edible and non-edible products. There are handicrafts, exports, climbers who harvest products, and women who make jaggery. It creates employment at many levels,” she explains. Large communities depend on the tree directly for income. (Photograph: Gio Shravan) Women’s collectives produce palm jaggery and craft products. Climbers harvest sap and fruit. Artisans weave leaves into baskets and utility products. Entrepreneurs make jams, squashes, and sweets from palm fruit. And then there is the environmental role. The tree helps reduce soil erosion, supports water retention, and acts as a habitat for multiple species. In coastal and dry landscapes especially, these ecological functions become critical. “It is not only useful for people. Many species survive because of these landscapes too,” she says. Where livelihoods climb trees During her fieldwork across Kanyakumari, Thoothukudi, and Villupuram, Preethi spent time with climbing communities whose relationship with palmyra stretches across generations. “There are huge climber communities, almost like fishing communities. Their identity and livelihoods are deeply connected to this tree,” she says. One such climber is 32-year-old Anto Brito, whose family has worked with palmyra trees for generations. “My grandfather was a climber, and my father was also in this profession,” he says. “After my studies, I got a job elsewhere, but I did not find satisfaction there. Here, I am physically fit, I am with my family, and I enjoy the work.” But what struck Preethi most was how invisible many of these value chains remain. (Photograph: Gio Shravan) His family remains deeply involved in the palmyra economy. While Anto climbs the trees and harvests sap and fruit, his parents prepare food products made from palmyra produce. Together, they also run two shops that sell handicrafts and food items derived from the tree. But what struck Preethi most was how invisible many of these value chains remain. Many people know palm fruit. Few know how much more exists. From neera-based beverages to jams, squashes, jelly, adhirasam, and paniyaram, communities continue creating products that rarely receive mainstream attention. For climbers like Anto, the work remains seasonal but can provide a meaningful income. Between April and October, he harvests enough sap to produce around two to three kilograms of karupatti (palm jaggery) a day, earning roughly Rs 1,000 daily during the season. “In a day, I climb more than 10 trees,” he says. “During the COVID period, I used to climb nearly 20 trees a day.” One of them was a fruit festival organised with local communities and hosted at Madras School of Social Work, where artisans and producers from Villupuram showcased dishes made from palmyra produce. To change perceptions around palmyra products, Preethi began organising palmyra trails and community events. One of them was a fruit festival organised with local communities and hosted at Madras School of Social Work, where artisans and producers from Villupuram showcased dishes made from palmyra produce. “About 150 people came and tried the food. Many had never tasted these products before,” she says. The moment that changed perspective One experience continues to stay with her. As part of her extended research, Preethi travelled through remote islands in Indonesia for 15 days, studying how communities there interacted with similar palm ecosystems. Instead of feeling distant, it felt familiar. “I was proud that this potential already existed in Tamil Nadu,” she says. Communities there used palm trees for food, crafts, and even musical instruments. “That was when I realised this tree connects communities across Asia. The community involvement travels with the tree.” The benefits are directly shared among the community and supported by the government. For Preethi, it serves as one of the strongest examples of community-based tourism. (Photograph: Gio Shravan) Rote and Sabu are remote islands in Indonesia. They conserve the palmyra — known locally as lontar — in every possible way. “More than conservation, I can say they co-exist with the tree. Sasando is a traditional harp-like musical instrument native to Rote Island, made from lontar. It is considered a symbol of identity, culture, heritage, and pride. You can see its influence everywhere on the island, from heritage monuments to modern décor inspired by its shape. There is even a Sasando-shaped building that serves as the official residence of the Governor of East Nusa Tenggara in Kupang. “Sabu Island is mostly covered with grasslands and lontar palms. The majority of people depend on the tree for their livelihoods. They make intricate handicrafts such as baskets and handbags, while also preserving their traditional products. “Namata village in Sabu has conical lontar-thatched houses, where visitors can observe animist and ancestral worship practices. Visitors can also experience ikat weaving and watch climbers collect sap from the trees, locally called tuak. The area is underdeveloped in terms of infrastructure, amenities, and sanitation facilities, but it is remarkably well-maintained and organised.” The benefits are directly shared among the community and supported by the government. For Preethi, it serves as one of the strongest examples of community-based tourism. How tourism can help revive community livelihoods For Preethi, tourism is ultimately about empowering communities by sustaining their livelihoods. “Community-based tourism can create additional economic opportunities while helping communities showcase their culture and knowledge systems,” she says. Visitors could experience both the edible and non-edible worlds of the palmyra ecosystem — tasting fresh palm products and traditional foods while also learning how leaves are transformed into handicrafts, utility products, and decorative items through skills passed down across generations. The benefits, she believes, extend far beyond tourism revenue. Visitors could experience both the edible and non-edible worlds of the palmyra ecosystem — tasting fresh palm products and traditional foods while also learning how leaves are transformed into handicrafts, utility products, and decorative items through skills passed down across generations. Women who already play a central role in producing jaggery, food products, and handicrafts could earn directly from visitors without relying on middlemen. They could price their products themselves, run their own enterprises, and continue living and working within their villages instead of migrating elsewhere in search of employment. “Tourists are not only visitors; they become consumers who understand the work, effort, and knowledge behind these products through direct experience,” says Preethi. That experience also creates a deeper understanding of the communities whose livelihoods depend on the palmyra and of the ecosystem that supports them. Unlike conventional tourism experiences, palmyra communities carry generations of ecological knowledge that exists nowhere else. They know the birds and insects that inhabit the trees, understand seasonal cycles, and recognise changes in flowering and fruiting patterns that come only from living alongside the landscape for decades. “They can narrate these experiences as stories, making the journey more memorable while sharing traditional ecological knowledge associated with the tree,” says Preethi. In her vision, tourism becomes a platform not only for conservation but also for collaboration. Palmyra artisans in Tamil Nadu could exchange ideas with palm-based craft communities elsewhere in the world through co-learning platforms, helping revive traditional practices while encouraging innovation in products and design. She also imagines dedicated celebrations that place the tree at the centre of public attention. “Why not have an exclusive Palmyra Day celebrated globally?” she asks. “The tree deserves recognition for everything it supports.” Greater visibility, she believes, could also encourage more research and development around palmyra products, crafts, and sustainable livelihoods. The outcome, according to Preethi, is not simply economic development but social development as well — one that supports inclusive growth, circular economies, and sustainable tourism models rooted in local ownership. Tourism, she argues, can strengthen the relationship between climbers and the trees they depend on by creating value through cultural experiences, palm-based products, and ecotourism. As communities begin earning more from the living tree, they gain stronger reasons to conserve palmyra landscapes, preserve traditional climbing skills, and protect the biodiversity that exists around them. A tree that cuts across faith What also fascinated her was how the palmyra quietly crosses religious boundaries. Muslim families use palm leaves during wedding decorations. Christian households use them for decorating homes. In Hindu traditions, sweets wrapped in palmyra leaves remain part of festivals like Karthigai Deepam. “It connects people in ways we do not always notice,” she says. The challenge no one talks about For all its benefits, the future of palmyra remains uncertain. The biggest concern is not the tree itself. It is the people. “Most climbers today are around 70 years old,” says Preethi. The younger generation increasingly avoids climbing work due to safety concerns, low earnings, and changing aspirations. As climbers disappear, traditional knowledge risks disappearing with them. “You cannot separate conservation from communities,” she says. “If we want the tree to survive, the people connected to it also need support.” Unlike conventional tourism experiences, palmyra communities carry generations of ecological knowledge that exists nowhere else. Her answer lies in tourism. Not mass tourism, but experiences rooted in local knowledge — trails, festivals, food experiences, and community-led storytelling that create livelihoods while reviving interest in traditional systems. Because for Preethi, saving the palmyra is not only about protecting a tree. It is about protecting everything that climbs with it — livelihoods, culture, memory, and communities that have spent generations looking up at these tall silhouettes and seeing not just trees, but survival.

title: Reflections on Suquamish and Nisqually Canoe Journeys
content: Reflections on Suquamish and Nisqually Canoe Journeys Country United States agnes Wed, 09/02/2026 - 09:21 Issues Languages and Cultures Program 5 Main Image By Phoebe Farris (Powhatan-Pamunkey) Annual inter-Tribal celebrations involving Pacific Northwest Indigenous communities were sparked by the 1989 Paddle to Seattle event, held as part of Washington State’s Centennial celebration. Since then, many canoe journeys from Canada, Alaska, and Washington State have voyaged from their traditional homelands to states in the Pacific Northwest. These canoe journeys have grown to about 100 participating canoe families from Native communities around the world, including the Māori from Aotearoa/New Zealand and other Indigenous Peoples from Japan, Mexico, South America, and Guam. After morning arrivals at the Tribal hosts’ shorelands, families request permission to land, offering prayers and short speeches in their traditional languages. Evening activities involve more prayers, music, dancing, gifting, and honoring. These ceremonies are designated as Protocol and can be in a longhouse-type environment or in an outdoor, tent-like enclosure. Inside Nisqually Protocol Tent. The host Tribe receives gifts from the participating families as a token of gratitude, and traditional foods are served during breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Participating Tribes share and explain their cultural practices and request that non-Native guests honor these practices by standing when asked during certain prayers and by refraining from photographing some dance performances, specifically those featuring dancers wearing large, wooden face masks. The first canoe journey I observed was hosted by the Suquamish Tribe from July 27-29. Indoor activities took place at the House of Awakened Culture in Suquamish, Washington. At this particular landing, the ocean was right below the Protocol building. Phoebe Farris with Cynthia Lozier. On my first day at Suquamish, I met Chaplain Cynthia Lozier (Muckleshoot and Puyallup), a retired Army veteran whose role as Chaplain is to comfort grieving Indigenous families during funerals, at hospitals, and in home or hospice settings. Her husband, Franklin Ross (Puyallup and Muckleshoot), is also a veteran. Lozier sang songs in her traditional language, and her husband drummed during Protocol. Chaplain Cynthia Lozier (Muckleshoot and Puyallup) and husband Franklin Ross (Puyallup and Muckleshoot). That same day, I met an Elder named Leona Canuta (Pacheedaht First Nations), who asked me to take photos of her family’s canoe, “People of the Sea Foam”—also the name of their family drum group—and her daughter, Emily Harmony (Pacheedaht), her nephew, Mike Smith, and her grandchildren. She said that Professor Sarah Wright-Cardinal at Northwest University helped secure grants for carving canoes from Macawmah Land. I ran into her the next week at Nisqually and watched her dance with other women at Protocol, in their red-and-white regalia. Leona Canuta (Pachedahtt) standing next to her family’s canoe. Phoebe Farris with Aimee Phair. While wandering around Suquamish, I met Aimee Phair (Lummi Nation), who has tattoos on her face, neck, arms, and hands. She briefed me on the differences between tattoo shops that use electronic tools and artificial dyes and those that use nature-based dyes and no electrical machinery. She explained that the colors are sometimes less bright and don’t last as long as commercial tattoos, but the pain is minimal, similar to the very mild sensation of an acupuncture needle. Aimee Phair showing her hand tattoos. Later in the evening, Phair danced in Protocol and said she was heading to participate as a puller for the Muckleshoot canoe landing in Muckleshoot territory. I would see her again at Nisqually, where she discussed the Lummi nonprofit film “Children of the Setting Sun” and encouraged me to visit the nearby nature reserve dedicated to the late Billy Frank Jr. (Nisqually), a social-justice fishing-rights advocate. Calina Lawrence (Suquamish) with “Looking Eagle” tattoo. I also ran into an old friend, Calina Lawrence (Suquamish), whom I had not seen in years. She has a shoulder tattoo titled “Looking Eagle,” created by tattoo artist Kyle Twiddy (Skokomish). It is called Looking Eagle because by moving his head fast, he can see in all directions and understand all perspectives. Canoe landing at Sequalitchew Creek. A few days later, I witnessed the canoe landing “Medicine Creek Potlatch: Healing Through Our Waters,” hosted by the Nisqually Tribe from July 31 to August 5. The landings took place on Sequalitchew Creek and involved a one-and-a-half-mile walk down a trail from the local park to the water landing. The Protocol ceremonies took place inside a large tent on the Nisqually reservation, several miles from the creek. Per custom, the host Tribe was honored and gifted by the various canoe families. Guests observed traditional dancing and were offered meals. In addition to the beautiful surroundings and the excitement of watching colorfully decorated canoes landing, the experience was marked by the warmth of the people involved—the pullers (rowers), the performers, the volunteers, the Tribal staff, and the visitors and guests from all over Turtle Island and beyond. Canoe landing at Sequalitchew Creek. I met John Halliday (enrolled Muckleshoot, Duwamish, Yakama, and Warm Springs descent), a visually impaired artist and retired BIA administrator. Halliday’s artist name is Coyote. He was introduced to me by his caretaker, Lucas Patricio, also an artist, whose Tribal heritage is southwest Pueblo. They explained some of the techniques involved in making the traditional vest Halliday was wearing. John Halliday (Muckleshoot). At both landing sites, the host Tribes provided campsites with outdoor showers and toilets. For the first time in my life, I engaged in activities I will probably never repeat: helping set up a tent, crawling on my knees in the dirt, digging holes, pulling out squiggly earthworms, and nailing down posts—all while destroying my newly manicured nails. It was sort of fun, but I am an urban Indian and stayed at the Suquamish Tribal Casino Hotel and two other local hotels. I would like to express special gratitude to Kelvin Penn, a musician whose day job is managing sound equipment and other technical responsibilities at events like the Nisqually Protocol. Penn respectfully stood up for the Blessing the Floor prayers and all other significant prayers, making sure that the entire film crew turned off their cameras when requested. Protocol events were livestreamed and shown in the Elders’ tent, but certain activities were not allowed to be filmed, and Penn was on the case. I would also like to thank Cheebo Frazier (Nisqually), Tribal Council Vicechairwoman; Kyles Gemmell (Suquamish), Cultural Activities Coordinator; and Hazle Pacquette (Suquamish), Activities and Events Planner, for graciously responding to all of my emails, text messages, and phone calls regarding press passes, transportation, and housing. And all the volunteer cooks for the free salmon, crabs, elk stew, bison burgers, fresh fruit and vegetables, strong coffee, homemade pastries, and bottles of water available day and night that kept us nourished. --Phoebe Farris (Powhatan-Pamunkey descent) is Contributing Arts Editor for the Cultural Survival Quarterly magazine. An art critic, curator, author, and photographer, she has written extensively on Indigenous visual, literary, and performing arts for over two decades. Farris is also a Professor Emerita of Art and Design at Purdue University and has curated and contributed to exhibitions highlighting Native and global Indigenous artists. Her work bridges scholarship, creative practice, and advocacy, amplifying Indigenous voices in contemporary art and media. Top photo: Suquamish canoe landing site. All photos by Phoebe Farris.

title: Indigenous plants offer Ghanaians an alternative to costly Western medicine
content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” This series offers insight into the lives and experiences of Indigenous peoples to build connections across regions, center Indigenous experiences, and share the stories of leaders, activists, community members, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.
The traditional medicine market in Ghana, West Africa, is thriving, offering countless cures passed down by generations of Indigenous Ga and Twi tribes. As prices for Western pharmaceuticals and Western medical care rise, Ghanaians are relying on the medical remedies they have always turned to: plants.
Dr. Kofi Donkor, deputy director of the Center for Plant Medicine Research, and an expert on the medical benefits of many traditional Ghanaian plants, noted:
The traditional medicine practitioners themselves, for them, it is a profession. It is something that has been passed down from generation to generation to them. So they know how to use plants properly. Indeed, let me admit that for us in research, our primary source of knowledge, and in botanical research is from the traditional medicine practitioners. It is the knowledge from the practitioners that we try to validate using scientific methods. What we are doing in research is basically trying to validate the traditional knowledge that we get.
Plant-based medicine is a big business in Ghana
In rural Ghana, women start picking medicinal herbs from both the bush and cultivated plots early in the morning to sell fresh in the capital city of Accra. By mid-morning, they’ve set up their booths piled high with fresh vines, leaves, stems, and bark to sell to customers.
Plant-based medicine is a big business in Ghana. The Center for Plant Medicine Research, created by the Ghanaian government in 1976, works with raw plant material to create natural products and treat patients. Their outpatient clinic sees roughly 16,000 patients a month.
About 60 to 70 percent of the Ghanaian population depends on traditional medicine markets for their medical care, according to a 2023 study in Frontiers in Pharmacology.
Donkor says many people in rural Ghana rely on traditional plant knowledge for three reasons: Accessibility, cost, and familiarity. In an interview with Global Voices, he explained:
Indeed the data shows that in most developing countries, in rural communities, traditional medicine forms 80 percent of primary health care… It actually contributes largely to us trying to meet the goals of universal health care.
The deep green forests and meadows of rural Ghana have been home to rural villagers for many years, so many villagers are already familiar with the various plants that can heal a disease. Living near these forests makes plant-based medicine an easy, cheaper option for treating disease in rural Ghana, when Western pharmacies are too expensive or far away.
Donkor said many rural Ghanaians already know the right plants to treat a problem, and may only visit an herbal practitioner when a more complicated disease is present. He said:
So sometimes when you are sick you don’t necessarily have to go to the traditional medicine practitioner in the community to get medication. You just go to your backyard and you know this herb is for malaria, this herb is for typhoid, this herb improves your hemoglobin levels, and you just pluck some, you boil, and you drink.
Ongoing research on West African plants
Botanical researchers at the Center for Plant Medicine Research are currently studying a full panel of West African plants for their ability to cure diseases, including a green shrub that has shown promising treatment against prostate cancer (croton membranaceous).
When asked whether consumers can trust the plants sold in Accra’s open-air markets, Donkor cautioned that though vendors are probably selling the right plants, the dosage is really important. If a practitioner knows what they are doing and prescribes the right amount of a plant, it can be a powerful cure for the client.
Featured in the above video is Patience, a plant healer who lives in Accra and regularly treats friends and family with traditional plants for many illnesses, including malaria, yeast infections, and colds. Patience shows how the common mother-in-law tongue plant (Dracaena trifasciata) can be prepared as a cold bath. She advises users to make a tea bath from the plant’s leaves, and then let it soak into the skin without drying oneself. She says the botanical brew calms anxiety and helps with good sleep. Spiritually, Patience says this plant can keep bad people away from one’s home if you keep it by the door.
The scientific research at the Center for Plant Medicine Research, which draws on traditional medicine knowledge, adds legitimacy and international attention to the deep Indigenous knowledge of these plants. As Western drug costs and gas prices continue to rise in Ghana and across West Africa, the traditional medicine market can provide a sustainable source of natural healing for the population.

title: New York's Muslims reclaim their city 25 years after 9/11 attacks
content: Asad Dandia was eight when he watched the Sept 11, 2001 attacks on television at his Pakistani-immigrant parents’ home in New York. Then came the backlash — years of Islamophobia as Americans processed attacks that had killed nearly 3,000 people. There was anger, suspicion and worse. At 19, Dandia experienced a police informant posing as a friend to infiltrate his family home, part of a now-disgraced surveillance effort purportedly seeking to detect extremism. Today, though, the 33-year-old historian finds a New York transformed: one with its first Muslim mayor, public prayers in Times Square and new mosques rising across the city. Asad Dandia conducts a guided tour about Malcolm X in the Harlem area of New York on Aug 22, 2026. — AFP “Twenty-five years after 9/11, we mourn and we grieve what happened, and at the same time, we recognise that I am not responsible for what happened,” he told AFP. “I don’t deserve to be targeted for what happened, and I am as much of a New Yorker as anybody else in that respect,” said Dandia, who leads walking tours centred on the city’s Muslim communities. Islamophobia surged in the United States after the 2001 attacks in which militants hijacked airliners and flew them into Manhattan’s World Trade Centre and the Pentagon outside Washington. A fourth plane crashed into a Pennsylvania field after a passenger revolt. Muslims reported increased public assaults and harassment, and some stopped wearing visual markers such as hijabs in a bid to conceal their religion. Meanwhile, US authorities monitored Muslims by requiring thousands of men and boys to register with the government, leading to many being deported from the country. “Everyone was in such fear,” said Mohammed Razvi, a native Pakistani who founded the Council of Peoples Organisation non-profit to support Muslims in New York after 9/11. “We had gunshots fired in our neighbourhood by individuals who felt that we were responsible,” he added. Razvi said he started introducing himself as “Mo” after 9/11 to avoid the stigma he encountered when saying “Mohammad”. “Muslims trying to live the American dream were being blamed for something they had nothing to do with or even control,” he said. ‘Terrifying’ In New York, police began surveilling hundreds of Muslims as part of their counterterrorism strategy, often targeting people without evidence of wrongdoing. Dandia experienced this as a 19-year-old college student, when a young Bangladeshi man joined a mutual aid charity he had started. The pair grew close: sharing meals, playing sports and even sleeping at Dandia’s home. But seven months later, the man revealed that he was an NYPD informant sent to monitor Dandia and his community. “It was heartbreaking, but it was also terrifying,” he recalled. “My relationship with the world around me shifted underneath my feet.” After his ordeal, Dandia and rights groups won a landmark legal settlement that restricted the NYPD from launching similar surveillance programmes and established a watchdog to monitor the force. For Gadier Abbas, an attorney with the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the NYPD programme was the prime example of the “anti-Muslim hysteria” that followed 9/11. But today, Abbas said, “there is a lot of hope”. “You see American Muslims in every single walk of life, almost at every single level, and that’s a testament to the vibrancy of the community.” ‘Power’ New York will soon boast the largest mosque in the state — one of more than 100 added since 2001 in New York — while Muslims are a rising cultural and political force. Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who took his oath of office on the Holy Quran, has become the new face of American leftist politics. Still, Islamophobia persists in the city where around nine per cent of the population is Muslim. In March, a far-right influencer organised a “Stop the Islamic Takeover of New York City” rally outside the mayor’s residence. Meanwhile, a conservative senator has said Mamdani should be sent to Guantanamo Bay, the US detention camp best known for holding 9/11 suspects. Some relatives of September 11 victims have called for Mamdani — an avid supporter of Palestinian rights — to skip this year’s 9/11 memorial, while other families have defended the mayor. Dandia acknowledged Islamophobia had not disappeared, but he was optimistic about how far New York’s Muslim community has come. “I’ve seen the growth of our institutional power, but also the recognition by other New Yorkers who are not Muslim, that we are all part of this city together,” he said. “I think that’s really valuable because, you know, Rome was not built overnight, and it was not built by one person or one group of people. It was built by the community.”

title: School in northern Vietnam marries modern design with highland ethnic heritage
content:
The school, located in Muong Khuong Commune, will serve as the central venue for the nationwide ceremony marking the inauguration of new schools and the opening of the 2026-27 academic year on Saturday.
Lao Cai Province will put into operation boarding schools for elementary and secondary students in the border communes of Pha Long, Y Ty and A Mu Sung the same day.
Mong Thi Duyen, principal of Muong Khuong Elementary and Secondary Boarding School, told Tuoi Tre (Youth) on Thursday that preparations for the inauguration and opening ceremony had essentially been completed.
The school covers nearly five hectares and comprises nine integrated buildings, providing facilities for studying and boarding for 980 students.
The project carried a price tag of over VND215 billion (US$8.2 million).
It is one of the province’s major education projects and is expected to bring significant improvements to the care and development of young people living in the province's border areas.
What sets the project apart is not only its scale of investment but also its approach to architecture, which places the cultural identity of ethnic communities in the highlands at the heart of the design.
The school draws inspiration from the cultural heritage of the Hmong and Dao peoples.
Traditional brocade patterns and the vivid colors of their traditional clothing have been incorporated into the contemporary architecture.
Its sports grounds are designed to evoke a highland market, creating a learning environment that combines modern educational facilities with a strong sense of local cultural identity.
The school spans nearly five hectares and comprises nine integrated buildings. Photo: Nam Tran / Tuoi Tre
As a boarding school, the institution has had to prepare not only classrooms, equipment and teaching staff, but also accommodation, meals and daily living arrangements to ensure that students can quickly settle into their new surroundings.
Ahead of the new school year, the school has helped students prepare textbooks and notebooks and distributed essential learning supplies.
It has also organized a range of extracurricular activities, including cultural and musical performances and clubs featuring the traditional folk music of the Hmong, Bo Y, Nung and Pa Di communities.
Students are mainly from the ethnic minority groups of Mong, Dao, Bo Y, Nung and Pa Di. Photo: Nam Tran / Tuoi Tre
Through these activities, students had the opportunity not only to preserve their own cultural heritage but also to learn about the traditions and identities of other ethnic groups represented at the school.
The school has big classrooms and modern equipment. Photo: Nam Tran / Tuoi Tre
Students play on the sports grounds. Photo: Nam Tran / Tuoi Tre
