title: A 76-year wait to bring a fallen father home
content:
LAI CHÂU — For 76 years, Hà Thị È waited to learn where her father was buried.
She was a teenager when Hà Văn Sinh was killed in 1950 while serving as a political officer with a local militia unit in what is now Lai Châu Province.
She was 93 when she finally stood before his grave.
The moment came after soldiers searching for the remains of fallen fighters discovered a small glass bottle buried alongside a set of remains.
Inside were a few pieces of information that helped investigators identify the dead man as Sinh, originally from Mường Kim Commune, Than Uyên District, Nghĩa Lộ Province, now part of Mường Kim Commune in Lai Châu Province.
“Every piece of information about a martyr is connected to a story, a life and a family that has waited for decades,” said Colonel Trần Thanh Bình, deputy political commissar of the Lai Châu Provincial Military Command.
On July 26, ahead of War Invalids and Martyrs’ Day, authorities formally confirmed Sinh’s identity and handed the decision to his daughter.
È was determined to see her father’s grave. But age and frailty meant she could not make the climb herself. Soldiers took turns carrying her up hundreds of stone steps to the hillside cemetery.
When she reached the grave and saw her father’s name on the headstone, she broke down in tears.
Colonel Bình recalled that È touched the headstone with her hand before embracing the grave.
“For her, at an age when she is nearing the end of her life, this was the fulfilment of a long-held wish,” he said.
For the soldiers involved in the search, the scene was a poignant reminder that behind every unidentified grave is a family that may have been waiting for decades, or even an entire lifetime.
A race against time
The discovery came as the country steps up efforts to locate and identify the remains of soldiers killed in past conflicts. A Government initiative, the 500 Day and Night Campaign, is intensifying the search for, recovery and identification of martyrs’ remains ahead of the 80th anniversary of War Invalids and Martyrs’ Day in 2027.
The campaign aims to locate and recover about 7,000 sets of remains, carry out DNA testing on about 18,000 samples and establish a genetic database of relatives of fallen soldiers. It also includes the clearance of unexploded bombs and mines in key areas.
Lai Châu, a mountainous province in the country's northwest, has already completed one of its main targets. By early June, authorities had collected all samples required for DNA testing under the provincial plan.
But DNA is only one part of the process.
“Collecting a DNA sample is an important step, but it is not the final goal,” said Colonel Bình.
The ultimate aim was to combine DNA results with military records, witness accounts and other evidence to establish the identity of each fallen soldier and inform their families, he said.
That task is particularly difficult in Lai Châu. The province's steep and fragmented terrain has changed significantly since the wars. Former battlefields have been transformed by erosion, natural changes and infrastructure projects. In many places, little remains to show that fighting once took place there.
The people who witnessed those events are also disappearing. Many potential witnesses are now elderly, while their memories have faded. Historical documents are scattered among different archives and records do not always agree.
In some cases, investigators have only a name, the military unit to which a soldier belonged or a vague indication of where fighting took place.
From there, search teams must reconstruct what happened.
“These cases require patience and the cross-checking of information from many sources,” Colonel Bình said. “We cannot rush the process.”
Every clue matters
Provincial authorities follow a simple principle of investigating information as it emerges and continuing the search as long as there is evidence or a possibility of finding the remains.
Local residents can play an important role. A seemingly insignificant detail, a remembered location, an old story or information passed down through generations, can become the clue that leads investigators to a grave.
For the search teams, difficult terrain and the passage of time are not reasons to stop.
Every unidentified soldier represents a family that has not yet received an answer.
Lai Châu Province plans to continue reviewing areas where remains may be located, collecting and comparing information, searching for witnesses and examining historical records. Authorities are also encouraging residents to come forward with information.
“Every piece of information, no matter how small, must be received, verified and handled seriously,” Colonel Bình said.
A single clue can mean days of searching and months of checking records, but È's story shows why the effort matters. After 76 years, her father has a name and her family finally knows where he lies.
“We understand that families have been waiting for decades,” Colonel Bình said. “For every family, knowing where their loved one is and whether they have been brought home is an immense wish.”
Many families are still waiting, and soldiers continue to search the mountains for traces of those who died generations ago. Every grave identified brings one more name home. — VNS

title: Okoko Item Celebrates Age-long New Yam Festival
content:
Latest Headlines
Okoko Item Celebrates Age-long New Yam Festival
Boniface Okoro in Umuahia
On Sunday, August 24, 2026, the LA School field in Okoko Item, Bende Local Government Area of Abia State, turned into a living canvas of colour, rhythm and purpose. Sons and daughters of Okoko Item, home and abroad, converged for the 2026 New Yam Festival — a gathering that blended thanksgiving, identity and community strategy in true Igbo fashion.
Okoko Item is one of the principal towns in Item Clan, the largest clan in Bende LGA and a community with deep cultural roots. For centuries, Item people have built their life around farming, self-help and strong town unions. Okoko Item carries that same DNA: a farming people, proud of heritage, and committed to “home first.”
The festival opened with age grades taking centre stage. Over 10 age grades, resplendent in uniform, marched in turns. There were cultural beats, medley, from many of the age grades: ogene, and ekwe, masquerades, and the symbolic cutting of new yam – the ancient rite that signals God and the ancestors have blessed the harvest.
Only after the traditional rulers and the elders cut and blessed the yam did the feasting begin. For Okoko people, it was not just food. It is a covenant: “There will be food in every home this year.”
More than a festival, New Yam is Okoko’s annual homecoming. From Aba, Umuahia, Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt and beyond, the indigenes returned. The field was divided by age grades, but united by one identity.
The Okoko Item Development Association used the platform to preach peace, review projects, and raise funds.
As President General, Chief Ogechi Kamkam, noted in his welcome speech, the day was about unity and peace. For a diaspora community, it is the one day the scattered family becomes one again.
This year, the cutting of yam doubled as a development drive. Each age grade made financial contributions toward community projects.
The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate in Abia State, Dr. Kelechi Anosike, was honoured as ‘Ezinwa Okoko Item’, illustrious grandson who has done the community proud led the charge. He donated N2.5 million during the yam cutting and N500,000 toward setting up and equipping the community vigilante.
Anosike’s mother is from Okoko and he attended primary and secondary school there.
As a special guest of honour, Anosike said “I am excited to return as a special guest to cut the new yam,” he said, adding, “My formative years started from here, Okoko Item. The new yam festival promotes not only our culture, it also promotes our identity and entrepreneurship spirit of every Igboman.
“Okoko people are great farmers. Over the years, they produce the food we eat in Abia State and beyond.
“As a government, we will promote our rich cultural heritage. Tourism will have a place in our government,” Anosike declared.
Anosike framed his governorship ambition around food and welfare. “If I become governor, my administration will promote agriculture and farming. There will be enough food, no Abia person will be hungry,” he declared.
He promised a “new cooperative economy” using well-structured cooperatives to give farmers, traders, artisans, women and youths access to affordable financing, SME loans, training and mentoring.
“Our objective is not simply to feed Abia. We want Abia to produce enough food to feed our people and generate surplus for trade,” he said.
He also noted that PDP has been repositioned ahead of 2027, describing it as a “new party, New mindset, new direction.”
He appealed to the people to see his ambition as their project, promising unprecedented development projects in Item.
Chairman of the occasion, HRM Eze Dr. David Kingston Okey-Dede, Eze Ndigbo 1 of Maitama, Abuja, added a political charge: “Okoko Item should present a single candidate in future elections through a political forum.” For him, Anosike is their son and therefore their own.”
All hands must be on deck to deliver Anosike 100 per cent in the nine villages of Item for governor.
This gave Anosike a massive boost and endorsement because Item has the largest voting bloc in Bende LGA with three big political wards.
Anosike further three light to guide the people that all those who gave PDP bad name in Abia State have left to join other parties. “This is a new PDP that their son leads in Abia State.”
Beyond politics, the festival sold Okoko Item to the world. The display of culture, the hospitality, the food — roasted yam, is a draw for visitors and a reminder of Item’s place in Igbo heritage. For tourists and indigenes alike, it is proof that culture can drive both pride and economy.
As dusk fell, the message was clear. The Okoko Item New Yam Festival 2026 was thanksgiving to God, a celebration of culture, a strategy meeting for development, a reunion for family, and a political rallying point — all in one.
In the words of the community: the yam is new, the unity is renewed, and the future is being planted today.

title: ‘Unlock your DNA’: More young S’poreans taking up dialect classes
content:
‘Unlock your DNA’: More young S’poreans taking up dialect classes
- More Singaporeans are learning Chinese dialects to reconnect with their heritage and strengthen family bonds.
- Clan associations report rising enrolments in dialect classes, with creative, fun methods used to make learning engaging and culturally rich.
- The government supports dialect learning alongside Mandarin, promoting cultural roots and local Chinese identity through various activities and programmes.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – When Eldred Wee started learning Hainanese at the Hainan Hwee Kuan in December 2025, the 34-year-old had practically no grasp of the language despite both his parents’ strong fluency.
His parents, who are both Hainanese, divorced when he was around nine, and he grew up speaking English with his mother.
“My dialect and culture were never handed to me.
“I am choosing as an adult, for myself and for my son, to rebuild a generational link that was broken,” said the entrepreneur.
Wee wants his four-year-old son, Eden, to know Hainanese. At home, he makes it a point to use simple Hainanese phrases like “boh gai dit” (thank you).
“My motivation is identity, intergenerational bonding and belonging,” he said.
The film Dear You may have sparked renewed interest in Teochew and dialects in general, but clan associations across Singapore told The Straits Times their dialect classes have become more popular in recent years.
Learners, who used to be mainly middle-aged and older, have become much younger, with many in their 20s to 40s.
For instance, Kong Chow Wui Koon’s (KCWK) advanced Cantonese class sizes doubled between 2022 and 2026, while the Singapore Hokkien Huay Kuan (SHHK) Cultural Academy has seen participation for its Hokkien classes jump about 15 per cent over the past three years.
Meanwhile, Char Yong (Dabu) Association started its Hakka class in April, with 19 students. Its second run has been expanded to 26 students, and there are three people on the waiting list.
Veteran radio newscaster Nigel Lim, who has been teaching Teochew at the Teochew Poit Ip Huay Kuan since 2003, noted the rising enrolment and the clear demographic shift.
“China has grown stronger, and more are seeking roots. Many are realising that speaking their dialect helps them connect with overseas relatives and even Chinese business partners,” he said.
For 20-year-old Joshua Loh, it was a Hakka song sung by a musician in a Shanghai cafe that inspired him to take up lessons at the Char Yong (Dabu) Association in 2026.
“He (the musician) told me something that really stuck: If you speak Hakka, you unlock your DNA. Learning Hakka has given me a sense of grounding, and I hope more young people get to experience that too,” said the polytechnic student.
He also hopes this can strengthen his relationship with his grandparents, whom he visits every other week.
“They would correct me if my pronunciation was different from what they grew up with,” he said. “It has become a nice bonding ritual between us.”
Accessible routes to cultural roots
Lim, the Teochew instructor, said the Government’s recent easing of its policy on dialect content is actually good for Singaporeans’ use of Mandarin.
In his Mandarin speech at the National Day Rally on Aug 23, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced that there would no longer be a cap on the number of screenings of dialect films, as long as a Mandarin-dubbed version is available.
He also spotlighted clan associations’ efforts to promote dialects here through classes and cultural activities, and said the Government will continue to support these efforts.
While the Government previously discouraged dialects to streamline communication across diverse Chinese groups, Lim believes dialects have the ability to unify, rather than fragment.
“Learning a Chinese dialect can actually boost one’s Mandarin, as mastering a dialect’s complex tones and structures makes Mandarin easier to grasp,” he added.
There are also students like Tan Song Ya, whose interest in Cantopop and Hong Kong dramas prompted her to enrol in a Cantonese class at KCWK in July.
“Perhaps I should be learning my own dialect, Hokkien, after this,” said the 34-year-old engineer, who grew up speaking English and Mandarin.
A budding interest in one’s dialect can also become an abiding interest in Chinese history and culture, noted Kong Chow Cultural Centre head and Cantonese instructor Wong Chee Meng.
“For the class in Chinese history and culture, many students enjoy learning classical poetry, especially Tang poetry, in Cantonese, because the richness in rhymes and tonal patterns often cannot be replicated in Mandarin,” he noted.
Clan associations here said they are experimenting with different ways to build on this momentum of interest in dialects.
For instance, the central plot device of Dear You is qiaopi, which were letters sent home by overseas Chinese along with remittance money. The letters were written with Chinese ink and traditional script, which flowed vertically from top to bottom.
SHHK has since incorporated this into its dialect programmes. It also organises intergenerational activities where youth and seniors are grouped together to make traditional food such as bak chang (glutinous rice dumplings) and to learn classic Hokkien songs together, said its marketing manager Jeremiah Soh.
Tapping into Singaporeans’ gastronomic obsessions, many of the lessons also touch on the dishes unique to each dialect group.
“Food is especially effective because it brings people together. We discuss dishes such as Hainanese chicken rice, kaya and yi bua, a Hainanese glutinous rice snack,” said Hou Wenxue, a teacher at Hainan Hwee Kuan.
“These dishes give students a way to understand the history and environment behind the culture.”
Meanwhile, KCWK’s elementary-level Cantonese class focuses on phrases for real-life situations, such as ordering food in a restaurant.
Lim said dialects also offer a stress-free way to access and appreciate one’s culture and traditions as there are no exams.
“There are also no strict standards to follow, as Singapore’s dialects are not ‘pure’ and have been influenced by other languages here.”
Hakka instructor Wong Chin Fee agreed. “Even in Dabu county, there are variations of the same Hakka dialect,” he said.
“I always tell my students: Just speak up and don’t be afraid of making mistakes.”
Students told ST that besides tapping on food, music and pop culture, what will sustain interest in dialects here is having more opportunities to use these languages in daily life.
This can include having more events where everyone attempts to speak in the same dialect, whether they are karaoke and movie nights or cooking classes.
“If dialect becomes something that we encounter more naturally in our everyday lives, I think more young people would be curious enough to give it a try,” said polytechnic student Alexis Foo, 18, who is learning Hakka.
“Sometimes, preserving a culture starts simply by making it easier for people to participate in it.”

title: In Odisha, drum-making traditions echo the rhythms of farm life
content:
In Pahandi, a small village in Bijepur block of Odisha’s Bargarh district, the rhythm of a traditional baja or drum begins long before it reaches a festival ground. It begins with the earth.
Of the roughly 530 households in the village, most depend on agriculture, growing paddy, millets, green gram, ground nuts and other crops. But for eight households of the Chamar community, making traditional drums and other percussion instruments has supplemented their livelihoods for generations.
For Judhisthir Sagar, locally known as “Kutru”, the two occupations have always existed alongside each other. He inherited the craft of making baja from his ancestors, along with the practice of farming.
“Making drums and musical instruments is our identity,” said Sagar while tightening the strips of a newly made mrudanga, a two-headed percussion instrument widely used in traditional music. “We have been doing it for generations. It is our livelihood. We are proud to continue it.”
Apart from the mrudanga, other percussion instruments made in Pahandi include the godi mrudanga, udand khol, madol khol, dubi-tabla, pankuch, dhol and nisan. Each has a different shape and sound and a place in the cultural life of western Odisha.
From soil and hide to sound
The craft begins with the khol, the body of the instrument.
The soil used to prepare the khol is carefully chosen. According to craftsman Baisakhu Rana, red or black soil without stones or other impurities is preferred.
The other essential material is animal hide, usually from goats or cattle. The hides are sourced from various parts of Odisha and, at times, from outside the state.
The process brings together materials closely connected to rural life. Soil comes from the agricultural landscape, livestock provide an important raw material, and the knowledge of transforming these materials into instruments has passed from one generation to another.
Once the basic structure is ready, the drum is decorated.
Amitabh Naik, 40, has been making traditional baja for more than six years. He learnt the craft from his paternal uncle and uses Sambalpuri printed canvas, bamboo strips, coloured threads and soil to decorate the instruments.
“My uncle taught me this work,” he said. “I have been doing it for more than six years now. I enjoy making the instruments, especially when I see them being used in our festivals.”
The connection with Bargarh’s textile tradition is hard to miss. The district has a large community of handloom weavers. Sambalpuri textiles are among Odisha’s Geographical Indication-registered products.
In Pahandi, that textile aesthetic becomes part of a musical instrument. Here, agriculture, livestock, textile traditions and music meet in the making of a baja.
Depending on its type, an instrument can take three to five days to complete. Its price varies according to the quality of the hide, its sound and the intricacy of its decoration.
Sagar says instruments made in Pahandi have travelled to districts of Odisha and other parts of India. Some have even reached Australia and Singapore through word-of-mouth orders and references.
But the value of these instruments goes beyond the markets they reach.
Instruments with a place in village life
A baja acquires meaning when it is played.
The mrudanga, godi mrudanga and udand khol accompany kirtans and nama yajnas, devotional chanting of the names of god. The madol khol is used during Karamsani Puja at harvest time, while the dhol and nisan accompany the Dalkhai dance and festivals such as Sital Sasthi, at which the wedding of Shiva and Parvati is re-enacted; Nuakhai, which celebrates the harvest; and Durga Puja, which marks the victory of the goddess Durga over the demon Mahishasura.
These occasions are closely woven into the social and agricultural calendar of western Odisha.
Nuakhai, for instance, is associated with the new harvest and the sharing of newly harvested food. Music and rituals bring communities together during these occasions, making the instruments an important part of village life.
Bargarh has a rich folk music and dance tradition that includes Sambalpuri, Sanchar, Pala, Khanjani Bhajana, Dulduli, Karamsani and Danda Nrutya. The traditional percussion instruments made by artisans such as those in Pahandi provide the rhythm for many such performances.
From village workshops to distant stages
Naresh Bhoi, a young folk musician from Bargarh, is a member of the Kalagram Adi Dhun Group, which promotes Odisha’s traditional musical instruments through performances. The group was founded by Rabi Ratan Sahu, an artist from Padampur in Bargarh who promotes folk culture through music. Sahu has been a research fellow with the Ministry of Culture and a general council member of the Odisha Sangeet Academy.
The group has performed at Rabindra Mandap in Bhubaneswar and Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium in New Delhi, as well as in Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh.
“Traditional instruments help carry the sound of western Odisha to audiences who may be unfamiliar with our folk traditions,” said Sahu. “A baja does not end its journey at the workshop. An artisan makes it, a performer brings it to life, and a festival gives it meaning.”
Keeping a tradition in motion
Traditional crafts face pressure from changing lifestyles, mass-produced alternatives and shifting market preferences. However, Pahandi’s drum makers continue to find work because their instruments remain part of rituals, festivals and performances.
Their knowledge is also sustained within families. Older artisans teach younger members, while performers continue to use the instruments in new settings.
The village remains rooted in agriculture. Its fields provide food and livelihoods, while its workshops sustain other form of rural knowledge. Soil, livestock, bamboo, textiles and inherited skills come together in objects that eventually become part of a festival, ritual or performance.
That makes Pahandi’s story larger than the survival of a traditional craft. It is a story of how different parts of rural life remain connected.
Some of the information for this article was provided by Abhishek Singha, who works as a District Project Coordinator with the Watershed Support Services and Activities Network, Bhubaneswar.
Pritesh Sundar Roy, Susant Sekhar Choudhury, Abhijit Mohanty and Bikash Das work for the Watershed Support Services and Activities Network.

title: '1,000 Martyrs Cup' — With joy and grief, Palestinian football marks return
content: Palestinian sports commentator Khalil Jadallah has spent the past three years mourning the athletes killed in Israel’s war on Gaza. As Palestinian football officially resumed this week, his return to the stadium proved bittersweet. Palestinian professional sports were brought to a halt in October 2023 when Israel began its military onslaught on Gaza, in which 1,014 Palestinian athletes were killed, according to the Palestinian Football Association’s tally. On Friday, Jadallah was back at Faisal Al-Husseini Stadium in Al-Ram in the West Bank to call the opening match of the first tournament organised by the association in three years. Though long awaited, the event was marked by contradicting emotions for Jadallah: “a feeling of joy at returning after such an absence, but also a feeling of loss.” “We lost players… fans, administrators and referees,” Jadallah told AFP. ‘1,000 Martyrs Cup’ The football association named the comeback tournament — which includes over 200 teams from the occupied West Bank, Gaza, and refugee camps in Lebanon — the “1,000 Martyrs Cup”. Throughout the war, Palestinian football authorities have accused Israel of killing football players and damaging Gaza’s sporting infrastructure. Israel has claimed 12 Palestinian football figures that it killed in Gaza, including a FIFA-registered referee, were members of armed groups, an allegation the football association has rejected. Large numbers of Palestinian security forces were deployed for the event, an unusual sight in the town more accustomed to Israeli military raids. Before the game, pitting Jabal Al-Mukaber Club against Shabab Al-Khaleel SC, children carried a Palestinian flag wrapped to resemble a dead body, before unfurling it across the centre circle as a band played the Palestinian national anthem. The sport authority also unveiled a memorial bearing the names of the killed Palestinian athletes outside the stadium, which stands in Al-Ram, not far from the West Bank separation barrier. Samir Issa, a prominent former player and veteran manager who had coached both teams, watched from the stands as the game kicked off. “Football has become more important than politics today,” he said. “The proof of that is the following the World Cup has had.” “Sport in general is the culture of the people,” he added, saying that Palestinians had “the right to practice sport normally and in all its forms, not just football”. At the 10-minute, 14-second mark, the referee ordered the game to stop for a minute of silence for the dead before the crowd grew loud again. “Football returns to Palestine,” read electronic screens around the stadium. Thousands of mainly young people attended the game, with families, women and children seated in a separate section. Maysan Suleiman, a 35-year-old from Al-Ram, said she came to commemorate “the martyrs”. ‘Football returns to Palestine’ “I don’t support either team,” she said. “I came to support the idea [of the tournamen] itself. After all, they’re all sons of Palestine.” The tournament opened simultaneously in Gaza, where Israeli strikes have left much of the territory in ruins and some football fields have been turned into makeshift camps for those displaced by the war. The opening match there was held in Deir al-Balah between Khadamat Rafah and Shabab Rafah as fans sat on plastic chairs around the small field lined with palm trees. “Football represented life for us before the war, and after the war the lives of players stopped altogether,” said Khalil Matar, a Khadamat Rafah player. Matar said holding the cup simultaneously in the West Bank, Gaza and refugee camps in Lebanon reflected “national unity” for Palestinians. But the West Bank teams are set to face major logistical hurdles as they travel between cities and Israeli military checkpoints in the occupied territory. “Still, we’re determined to continue sporting activities and developing our young people,” said Abdullah Abu Ghassan of the Shabab Jaba team competing in the tournament.

title: 'Ever evolving': PNG's unifying language celebrated in Tok Pisin Wik
content:
Members of Wellington's Papua New Guinea community say Tok Pisin is a versatile language that many people can use with relative ease.
Tok Pisin Wik is underway this week with a series of events around New Zealand celebrating Papua New Guinea's national language and traditional cultures.
The Ministry of Pacific Peoples has provided some useful resources for the week - Tenkyu tru!
Ancey Wamiri, a school teacher, told RNZ Pacific she uses Tok Pisin every day with family and friends, also teaches it during Tok Pisin Wik sessions.
Describing Tok Pisin as being in her blood and bones, Wamiri explained that the language has been been an "essential unifying factor" for people in a country of many diverse cultures.
"The wonderful thing about Tok Pisin is it has united us as a country, to be able to connect amongst ourselves as a nation.
"If we didn't have Tok Pisin then we'd be a completely divided people. So it was essential to have Tok Pisin become a part of the unifying language for our people.
Wamiri said Tok Pisin is very much a living language that is never stagnant.
"It's ever developing and ever evolving and changing," she explained.
"The great thing is it is a recognised language and not just a creole or a slight version of the English language - because it does have quite a bit of English in it - but somehow along the way it's gone into waves, dips and highs to be a language that we can speak."
Living language
If you're nervous about giving it a go, don't be. As the Wellington community say, it's versatile, and there's often no one right way to say something.
A common exchange may go: "Yu olrait? (How are you?)" responded to with "Mi olrait, tenkyu (I am good, thank you)"
Tommy Poliap Posangat told RNZ Pacific that from its origin, Tok Pisin was created as a way to bridge diversity.
"I believe Tok Pisin was created during he plantation period, when they brought all the islanders, Melanesians, together to work the plantations," Posangat said.
"And because PNG's got a variation of languages, over 800 languages, they've had to come up with a language that they can all speak and understand each other - not just the Papua New Guineans but you have the Solomon Islanders, Fijians and the Vanuatuans coming together, so that's how Tok Pisin was formed backed then, and it's just been evolving ever since."
Every day use
College student Naimah Leahy said the majority of her wider family still lives in PNG, so she makes an effort to stay in touch, which in turn helps keep her use of Tok Pisin alive.
"Apart from the time difference (two hours), I almost call them every day, message every day, make sure that I still am connected to those who are in Papua New Guinea because that's like my home," Leahy said.
Another college student from Wellington who is Papua New Guinean is Dziewanna Wamiri-Cokataki who said Tok Pisin is a beautiful language.
"It's like a wave, it's very up and down. You talk with a lot of emotion," she said, adding that using it with friends was a good way to keep growing the language.
"It's very cool to try and converse and learn, so that's what we try and do."
Em nau (that's right).

title: In Perù hanno rimesso in funzione i waru waru inca: 3.000 anni dopo aiutano ancora le patate contro il clima estremo
content:
In Perù hanno rimesso in funzione i waru waru inca: 3.000 anni dopo aiutano ancora le patate contro il clima estremo
Indice
Hanno rialzato la terra, scavato di nuovo i canali e rimesso le patate dove questo sistema le aveva protette per secoli. Ad Acora, nel dipartimento peruviano di Puno, sulle pianure dell’altopiano che circondano il lago Titicaca, le comunità aymara hanno recuperato cinque waru waru. La prima campagna agricola 2025-2026 è già arrivata al raccolto: patate native da mangiare, conservare come seme, trasformare in chuño e tunta e, quando avanzano, vendere.
Il progetto condotto nell’ultimo anno da World Monuments Fund Perú insieme all’Asociación Aymara Suma Yapu ha riportato in produzione una tecnologia agricola che la FAO fa risalire a circa 3.000 anni fa. Più che un reperto archeologico, è un sistema idraulico ancora perfettamente comprensibile: campi rialzati, acqua intorno, gravità e una conoscenza molto precisa del clima locale.
Il campo si alza, l’acqua resta nei canali
Un waru waru assomiglia a una grande aiuola agricola sollevata rispetto al terreno circostante. Tra una piattaforma e l’altra corrono canali capaci di raccogliere e distribuire l’acqua. Una geometria semplice che, vista dall’alto, può creare disegni spettacolari e che sul terreno svolge parecchio lavoro sporco: drena quando l’acqua è troppa, conserva umidità quando manca e modifica il microclima intorno alle colture. La stessa municipalità di Acora descrive questi campi come una forma tradizionale di adattamento alle pianure alluvionali del Titicaca.
C’è poi una specie di riscaldamento passivo incorporato nel paesaggio. Durante il giorno l’acqua nei canali assorbe calore; quando la temperatura precipita durante la notte, ne restituisce una parte, contribuendo a smorzare il gelo intorno alle piante. È un meccanismo documentato dalla FAO nei sistemi agricoli andini. Ad Acora siamo oltre i 3.800 metri di quota, dove siccità, gelate e forti escursioni termiche non sono precisamente inconvenienti marginali.
Anche il fango ha il suo mestiere. Sedimenti, alghe e materia organica si accumulano sul fondo dei canali e possono essere recuperati e riportati sui campi come materiale ricco di nutrienti. Acqua, terra e residui tornano così nello stesso ciclo produttivo senza bisogno di trasformare il paesaggio in una macchina particolarmente complicata. La sofisticazione, qui, sta tutta nel sapere dove scavare e come gestire ciò che c’è già.
Le patate raccolte diventano cibo, semi e scorta per i mesi difficili
Durante il primo ciclo dei cinque waru waru recuperati, le comunità hanno puntato soprattutto sulle patate native. Una parte del raccolto è rimasta alle famiglie e una parte è stata conservata per le semine successive. Altri tuberi sono diventati chuño e tunta, due sistemi tradizionali di conservazione che sfruttano proprio il freddo dell’altopiano. Il chuño è ottenuto disidratando le patate attraverso gelo e asciugatura; la tunta, di colore chiaro, prevede anche ripetuti congelamenti e permanenza in acqua corrente prima dell’essiccazione.
Il vantaggio è molto concreto: una parte del raccolto può essere conservata molto più a lungo rispetto alla patata fresca. E quello che supera i bisogni delle famiglie entra nel mercato locale, trasformando il recupero del waru waru anche in una piccola fonte di reddito. Alla fine di agosto, circa quattro tonnellate di patate native coltivate nei campi recuperati sono state portate a Lima da rappresentanti di quattro comunità di Acora per essere vendute, scambiate e utilizzate in degustazioni.
Il lavoro riguarda anche ciò che rischia di scomparire molto prima dei campi: la diversità delle sementi. Il Centro Internacional de la Papa (CIP) e MATER partecipano allo studio delle varietà di patate native coltivate dalle comunità, mettendo insieme conservazione genetica, conoscenze agricole e utilizzi alimentari. Nel territorio del Titicaca la diversità della patata è una faccenda tutt’altro che ornamentale: significa avere varietà con caratteristiche differenti davanti a freddo, siccità, suoli e tempi di maturazione diversi.
Il cambiamento climatico ha rimesso un sistema antico nell’elenco delle soluzioni utili
Nel 2025 i campi waru waru di Puno sono entrati nel World Monuments Watch, insieme a 24 altri luoghi culturali considerati vulnerabili o particolarmente importanti per le comunità che li custodiscono. La candidatura era stata presentata da Suma Yapu, associazione guidata da donne indigene, insieme alla Direzione decentrata della Cultura di Puno. Il Ministero della Cultura peruviano li ha indicati espressamente come patrimonio capace di contribuire alla resilienza e alla sicurezza alimentare nel contesto della crisi climatica.
Il recupero di Acora si inserisce poi nel programma globale Cultivating Resilience di WMF, dedicato proprio a paesaggi storici che conservano forme tradizionali di adattamento ambientale. Qui il patrimonio culturale ha una caratteristica abbastanza comoda: si può mangiare. E continua a funzionare soltanto finché qualcuno conserva semi, pulisce canali, ricostruisce piattaforme e tramanda il modo corretto di farlo.
I waru waru, infatti, difficilmente possono essere trattati come una tecnologia da esportare in blocco e montare altrove. La FAO sottolinea quanto questi sistemi richiedano conoscenze specifiche, manutenzione e lavoro collettivo. La loro forza nasce proprio dall’adattamento a un territorio preciso e da generazioni di prove fatte sul campo, con pochissimo spazio per il manuale d’istruzioni universale.
Ad Acora, però, cinque di quei campi sono tornati a produrre. Dopo tremila anni di siccità, gelate, abbandoni e ritorni, l’ultima innovazione agricola dell’altopiano peruviano ha ancora canali pieni d’acqua e patate sotto terra. Solo che è parecchio più vecchia di quanto suggerisca la parola “innovazione”.
Ti potrebbe interessare anche:
- Nei villaggi della Tanzania la crisi climatica si combatte con alveari, pollai e donne finalmente ammesse alle decisioni
- In Etiopia una cooperativa bruciava 2.305 litri di diesel in tre mesi: ora irriga i campi grazie all’energia solare
- A Nairobi sono le donne a tenere in piedi “le baracche” e i quartieri durante le alluvioni o il caldo estremo

title: Africa’s mother tongues are finding new life as youth connect with roots and relatives
content:
A television game show in Nigeria’s commercial hub of Lagos has an unforgiving rule: Speak English and you lose. For a US-born millennial in the audience and a student of her parents’ mother tongue, the high-stakes setting is a perfect classroom.
Meanwhile, a 15-year-old Canadian speaks to a teacher about 13,000km away in Zimbabwe, learning a language her parents feared she would never speak.
“Mhoroi,” Nyashadzashe Machingura says cheerfully with a pronounced Canadian accent while greeting in Zimbabwe’s vernacular Shona.
The scenes capture a new generation of interest and entrepreneurship around African languages once pushed to the margins by decades of colonialism. Often seen as secondary to English, French and Portuguese, they are enjoying a renaissance that is also creating business opportunities.
Between 1,500 and 3,000 languages in Africa
Africa is home to more than 1 billion people speaking roughly a third of the world’s languages, with between 1,500 and 3,000 across 54 countries, according to Unesco.
Experts say the revival in some of them is driven in part by second- and third-generation Africans in the diaspora finding it easier to reconnect with their roots and communicate with older relatives, thanks to social media, online learning, and entertainment.
“There were times I definitely felt left out because my family around me were all speaking Shona. And I just couldn’t understand them,” Nyashadzashe said after a lesson covering traditional greetings, proverbs and ancestral clan symbols. She said she had eaten the food and worn the traditional clothing but still felt left out.
But now her conversations with her grandparents in Zimbabwe are growing longer.
“Being able to connect with them on that level makes me really proud of my heritage,” she said.
African languages were never ‘modernised’
Her Zimbabwe-based tutor, Shungu Chidovi, left her banking career in January to focus full-time on ZimbOriginal, an online platform that teaches Shona through storytelling, book clubs and “buddy pairing” exchanges.
Now she teaches about two dozen learners in Zimbabwe, Canada, Australia, South Africa, Ireland and Scotland, charging $50 a month.
The business, part of a small but growing number of online initiatives teaching African languages, emerged almost by accident. Chidovi began writing a blog about Zimbabwean traditions in 2016. Readers began asking whether she taught Shona.
“I didn’t see it at the time that I was really writing about the Shona language,” Chidovi said.
Like many in Africa, she grew up with the understanding that to get ahead, she had to embrace Western languages rather than her mother tongue. English remains the dominant language for education, business and government affairs in the southern African nation that officially recognises 16 mostly indigenous languages.
“When you talk of Africa, you talk of English, French, Portuguese,” said Believe Mubonderi, a linguistics lecturer at Zimbabwe Open University. His research highlights the importance of ensuring that African languages have a place in the technologies that shape how people communicate, learn and trade.
“In most cases, African languages were sidelined. They were never exposed or modernised to be used in commerce, science and technology,” he said. ”When a language has a very low status, there’s a danger that that language eventually becomes endangered.”
Culture and connection are driving the new interest
Governments and international organisations are trying to reverse that trend.
The African Union’s 2022 decision to adopt Kiswahili, spoken in much of East Africa, as an official working language has raised its international profile. The United Nations declared 2022-32 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages.
And the AU continental body and Unesco are supporting efforts to document and revitalise African languages, including the use of artificial intelligence to generate and translate children’s books and teacher guides.
But there’s a steep digital disadvantage. Unesco says only 10 languages worldwide dominate the “internet ecosystem”, while less than 2% of African languages have a meaningful online presence. That leaves many with too little data to train artificial intelligence systems.
Still, momentum for change is growing, with much of it coming from Africans abroad.
“People of African descent have come to realise that we also have our own identity which we need to embrace and be proud of,” Mubonderi said. “You go on Facebook, you go on TikTok, you are seeing many different efforts. Younger diaspora Africans “are trying by all means to revive, to revitalise, to make use of these languages.”
Chindovi said she hears that desire from children and their parents.
“When people are away from home, they long for home more than when they are home,” she said.
Nigerian game show penalises English speakers
That hunger for connection is also reshaping culture.
In Nigeria, a game show called “Masoyinbo”, meaning “Do not speak English”, has turned Yoruba, one of the country’s most widely spoken languages, into prime-time entertainment. Contestants, including diaspora Nigerians, are tested on Yoruba language and culture, with prizes reaching thousands of dollars.
Host Olalekan Fabilola, who started the show in 2024, sees its popularity as part of a wider shift.
“If ‘Masoyinbo’ had started like 10 years ago, it wouldn’t have been what it is now,” he said. “But we are in the age of cultural resurgence. People want to go back to their roots. Everyone wants to know where they are from, and so it’s timely.”
Tomi Adeshokan, a New Jersey resident who is learning to perfect her Yoruba with Fabilola as a tutor, was part of the audience during a recent recording of the show. She said she lost daily exposure to Yoruba after moving out of her father’s home before the Covid-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, she joined Clubhouse (a live, audio-only social media app) just to hear the language and later began taking classes. Now she was back visiting family.
“It’s very important for us to immerse ourselves in our culture and not to fully identify with other cultures, like American or Western culture,” Adeshokan said.

title: Al rescate de los waru waru, la técnica ancestral de cultivo que puede ser nuestra tecnología de punta frente a un cambio climático fuerte
content:
Al rescate de los waru waru, la técnica ancestral de cultivo que puede ser nuestra tecnología de punta frente a un cambio climático fuerte
Comunidades aimaras recuperan una milenaria técnica de cultivo sobre lagunas: un espectáculo visual y productivo que ha permitido recuperar variedades de papas nativas.
Este resumen es generado por inteligencia artificial y revisado por la redacción.
En Puno, sobre los 3.500 metros de altura, el inmenso altiplano parece un territorio indomable. Las heladas nocturnas, las sequías y el friaje hacen difícil la vida en esta región del país. Sin embargo, en los últimos meses, este panorama aparentemente inhóspito se ha transformado. Ante la vista, aparecen ahora enormes y perfectos paisajes circulares, de más de una hectárea de extensión. En el interior de estas tierras flotantes, rodeadas de canales de agua, crecen robustas papas nativas y productos como la quinua y la cañihua. Y en el exterior, habitan patos y otras aves migratorias, lo que genera un ecosistema de abono orgánico y natural.
Esta técnica de cultivo, conocida como waru waru, fue desarrollada desde épocas antiguas por las comunidades aimaras del altiplano, pero fue paulatinamente abandonada en el transcurso del siglo XX, ante la falta de recursos y mano de obra comunal, debido a la constante migración de las nuevas generaciones hacia las ciudades. Sin embargo, en el 2025, cuatro comunidades del distrito de Acora, con el apoyo de Cultivating Resilience, un programa de World Monuments Fund (WMF), que promueve la conservación de jardines históricos y paisajes culturales en el mundo, han podido recuperar estos cultivos ancestrales, producir las primeras cosechas, y ofrecer soluciones efectivas a los embates del cambio climático.
Campos agrícolas
“La organización, a través del programa Watch, recibe cada dos años postulaciones de sitios culturales de todo el mundo que se encuentran en riesgo de perderse. En el 2025, postularon 200 lugares, y resultaron elegidos 25, entre ellos el proyecto de los waru waru”, cuenta Juan Pablo de la Puente, director ejecutivo de World Monuments Fund Perú. El funcionario precisa que luego el proyecto, bajo el título de “Campos agrícolas waru waru de Acora”, tuvo que participar en otro concurso –Cultivating Resilience–, donde quedó seleccionado para obtener los fondos respectivos, junto con proyectos vinculados a las chinampas de Xochimilco, en México; el Central Park, de Nueva York; el huerto del rey, en el Palacio de Versalles; el foso de la Torre de Londres.
Con este apoyo y financiamiento, las cuatro comunidades, a través de la Asociación Aymara Suma Yapu, se pusieron manos a la obra. A partir de faenas comunales se organizaron para diseñar y construir los waru waru de la misma manera en que lo hacían sus abuelos: elevar la tierra del fondo de las lagunas para formar plataformas elevadas (camellones), fijar los taludes inclinados de soporte, y transformar el altiplano en geométricos campos de cultivo. Esta arquitectura agrícola, rodeada por canales de agua, contribuye a regular la temperatura del suelo, optimizando el uso del recurso hídrico, y reduciendo el impacto de inundaciones o sequías.
Papas con energía
El primer ciclo de siembra y cosecha desarrollado a partir del proyecto no solo ha sido exitoso –se han cosechado cerca de cuatro toneladas de papas nativas–, sino también ha llenado de orgullo a estas comunidades. “Nosotros como aimaras estamos orgullosos del legado que nos han dejado nuestros abuelos, ellos nos han heredado más de tres mil variedades de papas y cada una tiene un diferente atributo y gusto. Nosotros, como institución, buscamos recuperar esta forma de criar la chacra, con respeto a la madre tierra”, dice Eliana Apaza, directora ejecutiva de la Asociación Aymara Suma Yapu.
Ella define a los waru waru como una tecnología de punta ancestral frente a un cambio climático fuerte, y destaca su función termorreguladora en una región de temperaturas extremas. “Tienen un controlador –explica–, si hay poca lluvia se cierran las compuertas de los canales para que se mantenga la humedad del suelo, y si hay mucha lluvia se abren para que salga el agua. Asimismo, si hay heladas fuertes, el agua de los canales se calienta con los rayos del sol durante el día y en la noche irradia ese calor al suelo para que las plantitas no mueran. Además, en el agua, hay todo un ecosistema, vienen los patitos, vienen las aves migratorias, y eso hace que exista un abono natural, con lo cual se puede cultivar orgánicamente”.
Uno de los retos actuales es lograr la sostenibilidad y permanencia de esta técnica de cultivo. De la Puente destaca la organización de talleres para el registro de este conocimiento, el desarrollo de exposiciones, como la desarrollada en Proyectoamil, en Barranco, y la promoción de las comunidades y de sus productos en la actual feria Fusión por Gloria. “Sabemos que ese es un reto grande, pero el primer paso era generar estos encuentros en Lima, dar a conocer este valor ancestral y cultural, así como su utilidad práctica para enfrentar retos actuales. En ese camino, hemos hecho aliados importantes como el Centro Internacional de la Papa y Mater para estudiar las variedades de tubérculos producidos en los waru waru”, añade.
Además…
A saber
El domingo 6 de septiembre representantes de las comunidades de Acora ofrecerán sus productos en el mercado de la feria Fusión por Gloria, en la explanada Costa Verde, en Magdalena del Mar.

title: Público puede acceder gratis a cómic bilingüe con 4 relatos del pueblo Nomatsigenga
content:
Cuatro relatos tradicionales del pueblo indígena u originario Nomatsigenga cobran vida en un cómic bilingüe que el Ministerio de Cultura pone a disposición del público de manera gratuita a través del Centro de Recursos Interculturales. Se trata de Igengitsare Nomatsigenga: Relatos Nomatsigenga, una publicación elaborada de manera participativa junto con integrantes de este pueblo de la región Junín.


El cómic reúne cuatro historias: “Imoro santani otisikë mogobati - La cueva del guácharo en el cerro Mogobati”, “Tsinane janainaro pobigëri sekari - La mujer enferma que envenenó al tigre”, “Opoata patyarija - La poza de sal” e “Ira pagitsa - El águila”.
Los relatos están basados en narraciones orales recopiladas en la comunidad nativa San Antonio de Sonomoro, ubicada en el distrito de Pangoa, provincia de Satipo. Fueron seleccionados por su contenido cultural, social y simbólico y posteriormente adaptados al formato de cómic, ilustrados y traducidos al nomatsigenga.
La publicación busca contribuir a la transmisión de estas historias a las nuevas generaciones, así como fortalecer el uso, valoración y preservación de la lengua y cultura Nomatsigenga. Asimismo, se desarrolla en el contexto de la Política Nacional de Lenguas Originarias, Tradición Oral e Interculturalidad al 2040 y la Política Nacional de la Lectura, el Libro y las Bibliotecas al 2030.
El proceso de elaboración tomó aproximadamente seis meses y se desarrolló de manera participativa entre el pueblo Nomatsigenga y el Ministerio de Cultura. En una primera etapa se recopilaron diversas narraciones orales compartidas por narradores locales. A partir de este material se seleccionaron cuatro relatos, que fueron adaptados al formato de cómic considerando aspectos narrativos, visuales y lingüísticos.
Posteriormente, las versiones en nomatsigenga y las ilustraciones fueron validadas con integrantes del propio pueblo a través de talleres realizados en la Comunidad Nativa San Antonio de Sonomoro, como parte del proceso de elaboración de la publicación.
El cómic puede consultarse de manera gratuita en el Centro de Recursos Interculturales del Ministerio de Cultura:
https://shorturl.at/ot2Af
Historias que se mantienen vivas
Las tradiciones orales pueden presentar distintas versiones de una misma historia, debido a que cada comunidad o familia puede conservar su propia manera de contarla. Por ello, el cómic no busca establecer una versión única u oficial de los relatos, sino recoger las versiones compartidas durante el proceso participativo.
De esta manera, la publicación acerca estas narraciones a públicos de distintas edades mediante un formato visual y bilingüe, y contribuye a poner en valor la memoria colectiva, los conocimientos y las expresiones culturales del pueblo Nomatsigenga.
Dato:
- 10 504 personas aprendieron a hablar en nomatsigenga, según los Censos Nacionales 2025.

title: With joy and grief, Palestinian football marks return
content:
With joy and grief, Palestinian football marks return
Palestinian sports commentator Khalil Jadallah has spent the past three years mourning the athletes killed in the Gaza war. As Palestinian football officially resumed this week, his return to the stadium proved bittersweet.
Palestinian professional sports were brought to a halt after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel and the ensuing war in Gaza, in which 1,014 Palestinian athletes were killed, according to the Palestinian Football Association's tally.
On Friday, Jadallah was back at Faisal Al-Husseini Stadium in Al-Ram in the West Bank to call the opening match of the first tournament organised by the association in three years.
Though long awaited, the event was marked by contradicting emotions for Jadallah: "a feeling of joy at returning after such an absence, but also a feeling of loss. "
"We lost players... fans, administrators and referees," Jadallah told AFP.
- '1,000 Martyrs Cup' -
The football association named the comeback tournament -- which includes over 200 teams from the occupied West Bank, Gaza, and refugee camps in Lebanon -- the "1,000 Martyrs Cup".
Throughout the war, Palestinian football authorities have accused Israel of killing football players and damaging Gaza's sporting infrastructure.
Israel has said 12 Palestinian football figures that it killed in Gaza, including a FIFA-registered referee, were members of militant groups, an allegation the football association has rejected.
Large numbers of Palestinian security forces were deployed for the event, an unusual sight in the town more accustomed to Israeli military raids.
Before the game, pitting Jabal Al-Mukaber Club against Shabab Al-Khaleel SC, children carried a Palestinian flag wrapped to resemble a dead body, before unfurling it across the centre circle as a band played the Palestinian national anthem.
The sport authority also unveiled a memorial bearing the names of the killed Palestinian athletes outside the stadium, which stands in Al-Ram, not far from the West Bank separation barrier.
Samir Issa , a prominent former player and veteran manager who had coached both teams, watched from the stands as the game kicked off.
"Football has become more important than politics today," he said. "The proof of that is the following the World Cup has had."
"Sport in general is the culture of the people," he added, saying that Palestinians had "the right to practice sport normally and in all its forms, not just football".
At the 10-minute, 14-second mark, the referee ordered the game to stop for a minute of silence for the dead before the crowd grew loud again.
"Football returns to Palestine," read electronic screens around the stadium.
Thousands of mainly young people attended the game, with families, women and children seated in a separate section.
Maysan Suleiman, a 35-year-old from Al-Ram, said she came to commemorate "the martyrs".
- 'Football returns to Palestine' -
"I don't support either team," she said. "I came to support the idea (of the tournament) itself. After all, they're all sons of Palestine."
The tournament opened simultaneously in Gaza, where Israeli strikes have left much of the territory in ruins and some football fields have been turned into makeshift camps for those displaced by the war.
The opening match there was held in Deir al-Balah between Khadamat Rafah and Shabab Rafah as fans sat on plastic chairs around the small field lined with palm trees.
"Football represented life for us before the war, and after the war the lives of players stopped altogether," said Khalil Matar, a Khadamat Rafah player.
Matar said holding the cup simultaneously in the West Bank, Gaza and refugee camps in Lebanon reflected "national unity" for Palestinians.
But the West Bank teams are set to face major logistical hurdles as they travel between cities and Israeli military checkpoints in the occupied territory.
"Still, we're determined to continue sporting activities and developing our young people," said Abdullah Abu Ghassan of the Shabab Jaba team competing in the tournament.

title: Mzilikazi commemorations grow into regional cultural spectacle
content:
Langalakhe Mabena, [email protected]
WHAT began as a commemoration of King Mzilikazi’s death anniversary turned into a major cross-border celebration of African culture and heritage on Saturday, as thousands of people from Zimbabwe and beyond converged at historic Mhlahlandlela in Bulawayo.
The gathering brought together Government officials, Bulawayo City Council leadership, amabutho, amaguqa, amatshitshi, cultural groups and members of the public, with visitors from South Africa, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia and China also joining the celebrations.
The usually quiet historical site on the outskirts of Bulawayo was transformed into a vibrant cultural hub, with music, dance, traditional performances and colourful regalia creating a fitting tribute to the founder of the Ndebele nation.
The celebrations began at 7am with a cultural parade from Matshobana Township, led by amatshitshi, amaguqa, abafana and amabutho. Dressed in traditional regalia, the participants marched through some of Bulawayo’s iconic suburbs, including Matshobana, Nguboyenja, Mzilikazi and Makokoba, before proceeding into the city centre. The procession made a stop at the statue of the late Vice-President Dr Joshua Mqabuko Nyongolo Nkomo before continuing to the Large City Hall car park, from where participants were transported to Mhlahlandlela for the main ceremony.
At Mhlahlandlela, generations converged to celebrate the legacy of King Mzilikazi, with elderly participants, children and cultural groups adding colour to the festivities.
Born near Mkuze in Zululand in 1790, King Mzilikazi is remembered for his leadership in building the Ndebele nation after breaking away from King Shaka in 1823. He died on September 9, 1868, and was buried at Entumbane in Matobo, about 20km from Bulawayo.
This year’s commemorations marked 158 years since his death and highlighted the enduring cultural links between the Ndebele people in Zimbabwe and other Nguni communities across the region.
Matabeleland South Provincial Affairs and Devolution Minister Albert Nguluvhe, who was the guest of honour, said the huge turnout reflected the significance of King Mzilikazi’s contribution to the development of the Ndebele nation.
“Your presence is a reminder that we are gathered on sacred ground. We gather not to just remember a king but a builder. King Mzilikazi kaMatshobane was not just a warrior, he was a nation builder, a unifier and a custodian of identity,” he said.
Minister Nguluvhe said culture remained central to how communities and the country conducted their affairs.
“Culture is the way we resolve conflict. It is the way we farm, it is the way we treat our elderly, it is how we lead and how we govern,” he said.
The commemorations also emerged as a platform for strengthening cultural ties beyond Zimbabwe’s borders. Royal guest Dumisani Mthembo Dube, chairman of the Umkhosi WeNxwala ceremony in Zambia under the kingship of Mpezeni, said attending the event had allowed him to learn more about Ndebele history and culture.
“It is a great thing for the nation to unite to revive African culture. It’s a great honour that I was invited to be part of this event. Coming from Zambia to Bulawayo to celebrate the King Mzilikazi commemorations gave me purpose because I am here to learn the history of our forefathers and further learn the way of life for the Ndebele nation.
“This was a great expedition, and what I learnt here, I will share it with other Nguni people in Zambia,” said Mr Dube.
Adding star power to the commemorations were South African entertainment personalities, including Maskandi musician Khuzani Mpungose and stars of the popular television series Shaka iLembe, Dawn Thandeka King and Mpilo Mbatha, who played Mkabayi and Mzilikazi respectively.
Khuzani, who has a large following among Maskandi fans, popularly known as the “blue nation”, said he was overwhelmed by the reception he received in Bulawayo.
“It’s my first time being in Zimbabwe, KwaBulawayo, and I am shocked by what I am seeing here. Being welcomed with such love is a beautiful gesture that I believe is mostly reserved for the kings and queens. Such a gesture humbles me.
“The cultural songs at this ceremony were sung in isintu, a great common thing that we do in KwaZulu. Basically, my experience here confirmed that indeed we are one people,” said Khuzani.
For acclaimed actress Dawn Thandeka King, the visit was equally personal, with the actress describing her return to Bulawayo as a homecoming. King previously visited the city earlier this year for Imiklomelo kaDakamela before travelling to Nkayi, where she immersed herself in local culture and interacted with communities.
“Being here already feels like home. Earlier this year, I was here and went to Nkayi, where I had a great cultural experience. Instead of staying for a short period of time, I had to stay much longer because I found purpose in this city, holding acting classes and doing other business.
“My return is to continue my cultural journey and discovery in this beautiful city. My roots are connected with the Khumalo people, and I felt like royalty to be invited for this great day, celebrating the legacy of King Mzilikazi,” she said.
Chief Dakamela of Nkayi, who delivered the closing remarks, said the massive turnout demonstrated that communities remained committed to preserving their cultural identity.
“What I see here is an embrace of who we are. I am proud that people came in their numbers to celebrate this day. This was King Mzilikazi’s dream when he created the Ndebele nation. I am sure he is happy wherever he is, because we united today to preserve his dream and legacy.
“This event was a success because of the people. Amabutho or chiefs were not going to make all this such a success alone. It is the people who left everything behind to come together and unite for this event,” said Chief Dakamela.
The main ceremony ended at 5pm, but the cultural celebration continued into the evening at a local leisure spot where the Maskandi Music Festival, headlined by Khuzani, took over.
Other performers included Bhila, Gazelimnyama and Imfanomsuthu, alongside Maskandi and Imbube artistes.
The scale and diversity of this year’s commemorations demonstrated that King Mzilikazi’s legacy extends beyond a historical remembrance, continuing to provide a cultural bridge connecting communities across Zimbabwe and the wider Nguni world.
Meanwhile, the Mthwakazi kaMzilikazi Cultural Association (MMCA) has hailed this year’s commemorations as a resounding success, expressing gratitude to the thousands of people who turned out to honour the legacy of King Mzilikazi, the founding father of the Ndebele nation.

title: $58m Aboriginal cultural centre opens at Darwin Waterfront
content:
Darwin's $58m Larrakia Cultural Centre opens to the public after 24-year wait
In short:
The Larrakia Cultural Centre on the Darwin Waterfront has opened its doors to the public, more than two decades since the idea was first developed.
The project cost $58 million and its design was inspired by a cultural centre in Whistler, Canada, and others around the world.
What's next?
Aboriginal Investment NT says it hopes the project will create more economic opportunities for Larrakia people.
A centre showcasing the culture, history and art of the traditional owners of the Darwin region, the Larrakia people, has opened to the public after 24 years of planning and development.
The $58 million Larrakia Cultural Centre, situated at Stokes Hill Wharf on the Darwin Waterfront, opened its doors for a sunrise tour this morning.
The idea for the centre was conceived in 2002, and negotiations between the Larrakia Development Corporation (LDC) and Northern Territory government on granting the waterfront location and developing the venue lasted from 2005 to 2022 before construction began two years ago.
LDC chair Mark Motlop said the new centre would "fill a void" in cultural education in Darwin.
"People rock up in Darwin, they want an Aboriginal experience and they want a Larrakia experience," he said.
"In the past we haven't had that, we've had dribs and drabs … this is a one-stop shop."
Centre takes worldwide inspiration
Mr Motlop said he had travelled the world looking at similar venues during the centre's planning phase, and that its design was influenced by cultural centres in Canada, Alaska and New Zealand.
"We had to get a model that was going to be sustainable and we didn't want this to be the golden goose that goes looking for funding later on," he said.
"It had to be a commercial model, and Whistler [in Canada] had that."
Alongside a museum space and art displays, the centre in Darwin includes meeting and office spaces, a retail shop, a cafe and a restaurant.
Aboriginal Investment NT chief executive Nigel Browne said he hoped the centre would not only provide cultural benefits to Larrakia people, but lasting economic gains as well.
"There's a cohort of full-time staff that are employed within the cultural centre … but there's a much bigger scope here,"he said.
"There'll be opportunities moving forward for Larrakia to engage in business and branch out from the centre itself.
"Over the years we've had a number of Larrakia people running their own tourism businesses … I'm sure that opportunities will come into the future to have those individuals linked with the cultural centre."
Cultural items and interactive displays
Mr Browne said the centre "takes the shape of the ancestral being", a bird in flight, which is "attached to the Larrakia sacred site" at the nearby Stokes Hill.
On display are 23 cultural items that have been repatriated to Larrakia land from interstate and overseas, as well as a replica of the Larrakia peoples' 1972 petition to Queen Elizabeth II for land rights and political representation.
There is also an interactive display where Larrakia people and visitors can learn about the history of the nine Larrakia family groups.
"A lot of people [in Darwin] will have come across or met or even fallen in love with Larrakia people over the years," Mr Browne said.
"Now's the opportunity to really come to one place where they can get a fuller appreciation of Larrakia history, of the story of Larrakia and what it's meant for Larrakia people ever since [George] Goyder sailed into our harbour in 1869."
The centre's cultural liaison officer, Donella Young, said she felt "so privileged" to see it finally come to fruition.
"It talks about culture, country, land rights and women and men that served in World War I and World War II and the Black Watch," she said.
"It also still talks about how the Larrakia community is still thriving to this day."

title: El rincón más recóndito de Gran Canaria lucha por que no se pierda su Baile de la Papa
content: La Asociación de Vecinos Rosa Nueva ha hecho un trabajo a contrarreloj para rescatar del olvido una tradición de un remoto pueblo de la isla Vivir a la sombra de Inagua y tener Horgazales enfrente ha conformado el carácter de la historia de El Hoyo, un remoto barrio del municipio más recóndito históricamente del resto de los de la isla de Gran Canaria, La Aldea de San Nicolás. Sus vecinos están luchando para poner negro sobre blanco una de las tradiciones más queridas de las Fiestas de San Pedro: el Baile de la Papa. Se trata de una de las manifestaciones coreográficas más singulares del patrimonio inmaterial de la comarca aldeana y, por extensión, de la isla de Gran Canaria. Pero pese a esta relevancia cultural y su presencia constante desde la mitad del pasado siglo, ha sido recientemente cuando la Asociación de Vecinos Rosa Nueva ha impulsado un estudio académico sistemático (ITPCI), con la financiación del Cabildo de Gran Canaria, y que ha llegado a tiempo para recabar los testimonios de los últimos testigos presenciales que lo bailaron o vieron cómo se bailó las primeras veces. Fragmento del mural ubicado en el barrio de El Hoyo en homenaje a su Baile de La Papa. El Baile de la Papa es la historia de personas trabajadoras que en el ocio encontraron espacios de encuentro, identidad y pertenencia. Todas las vecinas entrevistadas consideran El Hoyo, “el barrio más bonito de La Aldea”, aunque reconocen que “toda La Aldea es hermosa y especial”. “El truco está en no dejarse mover la papa” El Baile de la Papa, que no obedece ni a la fecha de su cosecha, ni tiene un arraigo religioso, ni aborigen, ha subsistido sin interrupción, salvo el año de la pandemia, por la plena voluntad de los vecinos de El Hoyo de divertirse y de que no desaparezca. Fue traído al barrio por Jorge Ojeda Montesdeoca, que pudo verlo en otros pueblos en fiestas donde ya se interpretaba el baile, recogido, tal vez, en la película que se proyectó en aquella época Serenata en el Valle del Sol (Duches of Idaho), de Robert Z. Leonard, un film en el que tiene lugar el Potato Dance, una competición al estilo de la realizada en El Hoyo, sujetando la papa con la frente, con las manos en la espalda, y aumentando la dificultad del baile a medida que se intensifica la música de la orquesta o del grupo que esté sobre el escenario. “El truco está en no dejarse mover la papa”, cuenta a esta redacción Gabriel Ramírez, que ha ganado hasta en cuatro ocasiones en esta competición, siempre con la misma pareja, su esposa Margarita González. Ella recuerda a sus 85 años cómo las fiestas de San Pedro se hacían antes de tener la talla del santo, cómo fue con otras dos niñas pidiendo para comprarla, cómo la trajeron al hombro a El Hoyo y cómo, años después, llegó El Baile de la Papa. Gabriel Ramírez sostiene a un niño en brazos junto a sus vecinos de El Hoyo en las fiestas de San Pedro. Años 60. Para ella, la mejor estrategia es mover la cintura y dejar quieta la papa en la frente, “la cabeza quietita”. Margarita no quiere que esta tradición se pierda y le da esperanza cómo los jóvenes se animan a bailarla en cada edición desde hace casi 70 años. Una parranda que empezó en un garaje Teresa Cárdenes tiene 83 años y en El Hoyo todo el mundo la conoce por Teresita. Llegó en 1959 desde Tejeda cuando tenía 16 años. Teresa Cárdenes Quintana, Nicolasa Ojeda Suárez, Carmen Ramírez, Margarita González Suárez, Gabriel Ramírez Montesdeoca y Ana María Díaz Suárez, vecinas y vecino de El Hoyo entrevistados para este reportaje. En su casa todos son amantes de la música y ella toca “la laúd” (sic). “Cantaba de chica en medio de los tomateros, pero ya no”. No es de extrañar que Jorge fuera su cuñado. Y ella recuerda cómo fue: “Él, un día que se cogieron las papas en El Hoyo, cogió un balde con las papas todas del mismo tamaño y el baile se hacía en el garaje de mi casa”, cuenta Teresita. “Los asientos eran cajas de tomates para que las madres pudieran vigilar si las hijas se pegaban mucho a las parejas”. Esta vecina recuerda que la introducción del baile no estuvo exenta de polémica y que algunas personas mayores del pueblo “acusaron a Jorge de inventar este baile para arrimarse más a las mujeres” (ríe). A la sombra del almácigo Nico Ojeda, de 76 años, recuerda aquellos momentos en que había fiesta antes que santo, ya que fue una de las tres niñas que fue pidiendo casa por casa. “Venía gente andando de todas partes, de Tasarte, Tasartico, desde por la mañana para la fiesta del mediodía y comían a la sombra del almácico (sic), almuerzo, merienda, bailes de taifas y después se iban a su casa”. Los vecinos de El Hoyo llevan a hombros a San Pedro en las fiestas.Año 1959. “Todo el que quería bailar la papa, la podía bailar. Se ponían enfrente, no se podía rodar la papa para el ojo, si se rodaba para el ojo te descalificaban”, explica la vecina. Había un jurado conformado por personas del barrio y de otros sitios, y si la papa se movía o se sujetaba con la nariz, tampoco valía. Luego se iba incrementando la dificultad: se bailaba a la pata coja, con las manos atrás, con las manos arriba, según la música se fuera acelerando, y después la pareja ganadora recibía un trofeo. “Había parejas que eran de la misma altura, que estaban acostumbrados a bailar juntos, más o menos la pareja se elegía pensando en todo eso”. La labor de la Asociación de Vecinos Rosa Nueva Begoña Saavedra, presidenta de la Asociación Rosa Nueva nos atiende en El Hoyo para contarnos cómo nació la inquietud de reactivar la labor que comenzaron hace 48 años los vecinos del barrio.“Mi padre fue uno de los constructores y socios fundadores, pensé que si teníamos el espacio y la asociación por qué no reactivarlo para todos y crear participación ciudadana, un sitio de encuentro, para recopilar costumbres, tradiciones de la zona, algo que nos parece muy importante para saber de dónde venimos”. Begoña Saavedra Ramírez, presidenta de la Asociación de Vecinos Rosa Nueva y vecina de El Hoyo. Begoña, auxiliar de vuelo, el tiempo que no está en el aire está en su barrio, del que ha aprendido que la distancia no es algo realmente importante, si la gente tiene realmente ganas de comunicarse. “Nos dimos cuenta de que la gente se nos acercaba cuando creábamos el espacio, empezando por actividades para los niños que implicaban a los padres, las clases de costura, pero había muchas ganas de compartir mucha información que todo el mundo guardaba y tenían necesidad de hablar y de hablar del pasado”. Fue en uno de esos encuentros, cocinados a fuego lento y con la espera adecuada, entre café y un poquito de agua guisada, donde se propuso que se hiciera algo por salvaguardar y difundir el baile. “El Baile de la Papa era uno de los puntos recurrentes en la memoria de los socios aunque sin datos muy claros, y, dado que tampoco existía información documentada, desde la asociación vimos la urgencia de comenzar a investigarlo para documentarlo; los motivos por los que este baile empezó aquí, en El Hoyo”. Primer estudio académico patrimonial Fue entonces cuando, en la búsqueda de financiación, dieron con la subvención de la Reserva de la Biosfera y Patrimonio Mundial, enclave en el que se encuentra El Hoyo. “Solo tener las conclusiones del estudio patrimonial en las manos ya fue un triunfo. Nosotras, desde la Junta Directiva, intuíamos que teníamos algo grande entre las manos aunque no viniera de los antiguos canarios, pero es algo que se ha hecho anualmente desde 1959 en un lugar remoto como este, de una determinada manera”. En el centro. Begoña Saavedra Ramírez, presidenta de la Asociación Rosa Nueva; junto a Guadalupe, miembro de la Junta Directiva; y la socia y profesora de costura, Mercedes, a la izquierda. Con el estudio en la mano, se ha solicitado que el Baile de la Papa sea considerado Bien de Interés Cultural Inmaterial a nivel autonómico o insular y la asociación continúa con su proceso de difusión y visibilización en colegios y centros culturales. “El Baile de la Papa tiene una amenaza”, advierte Begoña. “La principal es que no podamos recoger todo lo que las personas mayores puedan decirnos antes de que se vayan y también necesitamos implicar a las generaciones nuevas y por eso es fundamental que se conozca y que se interesen por él desde todas partes”. Para Guadalupe Godoy, miembro de la Junta Directiva, es fundamental que se difunda “tal y como se bailó en 1959, que no se pervierta”. “Un renacer” En conversaciones con este periódico, usuarias de la Asociación cuentan lo que ha significado para ellas tener un punto de encuentro en el barrio. “Las mujeres en el barrio no teníamos nada, ahora tenemos un sitio donde coser, donde tomarnos el buchito de café y recuperar las cosas de antes”, confiesa Carmen Ramírez. “Después de toda una vida de trabajos en la agricultura, el almacén de tomates, trabajar en el sur, tener hijos... ahora es mi tiempo”. Un grupo de vecinos viendo fotos en la Asociación Rosa Nueva. Nicolasa Ojeda explica la importancia de compartir en comunidad y salir del individualismo. “Los vecinos nos cuidamos y nos acompañamos porque eso es un paño que se pone en toda mesa, si no ayudamos a los demás, los demás no nos pueden ayudar cuando los necesitemos”. O Ana María Díaz Suárez, de 70 años, que explica cómo esto para ella ha sido “un renacer”. La profesora de costura Mercedes Hernández, jubilada de la docencia, aunque de eso una nunca se jubila, llegó a El Hoyo a dar clases de forma altruista y se enamoró de su gente y su paisaje. “Ya casi soy aldeana”, asegura. “Vienen muchas señoras que están jubiladas, hablamos, aprendemos y como todas se conocen es como una familia: ellas salen de casa y yo encantada”.
