title: With joy and grief, Palestinian football marks return
content:
AL-RAM (PALESTINIAN TERRITORIES) - Palestinian sports commentator Khalil Jadallah has spent the past three years mourning the athletes killed in the Gaza war. As Palestinian football officially resumed this week, his return to the stadium proved bittersweet.
Palestinian professional sports were brought to a halt after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel and the ensuing war in Gaza, in which 1,014 Palestinian athletes were killed, according to the Palestinian Football Association's tally.
On Friday, Jadallah was back at Faisal Al-Husseini Stadium in Al-Ram in the West Bank to call the opening match of the first tournament organised by the association in three years.
Though long awaited, the event was marked by contradicting emotions for Jadallah: "a feeling of joy at returning after such an absence, but also a feeling of loss.
"We lost players... fans, administrators and referees," Jadallah told AFP.
- '1,000 Martyrs Cup' -
The football association named the comeback tournament -- which includes over 200 teams from the occupied West Bank, Gaza, and refugee camps in Lebanon -- the "1,000 Martyrs Cup".
Throughout the war, Palestinian football authorities have accused Israel of killing football players and damaging Gaza's sporting infrastructure.
Israel has said 12 Palestinian football figures that it killed in Gaza, including a FIFA-registered referee, were members of militant groups, an allegation the football association has rejected.
Large numbers of Palestinian security forces were deployed for the event, an unusual sight in the town more accustomed to Israeli military raids.
Before the game, pitting Jabal Al-Mukaber Club against Shabab Al-Khaleel SC, children carried a Palestinian flag wrapped to resemble a dead body, before unfurling it across the centre circle as a band played the Palestinian national anthem.
The sport authority also unveiled a memorial bearing the names of the killed Palestinian athletes outside the stadium, which stands in Al-Ram, not far from the West Bank separation barrier.
Samir Issa a prominent former player and veteran manager who had coached both teams, watched from the stands as the game kicked off.
"Football has become more important than politics today," he said. "The proof of that is the following the World Cup has had."
"Sport in general is the culture of the people," he added, saying that Palestinians had "the right to practice sport normally and in all its forms, not just football".
At the 10-minute, 14-second mark, the referee ordered the game to stop for a minute of silence for the dead before the crowd grew loud again.
"Football returns to Palestine," read electronic screens around the stadium.
Thousands of mainly young people attended the game, with families, women and children seated in a separate section.
Maysan Suleiman, a 35-year-old from Al-Ram, said she came to commemorate "the martyrs".
- 'Football returns to Palestine' -
"I don't support either team," she said. "I came to support the idea (of the tournament) itself. After all, they're all sons of Palestine."
The tournament opened simultaneously in Gaza, where Israeli strikes have left much of the territory in ruins and some football fields have been turned into makeshift camps for those displaced by the war.
The opening match there was held in Deir al-Balah between Khadamat Rafah and Shabab Rafah as fans sat on plastic chairs around the small field lined with palm trees.
"Football represented life for us before the war, and after the war the lives of players stopped altogether," said Khalil Matar, a Khadamat Rafah player.
Matar said holding the cup simultaneously in the West Bank, Gaza and refugee camps in Lebanon reflected "national unity" for Palestinians.
But the West Bank teams are set to face major logistical hurdles as they travel between cities and Israeli military checkpoints in the occupied territory.
"Still, we're determined to continue sporting activities and developing our young people," said Abdullah Abu Ghassan of the Shabab Jaba team competing in the tournament.

title: Palestinian football returns amid joy, grief
content:
AL-RAM: Palestinian sports commentator Khalil Jadallah has spent the past three years mourning the athletes killed in the Gaza war.
As Palestinian football officially resumed this week, his return to the stadium proved bittersweet.
Palestinian professional sports were brought to a halt after the Hamas-led Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel and the ensuing war in Gaza, in which 1,014 Palestinian athletes were killed, according to the Palestinian Football Association’s tally.
On Friday, Jadallah was back at Faisal Al-Husseini Stadium in Al-Ram in the West Bank to call the opening match of the first tournament organised by the association in three years.
Though long awaited, the event was marked by contradicting emotions for Jadallah: “a feeling of joy at returning after such an absence, but also a feeling of loss”.
“We lost players… fans, administrators and referees,” Jadallah told AFP.
‘1,000 Martyrs Cup’
The football association named the comeback tournament – which includes over 200 teams from the occupied West Bank, Gaza, and refugee camps in Lebanon – the “1,000 Martyrs Cup”.
Throughout the war, Palestinian football authorities have accused Israel of killing football players and damaging Gaza’s sporting infrastructure.
Israel has said 12 Palestinian football figures that it killed in Gaza, including a Fifa-registered referee, were members of militant groups, an allegation the football association has rejected.
Large numbers of Palestinian security forces were deployed for the event, an unusual sight in the town more accustomed to Israeli military raids.
Before the game, pitting Jabal Al-Mukaber Club against Shabab Al-Khaleel SC, children carried a Palestinian flag wrapped to resemble a dead body, before unfurling it across the centre circle as a band played the Palestinian national anthem.
The sport authority also unveiled a memorial bearing the names of the killed Palestinian athletes outside the stadium, which stands in Al-Ram, not far from the West Bank separation barrier.
Samir Issa , a prominent former player and veteran manager who had coached both teams, watched from the stands as the game kicked off.
“Football has become more important than politics today,” he said. “The proof of that is the following the World Cup has had,” he added.
“Sport in general is the culture of the people,” he added, saying that Palestinians had “the right to practice sport normally and in all its forms, not just football”.
At the 10-minute, 14-second mark, the referee ordered the game to stop for a minute of silence for the dead before the crowd grew loud again.
“Football returns to Palestine,” read electronic screens around the stadium.
Thousands of mainly young people attended the game, with families, women and children seated in a separate section.
Maysan Suleiman, a 35-year-old from Al-Ram, said she came to commemorate “the martyrs”.
‘Football returns to Palestine’
“I don’t support either team,” she said. “I came to support the idea (of the tournament) itself. After all, they’re all sons of Palestine,” she added.
The tournament opened simultaneously in Gaza, where Israeli strikes have left much of the territory in ruins and some football fields have been turned into makeshift camps for those displaced by the war.
The opening match there was held in Deir al-Balah between Khadamat Rafah and Shabab Rafah as fans sat on plastic chairs around the small field lined with palm trees.
“Football represented life for us before the war, and after the war the lives of players stopped altogether,” said Khalil Matar, a Khadamat Rafah player.
Matar said holding the cup simultaneously in the West Bank, Gaza and refugee camps in Lebanon reflected “national unity” for Palestinians.
However, the West Bank teams are set to face major logistical hurdles as they travel between cities and Israeli military checkpoints in the occupied territory.
“Still, we’re determined to continue sporting activities and developing our young people,” said Abdullah Abu Ghassan of the Shabab Jaba team competing in the tournament.

title: Africa’s mother tongues are finding new life as youth connect with roots and relatives
content:
Associated Press
A television game show in Nigeria’s commercial hub of Lagos has an unforgiving rule: Speak English and you lose. For a U.S.-born millennial in the audience and a student of her parents’ mother tongue, the high-stakes setting is a perfect classroom.
Meanwhile, a 15-year-old Canadian speaks to a teacher about 13,000 kilometers (8,000 miles) away in Zimbabwe, learning a language her parents feared she would never speak.
“Mhoroi,” Nyashadzashe Machingura says cheerfully with a pronounced Canadian accent while greeting in Zimbabwe’s vernacular Shona.
The scenes capture a new generation of interest and entrepreneurship around African languages once pushed to the margins by decades of colonialism. Often seen as secondary to English, French and Portuguese, they are enjoying a renaissance that is also creating business opportunities.
Africa is home to over 1 billion people speaking roughly a third of the world’s languages, with between 1,500 and 3,000 across 54 countries, according to UNESCO.
Experts say the revival in some of them is driven partly by second- and third-generation Africans in the diaspora finding it easier to reconnect with their roots and communicate with older relatives, thanks to social media, online learning and entertainment.
“There were times I definitely felt left out because my family around me were all speaking Shona. And I just couldn’t understand them,” Nyashadzashe said after a lesson covering traditional greetings, proverbs and ancestral clan symbols. She said she had eaten the food and worn the traditional clothing but still felt left out.
But now her conversations with her grandparents in Zimbabwe are growing longer.
“Being able to connect with them on that level makes me really proud of my heritage,” she said.
Her Zimbabwe-based tutor, Shungu Chidovi, left her banking career in January to focus full-time on ZimbOriginal, an online platform that teaches Shona through storytelling, book clubs and “buddy pairing” exchanges.
Now she teaches about two dozen learners in Zimbabwe, Canada, Australia, South Africa, Ireland and Scotland, charging $50 a month.
The business, part of a small but growing number of online initiatives teaching African languages, emerged almost by accident. Chidovi began writing a blog about Zimbabwean traditions in 2016. Readers began asking whether she taught Shona.
“I didn’t see it at the time that I was really writing about the Shona language,” Chidovi said.
Like many in Africa, she grew up with the understanding that to get ahead she had to embrace Western languages instead of her mother tongue. English remains the dominant language for education, business and government affairs in the southern African nation that officially recognizes 16 mostly Indigenous languages.
“When you talk of Africa, you talk of English, French, Portuguese,” said Believe Mubonderi, a linguistics lecturer at Zimbabwe Open University. His research notes the importance of ensuring that African languages have a place in technologies shaping how people communicate, learn and trade.
“In most cases, African languages were sidelined. They were never exposed or modernized to be used in commerce, science and technology,” he said. “When a language has a very low status, there’s a danger that that language eventually becomes endangered.”
Governments and international organizations are trying to reverse that trend.
The African Union’s 2022 decision to adopt Kiswahili, spoken in much of east Africa, as an official working language has raised its international profile. The United Nations declared 2022-2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages.
And the AU continental body and UNESCO are supporting efforts to document and revitalize African languages, including using artificial intelligence to generate and translate children’s books and teacher guides.
But there’s a steep digital disadvantage. UNESCO says only 10 languages around the world dominate the “internet ecosystem,” while less than 2% of African languages have a meaningful online presence. That leaves many with too little data to train artificial intelligence systems.
Still, momentum for change is growing, with much of it from Africans abroad.
“People of African descent have come to realize that we also have our own identity which we need to embrace and be proud of. You go on Facebook, you go on TikTok, you are seeing many different efforts,” Mubonderi said. Younger diaspora Africans “are trying by all means to revive, to revitalize, to make use of these languages.”
Chindovi said she hears that desire from children and their parents.
“When people are away from home, they long for home more than when they are home,” she said.
That hunger for connection is also reshaping culture.
In Nigeria, a game show called “Masoyinbo,” meaning “Do not speak English,” has turned Yoruba, one of the country’s most widely spoken languages, into prime-time entertainment. Contestants, including diaspora Nigerians, are tested on Yoruba language and culture, with prizes reaching thousands of dollars.
Host Olalekan Fabilola, who started the show in 2024, sees its popularity as part of a wider shift.
“If ‘Masoyinbo’ had started like 10 years ago, it wouldn’t have been what it is now,” he said. “But we are in the age of cultural resurgence. People want to go back to their roots. Everyone wants to know why, where they are from, and so it’s timely.”
Tomi Adeshokan, a New Jersey resident who is learning to perfect her Yoruba with Fabilola as a tutor, was part of the audience during a recent recording of the show. She said she lost daily exposure to Yoruba after moving out of her father’s home before the COVID-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, she joined Clubhouse just to hear the language and later began taking classes. Now she was back visiting family.
“It’s very important for us to immerse ourselves in our culture and not to fully identify with other cultures, like the American, the Western culture,” Adeshokan said.

title: At 60, Vietnam's war orphans in US still search for their mothers
content:
Born in Vietnam as Nguyen Thi My Phuong, Murch was one of 150 children who survived the C-5A military aircraft crash during Operation Babylift, the 1975 campaign that evacuated over 3,300 presumed orphans from southern Vietnam to the United States.
As a generation of war orphans, they all left Vietnam when they were too young to make their own decisions. In the minds of many, there remains a constant yearning to fill the memories they "always never had" about where they came from and who gave birth to them.
Time is running out, but the children and many mothers are still waiting to find each other.
In 2005, Murch decided to return to Vietnam for the first time with a group of Babylift adoptees.
She had felt "strangely comfortable."
Unlike others in her group, she was not intimidated by her inability to speak Vietnamese and felt deeply welcomed. For the first time, the American adoptee saw so many people who "looked just like me."
She reunited with pre-1975 orphanage workers to express her gratitude.
"Because of them, we are alive. I printed out a photo taken with them and thought, 'Oh, I am Vietnamese.' That lingered in my mind," she says.
During that trip, she visited the field in District 12 where the C-5A crashed and held a small memorial.
Standing there, she felt more clearly than ever the fragile line between life and death that she and her companions had crossed.
She also returned to Vinh Long Province in the Mekong Delta, where she was born, and visited a local shelter, seeing her own reflection in the eyes of the children there.
However, she did not expect much from her search for her biological family, as there were few clues to offer hope.
Returning to the U.S., questions about her identity weighed more heavily. She did not know exactly where she was taken from or how old she was when she was separated from her mother.
Between her birth in June 1974 and admission to an orphanage in January 1975, intense fighting had swept across the Mekong Delta. No one knew what might have torn a child from their family.
"You realize you don't belong anywhere. I grew up in the United States, but I was born in Vietnam. So what country do I belong to?" she asks.
A series of questions haunted her: If the children are still struggling, can their mothers truly be at peace? A mother separated from her child, whether she chose to let the baby go or for another reason, might have thought about her child her entire life.
In 2024, after talking with a friend battling cancer, Murch realized that surviving the plane crash was a miracle.
"Death cannot take you away, as if you have a superpower and it defies death," the Babylift survivor says.
This inspired her to organize an event in Colorado called "Secret Ability to Fly," honoring those who had cared for, protected and raised the Babylift children. It was the first time she had met other Vietnamese adoptees.
"I realized the desire to be with one's biological family is truly powerful," she says.
At a "War Orphans" gathering in Boulder in March 2024, Murch received a gift: a piece of C-5A insulation material from the very plane that had crashed.
The gift came from Sister Mary Nelle, who worked for Friends For All Children (FFAC) in Saigon from 1972 until April 1975, assisting director Rosemary Taylor.
They received, cared for, and organized the evacuation of orphans. When FFAC closed at the end of the war, all documents, letters, and keepsakes that families had sent with their babies were destroyed.
However, Taylor had recovered the files that survived the destruction, and stored them at the Colorado office along with adoption-related items entrusted to her by others.
After Taylor's death, Nelle took over the collection.
Soon afterward, Murch visited her in a Colorado basement, and the nun handed her a file to look for clues about her identity.
Murch recounts: "I randomly opened the file on top. Miraculously, out of all 33 boxes of documents, my file appeared right before my eyes."
Caregivers at the To Am orphanage had given her the name Mimosa, after the flower.
She found documents detailing the exact day she arrived at the Vinh Long orphanage, her adoptive mother's handwritten letter, crossed-out adoption options leaving only her name, photos from second and third grades, health records, and U.S. immigration adoption updates.
Taylor of FFAC had documented about Mimosa from St. Paul de Chartres Orphanage, Vinh Long, Vietnam.
The child had been issued a birth certificate by a Vinh Long court on Aug. 15, 1974, confirming her status as an orphan with parents unknown.
The child was placed in FFAC's care for adoption on Jan. 15, 1975, and cared for until her departure on April 5, 1975.
Another document from FFAC director Wende S. Grant said: "I hereby certify that Nguyen Thi My Phuong, born on June 24, 1974, in Vinh Long, was surrendered to Friends For All Children for adoption. Her parents have never inquired about her since that day."
Murch says: "For the first time, I saw my name on an official list, on a faded hard copy rather than hearing it through someone else's words. I felt like a missing piece of the past had been put in its right place."
The surprise for her was that, for years, she only knew her Vietnamese name to be Nguyen Thi My Phuong from her adoption registration.
But after seeing the papers Taylor had left, she found that a girl named Tran Ngoc An, born Dec. 28, 1973, who had been raised at St. Paul's Convent in Vinh Long, had also been transferred to the FFAC facility in Saigon on Jan. 15, 1975.
But she did not have a birth certificate, and had been matched with documents bearing the name Nguyen Thi My Phuong.
Murch agonizes: "Am I Phuong or An? That is a missing piece I never knew."
When she was 82, Nelle wanted to find a home for the remaining 33 boxes, hoping they would help connect adoptees searching for their biological families.
"I’ll do it," Murch told her, accepting the responsibility to do something for others like her.
The boxes contained more than just adoption files: There were survivor and casualty lists from the plane crash, convoy manifests of transport companies, flight departure dates, destination addresses, child condition reports post-crash, volunteer lists, personal letters, news articles, film rolls, birth certificates, intake records, and early childhood photos.
Murch says: "These files are a heartbreaking, beautiful, and astonishing testament to war, life and death. They are a piece of my personal history and that of thousands of other adoptees."
She began sorting, categorizing, cross-referencing, and transcribing the records of Babylift children evacuated in April 1975.
One day, she suddenly realized that if it was so important to her, someone who had not even been searching for her past, what could it mean to others?
As if by destiny, Murch had been entrusted with a project to preserve thousands of records and documents from the wartime child-welfare organization.
She joined the Society of American Archivists.
She is now learning about cataloging, data management, descriptive formatting, risk management, privacy protection, and regulations for personal documents.
By organizing, digitizing, and indexing this collection, she hopes to preserve it for future generations.
Finding her biological parents brought healing to Huyen Friedlander, the last child placed aboard the final flight of Operation Babylift.
Following a trip to Vietnam in 1996, she became a therapist specializing in trauma, grief, and loss.
In graduate school, she focused her research on transracial adoption.
She says: "Most people do not understand the inner world of adoptees. These were the same painful experiences happening inside me before I found my mother."
Based on attachment theory, she says caregivers are the first to mirror a child's sense of self through interaction. For Friedlander, all her caregivers abruptly vanished in April 1975.
"I didn't know who I was anymore. That was deeply traumatic, even though I couldn't articulate it at the time."
A 2000 study by Ohio State University involving 169 Vietnamese war adoptees across 10 U.S. cities highlighted similar struggles. While 76% wanted to meet their biological fathers upon arriving in the U.S., only 30% knew their fathers' names. About 22% attempted contact, and only 3% succeeded.
Born to American military personnel and Vietnamese civilians, most of these children never knew their fathers' names or addresses.
Often, they possessed only a faded photograph or stories passed down from their mothers.
The cross-continental flights effectively closed the door on the past for many, particularly those aged four to nine. Initially fluent in Vietnamese, they lost their mother tongue entirely.
When Friedlander first arrived in the U.S., she could still sing a Vietnamese song.
She later realized that her cultural detachment was the result of severe psychological trauma.
Now in her 50s, Friedlander looks at photos from her early days in America and sees a profoundly traumatized, dissociated child avoiding eye contact with strangers. A psychological wall separated her past from her present, shielding her from the deep pain of her losses while allowing her to feel safe in a new life.
Despite having a loving adoptive family, she had felt isolated growing up mixed-race in the U.S. Surrounded by taller peers, having a different skin color, and facing discrimination at school, she constantly felt inadequate.
"When my biological mother left me at four, my true self died. I became a compliant child, seeking safety, fearing conflict, and terrified of displeasing people because I feared rejection. I lost myself," Friedlander says.
Within the roughly two weeks between leaving Vietnam and meeting her adoptive family, she lost everything familiar: her mother, relatives, home, language, food, and culture.
Later, when she visited Little Saigon in California, people spoke to her in Vietnamese. Unable to understand, she felt a heavy burden of guilt when asked why she could not speak her native language.
Working with hundreds of adoptees, Friedlander observes parallel traumas. Many share a collective pain of feeling unloved, rejected, or believing they had caused something terrible.
Common struggles include identity crises, self-rejection, racism, isolation, difficulty assimilating, feelings of inferiority, and body image issues.
For Friedlander, reclaiming control of her life meant reconnecting with her homeland.
In September 2025, she and a group of Babylift adoptees cycled through the Mekong Delta. Most were still searching for their biological mothers.
During a rest stop in Can Tho, 52-year-old group member Le My Huong suggested an idea: actively approaching Vietnamese families to find their mothers.
Adopted in Australia and surviving an abusive childhood, Le had endured her own traumatic search. She was kidnapped as a child and deceived for 47 years by her captor, who claimed to be her biological mother.
When she returned to Vietnam in 2004, she met with a family that falsely claimed her as theirs. It took 14 years for the truth to be known.
She says: "I was completely broken. Fortunately, I eventually found my real mother. That was the healing. After decades of living a lie, I am still learning how to carry the weight of the truth."
Over the past two decades, Le has helped many adoptees return to Vietnam to search for their families after being struck by the realization that the answers usually lie within the community and not in adoption paperwork.
Because most documents contain false information, many adoptees do not even know if their recorded names are real.
Le concluded that the only reliable way to find biological families is through DNA testing and cross-referencing global genetic databases.
The group agreed.
Friedlander, Le, Era Goodland, and Jane Joy went on to co-found Mother Search, a non-profit facilitating family reunions through DNA matching.
Launched in September 2025, Mother Search seeks to connect searching children and parents by sharing photos and information. Participants receive free DNA testing kits, which normally cost upwards of $50.
The samples are uploaded to major European and American databases, such as MyHeritage, which holds around 9 million profiles, and Ancestry, which has over 30 million, to increase the matching potential.
So far, five pairs of relatives have been matched and three reunifications involving two adoptees in France and one in the U.S. have been facilitated.
"If it weren't for DNA matching, they would never have found each other because all their paperwork was wrong," Le says.
Rather than rely on one-to-one matches, the project aims to expand the pool of DNA profiles from overseas adoptees while simultaneously collecting samples from mothers in Vietnam.
She notes that a Vietnamese family recently sent her a photo of an 83-year-old mother who is still searching for her long-lost son. Seeing the profound sadness in her face reaffirmed the urgency of their work.
"Mothers and children are still waiting to be found."
The organization believes that reconnecting with roots is essential for adoptees to reclaim their identities after an immeasurable loss. It hopes governments will eventually facilitate widespread, affordable, and accessible DNA testing.
"If state agencies in both Vietnam and the U.S. provided easily accessible archival information, it would help heal the wounds caused by this separation," Friedlander says.
Murch is pursuing the same goal.
Her questions and the 33 boxes of newly discovered files brought her back to Vietnam for a second time in May 2026. She visited national archives, locating thousands of documents related to wartime adoptions. At the end of her journey, she returned to Vinh Long simply to sit in quiet reflection in her birthplace.
She ruminates: "I know the chances of finding any clues are very slim, and I don't expect much. I just went there to walk around and reflect on what my life in 2026 would look like if I hadn't left Vietnam in the final days of the war."
Deep down, she still yearns for the memories she never had. For adoptees like her, discovering their origins is a form of validation.
Using the Friends For All Children archives, Murch and her colleagues are now tracking down Babylift adoptees across the U.S. to hand-deliver their personal files.
She says: "Witnessing history appear like a miracle, seeing your own name in the legacy of war, is incredibly important. A tiny piece of truth means everything to someone who knows nothing."
She says there are many other individual adoption cases beyond the records she has collected, highlighting the need for a central archive to consolidate records from various sources and help women find their children easier.
"I hope the governments of both countries can establish an agency to support the children of the war.
"And we need a compassionate community so that the complex legacy of the war isn't treated merely as a personal problem for those born at the intersection of history."
As the youngest victims of the conflict, these former orphans are still searching for an answer to the question that has vexed them for nearly six decades: Who am I?
Story by Hong Phuc, Kim Hoa

title: In Queens, Immigrant Women Sew a Truer Atlas
content:
In Queens, Immigrant Women Sew a Truer Atlas
The largely undocumented Latin American women of New York’s “costureros,” or needlework circles, are creating a countermap to archive the stories of their lives.
This article is part of a series focusing on underrepresented craft histories, researched and written by the 2025 Craft Archive Fellows, and organized in collaboration with the Center for Craft.
How can we delve into the archives of the present? Is it possible to unveil and touch the documents that communities are creating today to record and remember their history, or does understanding only arise with the passage of time? When does an object become an archive?
For the past two years, I have been working with two immigrant-led costureros: circles of women from all over Latin America that gather to create textiles together. Located in different community centers in Northwestern Queens in New York City, these spaces have become a safe haven for many undocumented, working-class immigrants who are enduring racial profiling and persecution under the current immigration crackdown. Amid this terror, the intimacy and secrecy of the costurero set a table where gossip and generosity sit side by side with threads and needles.
The first group, BordeAndo, was founded in 2018 as a community engagement initiative of the Queens Museum, though it soon grew beyond the institution to become an independent collective. Its name plays with multiple meanings in Spanish: bordar (to embroider), borde (border or frontier), and the suffix -ando, which evokes movement or walking. Most of its members come from the Ecuadorian highlands (la Sierra), though others are from the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, and Mexico. They range in age from 30 to 83 and have lived in the United States for between 10 and 50 years.
Las Comadres Bordadoras was founded in 2021 in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic by two Mexican immigrants, who sought to bring women out of isolation and foster a mutual support network. Their name, also difficult to translate, gestures toward camaraderie and kinship. The comadre refers specifically to women who are, in their words, “a midpoint between friend and family.” The comadres come from Mexico, Cuba, El Salvador, Uruguay, Colombia, Ecuador, and Argentina; range in age from 35 to 75; and have lived in the United States for between two and 30 years. They mostly embroider Mexican cloth napkins, but all forms of needlework are welcome. This costurero calls itself “nomadic” because it has moved around community gardens, public libraries, and schools in the area since its conception. Both circles are intergenerational, international spaces of confluence for transnational, working-class, largely undocumented immigrant women.
Last year, BordeAndo and Las Comadres Bordadoras were the protagonists of Thread of Voice / Un hilo de voz at the Queens Museum. The exhibition, which I curated, featured Andrés Altamirano’s photographs of the costurero members along with film by documentarian Eleonora Privitera. The visual narrative and documentation of this project was also done in collaboration with Altamirano.
I see these costureros as living archives — as sites where craft traditions converge, and concrete embodied and material practices connect geographies of affect and displacement, like a woman knitting a stitch learned by her grandmother back home or another embroidering a napkin for the altar of a dead loved one whose grave she cannot visit because of her migratory status. “Text” and “textile” share an etymological root — the Latin verb texere — that reveals both that texts are woven and textiles written. In this sense, textiles are texts that we have forgotten how to read, encoded with bodily gestures, storytelling practices, and materialities that could, if safeguarded, be called archives.

title: In Texas, a historic Route 66 neighborhood taps its deep roots for a revival
content:
In Texas, a historic Route 66 neighborhood taps its deep roots for a revival
Loading...
| Amarillo, Texas
David Rosas turns off Arthur Avenue and starts walking through the old Mexican American Barrio of his childhood.
The first landmark is an empty lot.
His grandmother’s house once stood here, Mr. Rosas says. It was a place where relatives streamed in and out, coffee seemed always to be brewing, and everyone came to learn the family news. He has called it the family’s “bank, library, meeting place.”
Why We Wrote This
Many American neighborhoods carry the history of the people who built them and helped them flourish. When time erodes the bonds that define a place, new energy can help a place like the Barrio in Amarillo, Texas, renew itself.
He remembers the railroad men walking home for lunch, then heading back to work. Afterward, his grandmother and a neighbor would pull out flour, water, and lard and begin making tortillas, the kitchen filling with the familiar rhythm of the rolling pins.
“I wish I could hear it right now,” he says. Walking down the street a few blocks, he passes a funeral home. But Mr. Rosas knows the building by an older name: El Salón Mexicano.
His grandfather, Mateo Lopez, a Santa Fe railroad worker, helped build the neighborhood hall with other residents in the 1930s as a place for dances, weddings, and quinceañeras. “The Barrio is a town within a town,” Mr. Rosas says. “We didn’t travel far.”
The short walk amounts to a century of Barrio history, a story about how American communities are made, and often remade in order to endure. In the late 19th century, Mexican railroad workers, brought in through programs of the Santa Fe Railway, arrived with their families and built homes, businesses, and a Catholic church – a world within a world, shaped partly by the segregation and discrimination that kept them apart from much of the city’s wider civic life. But the Barrio can be seen, too, as a recognizable American story of frontier towns in which neighbors helped out neighbors, and civic services became a fully communal affair.
Like so many small towns along Route 66, old boundaries have loosened, and families have scattered as regional economies reshape where people work and live. But the neighborhood is being rebuilt again. Their challenge is no longer how to create a community within those boundaries, but how to carry forward the belonging that grew there.
There is a Route 66 irony embedded in the Barrio’s story. Its 10th Avenue was part of the original highway in 1926 – the road Americans would celebrate as the “Main Street of America.” It was rerouted north in 1932.
Yet on the other side of Amarillo’s railroad tracks, Mexican American families kept building their version of the Main Street ideal: businesses, places to gather, familiar families, and a commitment to one another.
■ ■ ■
For Mr. Rosas, that older Main Street can be measured less in storefronts than in relationships.
“Back then when you met somebody, an elderly gentleman, they asked you who your parents were,” he says. He would give his name, and the older man would begin placing him.
Lupe’s son. Mateo’s grandson. Then would come the stories: Your father helped me with this. I knew your grandfather. “Being recognized by your parents and your grandparents, it’s a big deal,” Mr. Rosas says. “I mean, it carried weight.”
His grandfather was one of the first pillars of the Barrio. His father, Lupe Rosas, carried that ethic into a different era. A World War II veteran who later worked at Amarillo’s veterans hospital, he was one of the first members of the NAACP. In the 1950s, he and two Catholic priests conducted a sit-in at one of Amarillo’s whites-only restaurants.
Lupe also became one of the people neighbors sought out when they did not know how to navigate institutions beyond the Barrio. Someone needed help with a Social Security form. Someone had a problem with the city. Someone needed to know whom to ask.
“When people had problems, nobody had a lawyer,” says Mr. Rosas, who dropped out of school in the eighth grade and went on to spend four decades selling cars. “My dad could figure something out. And I do that for a lot of people.”
Mr. Rosas holds no public office. But neighbors call him when trash is not picked up or a dilapidated property becomes a problem. He goes to city meetings, pushes officials for neighborhood investment, and says Amarillo’s current mayor takes his calls.
People sometimes call him the “mayor of the Barrio.” Mr. Rosas has given himself an arguably grander title, printed on his business card: H.M.I.C. – “Head Mexican in Charge.”
His charm and levity, however, belie his seriousness. In 2017 he became part of a neighborhood revitalization process.
For him, the effort is about more than getting sidewalks or city money. His grandmother’s house is gone. Relatives have scattered across Amarillo and beyond. Mr. Rosas himself lives about five miles from the Barrio.
The old social geography is harder to see. “It’s getting lost,” he says.
■ ■ ■
Teresa Kenedy turns off Arthur Avenue onto 10th and drives slowly toward the railroad tracks, narrating the Barrio almost block by block.
There are the murals marking the entrance to the old neighborhood. Then the new trees. Banners celebrating Día de los Muertos with sugar skulls. Street lamps. Bike racks. Nine street benches painted in reds, blues, and greens. Most noticeably, there are sidewalks – wide, wheelchair accessible stretches of concrete in a neighborhood where, away from the businesses, sidewalks are scarce.
“What you’re seeing – none of that was here prior to April of this year,” says Ms. Kenedy, now the president of The Barrio Neighborhood Planning Committee, on which Mr. Rosas serves, too. For the old main street, it amounts to a $6.1 million makeover the organization helped facilitate.
But Ms. Kenedy does not describe the project as an attempt to make 10th Avenue look new. She talks instead about making the street announce where it is – and what came before.
For Mr. Rosas, the Barrio is an inheritance. He can walk its streets through generations of his own family. His argument for rebuilding the neighborhood begins with memory, but becomes a claim on the larger city: “We’ve paid taxes forever,” he says. “I want some of that money back here.”
Ms. Kenedy’s attachment is chosen. She did not grow up in the Barrio, but in tiny Snowville, Utah, near the Idaho state line, where hers was the only Hispanic family for about 20 miles. Her father died when she was age 2, leaving her mother to raise seven children. Ms. Kenedy says everyone chipped in; she began working at age 9, first as a babysitter and then as a dishwasher.
She arrived in the Amarillo area for college at age 20, studying to be a social worker, “connecting people with resources.”
Her biography appears almost geographically during the drive. She passes Caprock High School, where she worked for 13 years in drug prevention, and then Bowie Middle School, where she spent another seven.
Then she became the coordinator of a federally funded program to place the children of migrant farmworkers in school, even though they might remain for only weeks or months before their families moved on.
When she retired in 2015, Ms. Kenedy, a widow with no children, committed to volunteering in the Barrio, her home for over 45 years.
Together, she and Mr. Rosas represent the challenge facing the Barrio now. The first generations built a community from the ground up. Their descendants inherited its stories and obligations. The work of this generation is different: to turn that inheritance into something sturdy enough to survive change.
In 2018, Ms. Kenedy became something of the Barrio’s historian. She led a task force that interviewed older residents for a book that would preserve the neighborhood’s collective memory.
She conducted many of the interviews herself. When the group needed someone to turn the interviews into a book and nobody volunteered, Ms. Kenedy did that, too.
The book was also part of the committee’s effort to put together a historical map. The map and the memories fed into a neighborhood plan.
And the plan, eventually, became the trees, benches, and lights along 10th Avenue.
Memory, in other words, became infrastructure.
■ ■ ■
More than a century after an earlier generation built El Salón Mexicano because the Barrio needed somewhere to gather, Mr. Rosas and Ms. Kenedy are trying to create another such place – not to restore the confining boundaries of the old neighborhood, but to give its communal life a place to flourish again.
The group calls it La Plazita. Right now it’s an empty lot, but they are planning to turn it into a community park with a stage. Mr. Rosas was the one who spotted the property for sale. The city ultimately acquired it and deeded it to the planning committee.
For now, there is a mural, several benches, sponsored paving stones, and a storage building. Ms. Kenedy envisions a performance stage, food trucks, mariachi musicians, folklórico dancers, pop-up markets, movie nights, quinceañeras, and wedding receptions. There will be free Wi-Fi. The committee has already begun holding events on the unfinished lot so people will get used to coming there.
As she walks through the unfinished La Plazita, she also mentions the legacy of Mateo Lopez.
“Here’s someone who came as a young man with his wife from Mexico to the United States, came to Amarillo, helped build this railroad, helped build a community center – and his grandson is now helping renovate this neighborhood. It came full circle, right?”

title: Redfern Reckoning: Lily Shearer on Subverting the Colonial Gaze for the Stage
content: Redfern Reckoning: Lily Shearer on Subverting the Colonial Gaze for the Stage Country Australia agnes Thu, 09/10/2026 - 09:27 Issues Languages and Cultures Program 5 Main Image By Cristina Verán The word Moogahlin, in the Yuin and Bundjalung languages, means “to play” or “to fool around”. This spirited term—and the living philosophy behind it—expands through the work of the renowned Moogahlin Performing Arts, one of the most vital and culturally grounding forces in contemporary Australian performance today. Indigenous theater veterans Lily Shearer (Murrawarri/Ngemba), Fred Copperwaite (Bunuba), and Dr. Liza-Mare Syron (Biripi) co-founded the company in the deeply entrenched Aboriginal community of Sydney’s Redfern district, deliberately rejecting the standard western structures and strictures of theater to instead honor millennia of First Nations storytelling. Over the past decade and a half, Moogahlin has evolved from a grassroots, artist-run setup into a major force on the international stage; one that maintains a deep commitment to the community from which it sprang. Through landmark productions like Jane Harrison’s “The Visitors”—a touring work that inverts the colonial gaze to depict the arrival of the British First Fleet through the eyes of the land’s Original Peoples—and flagship platforms like the Yellamundie Festival, the company continuously champions independent First Nations creators and reclaims historical narratives. Beyond decolonizing performance spaces and redefining what theater can be, Moogahlin broadens its mission to include environmental and cultural advocacy through its biennial Baiame's Ngunnhu Festival, held alongside the ancient Brewarrina Fish Traps. Cristina Verán spoke with Moogahlin Performing Arts Co-founder and Artistic Director Lily Shearer about the political and social histories that shape their work, and how Indigenous storytelling remains essential to the larger projects of community healing and cultural survival. Lily Shearer and Natano Fa'anana (Samoan), Moogahlin's Executive Producer, en route to pitch a new play at the 2025 ISPA Conference (International Society for the Performing Arts) in New York. Cristina Verán: Tell us a bit about the beginnings of Moogahlin Performing Arts and the community it calls home. Lily Shearer: We, the company’s co-founders, started talking about forming something like this back in November 2007, following the passing of Uncle Kevin Smith (Walbung-Murramarang), a deeply respected actor and Aboriginal activist from Redfern, in Sydney. He’d been trying to establish a local Indigenous theater company, and his family asked if we’d pick up the baton and build something proper and lasting for the community. We officially incorporated on May 19, 2009. CV: While it’s become known for performances that can be defined as “theater,” Moogahlin doesn’t refer to itself as a "theater company,” as such. Why is that? LS: That was dead intentional. Western concepts of theater want to put artists in this box, requiring script-bound works and proscenium arches, whereas our mob has been telling stories for tens of thousands of years, across interconnected forms that combine dance, music, visual art, oral yaans, and songlines. Written scripts, in the Western sense, are a form First Peoples here have only really been using for about 50 years. Naming ourselves Moogahlin Performing Arts meant no one could lock us into a single Western performance genre, leaving us free to tell stories our way. CV: What was it like during those early years in terms of size, scale, resources, and before Moogahlin had a permanent home? LS: We started out as a grassroots, purely artist-run setup, working on a project-by-project basis. Each of us, the founders, kept outside jobs to pay the bills and keep roofs over our heads. For years, our office consisted of a single black filing cabinet that held all our documentation, dragged from place to place, wherever I was working. Though we lacked a fixed venue, we had strong relationships with the local Redfern community. CV: What makes Redfern so significant, symbolically and historically? LS: It’s universally recognized as the "Blak Capital" of Australia as well as the geographic and political beating heart of the modern First Peoples movement—where everything from the Aboriginal Legal Services to Koori Radio to the original National Black Theatre were born. Back in the late 1960s and ‘70s, our Indigenous civil rights activists here were exchanging ideas directly with members of the Black Panther movement in the United States. The central block of the neighborhood—known simply as "The Block"—is Aboriginal-owned land handed over under the Gough Whitlam-led federal government in 1972 after community members squatted in tents, right there on country, to demand land rights. This history also ties directly to the closing down of state and church-run missions from the late 1930s to the late 1960s. [Note: In Australia, the terms Blak and Blakfullas are used to refer to Indigenous Australians, not to people of African descent.] CV: What were the social dynamics like at the time, in terms of where people came from and what they were facing? LS: Those missions I noted were run like reservations, or residential schools, with the aim of total control, strict assimilation, and the cultural erasure of our People. When they eventually shut down, generations of displaced mob—many of whom had been stripped from their families under the country’s shameful Stolen Generation policies—had nowhere to go. They started coming to Redfern and setting up camp on The Block because nearby factories offered manual-labor jobs to people who’d been trained on the missions. Sadly, by the early 2000s, the accumulation of intergenerational trauma, poverty, and forced displacement led to serious issues for many residents with drug misuse, domestic violence, alcoholism, and crime. It also became a highly policed neighborhood. CV: Did these folks come primarily from Indigenous communities around Sydney, or from further afield as well? LS: Our people came from all over the nation after the missions were closed. First Peoples from as far as the Northern Territory were taken to Milleewas Half-caste home, Mulgoa NSW, in Western Sydney. Our people on the Mission in my hometown of Brewarrina came from QLD, VIC, and communities close by, but it was a handful of those communities all mixed up on the Mission, so they didn’t speak the same language and have the same ceremonies, they didn’t even have the same diets. When the missions closed, they came to Redfern looking for work, as they were trained as domestic servants and/or laborers. However, most importantly, they came in search of their families, to find out where they belonged. I was involved in a door-to-door survey taken in Western Sydney during the 1990s. There were mobs representing 63 different First Nations tribes and/or language groups living in the Blacktown LGA. Most of our people living in Western Sydney were relocated from Redfern as they were redeveloping The Block. CV: What were you engaged in at that time, and how did it relate to the movements you’ve mentioned? LS: Between 2005 and 2007, while working in Redfern for a mainstream company, Performance Space, I got involved at the Redfern Community Centre (RCC), and I helped launch “Gathering Ground,” a Community Cultural Development project, alongside Pact Youth Theatre. I then became the Cultural Development Officer at RCC, and Frederick Copperwaite stepped in to direct “Gathering Ground” (2008, 2010), while I acted as cultural advisor, to ensure 100% Indigenous creative leadership. Our focus was telling authentic stories through our own lens, as well as using that storytelling to process intergenerational trauma—which we did while also bringing in over 3,000 audience members a night. CV: How did urban development pressures in Sydney begin to impact this community? LS: Gentrification was forced upon it by the state government’s Redfern Waterloo Authority. Homes on The Block were knocked down, and families who’d lived there were forcibly relocated, again. The Aboriginal Housing Company was staunch in holding onto The Block, and began fundraising and working with University of Sydney design students to reimagine its future. CV: The advent of new arts spaces, and arts programming in general, seems to too-often herald and further encourage more gentrification, serving its newly anointed beneficiaries rather than the People already living there in community. How has that played out in Redfern? LS: Well, when Carriageworks Performing Arts Centre opened down the road in 2007, community mistrust around it was huge. People reckoned it’d be yet another elitist venue—like, for example, the Sydney Opera House—that would basically lock locals out. It took years of deliberate, unrushed relationship-building to bridge the Centre’s divide between itself and the local Aboriginal community, ensuring the People would be empowered to tell their own stories through its space and resources. CV: How did Moogahlin transition into a fully funded resident company there? LS: The major shift came in 2014 when the CEO of Carriageworks formally invited us to apply for residency, despite our lack of capital at the time. This provided our first actual office space, and partnering with them on grant applications gave us the organizational weight needed for multi-year operational funding. We secured our first four-year grant from the Australia Council for the Arts (now Creative Australia) for 2017–2021, and are currently in our third consecutive cycle with them, through 2028, matched by multi-year operational funding from Arts New South Wales (now Create NSW) since 2021. That baseline financial stability allowed us to stop surviving hand-to-mouth on project grants and actually engage in long-term strategic planning. Scene from "The Visitors" at the Perelman Arts Center in New York City. Photo by Maria Baranova. CV: Now let’s get to “The Visitors,” which has been touring across Australia and internationally in the past couple of years—including here at New York’s prestigious Perelman Arts Center (PACNYC). Tell us how this work came to Moogahlin and what its mission has become now that it is part of it. LS: It was written by playwright Jane Harrison (Muruwari), the author of Stolen, who had pitched the script originally under the title “First Contact” at Moogahlin’s National flagship platform, Yellamundie Festival, in our inaugural year (2013). Following seven years of dramaturgical development and community consultation around it, to ensure authenticity, it premiered at Carriageworks (directed by Fred Copperwaite and produced by Liza-Mare Syron) during the 2020 Sydney Festival. In 2023, “The Visitors” was re-staged under the directorship, Wesley Enoch (Quandamooka) and in partnership with Sydney Theatre Company, premiering at Sydney Opera House as part of their 50th Anniversary program. The play employs a kind of symbolic inversion of all the histories Australians are taught in school that are, in fact, contrary to our own Indigenous stories. Those British colonizers who recorded meticulous entries in their logs about us had operated under the assumption that First Peoples would never read them. But Jane went and found these documents, including many wherein British officers described Aboriginal People as, for example, "brutes" with "narrow heads, stocky bodies, short limbs, fish-like lips, and protruding eyes." Non-Indigenous audiences are often shocked to learn that some offensive language used in the play is, in fact, quoted verbatim from the official British records. She wanted to invert that colonial gaze. Scene from "The Visitors" at the Perelman Arts Center in New York City. Photo by Maria Baranova. CV: What should we know about the historical event around which the story is centered? LS: Set in 1788, “The Visitors” depicts six senior [Aboriginal] Law Men & Women, and one new initiate, from surrounding clans, convening in council at what is now known as Sydney Cove to discuss what they saw making its way toward them on the horizon: the British fleet. They begin to debate, per their own diplomatic protocols, whether to welcome, ignore, or resist the newcomers. Events in the play [such as a public hanging witnessed offshore] are drawn directly from colonial logs now reinterpreted through an Indigenous lens. CV: How has Moogahlin managed to design and adapt the staging for “The Visitors,” thus enabling the play to travel beyond major mainstage theaters and work well in different and smaller spaces? LS: We created three distinct production models. Version A is our mainstage configuration, built for major venues like the Sydney Opera House or the Public Theater in New York, and featuring a massive sandstone set piece we’ve nicknamed “Bertha.” Version B is a much more compact, flexible touring setup for use in regional theaters across Australia. And Version C, still being developed, will be further stripped back, ideal for performances on missions, reservations, and in community halls. It requires just the seven actors in business suits around a boardroom table, under basic lighting. When we were in New York earlier this year, to perform this at the Perelman Arts Center (PACNYC) in Manhattan, the cast even considered taking this version to a rock in Central Park to perform it right there. Scene from "The Visitors" at the Perelman Arts Center in New York City. Photo by Maria Baranova. CV: How have Indigenous Australian audiences been responding to it? LS: Mainstage venues often feel alienating to our mob, due to historical barriers we’ve experienced from such spaces. But during our 2024 national tour, regional venues reported record attendance for local First Nations community members—some venues, in fact, saying it brought out the most Blackfullas they’d ever hosted! They come to “The Visitors” because we’ve built real relationships with local communities, presenting a powerful narrative that had never been presented on stage through an Indigenous lens before. CV: I understand that some conversations that came out of the 2010 National Indigenous Theatre Forum led to the launch of your flagship platform, Yellamundie Festival. LS: Between 2008 and 2010, Wesley Enoch (Quandamooka), now chairperson of Creative Australia, had been in discussions with federal Arts Minister Peter Garrett about allocating $2 million toward a new National Black Theatre for Australia. We argued that funds should go directly to artists, script development, and commissions—not more “bricks and mortar.” In response, Wesley and Lea-Anne Buckskin (Narungga, Kaurna, Wirangu, and Wotjobaluk) convened the inaugural National Indigenous Theatre Forum you mentioned, in Cairns, so that First Nations practitioners from across the country could gather to map out sector priorities. When the number one of these policies was identified by a vote: reviving the National Aboriginal Playwrights Conference (which had been defunct for 17 years due to both drops in funding and a generational gap in the sector), Wesley looked out at all the attendees and asked: “Who will take on the responsibility?” The room went dead silent, because no company had either spare cash or extra staff to offer. Liza-Mare Syron and I looked at each other, though, and thought, “OK, we will!”—and thus committed Moogahlin to leading it (despite having bugger-all in our bank account). Creative Australia then backed us with $50,000 in seed funding and paired us with producer Wendy Blacklock at Performing Lines to help build and strengthen our own producing capacity. Moogahlin Performing Arts co-founders Dr. Liza-Mare Syron, Frederick Copperwhite, and Lily Shearer. CV: How did that commitment lead to producing festivals as part of its work of decolonizing performance spaces, and how has Moogahlin’s vision evolved over time? LS: We launched Yellamundie Festival—from the Dharug word for "storyteller"—in 2013, as a biennial national showcase dedicated exclusively to independent First Nations artists (We do not accept proposals for this from established companies). From the 50 to 60 applications we receive from around the country each time, we select six works for intensive workshop development, and showcase the works to the public and sector over 3 nights and 2 days. Under Fred Copperwaite’s direction from 2013 to 2019, the festival focused on script-based plays. When I became Artistic Director in 2020, I expanded the format to include two play scripts, two dance/movement works, and two music/composition pieces, returning us to traditional storytelling methods that treated movement and composition as equal to texts. Across its seven editions so far, Yellamundie Festival has developed 51 original works—21 of which have gone on to full mainstage productions with major companies nationwide. Moogahlin itself also commits to fully producing at least one work from each cohort. CV: Please describe what the broader landscape of Indigenous theater in Australia, especially Indigenous-led theater companies, looks like today, and what particular challenges are still being faced. LS: The sector remains relatively tiny, with just three dedicated Black companies nationwide: Ilbijerri Theatre Company in Melbourne, Yirra Yaakin Theatre Company in Perth, and Moogahlin in Sydney (a fourth company, Kooemba Jdarra in Brisbane, closed around 2008 due to funding and operational pressures). We do have several specialized dance and physical theater organizations to add to the list, including Bangarra Dance Theatre, Marrugeku, and BlakDance. Recognizing also our only national First Peoples-led training institution, the National Aboriginal & Islander Skills Development Association (NAISDA) Dance College. As to the challenges, we as First Peoples entities have to respond to demands that mainstream organizations rarely face, with our teams constantly balancing creative development with support for community needs—including the ongoing work of reconnecting families split by the country’s Stolen Generations policies. We’re also navigating the dynamics around what’s being called a “lost generation”: people who’d previously hidden their Indigenous identity due to systemic racism and discrimination, but now, without having grown up in community, proudly claim this heritage. Cast and crew of "The Visitors." Photo by Maria Baranova. CV: How did the familial and perhaps generational experiences of yourself and your Moogahlin counterparts shape your respective interests in and commitment to reclaiming historical narratives? LS: My generation grew up under Australia’s assimilation policies. First Peoples here were not granted full voting rights until 1967, and our equal access to education was only mandated around 1972. I remember well that, as a student in the mid-1970s, in a Catholic secondary school run by Good Samaritan nuns, we were taught that Captain Cook "discovered" Australia (and therefore us). I dared to challenge my history teacher on this point, insisting that, according to my father and grandfather, that man didn't discover us—our people discovered him when he arrived on our shores. For this, the teacher called me a "brazen toad" and threw me out of her class—permanently. My co-founders, who are also Indigenous, had quite different upbringings. Meanwhile, Liza-Mare Syron grew up away from community in the Sydney suburb of Balmain, while Fred Copperwaite grew up on the other side of the country in Fremantle, near Perth, with his white father’s family. It was at age 30 that he was finally able to connect with his (maternal side) Aboriginal family. CV: Moogahlin now also produces another festival, which connects culturally centered storytelling with environmental advocacy. Tell us about this, especially the significance of the place for its setting. LS: Baiame Ngunnhu Festival, established in 2015, uses performance and community gathering to fight for environmental justice. It takes place along the Ba-Wun (Barwon) River in my home community of Brewarrina (in New South Wales). The site features our traditional Fish Traps—called Ngunnhu—which comprise an ancient stone-pen system and represent the oldest human-made structures on Earth, predating the Egyptian Pyramids and Stonehenge. Despite its immense historical significance, unfortunately, the Australian government provides bugger-all protection or funding compared to those places it sees as global heritage sites. CV: And for the record, what are the most pressing issues for this community right now? LS: The river system has been severely degraded by imported cattle breaking down its banks, invasive European carp displacing native fish, and introduced weeds choking the water channels. Most damaging of all are commercial cotton farms—many owned by foreign corporate interests in America and China—that extract massive volumes of water from our river network, on the driest inhabited continent on Earth. The core message at Baiame’s Ngunnhu Festival is straightforward: if the natural country provided by the Creator is unhealthy, the people who rely on that land cannot be healthy either. Thus, we are able to link our cultural survival directly to environmental survival and, ultimately, to the survival of all our First Nations Peoples. --Cristina Verán is an international Indigenous Peoples-focused researcher, educator, advocacy strategist, network weaver, curator, and mediamaker. She was a founding member of the United Nations Indigenous Media Network and the UN Indigenous Language Caucus. As Adjunct Faculty at New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts and Affiliate Faculty of the NYU Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, she brings emphasis to the global histories, expressions, and socio-political impacts of Indigenous contemporary visual and performing arts, design, tech, media, and popular culture(s). Cast members featured in these images from "The Visitors" America Season, at PAC NYC in New York, include: Najwa Adams-Ebel, Beau Dean, Riley Smith, Sean Dow, Kyle Morrison, Guy Simons, James Slee, and Zoe Walters. (Additional members feature in the Australian and New Zealand Season productions.)

title: She Started Nursing 53 Years Ago. At 80, This Lakshadweep Nurse Is a Global Top 10 Finalist
content: On most mornings, Hindumbi Kaurom Kakkada still walks into the wards of Government Indira Gandhi Hospital in Kavaratti, ready for a shift that has continued, in one form or another, for 53 years. She is 80-years-old, and by any ordinary measure, her career should have ended when she first retired two decades ago. Instead, her name now sits among the Top 10 finalists of the Aster Guardians Global Nursing Award 2026, chosen from more than 134,000 nurses across 214 countries. For a woman who once ferried patients between Lakshadweep's islands by fishing boat, recognition has finally arrived on the world stage, decades after most of her patients had already stopped thinking of her work as anything unusual. A career shaped by scarcity Hindumbi was born and raised in Kavaratti, in a family with deep roots in India's freedom movement. Her father took part in the Dandi March alongside Mahatma Gandhi, and she grew up watching a generation that believed service came before comfort. She trained as a nurse at Kozhikode Medical College, at a time when leaving the islands for an education meant long, uncertain sea journeys. When she returned home, Lakshadweep's healthcare system was still in its infancy. Emergency patients were often moved between islands in fishing boats or naval vessels, and even essential medicines had to be sourced from Kochi on the mainland. Hindumbi trained as a theatre nurse and worked through those early gaps herself, at one point transporting a patient by fishing boat while administering a blood transfusion, and conducting a forceps delivery during a monsoon, when reaching a hospital in time was simply not possible. From fishing boats to hospital wards, Hindumbi has spent over five decades bringing healthcare to Lakshadweep’s remote islands. Photograph: (YourStory) There was no backup team to call in such moments, and no second attempt if something went wrong. She learnt, early on, to work with whatever the sea and the weather allowed that day. More than 20,000 lives touched Over 53 years, Hindumbi has supported more than 20,000 surgeries and emergency cases, often working through shortages of staff, equipment and transport. Beyond the operating theatre, she encouraged institutional deliveries across the islands, persuading women to give birth in hospitals rather than at home, alongside immunisation drives, hygiene awareness campaigns and preventive healthcare outreach. She also contributed to containing a cholera outbreak on the islands, and stayed on duty through two very different crises: the 2004 tsunami and the COVID-19 pandemic. Hindumbi once administered a blood transfusion to a patient aboard a fishing boat—one of many emergencies she handled when medical transport was scarce Photograph: (YourStory) Many residents of Lakshadweep still remember her today as the nurse who was present at their birth, or who stood by their family during a medical emergency. When she formally retired at 60, the break lasted barely three months before she returned as a contract nurse, unwilling to step away from a community she had served for most of her adult life. She remains in that role today. A national honour turns global In 2023, the President of India recognised Hindumbi's contribution at the highest national level, conferring on her the Florence Nightingale Award, India's top honour for nurses. That recognition has now been followed by something considerably bigger. In May 2026, Aster DM Healthcare announced her as one of 10 finalists for the Aster Guardians Global Nursing Award, a prize instituted to recognise nurses working in some of the world's most geographically isolated regions and difficult healthcare settings. After retiring at 60, Hindumbi returned to work within three months as a contract nurse, continuing to serve the community she had cared for all her life. Photograph: (WomenShine) Selected through a three-stage evaluation process overseen by Ernst & Young as independent process advisors, the finalists were drawn from a record pool of applicants across every continent, making Hindumbi's presence on the list a rare distinction for a nurse from India's smallest union territory. Azad Moopen, the award's founder chairman, said nurses' commitment, dedication and compassion make them the backbone of healthcare systems across the world. One of the 10 finalists will receive the grand title and a prize of US$250,000, while the rest, Hindumbi included, will receive global recognition for their work. The winner will be announced later this year at a ceremony being held in New Delhi. For Hindumbi, the outcome may matter less than the fact that, at 80, she remains the person Lakshadweep's islanders call on first. Five decades after she began her career navigating boats between islands with no hospital in sight, her work has quietly become part of a much larger story about what nursing looks like at the edges of the world, far from where such recognition usually reaches. Sources: 'Lakshadweep nurse among global top 10 finalists for prestigious International Nursing Award': by ANI, Published on 24 June, 2026 'The nurse who transformed healthcare in Lakshadweep': by YourStory Desk, Published on 19 May, 2026 '80 yr old Lakshadweep nurse among top 10 Global Nursing Award Finalists': by Awaz the Voice Staff, Published on 25 June, 2026
