title: ‘We’re all related’: Montana welcome greets children home from Carlisle after more than 100 years
content:
TRIGGER WARNING: This story has photos of caskets and contains disturbing details about residential and boarding schools. If you are feeling triggered, here are healing-informed resources from the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition in the U.S. The National Indian Residential School Crisis Hotline in Canada can be reached at 1-866-925-4419 or the Lamathut Crisis Line at 1-800-721-0066. If you’re in Treaty 4 territory, call 306-522-7494.
Charles Fox
Special to ICT
FORT PECK, Montana — Lana Fourstar never forgot the words of her grandmother, Freda Redstone Fourstar.
“My Aunt Christine needs to come home. She should have never been out there. She should have never died out there. She needs to come home. Someday, somebody needs to bring her home.”
Finally, after 135 years, Christine Redstone along with Richard Morgan and Peter Howe were returned to their homeland on Tuesday, Sept. 8, to the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes.
The three were part of a group that arrived at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School on April 15, 1890, after an 1800-mile journey to arrive at the school. During their time there, all three died of illnesses and were buried in the school cemetery.
On an especially windy day that some believed was the ancestors calling the children home, they completed the final leg of their return through the rolling hills and Badlands of North Dakota, arriving mid-afternoon in northeastern Montana.
At the eastern border of the reservation by the Big Muddy Creek Bridge a caravan of approximately 25 cars waited to welcome and escort the returning children.
Dana Buckles, 17, the great-grandson of Chief Leonard Crow Dog, sang an honor song for the repatriated students.
“It’s hard to know or even imagine what the pain or experiences they went through,” Buckles said while waiting for the group to arrive. “I couldn’t imagine being in their shoes. I’m grateful to live in the time I am today, and to be able to wear my moccasins or learn how to sing Indian. I’m just very grateful our culture’s still here.”
“It would be really difficult to be raised in one way of life, and then be taken away from your people, your families, and be converted to something that you’ve never, ever seen before,” she said.
Since Richard Morgan and Peter Howe did not have living relatives, organizers stressed that “the community will become the family,” making sure that no child will come home alone.
Because there were no known photographs of Richard Morgan, this was especially important since organizers wanted to make sure he was not reduced to a forgotten student, a faceless name on a school record. It was necessary to organizers that these three children were recognized as children born out of love with dreams and aspirations they never were able to accomplish.
“There’s really no way to express it in English. We have relatives who are buried in boarding school cemeteries. They’ve not been brought home. They’re still buried there. And for these children to come back and to be laid to rest amongst their people is an important thing,” said Melissa Buckles as she waited with three generations of family members to welcome the returning students.
“Their spirits can’t rest until they come home,” she said. “And now they’ll be laid to rest properly in our way. And especially for the two little boys. It was important to show up for them because they have no living family… We are all family. We’re either related by blood or marriage here. So we’re all Mitákuye Oyás’iŋ. We’re all related.”
The two young men were taken to the tribal repatriation cemetery in Poplar where teepees were erected in the darkness that evening and a fire started for an all-night vigil prior to their reburial on Wednesday, September 9.
Christine was taken to the Freda Fourstar Community Hall in Frazer. Ironically, the building is named after the same relative who for decades discussed the need to bring her home. She will be buried at Oswego Catholic Cemetery where many of her family members are buried, on Sept. 10.
“It is meaningful for our people that we open it up for the opportunity for creative community efforts and, and they have a place to show support or a place for them to grieve and relate to what’s going on,” Dyan Youpee, the tribe’s cultural preservation director told ICT. “And also to educate our younger people about the process for us to repatriate and the ceremonies. The inheritance of cultural responsibility is embedded in all of our community people.”
She continued, “We have a sacred duty and a responsibility to make sure that all the community is involved or participates or even prays from afar for the safekeeping of these ancestors coming home.”
A procession of runners, equestrians, motorcycles, and runners will be led to the reburial of Morgan and Howe by police and fire trucks.
‘I just sobbed’
The return home came following a very emotional week in Carlisle, Pennsylvania.
The Carlisle Indian Industrial School was the first federally run, off-reservation boarding school for Native Americans. Approximately 8,000 Native American students attended the school in the government’s misguided attempt at forceful assimilation into White civilization by cutting all links in their cultural chain. It became the model for more than 400 schools across 37 states and territories in the U.S. and provided a blueprint for Canada’s notorious residential school system.
Retracing the footsteps of ancestors who never made it home can be a wrenching experience. This was especially true for the relatives of Christine Redstone.
“I started to get emotional the minute I walked into the cemetery, and then when I saw where she was buried for myself for the first time… it just hit me, and then it made me cry, and I dropped to my knees and I just sobbed because it was so overwhelming,” said Michael Redstone.
Lana Fourstar, another relative of Christine Redstone, initially felt anger when she first walked into the Carlisle cemetery but feeling quickly turned to empathy for all the students buried there.
“The mother in me kicked in. I wanted to be able to just hold them all, just hold them all in my arms, and let them know that even though I wasn’t their relative, we’re all relatives in the Native way, and that we’re here,” she said. “We’re here for you, and that I’m praying for you, and someday I hope you’re at your homelands. And I felt a sense of peace, and all I could do was just keep praying that day.”
As a mother of three, there was a time when she knew that those could have been her children dying in a faraway place so far from a mother’s love.
It was under the outstretched limbs of a large oak tree, often referred to as the “witness tree,” that had been on the barracks grounds since before the school opened that Michael Redstone found some sense of peace and resilience.
“And then I got to stand under a tree that had been here since the time Carlisle was first opened, and I was thinking, ‘This tree’s seen my grandmother walk by. Now this tree gets to see her granddaughters walk by,’ and I just thought that was kind of a full circle moment. We’re still here despite what they tried to do to get us to abandon our way of life, but here we are still. Family’s just as strong as ever.”
‘Deep gloom’
The 1890 Fort Peck group that Christine, Richard, and Peter were part of consisted of 43 children, 22 boys and 21 girls, and were part of a larger group of 126 students recruited in Montana from various tribes.
School founder and superintendent Richard Pratt seemed particularly excited by the Fort Peck group as he wrote the Commissioner of Indian Affairs on April 25, 1890.
“The party from Fort Peck is worthy of mention as being taken almost wholly from the Agency school and gives evidence of good work in education and care,” he wrote.
Nine years later, he would again write the commissioner, mentioning that 25 percent of that Montana group died either while at the school or shortly after being returned home, and he questioned whether there was enough care making sure healthy children were chosen.
Christine was 15 when she arrived April 15, 1890. She expected to stay five years but after nine years at the school she died on July 19, 1899. The cause of her death is uncertain. Her student information card lists her as 5 feet tall and 96.5 pounds upon arrival at the school with both of her parents being deceased. Her records noted her stepfather lived at Porcupine Creek.
Four times during a five-year period, Christine stayed with the Russell family in Kemblesville located in Chester County of Pennsylvania as part of the school’s so-called “outing” program. The family obviously had grown close during the four summers she spent living with them.
Following her passing, Mrs. Russell sent a letter that appeared in the school newspaper, The Indian Helper, describing “the deep gloom” her death had cast over their family.
“Her sunny and affectionate disposition completely won our hearts, and she was to us as a daughter,” wrote Mrs. Russell, who had been writing a letter to Christine with a gift of money when she received news of her death.
Peter Howe arrived in Carlisle at the age of 16. He died on June 5, 1896, after becoming ill while on the school’s outing program in Solebury, Pennsylvania. The school held a joint funeral for Peter and fellow student, Fred Senasche, both having died after a battle with tuberculosis, according to school records. Both were described as “patient, hopeful sufferers to the last” in the school newspaper.
Although he may be in a group photo of the Fort Peck students, there is no known individual photo of Richard Morgan. He arrived as a 17-year-old with Peter and Christine, but died less than a year later of tuberculosis on March 25, 1891.
While his father had died, he still had a mother and stepfather. According to the school newspaper, he opted to spend his final days at school where he felt he would receive care rather than travel home.
Ongoing battles
The return of the students has been a long journey and has involved efforts by two generations.
At the Redstone family’s request, Dyan Youpee’s father, Darrell “Curley” Youpee, who died in May 2021, had tried to initiate bringing Christine home at the family’s request. Dyan Youpee was finally able to bring her father’s efforts to fruition.
Now what her father had started she was able to see through to fruition.
It was not without its share of obstacles, however.
“The journey to bringing these children home has been marked by decades of institutional bureaucracy and resistance,” Dyan Youpee, told The Glasglow Courier in August. “Fort Peck Tribes have had to fight through exhausting consultation battles, difficult administrative policies, and rigid ‘closet living relative’ requirements just to reclaim their sovereign relatives.
“Repatriation is a living, breathing exercise in tribal sovereignty and grief.”
Not every tribe has been able to navigate the institutional process to an end considered appropriate.
In 2024 the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska filed suit in federal court demanding that the U.S. Office of Army Cemeteries honor the tribe’s request to return the remains of two Winnebago boys who died at Carlisle more than a century ago.
The Army took over the Carlisle Indian Industrial School after it was closed in 1918.
The tribe argues that the federal Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, or NAGPRA, a 1990 law that spells out tribal rights governing returns of objects and remains, should be followed.
The Army maintains that NAGPRA doesn’t apply at Carlisle and that Army protocols supersede it. In April, a federal appeals court sided with Winnebago and sent the case back to a lower court.
Winnebago says it will continue pressing its case. The tribe’s chairman, Coly Brown, has stated that, “NAGPRA is an important statute our relatives fought for.”

title: Mexique : la jeunesse du Totonacapan résiste par le cinéma communautaire
content:
À Papantla, dans le Totonacapan de Veracruz, au Mexique, un collectif de jeunes totonaques se réunit chaque année depuis 2015 pour réaliser une semaine de campement et d’activités culturelles. Dans une région fortement affectée par la violence due à l’exploitation pétrolière, ces événements sont l’occasion de soutenir les liens communautaires et de faire vivre les savoirs culturels de la région.
À l’origine de cette initiative, un groupe de jeunes musiciens qui se réunit chaque semaine pour jouer ensemble, coordonné par l’activiste Omar Lázaro García. En 2015, les musiciens décident d’organiser un événement d’ampleur dans la région : une semaine de campement pour créer un espace d’échanges transgénérationnel et communautaire, avec des ateliers de musique, de théâtre, de poterie, de savoirs médicinaux… et des interventions de divers collectifs, comme celui des mères chercheuses, des défenseurs des droits humains, ou encore des anciens de la communauté.
En 2025, c’est le collectif de cinéma communautaire Xolo Films qui a été invité au campement annuel pour répondre au manque de formation artistique et audiovisuelle auquel font face les jeunes des zones rurales et indigènes. Organisé avec le Centre Interculturel pour la Soutenabilité de Papantla et financé par le Fond mexicain d’appui à la culture et à l’art (FONCA), l’atelier a réuni plus d’une vingtaine de jeunes activistes, provenant de la région ou des États voisins.
Faire avec les moyens du bord
Avec Xolo Films, on est loin des tapis rouges et des méga-tournages qui font la marque de fabrique de l’industrie cinématographique. Pour les membres de Xolo – 11 au total – le cinéma est surtout le moyen de faire communauté pour raconter son histoire. Partant de ce principe, les fondateurs ont créé Xolo en 2015, à la suite d’une formation basée sur l’éducation populaire, réalisée à Xalapa (capitale de l’État de Veracruz). Depuis, le collectif a tourné plusieurs court-métrages et réalisé plusieurs ateliers.
Pour le collectif, faire du cinéma horizontal, c’est permettre à chacun·e de raconter sa propre histoire avec les moyens du bord (et sans recourir à une technologie 2.0) comme le partage Joshua Espinosa Gutiérrez :
« Au final, le plus important, c’est l’histoire que tu veux raconter ».
C’est aussi forger le chemin d’une autre société. « Si on peut se réunir pour raconter une histoire et la filmer, alors peut être qu’on peut se réunir pour faire des choses plus grandes et plus complexes », explique le cofondateur et militant Emilio Braojos Fuertes.
Non loin d’une rangée de tentes, sous les quelques 30 degrés à l’ombre, les participant·es se sont essayé·es à la caméra, à l’équipement sonore, aux pratiques théâtrales et à la production. Et tout cela, avec une visée politique. Entre les repas fournis par l’hôte de la maison, plusieurs court-métrages communautaires ont été discutés par Ruben Dario Madrigal Ceballos, professeur et militant communiste, parce que le cinéma communautaire permet de « récupérer la valeur de ce qu’on a en propre », questionner la violence systémique vécue par les communautés et leurs multiples façons d’y résister.
« Documenter, c’est militer »
Raconter « l’Autre » histoire, c’est lutter contre l’homogénéisation des récits. Jésus Ramos Carballeda, un jeune étudiant des Hautes Montagnes proches d’Orizaba, en a fait l’expérience très tôt. Grand visionneur de films pendant l’enfance, il constate :
« j’apprenais du monde, mais je me rendais compte que beaucoup de films n’avaient rien à voir avec moi, ni avec mon lieu de vie [Et] quand tu n’as pas d’identité avec ton territoire, tu te sens perdu ».
Faire du cinéma communautaire permet de reprendre la main sur son récit, et éviter de « se faire raconter », comme l’explique Amairany Mora Vázquez, membre du Congrès National Indigène (CNI) Totonacapan : « Ces histoires doivent s’écrire depuis l’intérieur ».
Pour Rosa Laura Tezoco Tehuintle, jeune artiste des Montagnes de Zongolica, les histoires ne s’écrivent pas pour le regard extérieur, mais pour servir la communauté. C’est du moins ce qu’elle a appris en travaillant avec les enfants de son village :
« Quand on fait un travail communautaire ou rural, on ne va pas peindre pour l’étranger. Moi, ce que les jeunes me disaient c’était : « je veux pas que tu peignes ce que je connais déjà, je veux que tu m’écoutes, que tu écoutes l’histoire de mon enfance, je veux voir ce que me racontait ma maman ou mon grand-père » ».
Ce travail d’auto-documentation permet de remonter le fil de la mémoire. Une tâche cruciale quand on sait que cette mémoire est souvent muselée ou enfouie sous les décombres. Omar Lárazo García, conseiller du CNI Totonacapan, se souvient du massacre de janvier 1970, quand l’armée mexicaine a tué plus de 320 totonaques, à Monte de Chila: « Ils ont assassiné un village entier, et aujourd’hui il ne reste que les ruines. Ils ont voulu effacer cette mémoire. Alors, raconter notre histoire, c’est aussi demander que justice soit faite, ne pas se taire face à tout ça ».
Les récits ont un pouvoir invisible : celui de dessiner le réel. À ce propos, Dénétèm Touam Bona écrit : « C’est par une fabulation créatrice qu’une communauté, quelle qu’elle soit, recouvre la puissance d’agir ». Chikón, un jeune cinéaste qui a voyagé depuis les montagnes mazatèques de Oaxaca conclut : « Documenter c’est, d’une certaine manière, militer, et n’ayons pas peur de militer ! ».
Les histoires qui se rassemblent et se partagent sous la végétation luxuriante du Totonacapan, ne sont pas seulement des récits de lutte. Ce sont aussi des récits de vie quotidienne, tel que l’illustre Omar Lázaro García. :
« C’est important qu’on puisse se reconnaître. Un peu comme quand on se lève le matin, on se regarde dans le miroir, et on aime ce qu’on voit. C’est ça l’objectif : que les communautés se voient reflétées et qu’elles [se] disent : « Je me sens bien ». »
Se raconter c’est, finalement, faire émerger « ces autres mondes qui existent déjà et qui sont le point de départ pour construire quelque chose de mieux », selon Ruben Dario Madrigal Ceballos. C’est mettre à profit des histoires pour faire bouger les lignes.
Retarder la fin du monde
Ailton Krenak, activiste et écrivain botocudo du Brésil, écrivait : « Développons nos forces pour pouvoir toujours raconter une histoire de plus, un autre récit. Si nous y parvenons, alors nous retarderons la fin du monde ». Ces mots font écho à ceux de Leslie Marmon Silko, écrivaine autochtone de culture pueblo laguna : « Je vais vous dire une chose à propos des histoires… Ce ne sont pas seulement des divertissements. Ne vous y trompez pas. Elles sont tout ce que nous avons, voyez-vous, tout ce dont nous disposons pour lutter contre la maladie et la mort. Vous n’avez rien si vous n’avez pas d’histoires. » L’année dernière, les participant·es avaient tous cette aspiration: repeindre la réalité, détenir la fin du monde, recommencer.
Briany Lilith Lastiri Cruz, actrice et dramaturge originaire de Poza Rica a, par exemple, appris auprès du collectif Xolo à tourner un court-métrage sur la transidentité. Avec sa pièce Si réellement tu m’aimais, basée sur le théâtre de l’opprimé, Briany dénonçait les menaces qui pèsent sur les personnes trans et LGBTQIA+. En parallèle, elle a écrit une œuvre intitulée L’arbre de l’espérance, en référence au monument érigé à la mémoire des personnes disparues de Poza Rica.
Son travail a été récompensé pour « la meilleure direction » à Xalapa en 2024 : « J’ai profité de ces pièces pour mettre en place des espaces de dialogue à Poza Rica, pour dire : écoutez, il est en train de se passer ça, ça continue de se passer ! Parce que ces choses sont mises sous silence et c’est important de les rendre visibles ».
De son côté, Alejandro Jiménez Méndez est un danseur totonaque; il pratique la danse rituelle de la région connue sous le nom de « danse des voladores ». Avec la caméra, il cherche à documenter les activités quotidiennes de son village, comme la fête patronale, la culture du maïs, les rituels. La vidéo opère comme un moyen de préserver la mémoire communautaire auprès de ses habitants, mais aussi au-delà, en atteignant la diaspora.
Tout comme Alejandro, Rodolfo Bibiano Jiménez, s’est aussi fixé l’objectif de partager la mémoire vive, et les affectations de son territoire. Impliqué dans plusieurs organisations de lutte contre le fracking – une technique visant à extraire du gaz ou du pétrole en injectant sous haute pression une très grande quantité d’eau mêlée à des composés chimiques – Rodolfo souhaite dénoncer les dangers de l’exploitation pétrolière. Dans une région où les accidents pétroliers sont monnaies courantes, il veut cibler les jeunes générations en utilisant les réseaux sociaux parce que : « Tu as beau vivre dans la communauté, parfois, tu ne connais pas ton territoire ».
De son côté, Amairany Mora Vázquez, une jeune danseuse et actrice originaire de Amatlan de los Reyes, a commencé à se mobiliser à partir de ses 17 ans. Avec d’autres jeunes de sa ville, elle a organisé une série de festivals pour rassembler les habitant·es autour de problèmes communs. Aujourd’hui, membre du CNI Totonacapan et du collectif Por La Libre, Amairany veut s’appuyer sur ses connaissances en cinéma communautaire pour mettre en valeur l’usage de la langue náhuatl qui, peu à peu, se perd parmi les nouvelles générations de sa ville natale.
Autant de projets qui contribuent à retarder la fin du monde. Ils dessinent d’autres possibles face au rouleau compresseur du récit hégémonique. Entre les lignes, dans les silences ou dans les recoins de la pensée dominante, subsistent toujours d’autres histoires. Ce sont celles-là qui permettent de résister, et de résister par le rêve, cette forme de résistance dont parle le poète Marc Alexandre Oho Bambe.
Cet été 2026, le campement s’est de nouveau réuni; cette fois pour fêter les 30 ans du Congrès National Indigène, fondé en 1996, dans la suite du soulèvement zapatiste. L’année prochaine, il se réunira pour discuter des enjeux liés à l’eau et pour partager les pratiques et savoirs concernant sa préservation. Preuve si nécessaire, que le temps du rêve continue de couler dans les veines de ceux qui résistent.
– Claire Lapique

title: The Only Known Pelt of an Extinct Woolly Dog Has Returned Home to British Columbia After 160 Years
content:
For more than a century and a half, Mutton lay far from the place where his life story began.
The small, pale dog died in 1859, and his pelt eventually entered the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., where it survived while the woolly dogs once raised across the Pacific Northwest disappeared into extinction. Now, the only known pelt of this extinct dog breed has returned to British Columbia, on loan to the Museum of Anthropology at the University of British Columbia through August 2027.
For Indigenous artists who still practice traditional Salish weaving, Mutton’s return carries particular weight. Woolly dogs were once deliberately bred by Coast Salish communities for their dense fur, which women spun into yarn and wove into prized blankets, robes and clothing. Although the dogs disappeared in the 19th century and the weaving tradition was nearly lost under colonial rule, contemporary weavers such as Atheana Picha and Debra Sparrow have helped revive that knowledge.
“The woolly dogs were a big part of our family life,” Picha, a Tsartlip First Nation artist and weaver, told The Globe and Mail. “Having met this relative now, who left us 200 years ago, is pretty powerful.”
Mutton’s pelt also carries something oral histories alone could not preserve: its DNA. A 2023 study published in Science, built around Mutton’s genome and Indigenous knowledge, showed that woolly dogs represented a carefully maintained lineage stretching back thousands of years. It also challenged the idea that the dogs simply became obsolete when European-made textiles arrived.
A dog bred for wool
Woolly dogs were small, light-colored animals with pointed faces, curled tails and dense, crimped coats. Salish and Makah peoples raised them specifically for their fur, often mixing dog wool with mountain goat hair and plant fibers to make strong, warm yarn. Native Americans never domesticated native wild sheep, unlike peoples in Eurasia who managed livestock herds.
The woolly canines did not simply wander among other village dogs. Oral histories describe women keeping them apart, sometimes on small islands, to prevent crossbreeding. They were combed, shorn and given rich foods such as salmon and elk to maintain their coats.
“There was a very selective breeding process that ensured the quality of the fur,” Jordan Wilson, the museum’s curator of Pacific Northwest and Contemporary Indigenous Art, told the Vancouver Sun.
The genetics add weight to the folklore. Researchers compared Mutton’s DNA with ancient and modern dogs and found that about 85 percent of his ancestry came from precolonial North American dogs. His genome also showed signs consistent with generations of tightly controlled breeding. Among more than 11,000 genes examined, the team identified 28 associated with hair growth and follicle development, including genes linked to woolly or curly hair. The genetic and archaeological evidence suggests the distinctive lineage had been maintained for as long as roughly 5,000 years.
That is remarkable because Mutton lived decades after European dogs had arrived in the region. Even then, Coast Salish communities had managed to preserve much of a distinctive Indigenous dog lineage.
But how did the dog disappear?
The most convenient explanation is that machine-made blankets simply made woolly dogs unnecessary. But newer research points to a much harsher story.
The 19th century brought epidemics, displacement, the Gold Rush and colonial policies that suppressed Indigenous cultural practices and forced assimilation. Industrial textiles changed weaving economies too, but researchers concluded that they could not explain the disappearance on their own. Indigenous knowledge collected alongside the genetic study instead pointed toward the cumulative destruction of the social systems that had allowed people to maintain the dogs for generations.
“This dog was bred out of existence in large part because of all the transformations wrought by settler colonialism,” Wilson told Global News.
Mutton himself lived amid that transition. He was the companion of George Gibbs, a naturalist working on the Northwest Boundary Survey, although researchers do not know how Gibbs acquired him. Gibbs recorded that Mutton became ill and died at about 18 months old. The dog had been shorn at least once before his death, and his pelt eventually traveled to the Smithsonian with other specimens.
Today, Salish weaving has undergone a revival, and researchers are examining historic textiles for traces of woolly dog hair. Mutton’s sequenced genome could eventually help identify those fibers more confidently.
For Picha, however, the pelt’s meaning is already visible without sequencing.
“Seeing the fibres on the pelt, they’re already twisting,” she told The Globe and Mail. “They want to be spun. It’s just hungry to be turned into a blanket, turned into warmth.”

human_wellbeing_impact.evidence: contemporary weavers such as Atheana Picha and Debra Sparrow have helped revive that knowledge

social_cohesion_impact.evidence: Woolly dogs were once deliberately bred by Coast Salish communities for their dense fur, which women spun into yarn and wove into prized blankets, robes and clothing.

justice_rights_impact.evidence: the weaving tradition was nearly lost under colonial rule

evidence_level.evidence: A 2023 study published in Science, built around Mutton's genome and Indigenous knowledge, showed that woolly dogs represented a carefully maintained lineage stretching back thousands of years.

benefit_distribution.evidence: For Indigenous artists who still practice traditional Salish weaving, Mutton's return carries particular weight.

change_durability.evidence: on loan to the Museum of Anthropology at the University of British Columbia through August 2027

title: Proyecto educativo "La página oculta" visibiliza líderes afrodecescendientes
content:
Lundu Centro de Estudios y Promoción Afroperuanos y la agencia Cheil Perú se unieron para desarrollar el proyecto educativo y de memoria histórica "La Página Oculta", mediante el cual vienen distribuyendo 50 mil ejemplares impresos en instituciones educativas de Lima, Callao, Ica, Lambayeque y Piura. La iniciativa busca integrar en las aulas los aportes de líderes afrodescendientes del siglo XIX .


A partir de una investigación liderada por la historiadora Maribel Arrelucea y el uso de referencias históricas y familiares, el equipo creativo logró recrear los rostros y trayectorias de cuatro figuras clave: Alberto "Grumete" Medina, héroe de la Guerra del Pacífico; Catalina Buendía de Pecho, lideresa de la resistencia en Ica; Francisco Congo, fundador del Palenque Huachipa; e Ildefonso, combatiente de la causa independentista. Los materiales impresos han sido diseñados e insertados estratégicamente para complementar los textos escolares existentes.
"Con esta iniciativa queremos contribuir a visibilizar en la escuela a personajes referentes de los procesos de libertad y emancipación de las comunidades afrodescendientes. Al compartir estos ejemplares, vemos que se despierta la curiosidad del alumnado por conocer otros aspectos de la historia, transformando la percepción hacia los aportes afroperuanos más allá del ámbito musical, gastronómico o deportivo", destacó Brenda Garay, directora de proyectos de LUNDU.
El desarrollo de la iniciativa cuenta además con un video documental producido por Cheil Studio, el cual registra el proceso de investigación, diseño e impacto del proyecto en las escuelas.
El audiovisual, disponible en las plataformas digitales de Lundu, está musicalizado por los percusionistas Carlos Yamasaki y Gustavo Silva, e incluye análisis sobre ciudadanía e interculturalidad a cargo de la actual senadora Susana Matute, así como valiosos testimonios de exintegrantes de la organización, entre ellas su fundadora Mónica Carrillo y la comunicadora Ysabel Omega.
Lee también:
["La púrpura de la rosa, primer ópera prima de América, regresa a Lima 325 años después"]Con la distribución de estas 50 mil publicaciones en cinco regiones del país, "La Página Oculta" se consolida como una herramienta pedagógica que promueve una revisión crítica y representativa de la historia nacional en las nuevas generaciones.
Más en Andina
(FIN) CFS/CFS
Publicado: 10/9/2026

title: ‘Identity returned to us’: How Taiwan’s latest recognised indigenous group is reclaiming its voice
content:
‘Identity returned to us’: How Taiwan’s latest recognised indigenous group is reclaiming its voice
- The Siraya people of Taiwan gained official recognition as the island's 17th Indigenous group, reclaiming their identity after centuries of assimilation and discrimination.
- Recognition enables legal status, government funding, and efforts to revive the Siraya language and cultural traditions, benefiting descendants and future generations.
- Concerns exist among other Indigenous groups about resource competition and political representation, but experts encourage unity to strengthen collective Indigenous rights in Taiwan.
AI generated
TAINAN, Taiwan – As a child, Taiwanese indigenous language teacher Hanna Domok would lie to her classmates and say that her ancestors hailed from China.
Her darker skin made her look different from her peers, who called her derogatory names that meant “savage” or “barbarian”.
“It gave me an inferiority complex. So I would make things up and tell people, ‘No, no, you’re wrong, I am not who you think I am’,” the 54-year-old recalled in an interview with The Straits Times.
“I would tell them that my grandfather immigrated to Taiwan from China,” said Domok, who also goes by her Chinese name Mu Li-chun.
Her experience as a member of the Siraya, an Austronesian-speaking indigenous group native to south-western Taiwan, is not unique.
For centuries, the Siraya as well as other lowland plains – or Pingpu – indigenous communities often kept their background a secret to avoid social stigma and discrimination; many were forced to adopt Han Chinese customs and languages and assimilate.
But things have come a long way since the late 1980s during Taiwan’s transition to democracy, following the lifting of martial law in 1987.
On July 30, after decades of activism, the Siraya people finally won legal recognition from the Taiwanese government as the island’s 17th officially recognised indigenous group. There are 26 known indigenous groups in Taiwan, including those that are not recognised by the government.
Taiwan’s indigenous communities, which are traditionally divided into highland and lowland groups, make up about 2.7 per cent of the island’s 23.3 million people. They claim thousands of years of history on the island before the first foreign settlers arrived in the 17th century.
Taiwan’s first foreign settlers were the Dutch (1624-1662) and the Spanish (1626-1642), who built trading posts along the coast. To secure labour for farming, the Dutch encouraged the immigration of Han Chinese workers from mainland China, which marked the first significant wave of Chinese migration.
Han Chinese settlers grew to dominate Taiwan numerically, culturally and politically during the Qing Dynasty (1683-1895), and the indigenous groups became a minority discriminated against by the Chinese majority and forced to adopt Chinese surnames and pay heavy taxes. When the Kuomintang (KMT) government arrived from the Chinese mainland in 1949, indigenous people were forced to adopt Mandarin Chinese and suppress their cultural customs.
There is no official data on how many people of Siraya descent are in Taiwan, but the city government of Tainan, where they historically resided, recorded more than 11,800 people as Siraya in 2016.
The Siraya are also the first group to secure recognition under the Pingpu Indigenous Peoples Identity Act, which was passed in 2025 to redress the historic erasure of Pingpu groups. The other 16 groups are recognised under the Status Act for Indigenous Peoples.
The Siraya’s historic recognition will likely pave the way for more lowland plains indigenous communities to receive the same treatment in the future. But while the landmark ruling is cause for celebration, Siraya community leaders and activists say substantial work remains for full cultural and administrative integration.
“It feels incredible, because it’s like our identity has been returned to us,” said Domok from a Siraya-owned cafe in Tainan. “A lot more work needs to be done, but at least we can say that we have secured an entry ticket now (into legal parity).”
Taiwan President Lai Ching-te welcomed the news, having previously supported the Siraya people’s fight for cultural and legal recognition during his tenure as mayor of Tainan (2010-2017).
“This is a historic moment for the Siraya people and an important milestone in the pursuit of historical and transitional justice for indigenous peoples,” he wrote on Facebook on Aug 1, Taiwan’s Indigenous Peoples’ Day.
The milestone is not merely symbolic. Official recognition provides a clear legal basis and central government funding to restore the Siraya language and protect traditional customs such as the Siraya Night Festival, which honours their ancestral spirits while being an expression of thanks and blessings.
Eligible descendants can also begin to register at household registration offices to receive Plains Indigenous status on their official documents.
“Making our status official means the world to us,” said Vukin Takalomay, 28, a Siraya rights activist and language teacher.
“At university, even members of other Taiwanese indigenous groups would question my claim as a Siraya indigenous person. They’ll say I cannot possibly claim such a thing if it’s not made official,” he told ST.
While highland indigenous groups such as the Atayal and Bunun, who traditionally reside in Taiwan’s isolated mountainous areas, have been legally recognised since the Japanese colonial era (1895-1945), plains indigenous groups have struggled to receive recognition because they were deemed to be highly assimilated into Han Chinese society.
Their perceived loss of distinct cultural markers comes from centuries of intermarriage, language shifts and cultural integration with the Han Chinese settlers they lived alongside in the lowlands.
However, Siraya language and customs were largely suppressed not by choice but by a succession of dominant ruling powers.
As far back as the late 17th century during Qing Dynasty rule, Siraya families faced educational and societal pressure to adopt Chinese surnames and speak Chinese dialects. Then, when Japanese became the primary language of instruction in public schools under Japanese rule from 1895 to 1945, the Siraya language fell out of regular use altogether, and it was declared linguistically “extinct” by 1908.
Indigenous languages were further suppressed under the KMT government, with locals subjected to the regime’s strict Mandarin-only policy.
“If you spoke anything other than Mandarin, you could get punished in class,” said Lo Chao-teng, 71, chairman of the Tainan Siraya Cultural Association.
“The teachers would record it on the blackboard to humiliate you, and you could get beatings,” he added.
Linguists and language teachers have in recent years worked to reconstruct and promote the Siraya language, one word at a time. As the Siraya language has had no native speakers for such a long time, linguists relied heavily on historical texts, including a copy of the Gospel of Matthew, a book of the Bible, translated into Siraya by a Dutch missionary during the Dutch colonial period (1624-1662).
In 2008, activists published a comprehensive glossary containing thousands of Siraya words.
“There were certain words that we kept hearing from our elders but we didn’t even realise that they were Siraya words,” Domok said. “It’s amazing being able to learn these words again as my language, and teach them to the next generation.”
A few times a week, the freelancer teaches primary school-aged children Siraya words through songs in private lessons. “One of my seven-year-old students recently told me, ‘I can sing these Siraya songs by myself, I don’t need you to guide me any more.’ That made me so happy.”
Official recognition of the Siraya is expected to provide a legal and financial foundation to expand language revitalisation programmes, building on local efforts in Tainan where multiple schools already offer classes.
Jolan Hsieh, an indigenous studies expert at Taiwan’s National Dong Hwa University, who is also known by her Siraya name Bavaragh Dagalomai, noted the significance of learning one’s native language.
“Through learning the language, we can learn more about our history and culture, and that will make our identity stronger,” she told ST. “When you have that, more people can recognise and celebrate your group as distinct and just as valid as other indigenous groups.”
That is important given that official recognition of the Siraya has led to some anxiety among other indigenous communities over the possible dilution of government resources and benefits allocated to them, she said. For instance, there is a fear that it may become more difficult for them to secure political representation in the future.
Taiwan reserves six seats in its Parliament for indigenous people, which are directly voted on by eligible indigenous voters.
As the potential population of Pingpu descendants is estimated to be quite large, existing recognised indigenous groups fear they could easily overwhelm the vote, effectively squeezing their tribes out of parliamentary representation.
At the moment, officials are working on amending laws regarding political participation, social welfare, healthcare, education and other supporting measures for the Siraya, according to the Council of Indigenous Peoples, a Cabinet-level government agency.
“There is some concern that the more indigenous people are recognised, the more people there will be coming in to fight for a small share of resources,” said Hsieh.
“But actually I like to see it from the other perspective – the more of us there are, the more we can work together and negotiate for our collective rights.”

title: O grupo que mantém as tradições negras no interior de Goiás
content: <_cdata>Com oficinas e ensaios abertos ao público, movimento preserva ritos e engaja novas gerações Celebração do Dia da Consciência Negra em 2025 Allan Florentino / Divulgação Aos pés do Morro do Cachimbo, entre os tradicionais bairros Novo Paraíso, Vila São Joaquim e Jardim Santa Cecília, em Anápolis, Goiás, está localizado o Ponto de Cultura Onã Layó, no pequeno Residencial Florença. O nome, pouco conhecido pela vizinhança, tem um significado especial para a comunidade da Casa de Chico Preto. “Em iorubá, significa caminho de alegria”, explica pai Hugo Maurício, babalorixá do terreiro de Umbanda. Além das atividades litúrgicas, a Casa de Chico Preto agrega uma estrutura cultural e educacional, disponibilizando o espaço do templo para atividades abertas ao público, como oficinas gratuitas de samba de roda, jongo e maculelê, capoeira, ritmos afro – percussão e arte africana para crianças desde 2009. Em 2025, recebeu o título de ponto de cultura. Antes de ser contemplada pela primeira vez, no edital de 2025 da Política Nacional Aldir Blanc de Fomento à Cultura (PNAB), a casa já havia construído uma trajetória de voluntariado, atuação comunitária, cultural e de resistência. Em uma cidade com quase 400 mil habitantes, de maioria cristã, os mais de 1,3 mil autodeclarados de Umbanda ou Candomblé buscam uma organização contínua para os enfrentamentos, muitas vezes, necessários. Quando a Casa de Chico Preto foi fundada, há mais de uma década, expressar publicamente a fé e as tradições religiosas afro-brasileiras em Anápolis era um desafio ainda maior que hoje. Pai Hugo, iniciado na religião há 22 anos, testemunhou esse momento. “Quando eu comecei, você não achava terreiro [na rua]. Os terreiros eram todos escondidos.”, relembra. O babalorixá lembra que havia apenas um terreiro com placa de identificação na cidade. O espaço, em questão, era o terreiro Pai Benedito de Aruanda, localizado no bairro São Carlos, nas proximidades do centro da cidade. “Era o único que tinha nessa época, uma plaquinha discreta na porta, mas tinha”, completa. Com as graduações necessárias para o sacerdócio, ao lado de sua mãe biológica, também sacerdotisa, Mãe Cleonice de Oxum, ano após ano, conquistaram um espaço físico e simbólico na cidade. “A casa nasce no bairro Eldorado, em um lugar de aluguel. Depois de dois anos, mudamos para o centro da cidade, de frente para o prédio da Justiça do Trabalho. Ali a gente viveu um enfrentamento, usando placa. Nós íamos para a rua, ao mercado, restaurante, vestidos com a guia, do jeito que estava [no terreiro] e isso causou um boom na cidade”, relembra pai Hugo. 2ª Mostra Cultural Onã Layó Pedro Lucas / Acervo Pessoal Com a consciência de que um terreiro de Umbanda é uma comunidade, com pessoas diversas e atividades diversas, alguns pilares permeiam a casa desde o seu nascimento, como educação e cultura. Educador, a liderança reforça a perspectiva freiriana de que a prática educativa não ocorre apenas na escola, mas também através das relações e da participação comunitária. “Os grupos populares certamente têm o direito de, organizando-se, criar suas escolas comunitárias e de lutar para fazê-las cada vez melhores. Têm o direito inclusive de exigir do Estado, através de convênios de natureza nada paternalista, colaboração. Precisam, contudo, estar advertidos de que sua tarefa não é substituir o Estado no seu dever de atender às camadas populares e a todos os que e as que, das classes favorecidas, procurem suas escolas”, escreveu o patrono da educação brasileira, Paulo Freire, em 1992, registrado no livro Política e Educação, da Cortez Editora. Após a abertura da casa, o movimento que reivindica cidadania e direitos, termos muitas vezes negados aos povos de terreiro, começou a crescer na cidade. O processo é concomitante à instauração do Sistema de Cotas da Universidade Estadual de Goiás (UEG), em 2004, e da Universidade Federal de Goiás, (UFG), em 2012, que ampliou o acesso de grupos historicamente sub-representados no ensino superior. Na última década, os membros dos terreiros de cidade perceberam um reflexo direto: palestras e rodas de conversa com a presença de mestres e lideranças das tradições afro-brasileiras se tornaram mais comuns e enriqueceram o debate. “Foi muito libertador para a parte religiosa. Olhando para trás, a gente percebe que a Casa de Chico Preto fez parte desse enfrentamento, porque a gente sofreu, mas a gente sempre manteve a postura de somar com a comunidade”, destaca o babalorixá. A vizinhança do Residencial Florença, bairro periférico de Anápolis, que antes lidava com um espaço abandonado, matagal e o livre acesso de usuários de drogas, com a instalação do ponto de cultura passou a ver uma nova movimentação na rua, com sessões públicas, lotadas de carros. O comércio do bairro precisou se organizar para atender a demanda e situações de colaboração entre templo e o público externo se tornaram mais comuns. Além das ações do projeto Onã Layó, que tem como compromisso primordial o incentivo à educação e cultura como forma de manutenção dos saberes e manifestações tradicionais afro-brasileiros, contemplado pela Política Nacional Aldir Blanc, o templo sede o espaço para ensaios de grupos independentes já conhecidos na cidade com o grupo Sambadeiras do Cerrado, a banda Kalangorin e o homônimo Afoxé Onã Layó. Antes de tudo isso, da produção cultural, da participação em editais, foi a força da cultura negra que formou os filhos da casa, ensinamentos compartilhados através da oralidade, no dia a dia. Os aprendizados são fundamentos para centenas de jovens, crianças e adultos que escolheram trilhar os caminhos do axé. Para Pai Hugo, há uma diferença entre os ritos de terreiro e as atividades culturais. “O ponto de cultura é a Casa de Chico Preto, mas pelas suas atividades culturais e não litúrgicas”, explica. Ele dá alguns exemplos, como o Samba de Roda, o afoxé que leva para a rua aquilo que é celebrativo e festivo. “Temos o batuque, a dança, tudo aquilo que já é projetado para ir para a rua. Não é o retrato fiel da liturgia que acontece dentro do terreiro. Então, existe uma separação do que é produção cultural e do que é produção litúrgica. Mas o espaço, a instituição, as pessoas, os fazedores de cultura são os mesmos. É a comunidade de povo de terreiro mesmo”, enfatiza ele. O tambor tem sido mais escutado Com quase 20 anos de religião, a Ialorixá Cleonice de Oxum questiona: “Você já ouviu o tambor tocar?”. E completa: “O tambor toca a alma, toca o coração. Eu amo minhas vestes, sou apaixonada pela saia, pelo pano de cabeça. Eu não quero muito chique, basta ter a saia e o pano. Eu acho muito lindo”. Ao recordar da época em que frequentava a igreja católica e ainda não compreendia a escolha do filho, reflete que o imaginário social era de muito preconceito: “Antigamente as pessoas não sabiam discernir muito o certo do errado e tudo julgavam a religião. Diziam ‘Isso é de preto, isso é de branco’, mas sem observar o que está lá atrás.” Foi no terreiro que Mãe Cleonice se encontrou com a ancestralidade negra. A própria comida preparada por ela e repassada aos filhos é um exemplo da transmissão desse saber que faz parte de um processo histórico e também pessoal. “Em uma gira de baiano, tem o quê? Um bom acarajé! Na Preto Velho, comem o quê? Feijoada! Assim como na época da escravização, em que se comiam as sobras de porco que os senhores davam. A gente faz uma bela feijoada na gira, uma canjica, um docinho. Eles gostam de doce”, explica a liderança. Apesar dos avanços, com uma efervescência cultural inédita nos últimos anos em Anápolis, os líderes da Casa de Chico Preto concordam que, quando se fala em valorização da cultura negra na cidade, ainda há um longo caminho a ser percorrido. “Eu acho Anápolis ainda muito provinciana e isso trava o progresso. Falta engajar, expandir horizontes, trazer movimentos para cá, criar circuito de debates. Ainda é fraco.”, afirma Pai Hugo. A palavra de ordem é respeito, algo que, segundo ele, está na raiz do povo de axé. “Aprender a respeitar a diversidade, aprender a respeitar os mais velhos, os saberes daqueles que pisaram antes da gente no caminho”, conclui. Yá Cleonice complementa: “Se você não me respeita, se seu preconceito é grande, dá licença. Não baixo a cabeça jamais.” A pesquisadora Talita Michelle de Souza, doutoranda em História pela UFG, faz uma provocação de que o racismo linguístico, ainda hoje, é muito presente em Anápolis e destaca a necessidade do letramento racial para todos, a partir da educação básica. “Sueli Carneiro nos traz o conceito de epistemicídio, essas mutilações dentro da história e na educação. É necessário repensar os saberes. Os aquilombamentos tem sido feitos em Anápolis de forma consistente, mas tímida. Em Goiânia, eu já percebo esses aquilombamentos acontecendo de forma mais consolidada”, avalia. Ela também pontua que, em Anápolis, ainda é muito utilizado o termo ‘recorte racial’ para se referir às pessoas negras. “Nós não somos recortes. Trago para discussão o Nego Bispo, pensando em Goiás e na necessidade de trazer as narrativas negras e potencializar crianças”, afirma. Rompendo estigmas Romário Akinyode, criado no bairro Santa Cecília e ogã da Casa de Chico Preto, é um dos instrutores do projeto e co-fundador do Afoxé Onã Layó. Percussionista, iniciou a trajetória aos sete anos quando conheceu a capoeira e passou a se interessar pela cultura afro-brasileira. Na adolescência, foi auxiliar do Cidadão do Futuro, um programa municipal voltado para a aprendizagem de jovens, com foco em cidadania e desenvolvimento profissional. “Quando eu entrei para casa, expandiu o meu conhecimento, o meu entender da cultura dos povos de terreiro, do povo negro”, conta. Como ogã, função de grande responsabilidade dentro de um terreiro, Romário conheceu mais sobre a ciência dos atabaques e o poder dos cânticos. Agora, como instrutor do ponto de cultura, com alunos a partir dos sete anos, repassar esse conhecimento de forma lúdica para crianças se tornou uma descoberta diária. “São muitas crianças ali da comunidade, faço brincadeiras com elas, mostro o samba rural ou samba de coco, os vários ritmos que têm na cultura afro-brasileira”, explica. Mestre Luizinho, de Goiânia, filho do Mestre Bimba, referência da capoeira regional, é uma das inspirações de Akinyode. “Ele me passou muitos ensinamentos, até hoje me passa, é uma pessoa que eu admiro muito”, destaca. Segundo ele, trabalhar nesse segmento em Anápolis é um desafio, o espaço é pequeno e a movimentação é grande. “A galera, principalmente aqui em Anápolis, vê um tambor e pensa ‘é macumba”, relata. Segundo ele, o trabalho com as crianças é importante, porque permite a desconstrução desses estigmas desde cedo. “Tem muitas coisas que você passa para um adulto e a pessoa fica com pé atrás de aprender. Já a criança não, a criança você passa e ela se joga no negócio sem medo. Isso é o mais interessante.”, conclui. Continuidade Em julho, no Dia Internacional da Mulher Negra Latino-Americana e Caribenha, dezenas de pessoas se reuniram na Estação Ferroviária de Anápolis Prefeito José Fernandes Valente, no centro da cidade. O evento reuniu diferentes linguagens artísticas, como a poesia, samba de roda, desfile de moda e diversos shows fizeram parte da programação. À frente da organização, Mãe Carmen, sacerdotisa do Terreiro Pai Mateus de Angola e membro do Conselho Municipal de Promoção da Igualdade Racial (Compir) de Anápolis, destaca a necessidade de somar forças para reivindicar espaços de direito. Mãe Carmen na Câmara Municipal de Anápolis Allyne Lais / Acervo Pessoal Quase 60% dos anapolinos se autodeclaram negros, 52% pardos e 7% pretos, segundo o Censo de 2022. “Não sei se acontece só aqui em Anápolis, mas eu vejo que tudo que é de preto, de indígena, que é de pessoas em vulnerabilidade, as pessoas não querem nem ouvir, entendeu? Não fazem questão nenhuma de ajudar ou estender a mão”, lamenta. A memória, porém, traz à tona momentos em que a cidade se enchia de fé e cultura afro-brasileira. A ialorixá reforça que a cidade sempre teve presentes suas raízes negras, embora, por muito tempo, fossem refutadas. “Eu estou fazendo este ano 61 anos de idade, só de Anápolis eu tenho 60. Eu posso dizer com propriedade que Anápolis sempre foi uma cidade umbandista. Ao contrário do que os mais jovens que conheceram Anápolis, depois de um certo tempo, acham que a cidade é evangélica. Aqui nós temos de tudo, mas a cidade sempre foi umbandista”, afirma. Entre as recordações, carentes de registro físico, estão as procissões dos Pretos Velhos e de Ogum. Segundo ela, no final da década de 1960, uma multidão vestida de branco andava pela cidade, passava pela prefeitura com bandeiras e andores que carregavam as imagens sagradas. “Depois a gente ia para o terreiro acabar de festejar”, recorda. Até mesmo a Polícia Militar, com seu traje de gala, participava da celebração. “Naquela época, ter uma câmera fotográfica era muito difícil — só quem tinha muito dinheiro —, e os pais de santo não deixavam registrar a situação pelo respeito àquele momento”, completa. Os tempos mudaram, mas os terreiros, com mais ou menos visibilidade, continuam cheios de cultura. “A nossa comida é cultural, a nossa roupa é cultural, a nossa oralidade é cultural. Nosso povo preto, por não ter tido estudo, nem oportunidades, passava os conhecimentos com a oralidade. É uma coisa que dentro do terreiro a gente pratica até hoje. Nós respiramos cultura, nós vivemos cultura”, conclui Mãe Carmen.

title: Participatory budgeting behind bars: Durham, North Carolina, gives incarcerated residents a say
content:
Since Durham, North Carolina, implemented participatory budgeting in 2018, its organizers say they have been intentional about inviting as many residents as possible to take part in the citywide initiative. The process gives anyone who lives or goes to school in Durham and is at least 13 years old a direct say in how the city spends a portion of its budget.
People incarcerated in the Durham County Detention Facility have been allowed to vote on spending decisions from the beginning, but they couldn’t participate in idea generation, proposal development and deliberation, according to staffers with PB Durham, which oversees participatory budgeting in the city. Program leaders saw a missed opportunity.
“One of the really important things for participatory budgeting is to elevate all of the Durham resident voices,” Carmen Ortiz, Durham’s assistant director of community partnerships and engagement, told Smart Cities Dive. “We have residents who are incarcerated who have really tight, strong connections to the community. So, for us, it was really important to engage them in the process.”
The city redesigned its PB program so it could run idea-collection sessions inside the jail and worked with the Durham County Sheriff’s Office to identify incarcerated residents who could serve as budget delegates. The expanded program received a 2026 Smart Cities Dive Community Project Award.
The detention facility residents evaluated budget proposals, meeting biweekly over an eight-week period and working one on one with PB Durham staff. They used iPads to access data from the Durham Neighborhood Compass, a public data platform, and Google Maps’ street view to evaluate projects and inspect sites from inside the jail.
“The iPads were really helpful,” said Durham Innovation Manager Lyndsay Gavin. “We would [look at] a street view of a park, and then some of the participants would be like, ‘Oh, yeah, I do know that park. And I know that it doesn’t have enough play equipment,’ or something like that. It was much more engaging than if we had just printed things and brought them to them.”
“High expectations for our guys”
Before PB Durham could get greater participation from residents who are incarcerated, it had to enlist the cooperation of the county sheriff’s office. It was an easy sell.
“When they gave me the spiel, it really made sense,” said Durham County Sheriff Clarence Birkhead. Residents who are incarcerated “haven’t lost their right to vote and engage in conversations, so why not allow them to be part of the participatory budgeting process as well? It aligned with the things we’re doing inside the Durham County Detention Center.”
The sheriff’s office partners with education institutions for inmates who want to finish high school or get a GED and participates in programs including You Can Vote, which helps people who are incarcerated access absentee ballots, and Welcome Home, a city program that provides support to people returning to Durham after incarceration, Birkhead said.
“We have very high expectations for our guys,” said Justin Ellerbe, chief of detention services for the sheriff’s office, about those incarcerated at the detention center. “We want to raise their ceiling and their expectations.”
Ellerbe says he tells those who are incarcerated that while an event may have put them in the detention center, it does not define them. “The direction that we’re taking our facility is letting all of our detainees know you still have a voice, you still are productive,” Ellerbe said. “Let’s find your values, find your power and get it out there.”
Logistics of participation
In the most recent round of participatory budgeting, 10 residents from the men’s detention center participated in proposal development, 110 participated in idea collection and 230 voted, Ortiz said. (PB Durham hopes to open the program to women who are incarcerated next year, she said.)
The detention center staff screens and approves residents before they’re selected and treats the meetings like an attorney visit in terms of the search and security procedures, Birkhead said. PB Durham sent two to three staff members to each session.
The biggest hurdle the PB Durham team encountered was the residents’ fluctuating availability, the staff members said. Developing proposals takes many months, and inmates can end their terms, get transferred to another facility or lose their privileges, making them unable to participate, Ortiz said. Only three of the 10 residents stayed involved throughout the entire proposal-development phase, she said. “We didn’t anticipate that so many would drop out during the process for different reasons.”
The PB Durham staff members “met our residents where they were,” Birkhead said. “They didn’t talk down to them. They had conversations with them.” For her part, Ortiz said “the sheriff’s team was incredibly supportive.”
“This is, as far as we're aware, a first-of-its-kind approach [to] treating incarcerated residents not as passive recipients of a ballot, but as decision-makers with real authority in a public budgeting process,” Gavin stated in nominating the project. “This was an intentional structural redesign of who gets to hold power in a civic process typically closed to this population.”
“I’m going to see what my voice did”
The incarcerated residents overwhelmingly gravitated toward supporting youth-oriented programs and projects such as basketball courts and playgrounds, Ortiz said. “It’s almost like they’re looking at where they are and they’re like, ‘We want to make sure that our kids don’t end up here.’ There’s just so much power in that.”
Several participants said the experience increased their trust in government, gave them a stronger sense of connection and inspired them to vote or engage with the City Council after their release, according to Gavin. One participant said it offered him a chance to retain “some type of humanity in my situation,” she said. (Smart Cities Dive was unable to get comments directly from detention center residents who participated in the process by the time this article was published.)
The detention center participants took pride and a sense of ownership in being a part of the process, Birkhead said.
They learned that their voice and their ideas mean something, according to Ellerbe. “They had an opportunity to give back to the community and be part of something that’s bigger than they are,” he said.
Some of the participants had to leave the county facility to serve terms in other facilities, Ellerbe added. “They were excited to say, ‘Hey, when I come back home, I’m going to see what my voice did.”

title: Best wet season in decades gives life to living medicine cabinet
content:
Best wet season in decades gives life to Barkindji people's living medicine cabinet
In short:
A new community-made field guide shares cultural knowledge utilised by Barkindji people for thousands of years.
The Barkindji Edible and Medicinal Plants book share uses of locally-found native plants throughout Menindee, Wilcannia and Broken Hill, in New South Wales' far west.
What's next?
Barkindji and Malyangapa tour guide and co-creator of the book, Dave Doyle, hopes it will inspire young people to spend more time in nature and to also protect it.
To most travellers passing through Menindee, the bushland along the Darling-Baaka River is a striking outback landscape, abundant with wildflowers and greenery.
But where others see a stretch of native scrub, Barkindji and Malyangapa man Dave Doyle sees something more valuable — a living medicine cabinet, teeming with plants whose healing properties have been used by his family for generations.
There's emu bush, which can help with wounds and headaches; native lemongrass to soothe a sore throat, and river mint, which makes for a soothing tea and helps with digestion.
A particularly wet season in Far West New South Wales has seen flora in the region flourish in numbers not seen for decades, according to Mr Doyle.
"It was probably the 90s or maybe early 2000s last time we had a season like this," Mr Doyle explains to tour guests who admire the flowers from the back seat of his ute, which he occasionally pulls over to take a closer look.
Mr Doyle's cultural tours depart from Broken Hill and traverse the Darling-Baaka River and Menindee Lakes, sharing cultural knowledge of medicinal and edible plants that Barkindji people have utilised for thousands of years.
The recently released field guide, Barkindji Edible & Medicinal Plants, a collaboration between Barkindji community members and friends, encourages young people to get out into nature and learn more about the plants around them.
"I think the more that we see the environment as something valuable, the more we'll look after it," Mr Doyle says.
On a recent tour, the guide demonstrated the kind of knowledge he is trying to pass on to younger generations.
"We actually wrote it for people of teenage years to be able to understand, rather than something a little bit more technical, hoping that kids will have a look at it and get interested in plants," he says.
Thousands of years sustained by natives
Along Menindee Road, he pulls over to the road's shoulder, climbing out into a field of lilac Darling peas that have sprouted in the red dirt, seemingly from nowhere.
While hunting was a big part of Barkindji culture, Mr Doyle says that plants were often more vital to Aboriginal diets throughout history.
"For us along the river, plants, vegetables that we collect, are probably like a main staple, more so than proteins that people tend to associate with Aboriginal people: kangaroos, emus, goannas, that kind of thing," he says.
"It was the plants that sustained us, gave us energy, gave us the vitamins and minerals to be able to absorb the nutrients and proteins out of those bigger animals as well, to give us the energy to continue to do our day-to-day work.
"There's so many uses like medicines, and a lot of the plants also are fibrous, so making string for twine nets, fishing lines."
Mr Doyle first became interested in learning about native medicinal and edible plants during COVID, when supermarkets often ran out of fresh produce.
"Through COVID, people were having trouble sourcing food a lot of time, and we actually have a lot around us, but we forget it's there or don't know what's edible and what's not," he says.
His interest in native plants has since extended beyond cultural tours and he also runs a catering business focused on native plants and traditional bush tucker.
In Kinchega National Park, along the Darling-Baaka River, he hosts a morning tea for tour guests featuring locally-sourced native plants.
The menu includes quandong and finger lime tarts and river mint tea — the latter picked on a walk along the river while the kettle boils.
He picks Warrigal greens, handing the leaves around the group for tasting.
"A lot of these plants have more nutrition than things we buy in the shops," he says.
"Warrigal greens are actually comparable to English spinach, and we don't have to pay for it, we just go and collect it off the edge of the river."
A garden medicine cabinet
Mr Doyle, also hopes the field guide will inspire people to plant native species in their own gardens.
"So if we need them, they're actually right there for us to use, as well as they look really beautiful," he says.
"I reckon every time a house is built, we should be putting natives in there, especially for Aboriginal people.
"We should be putting things like emu bush [in the garden], that is one of the most important bush medicines we have out here.
"And we should be planting things that don't need much water, they don't need any fertilisers or insecticides.
"It would be great if you've got a rash or a sore and you can just go out in the backyard, pick it and use it."

title: [Magazine] En Corée du Sud, la relève chez les «femmes de la mer»
content:
Les haenyeo, ou «femmes de la mer», sont un symbole de liberté, de respect de la nature et de résilience féminine dans une Corée du Sud profondément patriarcale. Si cette tradition ne peut freiner son déclin, une nouvelle génération de plongeuses se forme.
Jin So-hee a gagné sa place parmi les plongeuses sud-coréennes qui récoltent des fruits de mer au prix de durs efforts. Elle fait partie à présent d’une nouvelle génération qui perpétue une tradition vieille de plusieurs siècles. La transformation économique rapide de la Corée du Sud a fait fondre le nombre de «femmes de la mer», ou «haenyeo», qui plongent en apnée pour récolter des fruits de mer. Cette profession proche de la nature mais très physique attire à nouveau des recrues, échaudées par un monde du travail sud-coréen déshumanisant.
Jin So-hee, 33 ans, a grandi à Busan, deuxième plus grande ville du pays, et a obtenu des diplômes d’esthéticienne et manucure avant de travailler comme aide-infirmière pour gagner sa vie. Découragée par la compétition au travail, des journées à rallonge et un maigre salaire, elle a décidé de mettre le cap vers la ville côtière de Geoje à l’âge de 25 ans. Elle y a rencontré des haenyeo septuagénaires et a été attirée par leur liberté et leur travail en communion avec la nature jusqu’à un âge avancé.
Au début, la jeune femme dit avoir perdu sept kilos en plongeant et avoir parfois été si fatiguée qu’elle «avait à peine la force de tenir une cuillère». Les haenyeo plongent avec pour seule protection une combinaison et des lunettes, qu’elles enduisent de salive et d’armoise pour éviter la buée, comme le veut la tradition. Elle a souffert de douleurs aux oreilles dues à la pression de l’eau, et de sévères migraines, des maux rencontrés par des générations de haenyeo. «La douleur était si forte que j’en avais les larmes aux yeux (…) je ne pouvais rien entendre.» Déterminée, Jin So-hee a appris des techniques modernes de plongée en apnée et en bouteille visant à égaliser la pression dans ses oreilles.
Pourquoi est-ce que je me battais si férocement en ville?
Choi Young-hee, 60 ans
Les haenyeo, dont le savoir-faire est classé au patrimoine culturel immatériel de l’humanité par l’Unesco, sont devenues un symbole d’indépendance et de résilience féminines dans un pays profondément patriarcal. Sur l’île de Jeju, au cœur de cette tradition, le nombre de haenyeo est tombé à 2 371 l’année dernière, contre 3 437 en 2021. Mais cette tradition existe ailleurs, notamment à Geoje.
S’intégrer à cette communauté des haenyeo plus âgées de Geoje a été un nouveau défi pour Jin So-hee et Woo Jung-min, autre plongeuse de la nouvelle génération. Les plongeuses se méfiaient de ces jeunes qui filmaient leur vie et publiaient des vidéos sur YouTube. «Nous voulions documenter le fait qu’il existe des jeunes haenyeo comme nous, pour que cela puisse un jour devenir une sorte d’archive et peut-être même un atout pour les générations futures», explique Woo Jung-mi, 40 ans.
Choi Young-hee, 60 ans, est devenue haenyeo à la fin de la quarantaine après avoir été pendant deux décennies vendeuse dans des grands magasins de Séoul. En visitant Geoje, elle a aperçu des silhouettes dans la mer qui plongeaient et remontaient sans cesse. Croyant d’abord qu’il s’agissait de dauphins, elle a compris ensuite que c’était des haenyeo. Fascinée, cette expérience l’a amenée à remettre sa vie en question, se demandant : «Pourquoi est-ce que je me battais si férocement en ville?» Aujourd’hui, elle dirige une association qui enseigne la culture des haenyeo et forme les futures plongeuses.
Malgré quelques jeunes recrues, le nombre de haenyeo ne cesse de diminuer. Le réchauffement de la mer perturbe les écosystèmes marins, raréfie les prises et rend leur dangereuse profession encore plus précaire. Un seul trou minuscule dans une combinaison de plongée peut être critique dans la mer glaciale en hiver, explique Woo Jung-mi. «Tu gagnes ta vie dans le royaume des morts et tu la passes dans le monde des vivants», dit un ancien dicton des haenyeo. «La mer est tellement dangereuse, et l’épuisement physique et mental si fort, que nous le considérons pratiquement comme l’au-delà», confie la quadragénaire.
Mais pour les deux plongeuses, la beauté saisissante de la mer vaut tous les efforts. Même si cette beauté elle-même s’estompe avec le changement climatique. Ainsi, les ascidies rouges – des invertébrés marins en forme de sac – qui transformaient le fond de l’océan en «champ de roses» chaque printemps, ont disparu, déplore Jin So-hee.

title: Country Women's Association celebrates 90 years in outback town
content:
Tennant Creek's Country Women's Association branch is celebrating its 90th anniversary this weekend, making it the longest continuously active CWA in the Northern Territory.
Founded when men outnumbered women more than ten to one in the town, the organisation continues to serve community members in the broader Barkly region.
What's next?
The organisation is now looking for the next generation to join and help the group reach its centenary year.
An outback branch of the Country Women's Association (CWA) is celebrating 90 years of service in one of Australia's most remote towns.
The Tennant Creek branch in the Northern Territory was founded in 1936 during a gold rush in the area, when local men outnumbered women ten to one.
It is the longest continuously active branch in the NT, and it still serves the town's population of about 3,000 people, nearly 1,000 kilometres south of Darwin in the Barkly region.
Founded in 1922, the CWA has more than 1,000 branches across Australia and aims to improve the lives of women and children through community service and supporting cultural and welfare projects.
Women vastly outnumbered
When CWA Tennant Creek formed, women made up 45 of the 600 residents, and after two years of informal catch-ups over cups of tea, the branch was officially launched.
President and life member Roddy Calvert said the CWA gave women and kids in the town a chance to find connection in the outback.
"I think it was for the companionship in those earlier days because a lot of these men … they were out on the field and often they just had their mine lease away from the town," she said.
"There just wasn't telephones and all that back in those days at all, so they just leaned on each other."
Service to the community
The Tennant Creek branch fundraises for various causes in the Barkly region, including supporting women's shelters in local Aboriginal communities and community groups.
The group also provided support during national emergencies, including to stationed soldiers in World War II and evacuees after Cyclone Tracy destroyed Darwin in the 70s.
For many volunteers, the community spirit in the CWA was instilled in them from childhood.
Volunteer Helen Kempe regularly travels more than 1,000km from Mount Riddock cattle station to Tennant Creek to ensure her family's long association with the organisation continues.
"Both my grandmother and my mother were CWA members, so I know what it's all about," Ms Kempe said.
"So I think it's a great honour to be a member and I'm glad I joined."
Looking towards a century
While excitement about the milestone is high, membership has fallen to fewer than 20 people in recent years, with fewer young people involved compared to the past.
However, branch member Alba Brockie said the CWA will always have a place in remote areas like Tennant Creek.
"The things that CWA have always fought for around isolated people, isolated children, women and children's health, those issues remain important," she said.

title: Triplets carry on father's FDNY legacy after 9/11
content:
Brothers pursue firefighting careers inspired by late FDNY father who died from 9/11-related illnesses
A firefighter father's 9/11 sacrifice is inspiring his triplet sons to serve.
NEW YORK -- The triplet sons of an FDNY firefighter who responded to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks are not identical, but they share a common past and will soon share a common future.
They're three of the thousands of children who lost a parent 25 years ago on Sept. 11 or in the years after due to 9/11-related illnesses.
William Gormley's sons - Raymond, Billy and Kevin - were just 3 years old when their father rushed to the twin towers on Sept. 11, 2001. While many children lost parents that day, the brothers grew up with their father, only later learning the toll his work at Ground Zero had taken on his health.
"We all, for the most part, have the same lives in a lot of ways," Raymond said while sitting on a couch between his two brothers. "The same trauma, the same upbringing, the same everything. No one understands me like these two understand me."
But for Kevin, Raymond and Billy didn't learn about what happened from the history books, they lived it and they always had each other to rely on.
"This is a huge point my father always made, he said, 'These are your people. You were born with them, and this is what you got til the end,'" Kevin said.
They don't remember what happened on Sept. 11, since they were so young.
"Now, 25 years later, we're understanding the full grasp of what happened that day," Raymond said.
William Gormley rushed to the twin towers after they were struck. Unlike many children, they didn't lose their dad that day. The reality of the work he did hit later in life.
Firefighter Gormley worked on the pile for months, looking for survivors and later, for the remains of victims.
"It makes you feel some pride knowing your father went in there selflessly to help others and do the best he could," Kevin said.
The family said the long-term effects of his work became apparent over time. Growing up, the brothers accompanied their father to numerous doctor appointments but did not fully understand the severity of his health problems.
"They never really told us anything really," Billy said. "But as kids we'd go to hospital waiting rooms in summer for doctors' appointments. But not knowing the severity."
Raymond added, "Growing up he had skin cancer, sinus issues. So growing up as a kid, I personally never really understood what that came from. It wasn't until he was diagnosed with bladder cancer in 2016 that we put two together and realized it was from his time spent at Ground Zero."
William Gormley died of bladder and lung cancer in 2017. According to a report, he was one of more than 400 fire and EMS workers who have died from 9/11-related illnesses.
Asked whether his father would have made the same decision knowing what is now known about the dangers faced at Ground Zero, Raymond said there was no doubt.
"One hundred percent, without hesitation," he said. "Not only him, but every single person he went down with that day would go down to the pile again, without a doubt."
Today, a street in Brooklyn bears William Gormley's name, near the firehouse where he worked.
Despite their father's advice to seek work outside the fire service, the brothers found themselves drawn to the profession.
"My father would always say, 'When you get older, get a job where you sit behind a desk and write checks for people,'" Kyle said.
"He'd always say, 'Work with your brain, not your hands,'" Raymond added.
He went on to say, "So I'm a firefighter right now, an FDNY firefighter working at the same house he worked at, Ladder 174. So it's full circle really, it's crazy from him telling me to work with your brain, not your hands, and it's crazy I'm sleeping in the same bed he did 20 years ago."
Billy hopes to join the fire service soon.
"So I'm an EMT with the fire department at the moment," he said. "Waiting to join fire as well."
Kevin has also applied to become a firefighter.
"You hope one day, you can fill those shoes," he said.
The report said Billy and Kevin could join the fire academy as soon as this month.
The brothers said they were inspired not only by their father, but also by the support they received from firefighters after his death.
"Once I saw the camaraderie, everyone coming together, people driving us around, his old coworkers taking care of us, the laughs, the tears," Raymond said. "After that in my mind, it was something I would really like to do."
"Yeah, what they did was incredible how they took care of us, made sure everything was in order," another brother added.
And this didn't just have an impact on the three brothers, it impacted the entire family, including their big sister, Bridget.
"I think there's a beauty in that it was never forced down their throats," said Bridget. "My dad was never like, 'You're going to be a fireman!' Our dad was like, 'You're NOT going to be a fireman!'"
Bridget has also dedicated her work to preserving the stories of those affected by Sept. 11. She works with 9/11 survivors and produced a documentary about the dangers of toxic dust exposure. It's called, "Dust: Lingering Legacy of 9/11."
"Along the way, I got to know my father's friends better," she said. "I mean, I lost my dad, but I've got [sic] thousands of uncles now."
For the Gormley siblings, the events of Sept. 11 continue to shape their lives and careers. They say their shared experiences and bond have helped them navigate a loss that has defined much of their lives.
"Just being there for someone on their worst day, being their hope when there's no hope is really something special, something we take a lot of pride in," Raymond said.
"We all, for the most part, have the same lives in a lot of ways, the same trauma, the same upbringing, the same everything, no one understands me like these two understand me," one of the brothers said.
As they continue their careers in public service, the brothers say they are carrying forward the values their father exemplified, together.
