title: Darwin soccer club helps migrants find community and a place to call home
content:
One of the city's oldest soccer clubs, Darwin Olympic SC, helping to connect migrants from more than 30 nations
In short:
A family who fled Myanmar after a military coup says joining soccer club Darwin Olympic is helping them settle into life in the Northern Territory.
Founded by Greek migrants in 1967, Darwin Olympic now has players and members from more than 30 nationalities.
What's next?
The club says migrants are continuing to shape the Darwin soccer scene as players, volunteers, coaches and supporters.
When Kaung Zayar-Thaw kicked a soccer ball for the first time at age 13, he was displaced in Thailand.
His father, Zaw Zaw Htoo, had been a member of Myanmar's parliament with the National League for Democracy and in 2021, the military junta seized their home in a military coup.
The family was forced to make the dangerous journey into Thailand, hiding in a forest for several days in fear of being caught and deported.
Soon after arriving in Thailand, Kaung said he spotted some people kicking a ball around and was intrigued.
From there, the so-called "world game" went on to play a role in helping him cope with adversity.
"Football is the only thing that helped me get through stuff," he says.
When he arrived in the Top End in 2024, Kaung joined the Darwin Olympic Sporting Club, where his teammates helped him practise his English as well as soccer.
Now 15, Kaung plays as a defender for Darwin Olympic, and he says football has become much more than a sport.
"Football is the only way out of things when I'm under stress from all the pressure from the schoolwork and stuff," he says.
"It's fun, and it just teaches me how to … communicate with my teammates.
"My teammates help me. I just feel [like I] belong, [and] I really like being a part of this Olympic team."
A club shaped by migration
The Darwin Olympic Sporting Club was founded in 1967 by Greek migrants to the city as a place for their community to come together through soccer.
Almost 60 years later, the club has grown into a multicultural community representing more than 30 nationalities.
Club president Yianni Prouzos believes the club's home base in Darwin's multicultural northern suburbs has made it a natural meeting place for migrant communities.
"Football is the world's most common language," Yianni says.
"You come here, you don't have to speak the same language — you just have to know how to kick the ball and pass the ball."
Yianni, who moved to Australia as a child, says migrants now contribute to the club well beyond the playing pitch.
"We've got a lot of our migrants that come and help us," he said.
"Every person has different experiences, has different cultures … so what do they bring? Knowledge."
A family starting again
After a period of uncertainty, Kaung's mother, Kyi Nwe Oo, says the family has felt safe since arriving in Darwin, but that adjusting to their new home has been challenging.
"The difficulty we faced is that people speak a different language, culture, and the food is really difficult for us," she said.
But football has given the family a reason to get involved in the community.
"When we are seen in the community engaging with others in activities, it makes us feel that we're involved in the community and part of the community as well," Kyi Nwe Oo says.
According to Charles Darwin University senior lecturer Devaki Monani, Darwin's small and diverse population can make those connections easier to build.
"You can actually really get a multicultural experience and … you're not excluded," she said.
"Sport has great potential in connecting communities and breaking down those language and political barriers.
"In a place like Darwin, sporting activities are critical for families to engage with other families, whether migrants or not."
Soccer brings sense of belonging
Football Northern Territory chief executive Jaime Monteith says for many migrants, their first preference when it comes to sport is soccer.
He says the game can give people a sense of belonging while also opening doors to volunteering, coaching and refereeing.
"What it does is it breaks down barriers, breaks down the ability for new arrivals, migrants, to find a home or a sense of belonging," Jaime says.
For Kaung's family, those connections are helping to turn Darwin from somewhere they arrived into somewhere they can call home.
"We are trying our best to look after each other and be welcoming and make this place our home," Kyi Nwe Oo said.

title: Veterans who died by suicide honoured at memorial
content:
Veterans who died by suicide honoured at memorial
- Published
Hundreds of people have gathered at the National Memorial Arboretum for the dedication of a permanent tribute to veterans and armed forces personnel who have died by suicide.
The Elysium Memorial, at the site in Elrewas, Staffordshire, is the first permanent memorial of its kind to be built in the UK.
More than 1,300 military veterans and personnel have taken their lives in the last 30 years, with the memorial aiming to provide a place for contemplation for those affected by the loss of a friend or loved one.
Edward Mackenzie, co-founder of the Elysium Memorial Foundation, which is behind the project, said he was "blown away" by the number of people that had turned up.
More than 300 motorcyclist rode to the arboretum from Burton-on-Trent on Sunday, with a convoy organised by community organisation Wheels for Wishes.
Mackenzie, who served in the army for more than 30 years and has lost over to 20 friends to suicide, including his best friend, said seeing those veterans' being recognised "means everything".
"This is why I did it, I did for for the friends, the families, the comrades, those that we've lost to suicide," he told the BBC.
"There's a lot of families here today that have been thanking me for achieving this memorial so I'm incredibly grateful."
There were 277 cases of veterans taking their own lives between 2006 and 2025, according to the Ministry of Defence.
"Any death by suicide is a tragedy that is felt across our community, and our thoughts are with those who have been impacted by the loss of a loved one," a spokesperson said.
"The welfare of our armed forces is at the heart of everything we do - more than £25m invested into Op Courage in the last year and our £50m Valour programme gives veterans in England access to specialist NHS mental health services and access to essential care, continuing our steadfast commitment to provide our forces and their families the wellbeing support they deserve."
Following the ceremony, people at the arboretum were invited to lay their own wreaths at the memorial.
Mackenzie said he was "very emotional" about the size of the turnout.
"I'm lost for words a lot of the time and I hope that this memorial will really help towards the mental health and families and basically taking the word suicide out of the shadows," he explained.
"I think that we still have amazing work to do to try and help everyone."

title: Nepal tunnel survivor finds solace in village homecoming
content:
Nepal tunnel survivor finds solace in village homecoming
- Sanjay Sah, a rare survivor of Nepal's glacier collapse disaster, returned home after nine days trapped in a hydropower tunnel and a week in hospital, bringing relief and grief to his village.
- The glacier collapse caused at least 1,386 deaths and over 5,000 missing, with many workers from hydropower stations still unaccounted for, including Sah's relatives.
- Sah was welcomed with traditional ceremonies and emotional reunions, expressing readiness to resume work despite the ongoing tragedy in his community.
AI generated
TILATHI KOILADI, Nepal – After nine days trapped in a hydropower tunnel and a week of hospital care following his dramatic rescue, Sanjay Sah, a rare survivor of a devastating glacier collapse in Nepal in August, finally returned to his village and family on Sept 13.
It was a homecoming marked by relief and joy but also grief.
“I was trapped in the tunnel... I felt trapped in the hospital room too. I finally feel free here in my village,” Sah, 30, said after arriving in Tilathi Koiladi, near the border with India.
At least 1,386 people have died and 5,130 are still missing across Nepal weeks after a Himalayan glacier collapsed near the Chinese border, unleashing a wall of mud and water that crashed through mountain valleys destroying everything in its path.
Around 900 power station workers remain missing. Sah, a mechanical foreman at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, was one of just three pulled from debris-buried tunnels extending deep under the mountains.
He survived in the darkness, drinking flood water and seepage from the mountain rock until rescue workers finally reached him.
Sah left the hospital in the capital Kathmandu on Sept 11 and the next day boarded a bus for an overnight journey home.
A tearful homecoming to a village still in mourning
Around 60 people, mostly women, awaited his arrival in Tilathi Koiladi on Sept 13.
Family members, including his parents, uncle, wife and daughter, performed a traditional welcome ceremony, washing his feet as part of a cleansing ritual.
After his mother dabbed a pink vermilion tika on his forehead, Sah bowed. They embraced and then broke down in tears.
“My son!” his mother cried, holding him tightly and kissing him on the cheek.
Women who had gathered to witness the reunion used their colourful saris to wipe the tears from their eyes.
Many in Tilathi Koiladi are still awaiting word of the fate of family members who had been working at hydropower stations hit by the flooding.
“There are more people from my village still missing after the flood,” Sah told Reuters.
One family, he said, phoned him while he was still in the hospital to ask if he had seen or heard from a missing relative who had been working at a different power station. He had to tell them he had not.
At home among family, Sah said he is ready to put his ordeal behind him.
“I will stay in my village for some time now. I want to meet all my people,” he said. “But if I am called back to duty, I will go.” REUTERS

title: 2 free children’s books bring Singapore’s past to life through kaya toast and ice-cream bread
content:
2 free children’s books bring Singapore’s past to life through kaya toast and ice-cream bread
- The Hainanese Cooked team created the picture book Bo’ Hou And The Grand Feast to teach children about Hainanese culture, cuisine and dialect phrases.
- The project features a web map highlighting heritage sites and eateries, aiming to make learning about culture a fun family activity.
- This book is part of the Temasek Foundation–NUS Heritage Champions programme, which supports student-led projects preserving Singapore’s heritage, including another book on ice cream hawkers.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – Many children love a good plate of chicken rice or a slice of kaya toast, but few know the story behind them – that these familiar dishes were introduced by Hainanese immigrants who made Singapore their home.
To help kids explore the roots of these beloved dishes, Koh V-Nying, 24, Ng Wee Liang, 27, and Yong Chuen Shin, 25 – collectively known as The Hainanese Cooked – have released Bo’ Hou And The Grand Feast, a picture book celebrating Hainanese culture and cuisine.
Available to read for free online at hainanesecooked.netlify.app, the story follows two animal characters, Bo’ Hou and Mai Tin, inspired by the traditional Hainanese tiger and lion dance.
Through their adventures, young readers are introduced to dialect phrases and lesser-known delicacies such as ge bia, a Hainanese-style mooncake made with orange peel and pepper.
“We hope young readers can learn Hainanese phrases and about delicacies they may not encounter in everyday life,” says Yong, who is of Hainanese heritage. “We want to spark their curiosity to explore more about our culture.”
To help families turn learning into a fun outing, the team has also created a web map.
It highlights local eateries serving traditional fare, an 1853 heritage temple and a troupe keeping the art of Hainanese tiger dance alive.
Bo’ Hou And The Grand Feast is one of 10 student-led community heritage projects developed under the inaugural Temasek Foundation-National University of Singapore (NUS) Heritage Champions programme.
Over two years, 125 tertiary students across two cohorts participated in the initiative, supported by NUS Libraries, Temasek Foundation and the National Heritage Board. The top five teams from each cohort received up to $7,000 to bring their projects to life.
Another project to emerge from the programme is My Ice Cream Uncle, a children’s picture book spotlighting roadside hawkers selling ice cream wrapped in bread.
Created by Scoops of Memory – comprising Totaan Aljean Choong, 20, Lai Xin Yu, 20, and Theint Theint Zaw Tun, 23 – the project also includes a YouTube documentary exploring the trade, titled Where Are Singapore’s Ice Cream Hawkers Going?.
“Ice-cream hawkers were a familiar part of many Singaporeans’ childhood, but they are slowly disappearing,” says Zaw Tun.
“Each cart represents years of hard work and community connection.
“We wanted to preserve these stories and make them accessible to a new generation.”
Families can look out for the e-book release on their Instagram page (@scoopsofmemory) by year-end.
Physical copies of the picture books from both teams will also be available at selected public libraries.
For NUS university librarian Natalie Pang, these projects highlight how important young voices are in keeping heritage alive.
“Singapore’s heritage is not only found in monuments and historic buildings,” she says. “It also lives in everyday experiences, memories, food, places and the stories of communities.
“When young people take ownership of these stories and find new ways to share them, they help ensure that our heritage remains relevant and meaningful to future generations.”

title: ‘Echoes of the Past’: Repatriations of three Fort Peck children bring joy, tears
content:
WARNING: This story has photos of caskets and contains disturbing details about residential and boarding schools. If you are feeling triggered, here are healing-informed resources from the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition in the U.S. The National Indian Residential School Crisis Hotline in Canada can be reached at 1-866-925-4419 or the Lamathut Crisis Line at 1-800-721-0066. If you’re in Treaty 4 territory, call 306-522-7494.
Charles Fox
Special to ICT
FORT PECK, Montana — The last handful of soil drifted through the air and down upon the casket, marking an historic moment in the decades-long quest by the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes to bring home their children.
More than 135 years after leaving home for the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, Christine Redstone, Peter Howe and Richard Morgan have been reburied under the big sky of Montana, with the whispers of a breeze coming off the Missouri River.
They finally are resting in the earth that contains the echoes of their past.
The three children were part of a group of 43 students who arrived after an 1800-mile journey from Fort Peck to the Pennsylvania school, arriving on April 15,1890. The school, the first federally run off-reservation boarding school, was known for its “kill the Indian, save the man” motto initiated by founder Richard Pratt to suppress Native culture and languages. Nearly 8,000 students attended during its 39 years of existence, and many, like Christine, Peter and Richard, never made it home.
Finally, this year, the three children were repatriated back to their homeland, bringing a lasting impact to their community.
Organizers had stressed in the weeks and months leading up to the homecoming of “the community becoming the family,” and the need to make sure “no child comes home alone.” Family members greeted Christine’s remains, but Richard and Peter do not have living relatives.
The messages translated into reality over three days, producing large processions and caravans, nightly community meals, and children dancing in the headlights of parked cars while preparations were made for all-night vigils.
“It’s been a wonderful time to see the families gather, to give love to one another, for us to laugh, for us to cry, for us to hold close to each other, and for our young people to learn how we’re all related and how all those connections connect to one another…not let it just be a temporary thing, but to strengthen those family ties for future generations,” Jonny BearCub said in her prayer at the service for Christine Thursday, Sept. 10, at the Freda Fourstar Community Hall.
“They (the children) are coming home at an opportune time to remind us that we’re only as strong as our families are strong. We’re only as strong as our tribe is strong. A nation is only as strong as its people,” BearCub continued in her prayer.
‘How fleeting freedom really is’
The level of participation and enthusiasm was especially evident by the procession leading up to the reburial of Howe and Morgan in the tribal repatriation cemetery. Students from Poplar High School ran the distance, while equestrians and a caravan of cars followed closely behind. They were led by an orange fire engine affectionately known as the “Big Orange Pumpkin.”
But the celebratory spirit did not mask the obstacles they overcame to bring the children home.
Well over a decade ago, Darrell “Curley” Youpee, who died in May 2021, and Ken Ryan had tried to initiate bringing Christine home at the family’s request.
For Richard and Peter, the difficulties were greater since they did not have living relatives, a requirement from the Office of Army Cemeteries that has been challenged by tribes in court.
Finally, the Office of Army Cemeteries agreed to let a tribal representative sign on behalf of enrolled members, and Dyan Youpee, the tribe’s cultural preservation director, was able to bring her late father’s efforts to fruition.
“He set the bar really high to be an anthropologist, an archeologist, historian, museum curator, and an archivist. … I learned to fight harder,” Youpee said.
“For people who never experienced repatriation, there’s the fighting with the agencies to bring [the children] back, the organizing, the planning, and the difficulties of getting different families together,” Youpee told the crowd at Christine’s pre-burial service. “I really fought a lot of battles, and I didn’t win all of them.”
But there was also sadness that many who worked hard for the day and dreamed of seeing the children returned home had passed away.
“I know that Ken [Ryan], my dad, and Lana Fourstar’s grandma and mom, they really wanted to be here and be a part of it,” Youpee said. “There were a lot of people in the community who wanted to witness this, and they’re not here.”
While the celebratory spirit and the return of the remains of the three children could bring some healing to families and the tribe, it would never produce closure to a period of Native American history that affected most every Native family and produced generational scars.
“We cannot comprehend the grief that our families went through long ago,” BearCub said as she led those assembled in prayer. “We can only be angry for them. But help us to understand that our rage and our anger that our ancestors felt, and use that as a power to fuel ourselves to be better than those who took our children. Help us to use that rage and anger to make us stronger, to make us more compassionate, to make us be able to understand people who are different from ourselves.”
She continued, “For with the return of our children, we understand how fleeting freedom really is. For in those days, the government came and took them.”
A message to future generations
Peter and Richard are now buried in the tribal repatriation cemetery in Poplar, while Christine lies to the west in the Oswego Catholic Cemetery, where she is reunited with other family members. Both locations are dramatically different from the cemetery at the Carlisle Barracks, where the act of stripping away individuality and culture were taken to a new level after death.
The students who were not lucky enough to survive Carlisle found themselves represented by identical, white gravestones lined up in straight lines like a formation of soldiers.
At Christine’s wake, Dylan Youpee, one of the spiritual leaders on the journey, described the cemetery and the emotions stirred by the visit.
“You think it’s just a cemetery, something that you see all the time on the side of the road,” Dylan Youpee said. “But when you go around that corner and you see those headstones of all those Indian kids, holy smokes. That lump comes up in your throat and your first reaction is to be sad, is to cry. And then you get another emotion. You get angry. You want to get angry because these people took our kids. These people took our children, brought them all the way over here, 1,800 miles over here, and beat the Indian out of them…Pretty soon you want to leave because of it. You want to leave that place. But then a part of you wants to stay… You want to make sure the relatives are brought back.”
At events over a three-day repatriation period in Montana, various relatives, spiritual and tribal leaders spoke about the experience of visiting the grounds of the former boarding school and the repatriation process. The emotional duress of walking in the footsteps of ancestors, especially those who never made it back home, dominated their talks.
But out of the somber darkness and raw emotions there was the light of inspiration created by the students who endured the experience.
“There were some difficult things that our ancestors went through like those young children dying, separated from their families,” said Barry Bighorn, a member of the Fort Peck Tribal Executive Board. “But for the majority of them, they didn’t lose what was inside of them, how they were raised, and they stayed strong. They learned. They succeeded. And that’s what stuck with me, is how, how well they did, how they overcame those difficult circumstances.”
Bighorn said there are lessons for the current generations.
“It’s a reminder to us today,” he said. “It brings that message home to us to love your families, love your children…. A lot of those children [in Carlisle] didn’t get to have that their whole life here. And a lot of the parents didn’t get to have time with their children because they were taken from them … It’s a different world that we live in now. There’s no reason for our children to go away like that anymore. So, consider that a blessing…We’re still here. We still have our identities and our families.”
‘She wanted to come home’
Throughout the homecoming, an inspiring image of Christine began to emerge, though little is known about Peter and not even a photograph can be found of Richard, who died of tuberculosis less than a year after arriving at Carlisle.
“Today, you look around what this young lady [Christine] brought us, it helps us understand the importance of compassion, empathy, caring, sharing, loving, our patience, our generosity,” said Michael Turcotte, who served as master of ceremonies for the reburials. “All these things she’s instilled in us, in our development of our own self.”
The five female relatives of Christine who traveled to Carlisle spoke about how they had gained a clearer image of who Christine was.
Michael Redstone describes how years ago, early in the process, she would imagine Christine.
“I would shut my eyes and I could see the prairie, and I could see that she wanted to come back, and she didn’t want to stay there,” she said. “I had to go back and get her. But, I didn’t know how.”
She learned along the way, with the help of Dyan Youpee. She also learned more about Christine, who spent nine years at Carlisle.
“When I got to Carlisle, I got to learn more about her,” Michael Redstone said. “She became more human to me, and not some ancestor that I’ve never known, but my actual grandma. I got to know her and know that she’s like us. She was a hard worker. She liked to play the mandolin and I’m pretty sure she had a wicked sense of humor… One of my cousins told me that she had a dream about Christine and that all she wanted was to be with her family and to hear a good song.”
But the emotions of Carlisle took their toll.
“I remember calling home three days in, and saying, ‘I’m done. I’m ready. I want to come home,’” Michael Redstone said. “I could just imagine what she had to deal with, being there for so long. But I like to think … the other Fort Peck kids all helped each other and all kept each other going and kept supporting each other.”
She, too, felt the impact of stepping into the cemetery.
“I started to get emotional the minute I walked into the cemetery, and then when I saw where she was buried for myself for the first time… it just hit me, and then it made me cry, and I dropped to my knees, and I just sobbed because it was so overwhelming,” she said.
“After so long, I was finally able to see her there. Like she was there in person.”
Now that the journey has reached its end, there is time for Michael Redstone to reflect and to heal with the hope that one day there will no longer be children in a cemetery in Carlisle.
“It does give me some peace because I feel like there’s a part of me that was missing, and it makes me feel more whole knowing that a member of my family got to come home and gets to rest with our relatives,” Michael Redstone said.
“It gives me some peace to know that she’s home and that she no longer has to be by herself where nobody can visit her and properly mourn her,” she continued. “What a privilege it is to be at the end of your life, to be buried next to your loved ones. There are kids over there that are still waiting. I keep hoping and praying that eventually, that cemetery’s going to be empty. That there’s nobody left there. Everybody’s going to get to go home, and everybody’s going to get to be with their families.”

title: Thousands flock to traditional ox race, floating market festival in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta
content:
The 2026 Ro Pagoda Traditional Ox Racing Festival officially opened on Sunday morning in An Cu Commune, An Giang Province, drawing 32 top pairs of oxen from the Seven Mountains area.
Ox racing is a long-standing cultural and sporting tradition among Khmer people in the Mekong Delta and has become a local tourism attraction in the Seven Mountains area.
Truong Thi Hong Tham, a visitor from Ca Mau Province, said it was her first time attending the Ro Pagoda ox racing festival.
The visitor was impressed by the skill of both the oxen and their handlers, as spectators cheered loudly as the pairs raced toward the finish line.
Nguyen Duy Phong, chairman of the An Cu Commune People's Committee, said the festival provides an opportunity for local residents to strengthen community ties and preserve Khmer cultural traditions.
The commune also hoped the event would help promote tourism in the Seven Mountains area to domestic and international visitors, he said.
The festival also featured a photo exhibition showcasing ox racing and the cultural life of people in the Seven Mountains area, along with the presentation of 100 bicycles to disadvantaged students and an exhibition of local OCOP (One Commune One Product) products.
Flood-season festival draws crowds in Hong Ngu
Also on Sunday, thousands of residents and visitors headed to a more than 2km-long embankment in Hong Ngu Ward, Dong Thap Province for the second edition of the Sac Nuoc Vung Bien festival.
The festival celebrated the Mekong Delta's annual flood season with activities including a floating market, boat racing, and duck-catching games.
Every year, from around August to December, water from the upper Mekong River flows into the Mekong Delta, turning vast areas into a sea of water.
Unlike a sudden flood, the water rises gradually, filling rivers before spilling over their banks and into the fields.
For Mekong Delta tourism and local communities, the annual flood season is seen as a gift from nature, bringing fertile alluvial soil and an abundance of fish, shrimp, fruits, and other local produce.
Dozens of decorated boats and sampans were arranged along the main festival area, creating a floating-market setting where visitors could sample local food and drinks and take photos.
Vo Nguyen Huy Nam, a local resident, said he was proud that Hong Ngu had developed a tourism event centered on the flood season, a distinctive feature of the area.
Phan Thi Hue, another local resident, said she sold roasted field shrimp with coconut water, teas and canarium products at the festival.
The event not only created a lively atmosphere and helped local vendors sell their products, but also conveyed a message about protecting the environment so that the annual flood season remains clean and healthy, she said.
Nguyen Thi Kim Yen, deputy chairwoman of the Hong Ngu Ward People's Committee, said this year's activities were designed to bring the flood season closer to residents and visitors through hands-on experiences.
Visitors could explore a floating market, enjoy don ca tai tu performances, join team boat races, and take part in other activities celebrating rural life during the flood season.
The festival also included an experiential program and a photo contest highlighting the beauty of Hong Ngu.
“The market tells the story of local produce. The boats tell the story of life on the waterways. Folk songs and traditional music tell the story of culture. Local dishes tell stories of memories. And the smiles of Hong Ngu people tell stories of kindness, friendliness, and hospitality,” Yen said.
“Through these familiar elements, we are not only creating a lively festival but also gradually building a distinctive cultural and tourism product for Hong Ngu.”

title: Nepal tunnel survivor finds solace in village homecoming
content:
National
Nepal tunnel survivor finds solace in village homecoming
Rescued after nine days trapped in a hydropower tunnel, Sanjay Sah returned to his family in a village still mourning workers missing after last month’s disaster.Reuters
After nine days trapped in a hydropower tunnel and a week of hospital care following his dramatic rescue, Sanjay Sah, a rare survivor of last month’s devastating glacier collapse in Nepal, finally returned to his village and family on Sunday.
It was a homecoming marked by relief and joy but also grief.
“I was trapped in the tunnel ... I felt trapped in the hospital room too. I finally feel free here in my village,” Sah, 30, said after arriving in Tilathi Koiladi, near the border with India.
At least 1,386 people have died and 5,130 are still missing across Nepal weeks after a Himalayan glacier collapsed near the Chinese border, unleashing a wall of mud and water that crashed through mountain valleys destroying everything in its path.
Around 900 power station workers remain missing. Sah, a mechanical foreman at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, was one of just three pulled from debris-buried tunnels extending deep under the mountains.
He survived in the darkness, drinking flood water and seepage from the mountain rock until rescue workers finally reached him.
Sah left the hospital in the capital Kathmandu on Friday and the next day boarded a bus for an overnight journey home.
A tearful homecoming to a village still in mourning
Around 60 people, mostly women, awaited his arrival in Tilathi Koiladi on Sunday.
Family members, including his parents, uncle, wife and daughter, performed a traditional welcome ceremony, washing his feet as part of a cleansing ritual.
After his mother dabbed a pink vermilion tika on his forehead, Sah bowed. They embraced and then broke down in tears.
“My son!” his mother cried, holding him tightly and kissing him on the cheek.
Women who had gathered to witness the reunion used their colourful saris to wipe the tears from their eyes.
Many in Tilathi Koiladi are still awaiting word of the fate of family members who had been working at hydropower stations hit by the flooding.
“There are more people from my village still missing after the flood,” Sah told Reuters.
One family, he said, phoned him while he was still in the hospital to ask if he had seen or heard from a missing relative who had been working at a different power station. He had to tell them he had not.
At home among family, Sah said he is ready to put his ordeal behind him.
“I will stay in my village for some time now. I want to meet all my people,” he said. “But if I am called back to duty, I will go.”

title: Nearly forgotten languages are finding new words for Colombia’s dragonflies
content:
Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries.
When researchers began cataloging dragonflies in Guainía, a remote region in eastern Colombia, the scientific record contained only about 10 species. By working with Indigenous communities, they’ve found nearly 120.
“When we started, very little was known,” Yiselle Cano, biodiversity leader of the Dragones Guainía project, told contributor Manuel Fonseca for Mongabay.
“I think we must be close to 120 species by now,” Cano said. “It’s a hugely diverse group, because it includes dragonflies native to the Orinoco, Amazonas, and dragonflies that are endemic to the Guiana Shield.”
The diversity makes Guainía a hotspot for dragonflies and damselflies. It may also provide insights on what is happening to the region’s water. These insects depend on healthy freshwater ecosystems, and their aquatic habitats are coming under growing pressure from mining, deforestation, poorly managed waste, and rapidly expanding tourism.
Cataloging the insects was only part of the work. Once the researchers had begun filling gaps in the scientific record, they held workshops to share their findings with local communities. There they encountered another gap: the language of biology meant little to people whose understanding of the landscape had been formed outside scientific taxonomies. Some participants didn’t speak Spanish at all.
Community leaders invited everyone, from young children to elders who retained ancestral knowledge. As researchers displayed the dragonflies found around puddles, streams, and rivers, participants tried to identify them in their own languages.
“This is something that sometimes leaves us speechless,” Delio Suárez, a Tucano Indigenous leader of the multiethnic community La Ceiba, told Mongabay. “This leaves us with the task of recovering their names, of looking back and asking the last remaining wisdom keepers that we have.”
Sometimes the words could be recovered. Sometimes they had to be invented. In the community of Remanso, members of the Puinave tribe created names in an ancestral language that is itself at risk of disappearing. Tucano and Curripaco communities have also begun naming the insects while working to recover their languages.
Communities are now developing their own means of monitoring dragonflies and, through them, the condition of the water on which they depend.
Read the full story by Manuel Fonseca here.

title: Western Arrernte man's journey of healing after problems with alcohol
content:
Western Arrernte man Tim McNamara yarns about alcohol problems, encouraging others to change
Hermannsburg/Ntaria traditional owner Tim Tjupurrula McNamara describes himself as "a leader, a cultural man and storyteller".
The proud Western Arrernte man is a mentor to boys and men in his community.
He passes on traditional knowledge and builds relationships through activities such as making spears and boomerangs, working with the Hidden Valley Camp Community Centre, the Tangentyere Men's Behaviour Change Program and other groups.
"I am the good leader of the community, good leader of my families," he said.
But Mr McNamara says he has been on a journey to become the man he is.
"Before, I was just nothing. I was just nobody," he said.
Taking ownership
About 10 years ago, Mr McNamara was ordered by a court to attend the Central Australian Aboriginal Alcohol Programs Unit (CAAAPU), a drug and alcohol support service in Alice Springs.
"I was really struggling with my life," he said.
"I got into trouble so many times, drink and drive, domestic violence, and all sorts of things that were related to alcohol."
Mr McNamara completed his mandated program and returned to his community, but says friends and family again tempted him back down the "wrong roads", so he decided to return to the rehabilitation program, this time of his own volition.
"It was my choice to change," he said.
"CAAAPU was the place we was healed from the things that we do … I learned more about what I need in my life."
Sharing the message
Since then, Mr McNamara said he had been on a journey towards accountability and ownership of his own life, describing it as "freedom".
"Freedom means that you are men in charge for everything that you needed not to take the wrong choice," he said.
"I have more freedom and more space and more sharing, stories, connection about countries, the knowledge that you use and pass it on to others, especially the little people, for my grandchildren.
"We need to continue to do these things, as a man, as an Aboriginal man."
Mr McNamara returned to CAAAPU to share his story with other men and show them change is possible.
"My journey takes me quite a while, but it's more to learn and more to teach others to be men, to understand each other, what is our responsibility," he said.
Positive examples 'a catalyst for change'
CAAAPU chief executive Demian Coates said it was "wonderful" to see Mr McNamara sharing his story.
He said while there was a lot of focus on issues such as substance abuse, domestic violence, crime and health gaps in Indigenous communities, there were "literally thousands" of examples of people overcoming and tackling these challenges.
"It's good to hear the other side, where people have been at rock bottom, and they've changed their whole life," he said.
"It's an inspiration. It's a catalyst for change."

title: “Digital House of Artsakh Culture” Presented in Yerevan
content:
“Digital House of Artsakh Culture” Presented in Yerevan
Digital House of Artsakh Culture - artsakhian.org, a digital platform created to collect, preserve, and promote the intangible cultural heritage of Artsakh, was presented in Yerevan. The platform was initiated by the We Are Our Mountains Development Agency, founded by Ruben Vardanyan, with the support of the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation.
Following the forced displacement of the Armenian population of Artsakh in September 2023, the natural continuity of cultural transmission was also disrupted. The dialect, folklore, rituals and customs, songs and music, traditional knowledge, and numerous expressions of everyday culture that had been passed down from generation to generation in their natural cultural environment now require particular attention, documentation, and preservation.
“It was important for us that Artsakh be represented in the digital world through the culture it has created. In this digital house, everything is interconnected — language, memory, people, and stories. Here, the culture of Artsakh is presented not as a closed chapter of the past, but as a living culture,” said Narine Aghabalyan, Deputy Director of the We Are Our Mountains Development Agency and Project Lead.
The structure of Digital House of Artsakh Culture is based on UNESCO’s five domains of intangible cultural heritage. It encompasses oral traditions and expressions, including folklore; performing arts; social practices, rituals and festive events; knowledge and practices concerning nature and the universe; and traditional craftsmanship. The platform also serves as a digital repository, bringing together a library, video archive, photo archive, audio archive, and dictionary.
Lernik Hovhannisyan, a member of the scholarly team involved in creating the platform, emphasized the significance of the initiative in the context of the threats currently facing the cultural heritage of Artsakh.
“Against the backdrop of recent developments, as Azerbaijan pursues a policy of cultural ethnocide aimed at erasing the Armenian presence in Artsakh, with the tacit consent of the international community, this platform enables us to present our homeland and ensure that the story of Artsakh - every page of it - remains open to all of us and is never closed,” Hovhannisyan said.
During the presentation, the team introduced the concept behind the platform, its structure, the principles guiding its content, and directions for further development. The project team also invited people from Artsakh, researchers, and families holding private archives to share photographs, videos, audio recordings, personal accounts, and other materials that can contribute to preserving the cultural memory of Artsakh.
In his professional assessment of the platform, historian and cultural studies scholar Hamlet Petrosyan emphasized the importance of scholarly accuracy and professional responsibility.
“Our success lies in presenting our culture in a detailed, precise, and impartial way. Under these difficult circumstances, a professional approach is also a moral standard. This platform is an exceptional undertaking, and I am truly impressed by what has been accomplished,” Petrosyan said.
The public presentation of the platform does not mark the completion of the work. Rather, Digital House of Artsakh Culture is entering a new stage of development. Its content and digital repositories will continue to expand through the inclusion of new scholarly and private archives, oral testimonies, and other materials. The aim is for the platform to become a continuously growing, open, and reliable source of knowledge that preserves the living cultural memory of Artsakh and passes it on to future generations.

title: Keeping Kadazandusun and Iban alive for the next generation
content:
But many are at risk of fading, with an estimated 65% of Sabah’s Dusunic community no longer speaking their mother tongue.
It might be surprising to learn that efforts to keep some of these languages alive are taking place in peninsular Malaysia. In 2010, Universiti Pendidikan Sultan Idris (UPSI) in Tanjong Malim, Perak, became the first higher education institution in the country to offer tertiary programmes in Kadazandusun and Iban.
Julita Norjietta Taisin joined UPSI that year to teach Kadazandusun, her area of expertise. At the time, Kadazandusun and Iban were offered only as minor programmes under the department of Malay language and literature.
In 2024, UPSI introduced Semai and expanded all three into majors under its Bachelor of Education programme.
Some students are also pursuing master’s and PhD degrees, helping to build a wider pool of teachers and specialists in these languages.
Iban was officially introduced in primary schools in 1968 and secondary schools in 1988, while Kadazandusun followed via pilot projects in primary schools in 1997 and secondary schools in 2006.
Yet a major challenge remains: there is a critical shortage of qualified teachers formally trained to teach these languages.
“I’ve noticed that more and more young people no longer use Kadazandusun in their daily conversations,” said Julita, who hails from Tuaran, Sabah.
“The biggest challenge is not simply that young people do not want to learn – they need to have the opportunities and reasons to use the language.”
She also highlighted the need for more learning materials, applications, and creative digital and social media content in Kadazandusun.
“As the number of native speakers dwindles, not only is the language itself threatened: expressions, folklore, proverbs, traditional knowledge and cultural values are also at risk of being lost.
“If we lose our language, we lose our identity,” she said.
Beyond the classroom, Julita said UPSI’s Sabah Native Student Association organises annual activities that give Malay, Chinese and Indian students the opportunity to learn Kadazandusun.
A similar effort is under way with Iban. Saripah Anak Banseng has been a lecturer at UPSI since 2020, specialising in the language. She initially pursued science before changing paths and eventually earning a PhD focusing on her mother tongue.
“I’m from Sri Aman, Sarawak, and I grew up in a longhouse community living the Iban way of life,” she told FMT Lifestyle.
“When I was young, we had no electricity, and we had to walk for more than an hour to school and travel by boat to reach the town.”
Saripah said all UPSI students currently taking the language programme are native speakers, but factors such as mixed marriages and living away from Sarawak mean Iban is not always part of their everyday lives.
Around 35 students are enrolled in UPSI’s Iban major programme, while an estimated 100 took the minor programme between 2024 and 2026. There are also 11 master’s and three PhD students.
“A language cannot simply be documented in a museum,” she said. “Even in my classes, I remind students that language does not exist only on paper – we need to use it outside the classroom.
“Perhaps one day, Iban may even become a medium of instruction in peninsular Malaysia.”
Although she grew up speaking Iban, Saripah said further study opened her eyes to the language’s intricacies, structure and uniqueness – aspects she had previously understood only instinctively.
“At first we may see language simply as a tool to communicate, but when we study it deeply, we understand the world better,” she added.
Speaking a week before Malaysia Day, Julita reflected on what the occasion means to her as a Sabahan living in peninsular Malaysia.
“Malaysia Day reminds me of Sabah’s role and position in the formation of Malaysia. I will continue to be proud to carry my Sabah identity and culture with me wherever I go,” she said.
For Saripah, Malaysia Day carries an equally important reminder: that Malaysia’s diversity must be understood and appreciated beyond a single day of celebration.
“We always talk about harmony, but harmony doesn’t only happen when we get together to celebrate one day. It is also about understanding one another’s way of life, language, history and culture.”

title: Niaguis au cœur de l’agroécologie : les femmes rurales portent la souveraineté alimentaire africaine
content:
Niaguis au cœur de l’agroécologie : les femmes rurales portent la souveraineté alimentaire africaine
À Niaguis, en Casamance, la cinquième édition du Camp International de Formation en Agroécologie Paysanne (CIFAP) réunit depuis ce matin des leaders, techniciens et animateurs venus de dix pays d’Afrique de l’Ouest, et pour une semaine. Ce rendez-vous, organisé par le Mouvement Pan-Africain Nous sommes la solution, s’est imposé comme un espace unique de transmission de savoirs, de renforcement de capacités et de mobilisation autour d’un enjeu vital : la souveraineté alimentaire africaine.
Mariama Sonko, présidente du mouvement, a rappelé que l’agroécologie est une pratique globale et interconnectée. Après avoir travaillé sur la revitalisation des terres, les biofertilisants, les semences horticoles et les bioprotecteurs, le CIFAP consacre cette cinquième édition à l’élevage. « L’élevage est une activité ancestrale qu’il faut transmettre aux nouvelles générations. Il garantit une alimentation saine, nutritive et économiquement rentable », a-t-elle déclaré, insistant sur le rôle central des femmes dans l’élevage de la volaille.
Face à la cherté de la viande et aux risques sanitaires liés aux poulets importés, elle a plaidé pour un retour aux espèces locales, plus saines et adaptées aux réalités des communautés.
Tabara Ndiaye, coordinatrice des fonds régionaux pour l’agroécologie en Afrique, a salué l’importance du CIFAP comme espace de construction de mouvements. Elle a rappelé que le Fonds pour l’agroécologie agit comme un pont entre bailleurs et organisations de base, facilitant l’accès aux financements et soutenant les communautés dans leur souveraineté alimentaire. « Produire ici pour consommer ici : voilà la clé de systèmes alimentaires durables », a-t-elle affirmé, en insistant sur l’appropriation par les femmes et les jeunes.
Le moment fort de la cérémonie a été l’intervention d’Idy Gomel Ba, adjoint au sous-préfet de Niaguis, qui a livré un discours vibrant. « En vous regardant, je vois le visage d’une Afrique debout, qui nourrit, qui refuse la dépendance et qui choisit la souveraineté », a-t-il lancé. Pour lui, l’élevage paysan est « de l’or entre vos mains », garant de la santé des enfants et moteur de l’autonomie financière des femmes. Il a exhorté les participants à devenir des « ambassadrices de l’Afrique souveraine et prospère », en repartant dans leurs pays respectifs avec les savoirs acquis.
Au terme de cette cinquième édition du CIFAP, une certitude s’impose : l’agroécologie paysanne n’est pas une simple alternative, mais une solution pour l’avenir. En valorisant les savoirs traditionnels, en renforçant les capacités locales et en plaçant les femmes au centre, Niaguis s’est imposé comme un symbole de la transition agroécologique africaine. Ici, au cœur de la Casamance, se dessine une Afrique qui choisit de nourrir ses enfants avec dignité, santé et souveraineté.Ce texte met en avant Niaguis comme lieu symbolique, le Camp International de Formation en Agroécologie Paysanne (CIFAP) comme cadre structurant, et l’intervention du sous-préfet de Niaguis comme voix institutionnelle qui légitime la démarche.

title: A Father’s Unfinished Dream Is Now Giving Hundreds of Seniors the Courage to Travel
content: “I couldn’t fulfil my father’s dream for him. But I could build something that would help hundreds of others fulfil theirs,” says Saakshi. For Saakshi Maheshwari (38), that thought became the beginning of something she had never planned to build. A travel writer and content creator for more than a decade, she had spent years helping others find places. But after losing her father in 2023, travel began to mean something different. It became a way of giving senior citizens the freedom to experience the journeys they had spent years postponing. Today, she runs ‘The Original Travel Company’ with her husband, Rajat Arora, taking small groups of seniors across India and overseas. Since launching the senior travel initiative in June 2023, she says she has travelled with approximately 350 senior citizens across more than 40 domestic and international journeys. But the story began with a man who believed retirement should not mean giving up on life. The man behind the idea Her father, Dr S K Maheshwari, was an army doctor who served for five years, including a posting in Tawang. Today, Saakshi runs ‘The Original Travel Company’ with her husband, Rajat Arora, taking small groups of seniors across India and overseas. He later worked with organisations including WHO and UNICEF on India’s polio eradication programme and with the Uttar Pradesh government on leprosy eradication and grassroots healthcare. Even during the COVID-19 pandemic, when most people were afraid to step outside, he travelled to villages around Agra to help people who had contracted the virus. “He was a doctor by profession, but service was at the core of everything he did. He believed that medicine was a way of serving people, and that compassion was as important as treatment,” she tells The Better India. He also had a particular concern for senior citizens. He wanted to spend more time visiting old age homes and using his medical experience to help elderly people. But work and family responsibilities kept pushing that dream into the future. He was also an enthusiastic traveller. He loved long drives, wanted to explore Kerala, and hoped to return to Tawang. He often spoke about travelling through the Northeast. Then, in January 2023, he was diagnosed with stage IV liver cancer. Two months later, at just 64, he died. One last holiday Just months before the diagnosis, Saakshi had travelled with her father to Kerala in October 2022. She remembers him dancing beside the sea, laughing whenever the waves touched his feet. “I didn’t know then that it would be one of our last trips together,” she says. His death made her question something many families take for granted. Time. “Like many families, we had assumed there would always be ‘later’,” she says. “Later to travel, later to slow down, later to fulfil dreams. His diagnosis, and then his death, taught me that later is never guaranteed.” She had already spent much of her adult life around travel. Born and raised in Meerut, she completed her BTech in Greater Noida between 2004 and 2008. She then worked with Accenture from 2008 to 2011 before pursuing an MBA in Mumbai from 2011 to 2013. She returned to the corporate world, working with companies and startups until late 2015. But travel had always been an itch she could not ignore. Around 2015, she began travel writing and content creation while still working. She later left the corporate world and spent more than 10 years travelling, writing for publications including AirAsia’s in-flight magazine and working with tourism boards such as Assam Tourism, Madhya Pradesh Tourism and Malaysia Tourism. “Travel taught me empathy, openness, and perspective. It was never just about seeing the world, but about understanding people, cultures and, ultimately, understanding myself,” she says. After her father died, she knew where she wanted to take that experience. In June 2023, she launched her senior travel initiative. In January 2026, she gave the venture a name of its own, The Original Travel Company. What was missing Before starting, she noticed that senior citizens were occasionally the focus of mainstream travel planning. The itineraries were mostly designed around speed. Wake up early, board the bus, visit several attractions, climb stairs, move to the next destination, and return late. That might work for younger travellers. For many seniors, it can turn a holiday into an exhausting exercise. “Most of them had not stopped dreaming about travel,” she says. “What had changed was their confidence, and the support available to them.” Companionship was another major barrier. Some had lost their spouses, while their children lived in other cities or countries, and friends who once travelled with them had stopped doing so, leaving many hesitant to join large groups of strangers. The founder felt the problem was not where seniors travelled, but how they were expected to travel. The founder felt the problem was not where seniors travelled, but how they were expected to travel. “What they needed was a slower, more thoughtful experience, one that put their comfort, confidence and wellbeing before ticking places off a list,” she says. That philosophy now decides every trip. It starts with a recce The couple does not take senior travellers to a destination until they have personally studied and experienced the route themselves. First, they research the destination. Then they travel there themselves, checking routes, hotels, attractions, and transport. They ask themselves one question. “If I were travelling with my own parents, what would I want them to experience?” They check hotels for accessibility, comfort, and location, and even ask hotel staff to show them the rooms and facilities over video calls when needed. In Japan, for instance, repeated visits taught them that hotel size matters because rooms can be considerably smaller than those in other countries. They also consider the number of stairs at sightseeing spots, the distance between attractions, the availability of lifts and the location of healthcare facilities. A first aid kit accompanies the group everywhere, even during short stops. “Health planning can never be an afterthought,” she says. The pace is deliberately slower, with breaks built in. Meals include a combination of Indian and local cuisine, while dietary requirements are considered individually. Every itinerary goes through multiple revisions. “The objective is not to maximise sightseeing. It is to maximise relaxation and enjoyment,” she says. Nothing is left to chance The attention to detail continues once the group begins travelling. The team tracks visa requirements, flight schedules, weather conditions and health advisories, particularly for international destinations. Before a recent Sri Lanka trip, they learnt about a dengue outbreak around Colombo. Travellers were informed and asked to carry full-sleeved clothing, while the co-founders carried anti-mosquito sprays. Even hotel check-ins are planned in advance. “We like to call the hotel two hours before we are about to reach there with the group to make sure that the rooms are ready, the ACs are turned on, the welcome drinks are ready,” she says. The goal is that seniors should never have to arrive after a long journey and wait at reception. Their groups are also capped at 12 to 14 people. Saakshi and Rajat personally accompany every group, meaning they know the travellers, their needs and their concerns. “We want to return as a family,” she says. The holiday is only part of it For many travellers, the friendships become just as important as the destination. They celebrate birthdays, remember anniversaries, and frequently see travellers who arrive alone leave with new friends and a WhatsApp group they are reluctant to close. Leena Menon, a retired children’s librarian who spent more than 20 years working with Auckland Libraries in New Zealand, travelled to Bhutan with the company. She was looking for something different from a conventional package tour. “The focus was not just on covering destinations but on creating memorable experiences,” she says. During the trip, the team surprised Leena and her husband with an anniversary celebration. “It made us feel that we were travelling with friends rather than a tour company,” she says. For 76-year-old Ahmedabad resident Mrs Pervin Phiroze Guard, the biggest concern was safety. After losing her partner, she was living alone and worried about travelling without a companion. Her daughter found the company on Instagram in April or May 2024. She was initially sceptical. The team answered her questions and even shared contact details of previous travellers so she could speak to them. Her first trip was a mother-daughter holiday to Goa in June 2024. “What touched me the most was Saakshi’s genuine care; she constantly checked on everyone’s comfort and made sure every senior traveller felt included, valued and cared for,” Pervin says. The experience changed her outlook. “The trip reminded me that age is just a number,” she says. The couple does not take senior travellers to a destination until they have personally studied and experienced the route themselves. Then there is 68-year-old Ranjana Dixit from Satna, who retired from Madhya Pradesh Electricity Board in 2020. Work, family responsibilities and health problems, including a knee replacement, had kept her from travelling as much as she wanted. She first heard about the initiative through her daughter in May 2024. Since then, she has travelled to Kashmir, Bhutan and Rajasthan with the company and celebrated her birthday on trips in 2024 and 2025. “Fulfilling my dreams has raised my confidence and made me want to travel even more,” she says. Even after undergoing another knee replacement in April 2026, she already has two trips lined up for October and November. She wants other seniors to remember one thing, “If your trip is led by Saakshi or Rajat, then you can keep your worries at home and enjoy the trip to the fullest.” 350 stories and counting So far, the founder says approximately 350 senior citizens have travelled with her across more than 40 domestic and international trips. Their destinations have included Japan, South Korea, Turkey, Bali, Bhutan, Vietnam, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Dubai and Abu Dhabi, as well as Kashmir, Ladakh, Meghalaya, Rajasthan, the Andamans, Sikkim, Varanasi, Ayodhya, Madhya Pradesh, Assam and the Rann of Kutch. Around 40 percent of travellers return for another journey. But the number that matters most is not 350. It is the person boarding an international flight alone for the first time at 68. It is the widow taking her first holiday after losing her husband. It is someone seeing the ocean for the first time at 70. And it is the children who call afterwards to say they have seen their parents happier than they have been in years. “We are a source to give them the confidence to step out, experience new places, and bring more joy and happiness into their lives,” the founder says. A legacy in motion The company remains intentionally small, with four core members. The couple works alongside a social media executive and an operations executive, supported by trusted local partners. Rajat left his corporate career of more than 15 years to join the venture full-time. There is no strict division of responsibilities between the couple. “From social media to marketing, from operations, from booking flight tickets to doing every little thing that needs to be done for a business, both of us are all hands on deck,” Saakshi says. For her, the company has become more than work. “I have to say that I wouldn’t have survived these three years if not for the senior travel company that I have built,” she says. “That kept me going.” The work has changed how she thinks about ageing too. “I have met people in their seventies who are more adventurous, more inquisitive, and more open to new experiences than people half their age,” she says. Her biggest lesson has been not to postpone life. “I have always believed in putting relationships before business, because when you invest in genuine relationships, the business naturally follows,” she says. The Original Travel Company’s next plans include destinations across Central Asia, Europe and Africa. But she wants growth without losing the personal care that brought the company this far. They check hotels for accessibility, comfort, and location, and even ask hotel staff to show them the rooms and facilities over video calls when needed. Her goal is not to become the biggest senior travel company. She wants to become the most trusted. She hopes families will stop seeing travel as a luxury for their ageing parents and begin seeing it as an investment in their happiness and wellbeing. And if her father could see what his daughter has built, she believes he would not care about the number of destinations or travellers. “He’d simply look at the seniors laughing together, and say, ‘This is exactly what I hoped for,’” she says. Her father spent his life helping people live healthier lives. Saakshi hopes she is helping them live happier ones. All pictures courtesy Saakshi Maheshwari.

title: How Assam’s Artisans Turn One Bamboo Plant Into Hundreds of Things We Use Every Day
content: 1 Plant, 100 Uses explores the many ways familiar Indian plants, leaves, fruits and trees have been part of everyday life — from food and farming to homes, traditions and natural remedies. Each story takes one plant and uncovers the surprising ways people have found it useful, often across generations. A bamboo plant can look rather ordinary. It may grow gently beside a home, along a field or across the hills of Assam, commonly becoming so familiar that people stop noticing it. But look a little closer, and the same plant can become a chair, a house, a basket, a musical instrument, paper, food, flooring or even a source of livelihood. India is home to 136 bamboo species, of which 125 are indigenous. According to the Government of India, the country has 13.96 million hectares under bamboo and is the second richest country in the world in terms of bamboo diversity. That versatility is perhaps best understood through people who have spent years working with it. In Jorhat, Assam, bamboo is not essentially a raw material for Prabhat Saikia. It has become the foundation of a business, a craft and a source of work for young artisans. From a bamboo pole to a piece of furniture When Saikia started a small bamboo and cane handicraft unit in 2006, he wanted to show that the plant growing abundantly around him could become more than an everyday utility. A bamboo plant can look rather ordinary. Photograph: (Organicbazar) His workshop now turns bamboo into furniture and decorative pieces, with around 20 young artisans working there. Some of them found a way to earn a living without leaving their villages for cities. He also learnt that bamboo’s strength depends on how it is treated. Working with the Rainforest Research Institute in Jorhat, he trained in bamboo treatment techniques and worked on making his products more durable. That made it possible for his bamboo to move beyond traditional handicrafts into furniture, cottages, and architectural spaces. The Government’s National Bamboo Mission lists construction, furniture, flooring, doors, windows, frames, trusses, and other building components among bamboo’s uses. The Indian Institute of Wood Science and Technology also notes that bamboo can be harvested in a two to four year cycle and has been used in board and panel forms for more than 1,000 documented applications. A home can begin with bamboo In many parts of India, particularly the Northeast, bamboo has long been part of the way homes are built. It can be used for walls, roofs, flooring, doors, windows, and structural components. Modern processing has also opened the door to laminated panels and engineered bamboo products. The Government of India’s National Bamboo Mission lists species used for construction, furniture, basketry, food containers, musical instruments, and other applications. This matters because bamboo is renewable and fast-growing. But using it responsibly still requires proper harvesting, treatment, and processing. Saikia’s experience is a useful reminder that only having bamboo is not enough. Skills and technology determine how much value can come from it. It can reach the dining table too Bamboo is not only something to build with. Certain species produce edible shoots, which are eaten in several parts of India and across Asia. The National Bamboo Mission lists edible shoots among the uses of species such as Melocanna baccifera, Dendrocalamus asper, and Dendrocalamus giganteus. The plant can also be made into food containers, kitchen products, and other household items. So, from the field to the kitchen, bamboo can have a place in everyday life. From craft to paper and fabric The usefulness of bamboo does not end when it leaves a craftsperson’s workshop. It is used as a raw material for pulp and paper. It can also be processed into fibres and used in textile products. The same plant can become a chair, a house, a basket, a musical instrument, paper, food, flooring or even a source of livelihood. Photograph: (Joynagar) The Telangana government’s bamboo mission lists pulp and paper, textiles, furniture, construction products and even energy production among bamboo’s applications. Its traditional uses are equally varied. Bamboo can become baskets, mats, lamps, storage products, and musical instruments. Different Indian species have their own uses, depending on their strength, size, and properties. In Assam, Saikia has taken some of these familiar forms and given them a place in contemporary homes. His furniture has reached markets beyond the state, while his skills have taken him to international workshops in Nepal. And then there is the land itself Perhaps one of bamboo’s most important uses is one we cannot always see. Its dense root system can help hold soil together and reduce erosion. Research and government-backed work in India has also explored bamboo for restoring degraded land. The Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser notes that a bamboo-based conservation system can reduce soil loss from 22 tonnes per hectare per year to 4.5 tonnes, while conserving 45 percent soil moisture. The same work records bamboo biomass production of 12 to 30 tonnes per hectare per year. Government material on bamboo also highlights its potential for carbon sequestration because of its rapid biomass accumulation. The humble plant also plays a role in protecting the ground on which people farm and live. One plant, many livelihoods The most meaningful use of bamboo is not an object at all. It is the work created around it. In Saikia’s Jorhat workshop, it passes through many hands before it becomes a finished chair or decorative piece. Artisans cut it, shape it, weave it, and polish it. Distributors take the finished products to new markets. Buyers take a piece of Assam into their homes. His story shows what happens when a resource that people have grown up taking for granted is given skill, treatment, design, and a market. The Government of India’s National Bamboo Mission has established hundreds of nurseries, treatment units, and product development and processing units as part of efforts to strengthen the bamboo economy. As of December 2024, the mission reported 528 product development and processing units and 104 treatment and preservation units. So perhaps the phrase “100 uses” is not really about counting every possible thing bamboo can become. It is about seeing the possibilities in something that has always been there. For someone like Saikia, that possibility began with a humble bamboo pole in Assam. Today, it can become a chair in Delhi, a building component, a basket, a meal, a sheet of paper or a livelihood that allows an artisan to remain close to home. In many parts of India, particularly the Northeast, bamboo has long been part of the way homes are built. Photograph: (www.vasoobambooarts.in) And sometimes, a plant becomes most valuable when we learn to look at it differently. Want to know how Prabhat Saikia turned Assam’s abundant bamboo into a healthy livelihood? Read his full story here.

title: Discovering the ‘others’ who make Malaysia what it is
content:
It happened at a combined celebration of the Kaamatan and Gawai festivities of Sabah and Sarawak that she first began to realise just how much of Malaysia’s cultural tapestry she had never known.
She met people at the celebration who introduced themselves by the names of communities she had never heard of. “I met people who said, ‘I’m Kelabit.’ Then someone else said, ‘I’m Kiput.’ I thought, what is this? I didn’t understand,” said Lim, who is better known as Faye Lim.
She admitted feeling ashamed when she realised there were so many communities and ethnic groups in Malaysia she knew nothing about. She began seeking out the people and stories behind those names, particularly communities whose identities had long been reduced to the catch-all category of “others”.
Finding Malaysia’s ‘family’
The journey grew through the Rojak Projek using art, food and culture to connect with people from different backgrounds. One of her early projects involved creating portraits of Malaysians using food such as onde-onde, laksa and nasi lemak.
Through the project, she began to realise that Malaysia’s diversity was far broader than she had ever known. She has gathered information on more than 250 ethnic and sub-ethnic groups so far.
“After meeting so many people, I can’t imagine my life without knowing them. I’ve gained so much knowledge, connections and experiences from this journey,” said the 36-year-old.
In 2025, her efforts took her deep into Sarawak after she received a Gamuda Foundation grant to trace and document the cultures of Orang Ulu communities.
Lim and her team initially set out to meet 15 communities, but eventually documented the stories of 18, including the Lun Bawang, Kedayan, Bisaya, Tabun, Berawan, Tering, Sa’ban, Kenyah, Penan and Penan Peruan.
Their stories were later shared on the social media platforms of the Rojak Projek and Canvas Art Malaysia.
“As someone from the peninsula, I realised that many of us simply don’t know them. But I also found Sarawakians who didn’t know these small communities. If I mention names such as Kiput, Sa’ban or other minority communities, many people in Sarawak might not even know who they are.
“But when we bring their stories to a wider audience and give them space to share, more people begin to learn that they exist,” she said.
Heritage under threat
For Lim, the small size of a community should never mean that its existence is overlooked, especially when its language, customs and culture face the risk of disappearing.
The migration of younger generations to cities meant older members were increasingly among the last people who still practised their communities’ customs and their heritage.
“Take the Tabun community, for example. There may be only about 20 to 30 people still recorded as Tabun. The rest are almost gone,” she said.
The effort to document these communities also took Lim and her team deep into the interior, including journeys by boat.
“Once, we were stranded after dark without phone reception. I ended up crying, but fortunately, one of us managed to get a signal and call for help,” she said.
But the experience only strengthened Lim’s determination to continue telling the stories of communities that have long gone unnoticed.
For her, getting to know these communities is about understanding the country itself. We have to make an effort to get to know our ‘family’ in Malaysia. We are what makes Malaysia what it is,” she said.

title: In Qatar, Uzbek master artist Toshev carries Bukhara’s artistic legacy forward
content:
Preservingô traditionalô artsô requiresô moreô thanô safeguardingô oldô worksô inô museums;ô endangeredô techniquesô mustô continueô toô beô practised,ô taught,ô andô adaptedô forô futureô generations,ô Uzbekô masterô artistô Davlatô Toshevô toldô Gulfô Times.
ô
ô
Toshev,ô anô artistô inô residenceô atô theô Museumô ofô Islamicô Artô (MIA),ô hasô devotedô muchô ofô hisô careerô toô preservingô theô artisticô heritageô ofô Bukhara,ô includingô theô revivalô ofô theô nearlyô forgottenô Abru-Bahor,ô orô ãSpringô Cloudã,ô paper-marblingô technique.
ô
ô
Itô isô aô centuries-oldô Uzbekô artô formô combiningô paperô marblingô andô miniatureô painting,ô withô deepô rootsô inô theô culturalô heritageô ofô Bukhara,ô Uzbekistan.
ô
ô
ãAbru-Bahorô isô farô moreô thanô aô techniqueô forô creatingô patternsô uponô paper,ô itô isô aô delicateô andô singularô threadô withinô Bukharaãsô culturalô heritage,ãô Toshevô said.
Heô becameô involvedô inô revivingô theô techniqueô afterô recognisingô howô closeô itô hadô comeô toô disappearingô inô itsô historicalô homeland.
ô
ô
Workingô withô researchersô fromô Bukharaô Stateô University,ô heô reconstructedô theô traditionalô recipesô andô methodsô usedô toô createô theô distinctiveô marbledô patterns.
ô
ô
ãTheô truestô wayô toô preserveô aô vanishingô traditionô isô notô toô enshrineô itô asô aô museumô piece,ô butô toô giveô itô lifeô onceô more:ô toô practiseô it,ô toô studyô it,ô andô toô passô itô onô toô youngerô generations,ãô heô said.
Forô Toshev,ô theô importanceô ofô Abru-Bahorô goesô beyondô theô survivalô ofô aô particularô artisticô technique.
ô
ô
ãInô revivingô Abru-Bahor,ô weô preserveô notô onlyô aô technique,ô butô aô fragmentô ofô ourô ancestorsãô worldviewô ãô theirô aestheticô sensibility,ô andô theô richnessô ofô theirô creativeô imagination,ãô heô said.
Hisô widerô preservationô workô includesô miniatureô painting,ô classicalô calligraphyô andô theô restorationô ofô historicô booksô andô manuscripts.
ô
ô
Moreô thanô 100ô studentsô areô currentlyô learningô theseô disciplinesô underô hisô guidanceô atô theô Ustoz-Shogirdô Centre,ô whereô Toshevô seeksô toô combineô preservingô traditionalô knowledgeô withô theô creativeô freedomô ofô youngerô artists.
ô
ô
Heô saidô oneô ofô theô biggestô challengesô isô attractingô youngô peopleô toô artisticô disciplinesô thatô demandô patience,ô concentrationô andô yearsô ofô practice.
ãWeô liveô inô anô ageô ofô speedô andô information,ô whileô miniatureô painting,ô calligraphyô andô theô manuscriptô artsô askô insteadô forô carefulô attentionô andô quietô devotion,ãô Toshevô said.
Anotherô challengeô isô ensuringô thatô masterô artistsãô accumulatedô knowledgeô isô transferredô directlyô toô theô nextô generation.
ô
ô
ãTraditionalô artsô cannotô beô learnedô fromô booksô aloneô ãô theô hand,ô theô eye,ô theô accumulatedô experienceô andô theô spiritualô approachô ofô theô masterô matterô immensely,ãô heô said.
Thisô isô whyô Toshevô seesô hisô centreãsô missionô asô extendingô beyondô technicalô instruction.
ãTheô trueô missionô ofô theô Ustoz-Shogirdô Centreô isô notô simplyô toô teachô tradition,ô butô toô keepô itô alive,ãô heô said.
ô
ô
Theô artistô believesô thatô theô survivalô ofô Bukharaãsô artisticô heritageô ultimatelyô dependsô onô youngô artistsô makingô theô traditionsô theirô ownô andô introducingô themô toô newô audiences.
ô
ô
ãIfô youngô artistsô continueô toô carryô forwardô theô traditionsô ofô Bukharaô miniatureô painting,ô calligraphy,ô theô manuscriptô artsô andô Abru-Bahor,ô andô introduceô theô cultureô ofô Uzbekistanô toô theô worldô throughô theirô ownô creativity,ô Iô wouldô considerô thatô myô greatestô achievementô ofô all,ãô heô said.
ô
ô
Toshev,ô whoseô workô hasô beenô exhibitedô inô culturalô centresô acrossô Europe,ô theô USô andô elsewhere,ô saidô hisô greatestô legacyô wouldô notô beô theô artworksô heô leavesô behind,ô butô theô knowledgeô andô loveô ofô artô heô passesô onô toô thoseô whoô follow.
ô
ô
Heô alsoô hopesô Bukharaãsô artisticô traditionsô willô increasinglyô beô recognisedô beyondô theirô nationalô context.
ô
ô
ãIô hopeô thatô theô artô ofô Bukharaô willô continueô toô beô recognisedô andô cherishedô ãô notô onlyô asô partô ofô Uzbekistanãsô heritage,ô butô asô partô ofô theô sharedô culturalô heritageô ofô allô humanity,ãô heô said.
Forô Toshev,ô thatô legacyô ultimatelyô comesô downô toô helpingô youngerô generationsô remainô connectedô toô theirô roots.
ô
ô
ãWeô mustô neverô forgetô ourô roots,ãô heô said.ô ãOnlyô thoseô whoô understandô theirô historyô andô cultureô deeplyô areô trulyô capableô ofô shapingô theô future.ã
