title: Turtle Mountain chairman encourages civic, youth engagement
content:
This story was originally published by North Dakota Monitor.
Jack Dura
North Dakota Monitor
Tribal leaders should support their community’s youth to spur growth and break away from old politics that hinder opportunities, the leader of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians told college students, instructors and other tribal officials Thursday, Sept. 10.
Tribal Chairman Jamie Azure said he wanted to break away from that “standard approach” soon after his entry into tribal government as a council member in 2016. He outlined how his tribe worked to engage youth and drive toward goals for the Turtle Mountain community after trainings on strategic planning for Native nations showed why opportunities were lacking.
“We learned that if we are going to move forward as a nation, we needed to start planning on moving forward by using correct data, by using higher education, by showing people that our sovereign nations weren’t just little specks on a map,” Azure told an audience at the 29th Tribal Leaders Summit in Bismarck.
In 2018, Turtle Mountain leaders and the Native Governance Center organized a youth summit with roundtables to ask young people what challenges, opportunities or lack thereof they saw in the community, Azure said.
The tribe began a 10-year strategic plan based on that feedback, “and that’s still going through to today,” the chairman said.
The tribe built a water park for a safe, fun place for families and job opportunities for young people, and a recovery center to help people move forward from addiction, Azure said.
The tribe raised its minimum wage to $15 an hour and made youth employees eligible for a 401(k) retirement account and insurance after six months, he said.
“That to me is sustainable security for our people for the next 40, 50 years,” the chairman said.
Additionally, the tribe’s natural resources group and 25 to 50 youth workers cleaned up and transformed the beaches of Gordon Lake into Sky Chief Park. The youth asked the tribal council to prohibit alcohol at the lake, which passed, Azure said. And those teenagers began to enforce the rules, he said. Parking and camping areas got cleaner, he said.
“You can sit back and you can watch our young ones really just take a grasp and say, ‘This is who we are.’ That’s true sovereignty. That’s people coming together and saying, ‘We have the power,’” Azure said.
Tribes can take the example of the youth at Turtle Mountain and other tribes and “say we need to come together unitedly” and move forward on issues together, he said. He noted Turtle Mountain and Spirit Lake brought a voting rights lawsuit regarding North Dakota’s legislative redistricting that is ongoing.
“We continue to fight and we continue to move forward,” Azure said.
He said he’s become more connected with other tribal leaders across North Dakota the last two years, especially over developments at the federal level, such as tribal college funding cuts.
“Sovereignty does not mean that we work alone,” the chairman said.

title: Dr Te Ripowai Higgins: An unrelenting champion of te ao Māori
content:
"Mō tēnei hōnore i homaihia nei, kei au te waimarie, nā te mea i a au e tipu mai ana e patua ana i te kura mō te kōrero i tō tātou reo. Ka mutu, koirā anake te reo i mōhio mātou."
Recognition like this is poignant, especially considering I was among the generations beaten at school for speaking our language, it's the only language we knew.
- Dr Te Ripowai Higgins, QSM, ONZM
Beaten for speaking te reo Māori at school, Dr Te Ripowai Higgins (Ngāi Tūhoe) dedicated her career to keeping her language and culture alive.
Her relentless dedication to a language she was punished for speaking has been recognised by the Governor-General at an investiture ceremony this week, where she received the Officer of the New Zealand Order of Merit (ONZM) for more than 43 years of service to education and Māori.
Dr Higgins reflected on the acknowledgement and shared her thoughts with Pūkāea.
"Mō tēnei hōnore i homaihia nei, kei au te waimarie, nā te mea i a au e tipu mai ana e patua ana i te kura mō te kōrero i tō tātou reo. Ka mutu, koirā anake te reo i mōhio mātou."
I find this type of recognition quite poignant, especially considering I was among the generations beaten at school for speaking our native tongue.
The assimilationist education system of the time prioritised English and contributed to the suppression and decline of te reo Māori.
But the punishment had the opposite effect on Dr Higgins.
She says kaumātua and kuia taught her generation to withstand those pressures and turn adversity into opportunity.
"Nā rātou i tohu, 'kia kaha koutou, ahakoa patua koutou, me ako koutou i taua reo. Kei te pai tō koutou reo Māori. Kua nui ake ngā Pākehā e haere mai ana, me ako koutou i tā rātou ake reo, kia mōhio ake tātou kei te aha ngā kōrero'."
They told us not to let the beatings break us; they helped us recognise that learning their language didn't mean we had to abandon our own. They said Pākehā would not stop coming, they told us we had to adapt and master their language so we would always know what they were saying."
The ability to navigate two worlds became a defining feature of Dr Higgins' career.
She went on to help establish initiatives that created pathways for te reo Māori in education, broadcasting and public life.
In 1982, she became a foundation board member of Te Ataarangi, the Māori language revitalisation movement.
She remained involved for 42 years, helping generations learn te reo Māori while sharing the approach with Indigenous communities overseas.
Her influence extended into Māori broadcasting.
She served three terms on the board of Te Māngai Pāho and was instrumental in establishing Te Upoko o te Ika, recognised as Aotearoa's first Māori radio station.
Those initiatives established foundations for the ongoing development of more education and media initiatives dedicated to fostering te reo Māori.
Dr Higgins says her aspiration is to ensure generations to come maintain pride in their identity.
"Karekau e tino aro atu ana ki ngā tohu pēnei. Ko te āhua kei te tino hiahia kia kitea, ko te whakakaha ake i te nui o ngā tāngata e kōrero Māori ana, heoi i tū atu I te reo, kia whakatauira ai rātou i te mana me te mōhio o ngā kuia, kaumātua."
Things like this have never interested me. The work I have done over the years is focussed on supporting the establishment of initiatives that encourage Māori to embrace their language, beyond that. I want future generations to take pride in their identity and represent their culture with integrity, I hope they, like me aspire to make their kaumātua and kuia proud."
Dr Higgins' daughter, Dr Rawinia Higgins is demonstrating the impact of her mother's work through her own role as Māori Language Commissioner, helping lead the revitalisation of te reo Māori.
Speaking to Radio New Zealand about the importance of Te wiki o Te Reo Māori, Higgins said the growing number of people learning the language is encouraging, and the commission's rangahau (research) continues to show that many New Zealanders see te reo Māori as a valuable part of the country's identity.
"This is a three generation kaupapa," she said.
"Every little step that each generation takes is really important."

title: Erinnerung an Holocaust-Opfer: Wie ein Münchner zufällig herausfand, dass seine Großmutter von Nazis getötet wurde
content:
Als Toni Heilmaier vor 23 Jahren in der Stadtbibliothek Hadern ein Foto entdeckt, durchzuckt ihn ein Gedanke: „Das ist ja meine Oma!“ Das Bild seiner Großmutter Anna Paroubek ist dort Teil einer Ausstellung, die in der nahen Mittelschule an der Guardinistraße entstanden ist, im Rahmen eines Projekts über die Lebensgeschichten von vergessenen Jüdinnen und Juden aus dem Münchner Stadtbezirk.
Toni Heilmaier ist mittlerweile 92 Jahre alt, aber erinnert sich noch daran, wie die Gestapo seine Großmutter im Sommer 1942 abholte und ins Ghetto Theresienstadt deportierte. Er war acht Jahre alt, als er sie das letzte Mal sah. Über ihr Schicksal wurde in der Familie danach kaum gesprochen. Die Oma sei ins Altenheim gekommen, habe ihm seine Mutter damals erzählt, sagt Heilmaier. Umso mehr wühlte es ihn auf, als er viele Jahrzehnte später in der Ausstellung plötzlich auf die Kennkarte seiner Großmutter stieß. Auf diesem Vorläufer des Personalausweises prangte ein großes rotes J – der sogenannte Judenstempel.
Anna Paroubek starb im September 1943 an den unmenschlichen Lebensbedingungen in Theresienstadt. 83 Jahre später ist nun ein Erinnerungszeichen an ihrem ehemaligen Wohnort in der Großhaderner Straße 18 angebracht worden – im Beisein ihres Enkels Toni Heilmaier, ohne dessen Entdeckung in der Bücherei es heute keinen Gedenkort für seine Großmutter gäbe. Denn im Nachgang seines Ausstellungsbesuchs nahm er Kontakt zu Ursula Saabel auf, die das Schulprojekt organisiert hatte. Und die Lehrerin versprach ihm, dem Schicksal von Anna Paroubek genauer nachzugehen.
Das tat Ursula Saabel nach ihrem Eintritt in den Ruhestand von 2010 an, zusammen mit Barbara von Broekhoven: Gemeinsam recherchierten die beiden Frauen in Archiven, fuhren nach Theresienstadt und brachten so die traurige Lebensgeschichte von Anna Paroubek zutage. 1870 in Čelechovice im heutigen Tschechien geboren, zog sie noch vor der Jahrhundertwende nach München, wo sie im Jahr 1900 den katholischen Herrenschneider Anton Paroubek heiratete. Er führte ein gut gehendes Geschäft, in dem auch seine Frau arbeitete. Sie gehörte zwar dem jüdischen Glauben an, praktizierte jedoch nicht. Ihre 1904 geborene Tochter Emilie Paroubek erzogen die Eltern katholisch.
Das war ein bewegender Moment für uns und ein Stück gelebte Familiengeschichte.Toni Heilmaiers Sohn Christian
Nach der „Machtergreifung“ der Nazis wurde die Witwe – im Jahr 1932 war ihr Ehemann verstorben – zunehmend drangsaliert und ausgegrenzt. Als sie von September 1941 an in der Öffentlichkeit den Judenstern tragen musste, verließ sie ihre Wohnung nicht mehr. Sogar die eigene Tochter, die nur einen Steinwurf entfernt lebte, konnte sie nicht mehr besuchen. „Weil unser Hausherr damals gesagt hat: In mein Haus gehören keine Juden“, erinnert sich Toni Heilmaier.
Er sah als Achtjähriger, wie die Gestapo seine Großmutter am 23. Juli 1942 abholte. „Ich war damals ein kleiner Bub und habe vom KZ nichts gewusst“, erzählt Heilmaier. „Deshalb hat meine Mutter zu mir gesagt: Die Oma ist ins Altenheim gekommen.“ Tatsächlich aber wurde Anna Paroubek zusammen mit 49 weiteren Menschen ins Ghetto Theresienstadt deportiert. Dort litt sie unter Unterernährung und Isolation, ehe sie im September 1943 im Alter von 73 Jahren verstarb. Ihre Asche wurde an unbekannter Stelle verstreut, ein Grab gibt es nicht.
Nach ihrem Tod geriet Anna Paroubeks Geschichte in Vergessenheit – bis im Jahr 2003 die Schulklasse von Ursula Saabel auf die Jüdin aus Hadern stieß. Auf Initiative der Lehrerin sammelten der Geschichtsverein Hadern und die Familie von Anna Paroubek Spenden für eine Gedenktafel, die vor wenigen Wochen im Kolumbarium der Gedenkstätte Theresienstadt enthüllt wurde, unter den Augen von Toni Heilmaier, seinem Sohn Christian Heilmaier und dessen 17-jähriger Tochter Emilia Heilmaier. „Da waren drei Generationen zusammen“, erzählt Christian Heilmaier. „Das war ein bewegender Moment für uns und ein Stück gelebte Familiengeschichte.“
Um Anna Paroubek auch an ihrem früheren Wohnort zu gedenken, beantragte der Geschichtsverein Hadern ein Erinnerungszeichen, das nun an ihrer letzten Adresse an einer Stele angebracht wurde.
In ganz München gebe es mittlerweile circa 350 solcher Denkmäler für die Opfer des Nationalsozialismus, sagte Stadträtin Nimet Gökmenoğlu (Grüne) bei der Gedenkveranstaltung im Kulturzentrum Guardini90. Dadurch werde das Erinnerungsnetz zunehmend feinmaschiger, „und wir bewahren immer mehr Namen und Lebensgeschichten vor dem Vergessen“.
Zu diesen zählt jetzt auch das Schicksal von Anna Paroubek – dank ihres Enkels, dank des Engagements von Ursula Saabel und dank des Zufalls, der Toni Heilmaier im Jahr 2003 in die Ausstellung in der Stadtbibliothek führte.

title: Hebron’s Jewish community finishes restoring tomb belonging to ancestors of biblical King David
content:
Hebron’s Jewish community completed a four year restoration of the Tomb of Yishai and Ruth atop Tel Hebron in the West Bank on Tuesday.
The work was spearheaded by the community’s international spokesperson, Yishai Fleisher, a member of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party.
He also serves as a member of the Efrat Local Council, and is a widely recognized English-speaking voice for Israel abroad, with his YouTube channel having more than 300,000 subscribers.
The tomb is believed by Jewish sources to be the burial place of the biblical King David’s father, Yishai, and his great-grandmother, Ruth the Moabite.
“The location of the site in Hebron, city of the Patriarchs and Matriarchs, the first acquisition of the Jews in the Land of Israel, made by our forefather Abraham, carries important spiritual significance,” explained Fleisher. “There is a connection between the Tomb of Yishai and Ruth and the Cave of the [Patriarchs].”
“The sources state that there are four 'wheels' in the Chariot of the G-d: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and David. Why specifically David? Because David is the one who fulfills the dream of the Patriarchs and Matriarchs, the dream of a united and strong people in their land, living in holiness."
Bringing Safed to Hebron
Fleisher, working closely with a team of historians and artisans, drew up a design drawing on the turquoise color usually associated with Safed, departing from the site's traditional browns and greens.
"We wanted to bring the sanctity of Safed's turquoise into the heart of Hebron," Fleisher said.
The graves of Yishai and Ruth themselves were redesigned using stone, calligraphic inscriptions, a Star of David, and a wheat motif to represent Ruth's biblical story.
Renovations for the tomb, as well as the establishment of a new synagogue and study hall at the site, were completed using mainly local Hebron stone, wrought iron, and wood.
The project cost roughly one million dollars fundraised by Fleisher from donars around the world.
Connecting site to younger generations
Additionally, a chamber dating back to the Byzantine and medieval periods was restored and converted into a a working studio, where a scribe writes on parchment using traditional methods, in view of visitors.
The completed site also includes shaded seating areas, water fountains, restrooms, a small event hall, a courtyard, parking, and direct access to the Tel Hebron archaeological park.
"If young people saw the place as it used to be, they wouldn't connect to it, and they wouldn't feel that this is a place of holiness,” Fleisher stated. “My view is that these places we love, places that are our heritage, need to be beautiful, need to expand the heart, to believe that this is truly something great.”
“I'm looking forward to applying my experience in beautifying Hebron to beautifying the whole Land of Israel through the Knesset.”
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

title: First Nations netballers driving change, bringing cultural safety
content:
Netball's First Nations Tournament part of creating culturally safe spaces
While netball may be Australian girls' and women's top participation team sport, it has long fallen short of producing — or at least nurturing — elite Indigenous talent.
Just three Indigenous Australian women have represented the Diamonds: Marcia Ella-Duncan, Sharon Finnan-White and, after a 22-year gap, Donnell Wallam.
In 2024, Wallam left Australia for New Zealand, taking a swipe at her former club, the Firebirds, on the way out.
At the time, she wrote that the New Zealand clubs' "respect for inclusion and culture" was a key factor in her decision to leave, while she eventually returned to the Sunshine Coast Lightning this year.
Netball Australia was not idly watching.
As accusations of a 'toxic culture' at the Firebirds were aired, the governing body launched an investigation and kickstarted a series of measures to enshrine 'cultural safety' for First Nations athletes in the sport.
This included the introduction of Australia's inaugural First Nations team, the Black Swans, following the appointment of Ali Tucker-Munro, Netball Australia's General Manager First Nations and former Diamonds squad member.
Tucker-Munro was also influential in establishing the First Nations Tournament, a yearly national championship currently being held in Melbourne, and the Spirit Series, which launched in 2026 and saw the Black Swans go undefeated against Australia's Pacific neighbours.
Speaking from the State Netball and Hockey Centre, Tucker-Munro, alongside players Gabby Coffey and Scarlet Jauncey, said the measures had begun to address the lack of visible role models for First Nations netballers, with more work to be done.
Embraced in Alice Springs
Twenty-six-year-old Coffey, representing the Northern Territory, is one of several First Nations netballers who have been stuck at the cusp of national competition.
The defender spent four years as a Melbourne Vixens training partner before eventually making the decision to move to the UK to further her netball career.
She represented Birmingham over two seasons, and has since returned to Alice Springs.
Coffey had seen the writing on the wall at the Vixens.
"I knew there wasn't much movement in their defensive end, and the same with a lot of defensive ends around Australia," Coffey told ABC Sport.
While she has not given up on a professional career, she is also at peace with the idea that her role may be to support other First Nations athletes with their sporting aspirations.
The Wiradjuri woman grew up in Alice Springs, away from mob and country, but remembers being embraced by the community in Arrente.
"When you grow up on other Indigenous land and tell people you're Indigenous, they pull you into their culture, so [my family and I] were super lucky and blessed to grow up in the centre of Australia where arguably their Indigenous culture is very sacred and traditional," she said.
Determined to pursue netball, she was advised by coach Gillian Lee to move down south, and remembers the transition to Melbourne as a difficult one.
"It was really hard being away from home," Coffey said.
"I was really lucky with the team I entered [the Vixens] and the support I did have, but it's not the same for everyone. There's a lot of girls who do get those opportunities to move and then don't last because there's just not that support in place."
Hailing from the Northern Territory, Coffey said, was an additional barrier.
"Even with competitions like these, we don't get together until we're here, and we're training away from each other, so it can be quite a challenge."
Visible Indigenous role models key
Asked what more could be done to help First Nations netballers make it to the elite level, Coffey said role models were key.
"If you can't see it, you can't be it," she said, pointing out that there are only two Indigenous players currently in Super Netball.
Coffey said her own experience of spending multiple years as a train-on player, without breaking into the elite environment, showed how difficult it was to make it into a professional team in Australia.
"We get a number of internationals [coming to Super Netball], which I think makes the game better and more exciting, and I don't think [that] should be restricted," she said.
"But I do think there should be more focus on bringing Indigenous girls into the elite level."
She pointed to Netball Australia's plans to introduce two new teams into the competition, saying this would open further list spots.
A New Zealand team, she added, may take pressure away from the Australian players vying for contracts.
Scarlet Jauncey has spent the last year as a training partner for the West Coast Fever, pinching herself to line up on names like Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard at training.
A Yaruwu woman from Rubibi/Broome in Western Australia, Jauncey agreed with Coffey that cutting international talent was not a solution.
"We're happy to be playing against the best in the world, that's what we want," the defender said.
Like many of her teammates, Jauncey grew up idolising Wallam.
"I think it just gives us something to strive towards, knowing that we can be in that space," she said.
In 2025, Jauncey captained the Black Swans, in turn becoming a role model to other First Nations players.
"It was the best tournament I've played in, the best teams I've been with," she said.
"I think just being able to come to First Nations tournaments and having that connection with each other has been really great."
Coffey agreed, saying the experience had given her "goosebumps".
"I think it gives not only myself, but a lot of players so much power and push to keep going and play at the highest level," she said.
Cultural safety means listening to community
Tucker-Munro smiles when hearing the players' responses to playing for the Black Swans.
It has been one of her signature initiatives, alongside the First Nations Tournament and Spirit Series.
"These tournaments are aspirational in terms of trying to inspire the next generation of our kids — who we know love sport and netball in particular — to trial for their respective state and territory," she said.
"It's about the kids that are here this week wanting to aspire to take that next step into the big leagues in terms of Super Netball and Australian representation as well."
Tucker-Munro acknowledged that while it was important to bring First Nations netballers into elite environments, those environments had to be culturally safe.
"First Nations people come into these spaces with our culture and community on our back, as well as cheering us on, so you want to do them proud," she said.
"It's also a tough journey, especially for the kids who have to relocate, so it's about thinking strategically about how we can support them."
Since her appointment, the code has put in place a First Nations Cultural Council, and last year ran a cultural safety review in collaboration with community.
The review considered the perspectives of the wider netball workforce, including coaches and umpires as well as athletes
Tucker-Munro conceded there are "multi-faceted" barriers to having more elite Indigenous netballers, including financial constraints and geographical barriers to access.
"For too long our voice has been very silent," Tucker-Munro said.
"We're not a homogenous people, so it's really important that we make sure we're hearing the voices of many.
"One thing we're really big on in our community is not to do things for us or to us, you've got to do it with us.
"There's real intent and good will to actually drive some of this change across the sporting landscape of netball in Australia."

title: Hundreds of children embracing te reo swim safety lessons
content:
Kapiti Coast hosts te reo swimming event
A swimming sports event on the Kāpiti Coast has given a few hundred local kids the chance to flex their skills in the water - while speaking entirely in te reo.
Three schools from Ōtaki, Te Kura Kaupapa Māori o Te Rito, Te Kura ā iwi o Whakatupuranga Rua Mano and Te Kura o Ōtaki, took part in Kauroa Ahurei in Paraparaumu on Thursday, learning about water safety in a space created specifically for te reo Māori.
Kauora Ahurei organiser Terina Raureti said the idea for the event came from her nieces and nephews, who wanted the chance to use their swimming skills in a competitive setting.
"It's really important to me that they don't have to change who they are to come to Kauora, and that's the whole point that it was created, because we want our kids to be able to fully immerse in their mātauranga, in their worldview, in their reo Māori, to learn how to swim and to engage in the taiao and the wai in a way that is actually reflective of how they live their lives."
The events are based on the pūkenga wai (water competencies) of Kauora, one of those pūkenga is kauawhi, which involves putting on a lifejacket before jumping in the pool.
"It's just knowing that they are in these competitive environments putting on a lifejacket, the stress and just having that moment to think, 'oh yeah, that's how you put it on properly', and we've got to put it on properly before that buzzer goes off.
"So yeah, it's just kind of teaching everyone about the importance of equipment as well, and it's not just about the swimming skills, it's about all the resources around it as well."
Raureti said a lot of the time whānau aren't actually going to the water to swim, they're going to dive or to fish, so it's crucial that kids learn about the equipment too.
There were a lot of inequities in water safety statistics between Māori and non-Māori, and that was reflected in the inequities in access to aquatics and water safety programmes, she said.
"So teaching our kids to love the water, rather than teaching them about all the dangers and all the things. Because we do get stereotyped as a community that we are at high risk... but we're actually a really beautiful water community, and it's just about making sure that our tamariki know that about the water, and where the risks are versus what you can do safely."
Jade Ratapu works at Te Kōhanga Reo o Raukawa but she was also there as a parent, with her son taking part in his first swimming sports event.
"I te hīkaka i te ata nei, oho moata, whakariterite i ōna kākahu. I tae mai ki te puna i kitea i te marea i āhua pā te āmaimai ki ā ia, engari kātahi anō i tutuki pai i tōna reihi."
He was excited this morning, woke up early and got his clothes ready, but when we arrived at the pool and saw all the people he felt a bit nervous, but his race ended well.
Ratapu feels very lucky that her son can attend a swim class every week, also run by Kauora, that is conducted in te reo.
"Ka timata āhua āmaimai ngā tamariki, kāre e pīrangi kia ruku, kia māku ngā karu, engari i te mutunga iho kua kaha kitea ngā painga i tēnei rā, ki ngā tamariki kōhanga o mua kei rō i te puna papaku i te puna hōhonu hoki i tēnei rā, kua kite i te māia."
[The kids at Kōhanga Reo] often start off nervous, they don't want to dive in or get their eyes wet, but we have really seen the benefits today for the kids who used to be in Kōhanga and are now in the shallow pool or even the deep pool, we've really seen the confidence in them.
Nukuao and Hawaiki are just two of the volunteers who help keep the Ahurei running.
"Ki au nei ko te whakahirahiratanga ko tō tātau nei reo Māori me te kite i te pakaritanga ō ngā kura Māori, me ētahi kura Pākehā anō hoki e kaha aro ana ki tō tātau nei reo, waihoki ki ō rātau pakaritanga i roto i te reo," Nukuao said.
To me what is most important about this event is our language, and seeing the strength of the Māori schools, and some of the Pākehā schools who are paying attention to the language, in speaking te reo.
Hawaiki said the event was about whakawhanaungatanga, kotahitanga and friendly competition between the three kura.
"It's cool to teach all the kids Kauora and te reo Māori and to teach them swimming in a Māori way."

title: Intergenerational Two-Spirit head dancers find joy in expressing themselves freely
content:
Editors’ note: Theo Wright’s pronouns are he/they, and per Underscore and ICT’s style guides, Theo is referred to both he/they interchangeably throughout the story.
Nika Bartoo-Smith
Underscore Native News + ICT
PORTLAND, Oregon — After adding the finishing touches of their makeup, little blue stars falling down their cheeks, Theo Wright gently pulled their jingle dress over their head, adjusting it into place with the soft tinkle of jingle cones ringing in the air.
Theo smiled before joining his dad as the pair helped add the final pieces of each other’s regalia before grand entry at the Native American Youth and Family Center‘s 14th Annual Neerchokikoo Powwow in Portland.
Starting the day in a jingle dress made from hand by his father, Theo ended the night in grass dance regalia, also made by his dad.
“There’s not a lot of places where I can openly dance both jingle and grass, and so when I was asked to be a Two-Spirit head dancer, I was, like, immediately yes,” Theo, 22, said.
Theo, Klamath and Oglala Lakota, is Two-Spirit, nonbinary and trans masculine. They define their queerness in powwow terms.
“Being able to be a Two-Spirit head dancer is not having to choose between being queer and Native, and being not only allowed but encouraged to be both,” they said.
Now in its 14th year, the center powwow first introduced a Two-Spirit head dancer title to join men’s and women’s head dancers in 2023.
At most powwows across the country today, jingle dancers are expected to be women and grass dancers are expected to be men. However, there has been a push to create more spaces of queer joy and a disruption to gender norms at powwows.
“There were a lot of powwows that were starting to have the Two-Spirit flag and say ‘everyone is welcome here and these are safe spaces,’ and we were inspired by that,” said Tamara Henderson, Laguna Pueblo, chief operating officer and powwow organizer at the center.
“And frankly, some powwows will have Two-Spirit dancers [and] Two-Spirit powwows, and so I said if we’re truly trying to create a safe space for our community, then what we really have to do is have our own Two-Spirit head dancer and keep it consistent,” she continued.
This year, accessibility and belonging are central themes of the Neerchokikoo Powwow. Along with continuing to host a Two-Spirit head dancer, NAYA staff and community also celebrated an elevator on campus that opened in February 2026.
The elevator, years in the making, has been a priority for the NAYA community in order to expand building access for elders and people with disabilities.
“Accessibility and belonging are both really, really important,” Henderson said. “They’re really important to us to make sure that our community always feels like they can be safe here and knows that they have a home away from home.”
Hearing about the elevator for the first time at this year’s powwow, both Theo and his dad perked up with excitement.
“It’s really awesome because both the kid and I are disabled,” Asa Wright, Theo’s dad, said.
Following in his father’s footsteps
Last year, Asa held the title of head Two-Spirit dancer at the Neerchokikoo powwow. This year, he is a proud father, watching Theo follow in his footsteps.
“I’m really honored that I was able to be the Two-Spirit head dancer last year, and then now my kid was able to do it this year,” Asa said, after finishing up braiding Theo’s hair to help them get ready to dance. “It feels really awesome, and just really cool that they’ve grown up in a different world than I have and got to express themselves freely.”
“They just make me super proud,” the 46-year-old continued.
Asa, Klamath, Modoc and Yahooskin, is Two-Spirit and trans masculine. He is also the founder of Portland Two Spirit Society.
“I think it’s interesting how we look at historical roles of Two-Spirit people, and then contemporary Two-Spirit people, and we end up finding the roles that reflect what we’ve had historically, without even knowing that,” Asa said. “It’s who Creator made us to be to fill those roles.”
Asa grew up dancing in a powwow family.
At 17, Asa began school at Portland State University and also started dancing grass. He remembers getting threats from other male dancers. For a while, he was scared to put on his regalia.
“As a 17-year-old who started at PSU, I could have never imagined being a Two-Spirit dancer or seeing another Two-Spirit dancer,” Asa said.
But he continued to dance grass anyway, following his heart and the movement of his footsteps. As a father, Asa has raised a child who knows they can dance whichever style they choose, be whoever they are and know they will be loved unconditionally.
“I’m so glad that we’ve come so far that my kiddo doesn’t have to think about that [fear],” Asa said. “Their whole dancing experience for their 22 years has just been positive. It’s just been joy-based, and I’ve really tried to shelter them from any kind of hate or negative talk.”
Though Asa continues to dance himself, it has gotten harder as he has aged. Asa has a disability, along with bad knees, and is a survivor of kidney cancer.
Even though dancing is hard on his body and requires more breaks, he continues and finds healing through grass dancing. The time may come when he may not be able to dance anymore, but Asa’s eyes fill with pride as he thinks about his child following in his footsteps.
“It’s cool that Theo has adopted grass dance now for himself and I get to live that through watching him dance now,” Asa said.
In 2023, Theo first danced grass during a switch dance special at the University of Washington annual spring powwow. His dad asked if he wanted to use his regalia, and Theo remembers as soon as he slipped it over his head, he realized how good it felt to wear grass dance regalia. Following that first time dancing grass, Asa made Theo his own regalia.
For Theo, when he first came out as trans, he worried it meant he would no longer be able to dance jingle, which he had done his whole life. But, instead, Theo has found spaces, like the Neerchokikoo powwow, where they can dance as fully themself, embracing two different forms of dance.
“It doesn’t have to be one or the other,” Theo said. “I don’t have to be a jingle dancer or a grass dancer. I can be a jingle and grass dancer because no one looks twice at you if you’re a fancy shawl and jingle dancer or if you’re a traditional bustle and grass dancer. But they’ll be confused if you’re a jingle and a grass dancer because those aren’t supposed to go together. Both of those styles live in my feet and in my body, and that’s not something that can be taken away by anyone.”
As Theo dances this year, they reflected on watching their dad hold the role of head Two-Spirit dancer at last year’s powwow — and what it means to be part of an intergenerationally Two-Spirit family.
He looks up to the work his dad has done in the community: creating space and conversations for Two-Spirit people across the Portland Metro area and beyond.
“I think he’s really a trailblazer for a lot of that,” Theo said. “It’s been really cool to acknowledge all of the work that he’s done and then be like, okay, what can we do next?”
This story is co-published by Underscore Native News and ICT, a news partnership that covers Indigenous communities in the Pacific Northwest.

title: Country Life: 'Looking for an edge' on a Māori-owned farm
content:
In the past 16 years, the Pukepoto Farm Trust near Taumaranui has never not made a profit for its more than a thousand shareholders, descendants of Ngāti Maniapoto.
It's something the trust prides itself on, as it allows them to give back to the community.
"We can't do a lot on 1000 effective hectares, but we can certainly do a little bit," Trustee Weo Maag told Country Life.
Now it's sharing the secrets to its success with other neighbouring farmers as part of Beef and Lamb's Hub Farm Programme.
'Looking for an edge': Data driven decisions on a Māori owned farm
Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.
Meaning 'little hill', Pukepoto was established by the Māori Land Court in 1978.
Trustee Weo Maag inherited his shares from whakapapa on his mother's side.
"I've always maintained that the land should provide to our people."
He said the trust initially started by paying dividends to shareholders, then moved to providing education grants and most recently, kaumātua grants.
Returning a profit to the shareholders comes from careful planning, he added.
"We draw up plans production-wise and expectations based on one season from the other, and then we look to what is it we're going to produce, what then can we sell.
"We can't control what the prices are - we're at the mercy of the processors, but we can control what we produce."
Another important part was having a "yardstick to measure our success".
For Maag this meant "benchmarking" to help when explaining farm operations and results to the shareholders.
"It's about managing expectations," Maag said.
"I can go, 'hey, how come we didn't produce that many [lambs]? What happened? What went wrong? Did you miss a paddock with the ram or something?' You know, whatever it might be. But if you don't have anything in writing, then you're just flying by the seat of your pants."
The Pukepoto Trust farm joined Beef and Lamb's Hub Farm Programme in October 2025. The programme follows a farm business over several years to help farmers see what change looks like over time in a real system.
Maag said he hoped the programme would help with providing more detailed data as part of the trust's own benchmarking processes.
"With the hub farm, we're going to be able to get accurate measurements around grass growth," he said.
"We've got an idea historically because [of] our irrometer (a tool used to measure soil moisture) and knowing how many sheep we've had, 'oh yeah, we'll be right'. We know the rainfall.
"But this is going to provide real live data that we can then go... yeah, we were pretty accurate."
It's also about providing tested data and information for future generations, he said.
"At some point, someone's going to replace us. I see the hub farm and the learning from the hub farmers, essentially going to be able to provide information [to] the new trustees who come along, who may not have a greater knowledge in farming, but have a lot of understanding in governance and finance."
On the bright autumn day Country Life visited, about 80 farmers, trustees and other rural professionals turned out for the field day where early results were shared.
"It feels really great to be up there amongst top performing farms in the district."
Trust chairperson Aloma Shearer said there were wider benefits to being part of the programme too.
"It's about bringing other people, sharing knowledge that you have with other farmers about performance and what we do here, what can help others, that sort of thing.
"I'm just hoping that what we've got to share with farmers here today, with the industry, is going to be helpful for what their plans are for the future."
The field day highlighted how the trust was lifting performance through genetics, making better land use decisions, and integrating technology like the new eShepherd virtual fencing collars from Gallagher.
"We're always looking for an edge just to get ahead, to make more money, grow more grass," she said.

title: 2 College Friends Built Free Mini Libraries in Ahmedabad Parks. Here’s How You Can Too
content: Every evening at Ahmedabad’s Parimal Garden, people gather for different reasons. Some arrive for long walks after work. Children run across pathways with cricket bats in hand, while elderly residents settle onto benches beneath old trees. Amid the movement and chatter sits a small wooden cabinet lined with books, drawing people towards it. A child pauses to pull out a comic book. An elderly man carefully flips through a novel before placing it back. A college student stands there reading for nearly twenty minutes before leaving with a paperback tucked under his arm. Nobody monitors the shelves. There are no membership cards, fines, or formal procedures. The library functions entirely on trust. The idea came from Ahmedabad-based friends Heet Doshi and Om Thakkar when they were still college students. Through their reading community, ‘Your Reading Circle’, the duo began setting up free mini libraries in public parks to make books more accessible. What started with one library at Parimal Garden in June 2024 has now grown into 13 libraries across Ahmedabad and Vadodara, with three more set to open soon. In March 2026, they also registered an NGO called ‘Virakt Foundation’ to expand the initiative further. For Heet, the journey began with a small observation. “We realised there were a lot of people who loved reading, but there were very few places where readers could actually meet each other and share that interest,” he says. The duo started Your Reading Circle in Ahmedabad in September 2023. The group brought together people who enjoyed books but lacked spaces to discuss them outside social media or academic settings. The founders had no larger plans at the time. They just wanted to create a reading culture around them. Then they came across a social media reel about Perumkulam in Kerala, where libraries are spread across the settlement every few hundred metres. “That idea stayed with us for a long time,” Heet tells The Better India. “We kept thinking that if a village in India could create something like that, why couldn’t we try doing it in Ahmedabad?” A small bookshelf, and weeks of figuring out permissions In April 2024, the two friends began discussing how they could set up a small public library inside a city park. They made a basic list of what they would need: permissions, funding, fabrication and books. The duo started Your Reading Circle in Ahmedabad in September 2023. What they did not anticipate was how difficult the permission process would become. “The biggest challenge was understanding where to even go because nobody had dealt with something like this before, so we found ourselves visiting multiple departments just to figure out who could actually give us permission,” he says. The team spent weeks moving from one office to another. Some officials redirected them elsewhere, while others were unsure which department held the authority to approve a library inside a public garden. “It sounds like a very small thing when you say you want to place a library in a park,” he adds. “But practically, it takes a lot of patience.” Eventually, after several follow-ups and discussions, the team received permission to install their first mini library at Parimal Garden, one of Ahmedabad’s busiest public spaces. On 23 June 2024, the first library officially opened to the public. Initially, the founders approached it as an experiment rather than a large project. “We just wanted to make one library and see how people reacted to it,” says the co-founder. The response came almost immediately. Children began gathering around the shelves after finishing their games. Elderly residents stopped to browse through books during their evening walks. Some visitors borrowed books and returned days later, carrying another one from home. The system worked on a straightforward principle. Anyone could take a book as long as they contributed one in return. “The public mini-library runs entirely on trust,” he explains. “People take a book, people keep a book. That is how we started, and that is how it still works.” The founders were fully prepared for books to disappear or the shelves to remain empty after a few weeks. Instead, they witnessed complete strangers voluntarily maintaining the libraries. “There were people we didn’t even know who started cleaning the shelves or arranging books properly,” he adds. “Some of them told us they regularly visited the library just to maintain it.” Those moments reassured the team that the idea could survive beyond their direct involvement. Why parks became the chosen space As the libraries began attracting attention online, many people asked why the founders specifically chose parks and gardens instead of railway stations or bus stops. For Heet, the answer was always linked to the atmosphere of these spaces. “A park is a place where people naturally slow down, spend time with family, sit in silence, and relax, so we felt reading would fit very naturally into that environment,” he says. The founders also noticed that many visitors spent long stretches scrolling through phones while sitting outdoors. “We wanted to create another option,” he explains. “If somebody spends even ten minutes reading instead of being on their phone, that itself matters.” Today, the team has installed 11 libraries across Ahmedabad and two in Vadodara. Two more are being prepared in Vadodara and another in Ahmedabad. One particularly memorable moment came shortly after they opened a library at Kamati Baug in Vadodara. Within two days, almost all the books had disappeared from the shelves. “We were honestly disappointed because within two days the shelves had become empty, and we thought people had taken the books away and that the library probably would not work in this place,” he admits. A week later, a local social media page featured the library. Residents began discussing it online and promising to donate books. Soon afterwards, one of the team’s volunteers visited the site and sent them a photograph. The shelves were full again. “We had not added any books ourselves,” he says. “The people of Vadodara had filled the library back up.” What it takes to start a public library in your city Over the past year, Heet and Om have received messages from people across India asking how they can create similar public libraries in their own cities. Having gone through the process themselves, the founders now openly share the steps they believe are most important. 1. Begin with permissions before anything else According to Heet, the first step is approaching the municipal corporation and the city’s garden department directly. “Do not begin by building the structure because permissions take the longest time, so the first thing people should focus on is getting approval from the authorities,” he says. In April 2024, the two friends began discussing how they could set up a small public library inside a city park. He advises preparing a simple proposal that lays out the idea clearly. The document should include the size of the library, where it will be installed, whether it will remain open or locked, how maintenance will happen, and who will manage it. “They mainly want to understand whether you can responsibly maintain the library,” he adds. He also believes approaching senior officials directly can speed up the process considerably. “If the message reaches the higher authorities, the process becomes smoother,” he explains. 2. Start with the people who already love books Long before the first library was installed, the duo had already built a community of readers through Your Reading Circle. That network helped them find books and early supporters. “Every city already has readers; you just need to bring them together and create spaces where they can connect with books and with each other,” he says. The first library itself was funded partly by the team and partly by a retired principal and professor named Indira Nityanandam, who became one of the initiative’s earliest supporters. “She kept telling us to focus on permissions and the rest would somehow work out,” he recalls. He says their experience showed them that people were often willing to support the idea once they understood what the team was trying to do. 3. Invite public figures to build trust The founders also realised that involving respected public figures during inaugurations helped the libraries gain visibility and community trust. “Even a small library can create a big impact,” the co-founder says. “If people see respected individuals supporting it, they take the initiative seriously.” The team has collaborated with radio personalities, local creators, and community leaders to spread awareness about the libraries and encourage participation. 4. Do not wait for everything to be perfect One lesson the co-founder particularly emphasises is the importance of beginning. “We got the idea in April 2024 and started working on it soon after,” he says. “If your intention is genuine and you keep taking action consistently, things slowly start happening.” That approach now shapes the way they advise others who want to replicate the model. ‘Our readers keep us going’ While the initiative continues to grow, it is the personal moments around the libraries that have remained most meaningful for the founders. One such story came from a supporter named Parth Jala, who decided to sponsor a library in memory of his grandmother. “His grandmother could not read, but she loved listening to him talk about books, so after she passed away, he decided to open a library in her name so that many others could experience the joy of reading,” Heet explains. For the founders, Parth’s gesture showed how a library could carry a personal memory into a public space. Today, the team has installed 11 libraries across Ahmedabad and two in Vadodara. Another moment came when elderly residents began calling the team directly to thank them for reviving their reading habits. “There were uncles in their seventies and eighties telling us they had started reading again after many years,” he continues. “Some even brought books from their personal collections and donated them.” The founders also noticed women in some parks gathering regularly around the libraries to read together and discuss books informally. These interactions showed them that the libraries were becoming places where people could read together and talk about books. Now, they want the idea to travel beyond city parks Mini libraries remain at the centre of their work, but the duo are now taking the idea into rural India as well. The foundation has already opened its first village library in Bherunda near Modasa in Gujarat. Around 200 books are placed inside the gram panchayat building, along with a register system through which residents can borrow books for 14 days. “For someone who has never travelled outside their village, books can become a way of seeing the world,” the co-founder says. The team is now converting the first floor of the gram panchayat building in Sudamda village in Surendranagar district into a fully functioning community library where residents can sit and read. Unlike the mini libraries inside parks, this space will operate as a proper reading centre with seating, shelves, and a larger collection of books. The founders eventually hope to build similar libraries across villages in Gujarat before expanding into other parts of India, including border regions and underserved communities. For Heet, trying an idea they had once encountered through a social media reel has also changed what feels possible. Heet and Om have received messages from people across India asking how they can create similar public libraries in their own cities. “This initiative changed us psychologically because it made us believe that if your intention is pure and you continue taking action consistently, almost anything is possible,” he says. For now, the idea continues to rest on the same thing that made the first cabinet at Parimal Garden work: strangers choosing to take care of a shared shelf of books. All pictures courtesy Heet Doshi.

title: Cross-border project explores growing up after GFA
content:
A cross-border project examining what peace means to the generation that grew up after the Good Friday Agreement in 1998 will culminate in a theatrical performance that will be streamed live tomorrow, the UN's International Day of Peace.
Thirty young people aged 18-25 from North and South, who lived together during the summer, will perform 'Project Lighthouse,’ in the Hawk’s Well Theatre in Sligo.
The Hawk’s Well Director Kieran Griffiths said the project examines "what conflict means to a generation that inherited peace," while "exploring difference and hoping to celebrate it".
The production is a partnership between the Hawk’s Well Theatre, the Millennium Forum in Derry and the John and Pat Hume Foundation, supported by the Special EU Programmes Body.
The project participants, some of whom had no theatrical experience, were selected after they responded to advertisements, in a production guided by artists Abby Oliveira and Bob Kelly.
Mr Kelly describes the production as "a tasting board" of the young people’s discussions, using an open-mic format that expands into dance, movement and abstract theatre.
"What we’re hoping the audience will experience isn't so much a cohesive dramatic arc, but that they have had an encounter with these very interesting young people," he said.'
Grace Doherty from Derry City said the production "was great craic from day one," adding that it was a real success in terms of collaboration.
"Personally, for me, peace means that everyone, regardless of creed, race, religion, whatever, can just live and exist in the world without fear," she said.
Ms Doherty said participants, such as herself, were "very aware of the privilege" and "the safety" that the Good Friday Agreement brought, noting it was "talked about a lot".
She alluded to what the group believes is required for society to move forward as a key point of their discussions.
"A big issue that's been discussed is the rates of violence against women in the north, as well as the male suicide epidemic that the north is grappling with…
"So, there's a balance of being aware of the privilege that we have, while also being aware of what's needed moving forward," Ms Doherty said.
Luke O’Grady from Derry city, who has a background in writing, said he had never experienced theatre and found that he enjoyed "acting and loved improvisation."
"My understanding of peace after taking part hasn't really changed for me, but that's not a bad thing. I've always been quite an open person.
"The dialogue in the group was fantastic. I thought we all got on well, very quickly. It helped that the Sligo people had to stay in Derry; we were seeing each other every day."
Participant Kaylee Finnegan from Limavady, who composed a solo piece for the production, said "peace means collaboration".
Patrick Donlan from Ballintrillick in Co Sligo said he really enjoyed this project and hopes the group can remain in contact.
"Being up there really changes your perspective. It's a recent history. It's not something long gone, and it's something that still needs to be learned about," he said.
Evan Ennis from Dromahair in Co Leitrim said the group wrote their scenes together and will be on stage together, throughout the production.
"It’s so important to have that dialog, not just talking about differences, but being able to create, and highlight how similar we are and how brilliant it is that we can all come together."
Oleksandra Pidopryhora from Ukraine, who lives in Sligo said it was an amazing opportunity, to learn more about Irish history, and to discuss Ukraine’s situation as well.
"This is so great to see how people found this peace, after the troubles and this hard history and I wish that one day our people in Ukraine will live the same way in a peaceful country."
‘Project Lighthouse’ can be viewed online on The Hawk’s Well website tomorrow morning, however, online registration is required.
The production is also the subject of a fly-on-the-wall documentary, which will be included in a digital resource for schools, and it will inform another project, currently in development.
The White Dove, which will be staged at the Hawk’s Well Theatre and the Millennium Forum in 2029, will complete a trilogy of ‘The White Handkerchief’ and ‘Hume: Beyond Belief.’
Chief Executive of the Millennium Forum David McLaughlin said the cross-border initiative is a fantastic example of what can be achieved with a shared ambition.
"It demonstrates how collaboration across the island can strengthen the arts, create meaningful opportunities for the next generation and showcase the creativity and stories of this region on an international stage," he said.

title: Ministra Rachel Barros visita Casa da Igualdade Racial de Contagem (MG)
content:
A ministra da Igualdade Racial, Rachel Barros, visitou, na terça-feira (15), a Casa da Igualdade Racial de Contagem, na Região Metropolitana de Belo Horizonte (RMBH). Inaugurado no último dia 10, o equipamento é o sexto do país e o segundo de Minas Gerais a integrar o projeto-piloto do Programa Mais Igualdade, do Ministério da Igualdade Racial (MIR).
Casa funciona como espaço de acolhimento, orientação e apoio especializado
A Casa funciona como espaço de acolhimento, orientação e apoio especializado à população negra, comunidades tradicionais e outros grupos atingidos pela discriminação racial e étnica. Entre os serviços previstos estão atendimentos psicológico, social e jurídico a vítimas de crimes raciais e outras violações de direitos.
Durante a visita, Rachel Barros foi recebida ao som de atabaque e berimbau pelo grupo de capoeira Eskiva Brasil. A atividade contou com a presença de representantes da Prefeitura de Contagem, do Conselho Municipal de Promoção da Igualdade Racial (Compir), de comunidades quilombolas, povos de terreiro, congados e reinados.
A unidade integra o Programa Mais Igualdade e o Sistema Nacional de Promoção da Igualdade Racial (Sinapir). O projeto-piloto contempla seis municípios: Fortaleza (CE), Rio de Janeiro (RJ), Pelotas (RS), Salvador (BA), Itabira (MG) e Contagem (MG).
Cinco eixos
As ações desenvolvidas na Casa da Igualdade Racial estão organizadas em cinco eixos. O primeiro é a justiça racial, voltado ao apoio às vítimas de crimes raciais e de outras violações motivadas por discriminação racial e étnica.
O segundo é a inclusão produtiva, que busca ampliar oportunidades de desenvolvimento pessoal e profissional, com prioridade para mulheres negras e jovens negros. Já o eixo de cultura e educação prevê atividades educativas e culturais, especialmente a partir de referências afro-brasileiras.
O eixo convivência comunitária tem como objetivo fortalecer vínculos sociais, identidade e pertencimento das comunidades atendidas. Por fim, a pactuação federativa busca ampliar a articulação entre União, estados e municípios na implementação de políticas públicas de igualdade racial.
O Ministério da Igualdade Racial define as Casas como equipamentos destinados à redução das desigualdades raciais e ao fortalecimento dos vínculos sociais e culturais da população negra e das comunidades tradicionais.
Em Contagem, a Casa está localizada na rua Manoel de Matos, nº 162, no bairro Central Park. O atendimento é gratuito e ocorre de segunda a sexta-feira, das 8h às 17h.
Diálogo com povos tradicionais em Belo Horizonte
Também na terça-feira (15), o Ministério da Igualdade Racial promoveu um encontro com povos e comunidades tradicionais de Minas Gerais no Centro Nacional de Africanidade e Resistência Afro-brasileira (Cenarab), em Belo Horizonte.
O encontro reuniu representantes de povos de terreiro, comunidades quilombolas, reinados e congados. Durante a atividade, os participantes apresentaram demandas ao ministério e destacaram necessidades relacionadas à proteção dos povos tradicionais.
Além do momento de escuta, foram entregues reconhecimentos a pessoas e trajetórias ligadas à preservação da ancestralidade africana e à luta pela igualdade racial.

title: Coletivo Katihirene lança mapeamento do cinema das mulheres indígenas no Festival de Brasília
content:
Quantas línguas cabem no cinema brasileiro? Essa provocação faz parte da apresentação da rede audiovisual das mulheres indígenas Katahirine e sintetiza a urgência e o pioneirismo do coletivo. O trabalho do grupo e o levantamento de informações foram sintetizados no livro “Ler o vento, filmar o mundo: Pesquisa-mapeamento do cinema das mulheres indígenas no Brasil”, lançado durante o 59º Festival de Brasília do Cinema Brasileiro, sediado no Cine Brasília.
A pesquisa ouviu 60 realizadoras de 40 povos indígenas, falantes de 35 línguas originárias e procedentes de todas as regiões do país. O resultado traz um diagnóstico aprofundado sobre a presença e a circulação dessas cineastas, que são ao mesmo tempo uma realidade vibrante nas telas nacionais e internacionais, mas encontram gargalos estruturais, linguagens excludentes e barreiras burocráticas no acesso a financiamento.
Katahirine: a rede, a pesquisa e o livro
Na língua do povo Manchineri, Katahirine significa “constelação”. A metáfora traduz a essência da Rede e sua articulação plural voltada ao apoio mútuo, à visibilidade e à autonomia de realizadoras originárias em todo o país. Mais do que uma organização coletiva, a rede constitui um território de acolhimento e fortalecimento de narrativas, integrando a força do coletivo com a singularidade e o protagonismo de cada cineasta.
A agrupação é formada por mulheres do audiovisual com raízes fincadas em seus territórios ancestrais. Hoje, a Rede Katahirine reúne 92 cineastas, falantes de 30 línguas indígenas, abrangendo 48 povos do Brasil e três de nações vizinhas — Bolívia, Chile e Equador. Essa constelação atravessa a Amazônia, o Cerrado, a Mata Atlântica, a Caatinga e o Pampa, levando narrativas e presenças que atuam nas próprias comunidades e ecoam no mundo não indígena.
Esse movimento nasceu de pé no chão, durante um encontro de realizadoras indígenas no Acre, em 2022. Na ocasião, o Instituto Catitu — instituição pioneira na formação e no estímulo à produção audiovisual feminina indígena — compartilhou a semente da criação de uma rede própria. A partir dali, gerida e construída a muitas mãos, a constelação ganhou corpo.
De acordo com a cineasta e comunicadora Moiara Kaxuyana, a elaboração do livro “Ler o vento” partiu de um amplo processo de pesquisa-mapeamento voltado a identificar a realidade e a pluralidade das realizadoras originárias no Brasil. Moiara é oriunda dos povos Kaxuyana e Tiriyó, do Território Indígena Parque do Tumucumaque e natural de Macapá (AP). Ela reside em Brasília desde 2009 e dirigiu o curta “Eu sou Kaxuyana” (2021).
Ela ressalta que o estudo nasce com o compromisso de não reduzir as entrevistadas a estatísticas frias. “Afinal de contas, a gente não está falando de números. A gente está falando de mulheres, de mães, de benzedeiras, de líderes comunitárias, que se encontram nessa pluralidade de etnias, de territórios, de povos, de línguas, uma prática em comum. E essa prática é o cinema”, resume.
Circulação do cinema originário
Os dados levantados também expõem a forma como o audiovisual se insere nas dinâmicas territoriais e as barreiras que cercam sua difusão. Moiara afirma que “mais de 73% dessas mulheres atuam profissionalmente no setor, mas sem desvincular a câmera de suas responsabilidades comunitárias e da urgência de registrar saberes ancestrais”.
Segundo Moiara, o estudo revela um paradoxo no eixo dedicado à circulação, pois, embora cerca de 81% das realizadoras já tenham exibido suas produções em festivais e mostras, 61% relatam não dominar os trâmites de inscrição em editais e eventos competitivos, “em grande parte pela barreira da língua portuguesa, pela falta de internet e pela burocracia documental”.
Para ela, esse descompasso reafirma que a circulação do cinema originário obedece a outra lógica. As exibições nas próprias aldeias caminham lado a lado com os grandes festivais, consolidando um cinema que, longe de visar apenas ao mercado, busca quebrar preconceitos históricos e fortalecer a memória viva de seus povos.
“O compartilhar no território, devolver as imagens para o povo que fez com que esse filme fosse possível de ser feito é a nossa prioridade máxima. Enquanto cineasta, é ter essa devolutiva”, afirma.
A fundadora do Instituto Catitu e única não-indígena idealizadora da Rede Katahirine, Mari Corrêa é educadora com trajetória no audiovisual desde 1988 e atuação junto a comunidades indígenas iniciada em 1992. Ela informa que o coletivo abriu espaço para a inclusão das cineastas no grupo com “entrevistas aprofundadas conduzidas pelas próprias mulheres da rede e com duração média de duas a três horas cada. O roteiro abordou desde a caracterização de perfil até eixos críticos como formação artística, modos de criação, circulação das obras, gargalos de fomento e a salvaguarda de acervos”.
As cineastas indígenas estão presentes em diferentes biomas, com maior concentração na Mata Atlântica (35%) e na Amazônia (31,7%), seguidas pelo Cerrado (18,3%), Caatinga (13,3%) e Pampa (1,7%). Quanto à moradia, 53,3% vivem em aldeias, 40% em cidades e 6,7% transitam entre os dois espaços, evidenciando a diversidade territorial e os diferentes contextos de produção audiovisual indígena.
Segundo o livro, esses dados ressaltam o fato de que “a distribuição territorial desfaz outra imagem simplificadora: a de que as cineastas indígenas viveriam em territórios remotos ou, ao contrário, seriam todas urbanizadas, a partir de um entendimento equivocado de que, para acessar equipamentos audiovisuais, seria preciso viver em grandes centros urbanos. A realidade territorial das cineastas indígenas é mais complexa e mais viva, pois o fato de morar na aldeia não significa estar apartada, e morar na cidade não implica, necessariamente, afastamento da comunidade”.
Rompendo barreiras
Para Mari Corrêa, a produção sistemática de indicadores é o único caminho viável para romper a barreira da invisibilidade e exigir transformações reais no setor cinematográfico, pois a sistematização das respostas permitiu mensurar a realidade de um setor historicamente subnotificado. A iniciativa foi desenvolvida pelas mulheres indígenas em conjunto com profissionais não indígenas parceiras.
“E a gente sabe a pouca visibilidade que têm essas produções dos cineastas e das cineastas indígenas, e é preciso que o Estado enxergue esse grupo do cinema brasileiro, não há políticas públicas sem dados”, aponta. Ao fundamentar as demandas em estatísticas sólidas, o mapeamento busca subsidiar tomadores de decisão, comissões de seleção e gestores públicos com diagnósticos precisos sobre onde e como investir, indo além de mecanismos paliativos.
“Olhem aqui como está essa questão da formação, olhem aqui como está a questão da produção, ou seja, deixar mais claro como é pensado e feito esse cinema, para as pessoas entenderem que precisa de políticas públicas que funcionem para esse cinema. A gente fala muito dessa questão de cotas, mas não é o suficiente, tem questões que vêm antes”, enfatiza a fundadora do Catitu.
Segundo o livro, entre as cineastas entrevistadas, 58,3% são mães, enquanto 28,33% afirmam não viajar sozinhas, dependendo da companhia de familiares, especialmente filhos e netos, para sair de seus territórios. Em relação ao estado civil, 48,3% são solteiras e 41,7% são casadas ou vivem em união estável. Os dados evidenciam como responsabilidades familiares e redes de parentesco influenciam as condições de produção e circulação dessas mulheres no audiovisual.
Quanto à faixa etária, 46,7% das cineastas têm entre 30 e 39 anos, e 65% têm 30 anos ou mais. Segundo a pesquisa, essa concentração está relacionada à trajetória do cinema indígena brasileiro e às oficinas de formação audiovisual realizadas nas últimas três décadas, que contribuíram para a formação das primeiras gerações de mulheres indígenas produtoras de suas próprias imagens.
Cinema indígena feminino
O trabalho da Rede Katahirine também envolve a elaboração de diretrizes para um audiovisual ético com povos indígenas para propor relações mais justas e respeitosas entre as aldeias e instituições, festivais, curadorias, produtoras e profissionais do setor audiovisual. Essa parte da publicação nasce das experiências vividas por mulheres indígenas em produções, festivais e curadorias.
Segundo Mari, “o documento reúne orientações direcionadas para profissionais e organizações do setor audiovisual com a proposta de prevenir práticas discriminatórias, exploratórias e desiguais e estimular parcerias baseadas na escuta, no cuidado, na reciprocidade, no consentimento, na remuneração justa e no reconhecimento dos modos indígenas de fazer e pensar o cinema nas suas formas de viver”.
Mari Corrêa parafraseia a antropóloga e fotógrafa Francy Baniwa para descrever a particularidade indígena produzir cinema:
“Crescemos aprendendo a ler o vento antes de ler livros. Aprendemos a ler as constelações antes de conhecer o calendário. A decifrar o canto dos pássaros antes de decifrar o alfabeto. Nosso cinema nasce dessa percepção ancestral e vítima do Brasil. As mulheres dos territórios indígenas têm olhares diferentes e únicos. O que vemos com os olhos de quem cuida, de quem preserva, de quem guarda, de quem transmite. E esse olhar levado para as telas transforma o próprio cinema. Para nós, o cinema raramente pertence a uma só pessoa. Ele pertence à comunidade que o viveu e ao território que o inspirou. Nós somos como as famílias, somos muitas e sempre andamos juntas. O que nossas avós faziam com a palavra o canto, com o canto, nós também fazemos com a imagem.”
A multiartista Barbara Matias Kariri é diretora de filmes documentais e ficcionais como “Santa Pedra” (2020), “Corpo Memória Submersa” (2021), “O que me leva não é mercadoria de bolso” (2022). Para ela, a relação com o cinema produzido na perspectiva indígena é uma forma de apropriação e “passa a ser um instrumento para documentar, para expor as violências, além de servir como um exercício de autoestima e também provocação à linguagem cinematográfica”.
“A câmera, ao contrário do milho, não faz parte do nosso terreiro e da nossa estrutura enquanto realidade de vida. Mas a câmera, assim como o cavalo para os Mapuche, que é uma etnia indígena do Chile, entra nas nossas aldeias. A gente luta com a câmera, assim como os mapuches fizeram com os cavalos”, destaca Barbara, oriunda do povo Kariri, nascida na comunidade do Marreco, no Ceará, doutora em Artes pela UFMG e coordenadora e conselheira da Rede Katahirine.
Ela aponta que o cinema indígena não constitui uma categoria homogênea, mas reúne diferentes formas de criação vinculadas aos modos de vida e aos territórios de cada povo. Para ela, uma das características desse audiovisual está no processo de adaptação de práticas culturais para a linguagem cinematográfica. Essa perspectiva também se manifesta na escolha das narrativas, na valorização da oralidade e na construção coletiva dos filmes, que podem envolver diversas pessoas na direção e na criação. “Os povos indígenas também vão artesanando o seu modo de criar também cinema”, afirma.
Esse modo de produção também está relacionado à temporalidade, à espiritualidade e à relação com os territórios. Barbara explica que as realizadoras trabalham respeitando o ritmo das comunidades, que inclui atividades como roça, pesca e convivência familiar, e não segue necessariamente o tempo acelerado da produção cinematográfica convencional. Em alguns casos, o processo começa com práticas espirituais: “Antes de começar com algum trabalho, temos que fazer uma reza que limpa a nossa alma”, relata.
Para a cineasta, essas dimensões também produzem uma estética própria, presente no enquadramento, na oralidade e na maneira de contar histórias. “A oralidade é um recurso estético que é muito da natureza das comunidades indígenas”, afirma.
Larissa Tukano , é cineasta, artista visual, artesã e articuladora do povo Ye’pa Mahsã, originária da comunidade de Taracuá, na Terra Indígena Alto Rio Negro, no Amazonas. Em entrevista ao Brasil de Fato DF, a diretora de “Wehsé Darase – Trabalho da Roça” (2017) explica que o cinema produzido por indígenas parte de uma relação direta com o cotidiano e com aquilo que faz sentido para cada comunidade, em contraste com representações externas que frequentemente privilegiam paisagens e imagens estereotipadas.
Segundo ela, enquanto produções não indígenas podem apresentar uma visão mais enquadrada e distante, os filmes realizados pelos próprios povos incorporam a participação de quem está diante das câmeras, inclusive na tradução e na explicação de práticas culturais. “Pode ser a mulher torrando farinha, pode ser eles comendo, ou eles trabalhando”, explica. Para a cineasta, essa diferença está relacionada ao lugar de quem filma: “são olhares diferentes”, porque uma pessoa que não pertence àquela realidade pode tentar retratá-la, mas dificilmente conseguirá transmiti-la da mesma maneira.
Essa produção também é marcada pela construção coletiva e pelo respeito às especificidades culturais de cada povo. Larissa afirma que cada comunidade possui “seu próprio sistema de como fazer um documentário”, definindo o que pode ou não ser filmado e divulgado.
Esse processo envolve consultar a comunidade sobre a representação de grafismos, adornos, rituais e outros elementos culturais, evitando transformar essas manifestações em imagens estereotipadas. Para ela, os filmes também cumprem uma função de preservação da memória, especialmente diante da perda de anciãos e outros membros das comunidades: “Muitos daqueles que foram filmados já não existem mais”. Assim, o cinema indígena registra narrativas e modos de vida que podem permanecer como memória para as gerações seguintes.
Larissa também destaca o retorno que as produções de cinema e vídeo oferecem para as aldeias: “O documentário que fiz é um dos filmes que contribuiu para que reconhecesse o sistema agrícola do Rio Negro como um dos patrimônios dos 23 povos indígenas lá. Então tem o meu, tem o dos outros, que fazem parte dessa documentação pra que reconheçam que esse conhecimento, tanto material e imaterial”, é patrimônio dos 23 povos indígenas”, conclui.

title: Archaeologists are racing to save precious artifacts in Alaska after last year's storm
content:
Archaeologists are racing to save precious artifacts in Alaska after last year's storm
Last October, remnants of Typhoon Halong swept through western Alaska — causing widespread flooding and displacing over a thousand people in multiple far-flung villages off the state's road system.
In the coastal village of Quinhagak, the storm shook houses and damaged some buildings and infrastructure. And the day after it hit, Jenny Matthew and her husband rode four-wheelers along the torn-up beach, assessing the damage.
The wind and floodwaters had peeled the tundra up like discarded carpeting. And as Matthew scanned the debris, suddenly, something caught her eye.
"I said to my husband, 'Look, what's that?' We stopped. He got up and took it, and it was that bowl," Matthew remembered.
The bowl was wooden and smooth. It was carved by Quinhagak residents somewhere between 400 and 600 years ago and was one of thousands of cultural objects scattered along the coastline.
The storm had unearthed it from an archaeological dig site called Nunalleq that sits near the village. It's renowned as one of the best examples of Alaska Native Yup'ik culture before Western contact and serves as an important link to Quinhagak's past. Not only had the storm scattered many objects from the site, it also increased the risks for what was still in the ground by eroding more of the land buffer between the Bering Sea and where these artifacts are buried.
This past summer, a team of archaeologists came to the village for an emergency dig to recover as much as possible before the next big storm.
Precious objects slowly being excavated
Archaeologists have been working at this dig site since 2009, according to lead archaeologist Rick Knecht. He says that after thawing permafrost revealed significant numbers of these objects in the early 2000s, the village deliberated and decided to try to save these pieces of their culture.
They include hand-carved animals, grass rope, sewing needles, ornate wooden masks and pieces of kayaks.
According to the archaeologists, the frozen ground has helped preserve artifacts composed of organic material, which they say would have likely eroded under different conditions.
The team, Knecht says, is mostly made up of volunteers and has a shoestring budget with funding from the Pacific Northwest Archaeological Society and the Daughters of the American Revolution, among others.
The whole archaeological site is about the size of two Olympic-size pools, but the emergency dig area is smaller, about the size of a backyard pool. It's a hole that has been dug around the buried remnants of several sod houses that date back 400 to 500 years.
Digging against time
Charlotta Hillerdal, who has been part of this excavation for over 15 years, was home in Scotland when she heard about the storm damage.
"I was crying," Hillerdal said. "It was a horrible feeling."
Knecht said that since the dig began, they've watched the Bering Sea creep closer and closer to the site. Shorelines in this part of Alaska are now more vulnerable to erosion due, in part, to decreasing sea ice and permafrost thaw. Both are fueled by human-caused climate change.
Last October's storm closed the distance even more. Now, at some high tides, seawater can reach into the pit.
"It's every bit as tough as working in front of bulldozers," Knecht explained.
In October, the flooding was so extensive that the site was covered by feet of water. When it receded, it took many valuable objects with it. They're worried that could happen again.
Knecht said they hope to return to the site next summer, though they're still raising the money to do so through a GoFundMe campaign and Quinhagak Heritage Inc., the nonprofit that oversees the dig.
"I'll be damned if I'm going to leave this for the waves," Knecht said. "It's like you might as well take those pieces of artwork we're finding and skip it off into the Bering Sea."
"When you know that you come from a people that were so resilient … you get a boost"
At the Nunalleq Culture and Archaeology Center — a museum-style building and lab — these pieces of Quinhagak's past are available for their direct descendants to access, along with the public.
"We all as humans want to know who we are and where we come from, and having the Nunalleq there for us strengthens that," said Elizabeth Church, director of Quinhagak Heritage Inc., which manages the center as well as the dig.
Church said seeing the artifacts exploded onto the beach was traumatic. It underscored the community's desire to steward their ancestors' belongings.
"They are interwoven into us as people, and we feel a great sense of responsibility to care for them well, and to take them into the future with us," Church said.
There's evidence of people adapting to environmental change and making technological progress.
"When you know that you come from a people that were so resilient and so capable and so talented and so smart — you get a boost," Church said. "It's amazing."
She said that with fall storm season fast approaching, the scramble is urgent to recover what they can of this past.
