title: Hundreds recruited to help foster kids visit birth families in NSW
content:
NSW overhauls supervised foster care visits with new Family Time team
In short:
NSW's approach to foster care supervised visits has been revamped with new specialist workers.
Family Time helps kids build connections with their birth families, and ease the impact of separation.
Parents and children will now catch-up at "beautiful venues" like parks or ice skating rinks to create "positive memories".
Thousands of children in foster care are improving ties with their birth families, as part of an overhauled supervision system in New South Wales.
More than 300 specialist workers have now been recruited by the Department of Communities and Justice to accompany children on supervised family visits.
These Family Time visits can vary widely in setting — from picnics and sports events, to theme parks and zoos.
Kylie Stone is among the recent recruits, whose own childhood experience of family separation motivated her to join the team.
She grew up in outer-western Sydney, where her father grappled with addiction and went to prison when she was aged 11.
"I just remember waiting for all my letters to come or waiting for phone calls and wanting to go and see my dad," she said.
Now, Ms Stone is determined to make a difference to other families' lives in her old neighbourhood.
One of her proudest moments in the job involved a young mother and her child who had been removed from her care while she sought treatment for an addiction.
"I started working with her when her baby was three months old. We shared her first Easter, her first birthday, her first Christmas together,"she said.
"There were days that she did struggle and she's like, 'I don't know if I can do this', and she's actually now gone through final orders and she's getting her little girl back.
"Honestly, it gives me goosebumps."
Ms Stone acknowledges while permanent family reunification is not always feasible, supervised contact provides a "safe place" to build connections and ease the impact of separation.
Supervised family visits have long been a feature of the state's foster care system, but previously they were run by caseworkers in the private sector.
It was a system that Families and Communities Minister Kate Washington argued was plagued by poor training and a high staff turnover, which would often make it a distressing experience.
"When a different person was turning up to their door every single time, they didn't know the child, they didn't know the families,"she said.
Ms Washington said bringing the program in-house had ensured there was rigorous oversight and training of workers.
There is also a strong focus on making sure Family Time workers are culturally-matched, and to date, almost 20 per cent of the team identifies as Aboriginal.
Growing focus on Aboriginal kinships
One of the new program officers is Cody McGrady Miller, a Gomeroi and Wonnurua man who was 12 years old when he was removed from his mother's care by caseworkers and police.
He and his sister were placed in the care of his great-aunty in south-west Sydney, and said the turnover of casework teams "make it really difficult".
"Back then, there was not much understanding around Aboriginal kinship systems and the way in which our communities support children," he said.
Now he works with the Family Time team in Tamworth, and has led efforts to ensure supervised visits are culturally appropriate.
"For us as Aboriginal people, I think that connection is one of the most significant parts of culture, and with the lived experience, I feel like that I can really contribute to ensuring that there's a better experience for children and young people in care," he said.
Building a 'legacy' for families
Supervisors typically write detailed reports after each visit, which is often used for family law or court proceedings.
But Nicholle Andreuzza from the Department of Communities and Justice said there had been a move away from the "clinical" approach to supervising family visits.
"What we're seeing now is beautiful venues," Ms Andreuzza said.
"We're seeing kids and mum and dad at soccer fields with the support of their Family Time work, we're seeing kids having experiences like ice skating, we do some visits in home when safe to do so."
Ms Andreuzza said the Family Time workers also played an important "legacy" role, by taking pictures during the visits.
"So for kids when they get older … they're able to look at photographs and look at all of the positive moments that they've had with their mums, dads, brothers, sisters, uncles, aunties," she said.

title: Einer der ältesten Bräuche – «Fürio de Bach brönnt»: Aarau feiert Jubiläum des Bachfischet
content:
Es ist dunkel, wo sonst Strassenlaternen die bekannten bemalten Giebel beleuchten und in Schaufenstern Uhren glitzern. Am Strassenrand der Altstadt drängen sich die Menschen. Trommelschläge der Tambouren kündigen den nächtlichen Umzug an. Ein Raunen geht durch die Menge. Die Kinder ziehen durch die Stadt, der Schein ihrer selbst gebastelten Lampions erhellt die Gesichter und Fassaden. In Aarau ist Bachfischet.
-
Bild 1 von 5. Mit Lampions und Gesang ziehen die Aarauer Schulkinder durch die abgedunkelte Stadt. Fische sind ein beliebtes Motiv. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
-
Bild 2 von 5. «De Bach isch do, de Bach isch do», singen die Kinder am Bachfischet. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
-
Bild 3 von 5. Schulklassen und Jugendvereine basteln eigene Lampions. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
-
Bild 4 von 5. Der Bach ist eines der Themen, die immer wieder auftauchen. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
-
Bild 5 von 5. Am Ende des Umzugs wird ein Teil der Lampions verbrannt. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
Der Bachfischet wird dieses Jahr wohl schon zum 500. Mal gefeiert. Bereits 1526 wurde der Bachfischet nämlich erstmals in einem Ratsprotokoll der Stadt Aarau erwähnt. Aarau hat keinen natürlichen Fluss, das Gewässer wurde künstlich angelegt. «Der Stadtbach war die Lebensader der Stadt, bis die ersten Quellen gefasst werden konnten», betont Historikerin Stefanie Mahrer. Eine mittelalterliche Stadt konnte ohne Bach nicht überleben. Man habe Trinkwasser, Löschwasser und Wasserkraft für das Gewerbe gebraucht.
-
Bild 1 von 2. Der Bachfischet-Umzug zieht durch die Rathausgasse in der Aarauer Altstadt. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
-
Bild 2 von 2. Die Lampions erleuchten die sonst stockfinstere Stadt. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
Einmal jährlich musste die Stadt Aarau das Bachbett des Stadtbachs reinigen. Dafür wurde der Bach gestaut. Die Reinigung dauerte in der Regel vier Tage und wurde als Fronarbeit erledigt. Vier Tage ohne Trink- und Löschwasser – eine Herausforderung für die Bewohnerinnen und Bewohner. Deswegen legten Haushalte einen Wasservorrat in Kesseln und Zubern an.
Der Bachfischet 1950
-
Bild 1 von 4. Einmal jährlich wurde der Aarauer Stadtbach gestaut und geputzt, wie die Aufnahmen der Schweizer Filmwochenschau von 1950 zeigen. Bildquelle: Schweizer Filmwochenschau 1950.
-
Bild 3 von 4. Für vier Tage musste die gesamte Stadt ohne Wasser auskommen, bis der Brunnenmeister die Schleuse wieder öffnete und der Bach wieder in die Stadt fliessen konnte. Bildquelle: Schweizer Filmwochenschau 1950.
-
Bild 4 von 4. In Suhr schickten die Kinder Kerzen mit dem Stadtbach nach Aarau. Bildquelle: Schweizer Filmwochenschau 1950.
September sei für das Putzen des Bachs die ideale Zeit gewesen, sagt Stefanie Mahrer. Nach der Ernte und vor der Weinlese, weil da die Arbeitskräfte und die Kessel zur Verfügung gestanden hätten.
1784 musste die Bachreinigung frühzeitig abgebrochen werden – wegen eines Grossbrands. Daraufhin wurde der Stadtbach «notfallmässig vorzeitig geflutet», wie die Heinerich Wirri-Zunft schreibt, die sich der Pflege der Aarauer Bräuche verschrieben hat, insbesondere des Bachfischet. Zahlreiche Gebäude seien niedergebrannt, der Brandstifter habe seine Tat vor der Hinrichtung gestanden.
Heute gilt der Bachfischet laut der Heinerich Wirri-Zunft «als ältester dauernd gelebter Brauch in der Schweiz». Dass der Brauch so lange überlebt hat, ist nicht selbstverständlich. Im Laufe des 19. Jahrhunderts sei er in Vergessenheit geraten, der Bach habe wegen der modernen Wasserleitungen an Bedeutung verloren, erklärt Historikerin Stefanie Mahrer. «1922 muss der absolute Tiefpunkt gewesen sein, als nur noch ein paar Vereinzelte am Bachfischet teilgenommen haben.»
Daraufhin wurde die Heinerich Wirri-Zunft gegründet, die sich des Brauchs annahm. Initiiert wurde die Zunft vom Arzt und rechtsnationalen Aarauer Politiker Eugen Bircher. Zwar seien die Anfänge klar im rechtsbürgerlichen Milieu. Der Bachfischet sei aber absolut unpolitisch, betont Mahrer, die als Co-Autorin die Geschichte der Stadt Aarau erforscht. «Ohne die Heinerich Wirri-Zunft hätten wir das wunderbare Fest, wie wir es heute haben, nicht mehr.»
Wenn am Ende der Reinigung der Stadtbach wieder in sein Bett geleitet wurde, war das ein feierlicher Moment: Die Kinder in Suhr setzten Schiffchen mit Kerzen auf den Bach, die Kinder in Aarau empfingen diese, zogen in einem Umzug durch die Stadt und sangen das Bachfischet-Lied.
Früher trugen die Kinder ausgehöhlte Kürbisse oder Räbeliechtli, heute sind es selbst gebastelte Laternen an Haselruten. Beendet wird der Umzug mit dem «Mords-Chlapf», einem grossen einzelnen Böllerschuss. Auf einem grossen Feuer werden die Haselruten und teilweise auch die Lampions verbrannt.

title: Nunas Nede, Ritual Adat Masyarakat Kesik Jaga Mata Air
content:
- Nunas Nede menjadi ritual tahunan masyarakat Desa Kesik untuk menyambut musim hujan sekaligus menjaga hubungan dengan sumber air. Warga membawa hasil bumi dan mengambil air dari tujuh mata air yang kemudian disatukan dalam prosesi adat. Bagi masyarakat Kesik, ritual ini bukan sekadar permohonan agar hujan turun, tetapi juga pengingat bahwa keberlangsungan kehidupan dan pertanian bergantung pada kelestarian sumber air.
- Perubahan musim dan krisis iklim membuat keberadaan ritual semakin penting bagi petani. Masyarakat mulai merasakan musim hujan yang tidak menentu, penurunan debit sejumlah mata air, serta kesulitan menentukan waktu tanam. Nunas Nede kemudian tidak hanya dipandang sebagai warisan leluhur, tetapi juga sebagai bentuk kesadaran masyarakat menghadapi perubahan lingkungan.
- Ritual diikuti aksi nyata menjaga ekosistem mata air secara gotong royong. Selain berdoa, warga membersihkan mata air, mengangkat lumpur dan sampah, memperbaiki saluran air, serta menanam pohon di sekitar sumber air. Mereka juga mempertahankan aturan adat seperti larangan menebang pohon tertentu dan membuang sampah sembarangan karena memahami hubungan antara vegetasi dan keberlangsungan mata air.
- Nunas Nede menjadi sarana mempertahankan pengetahuan ekologis dan mentransmisikannya kepada generasi muda. Anak-anak dan remaja dilibatkan dalam pembersihan mata air, prosesi ritual, serta mendengarkan sejarah sumber air dari para tetua. Bagi masyarakat Kesik, mempertahankan tradisi berarti sekaligus mempertahankan pengetahuan lokal tentang cara menjaga air, pertanian, dan lingkungan di tengah perubahan zaman.
Puluhan orang memadati halaman rumah Amaq Marni siang itu. Sembilan hari menjelang pelaksanaan ritual Nunas Nede, para petani di Desa Kesik mulai mengantarkan hasil pertaniannya ke rumah perempuan 73 tahun tu. Nantinya, hasil tani berupa beras dan ketan itu akan warga olah menjadi makanan tradisional pelengkap ritual.
Di bawah tenda sederhana di halaman rumah, para perempuan tampak sibuk menampi beras, menyiapkan kelapa, dan mengaduk adonan ketan dalam wadah besar. Di sudut lain, sejumlah laki-laki bercengkrama sambil menyusun perlengkapan ritual.
Dua hari setelahnya, satu per satu warga Desa Kesik mulai berjalan menuju sumber mata air di kaki perbukitan. Di tangan mereka terdapat dulang berisi hasil bumi, ada padi, ketan, buah-buahan, ayam kampung, dan kendi kecil yang akan diisi air dari mata air yang mereka jaga turun-temurun.
Bagi masyarakat Desa Kesik, Kecamatan Masbagik, Kabupaten Lombok Timur, Nusa Tenggara Barat, perjalanan menuju mata air bukan sekadar prosesi budaya. Ia adalah perjalanan spiritual, perjalanan ekologis, sekaligus sejarah yang mereka warisi dari para leluhur. Ritual itu populer dengan sebutan Nunas Nede, tradisi tahunan yang warga gelar jelang pergantian musim dari kemarau menuju musim hujan.
Berawal dari kekhawatiran
Di desa yang sebagian besar penduduknya menggantungkan hidup pada pertanian itu, perubahan musim bukan perkara sederhana. Hujan menentukan apakah sawah dapat mereka tanami. Ketika kemarau terlalu panjang, sumber mata air menyusut. Sawah retak. Petani mulai cemas. Karena itulah, ritual Nunas Nede lahir dari kegelisahan kolektif masyarakat terhadap alam yang menjadi sumber kehidupan mereka.
Tradisi ini warga gelar setiap tahun pada akhir musim kemarau. Prosesi mulai dengan pengambilan air dari tujuh mata air yang tersebar di Desa Kesik. Air dari tujuh sumber itu warga satukan sebagai simbol persatuan kehidupan dan keberkahan alam. Ritual berlanjut dengan doa bersama, arak-arakan hasil bumi, zikir, serta makan bersama.
Di balik ritual nan sakral dan meriah itu, tersimpan pesan yang jauh lebih dalam yaitu hubungan manusia dengan air.
Menurut berbagai catatan budaya dan penelitian akademik, Nunas Nede merupakan bentuk permohonan kepada Tuhan agar hujan turun dan pertanian kembali subur. Namun bagi masyarakat Kesik, ritual ini juga menjadi pengingat bahwa air tidak akan pernah ada jika manusia berhenti menjaganya.
Amaq Marni, Pemangku adat Desa Kesik, mengatakan, ritual itu sebagai cara menjaga keseimbangan alam dan mengingatkan masyarakat agar tidak merusak sumber kehidupan mereka.
“Air itu bukan cuma untuk manusia. Air itu hidup untuk semua makhluk. Kalau mata air rusak, sawah rusak, kehidupan juga ikut hilang,” katanya saat Mongabay temui di sela prosesi ritual.
Bagi Marni, ritual adat ini bukan sekadar seremoni tahunan, juga bentuk komunikasi antara manusia dengan alam. Karena itu, setiap tahapan ritual memiliki makna, mulai dari pengambilan air, membersihkan mata air, hingga menanam pohon di sekitar sumber air.
Tradisi itu juga menunjukkan bagaimana masyarakat Sasak di Desa Kesik membangun pengetahuan ekologis secara turun-temurun. Di tengah modernisasi pertanian dan perubahan pola hidup masyarakat desa, mereka tetap mempertahankan ritual yang menempatkan alam sebagai pusat kehidupan.
Tak ada sekat sosial
Pagi itu, warga berjalan beriringan menuju salah satu sumber mata air. Para perempuan membawa dulang berisi makanan tradisional. Anak-anak muda ikut membantu membawa perlengkapan ritual. Sementara para tetua adat memimpin doa dan pembacaan zikir.
Di sepanjang perjalanan, warga saling menyapa dan bercengkerama. Tidak ada sekat sosial. Semua melebur sebagai bagian dari masyarakat tani yang memiliki ketergantungan sama terhadap air dan tanah.
Suasana seperti itu membuat Nunas Nede tidak hanya menjadi ritual spiritual, tetapi juga ruang memperkuat solidaritas sosial warga desa. Penelitian dari Universitas Mataram menyebut tradisi ini berfungsi mempererat hubungan sosial masyarakat sekaligus mempertahankan nilai gotong royong antar petani.
Muhamad Kadri, Kepala Desa Kesik, mengatakan masyarakat desa masih mempertahankan ritual itu karena mereka memahami betapa pentingnya air bagi kehidupan pertanian di Kesik.
“Kami hidup dari sawah. Kalau sumber air hilang, masyarakat akan kehilangan penghidupan. Jadi ritual ini bukan sekadar adat, tapi cara masyarakat menjaga kesadaran bersama tentang pentingnya air,” katanya.
Dia bilang, Desa Kesik memiliki sejarah panjang sebagai desa agraris. Sebagian besar wilayah desa berupa lahan pertanian yang bergantung pada sistem irigasi dari mata air alami. Karena itu, masyarakat sejak dulu memiliki aturan adat untuk melindungi kawasan mata air.
Apalagi, dalam beberapa tahun terakhir, kekhawatiran masyarakat terhadap perubahan iklim semakin besar. Musim hujan tak menentu. Debit air di beberapa sumber mulai menurun. Sebagian petani mengaku mulai kesulitan menentukan waktu tanam.
Kondisi itu membuat ritual Nunas Nede terasa semakin relevan.
Bagi Amaq Sati, petani yang sejak kecil mengikuti ritual itu, perubahan cuaca sekarang jauh berbeda ketimbang masa lalu. “Dulu musim gampang ditebak. Sekarang kadang hujan terlambat, kadang terlalu deras. Kami petani jadi bingung,” ujarnya.
Masyarakat desa mulai merasakan dampak nyata perubahan lingkungan. Karena itu, ritual adat kini bukan hanya tentang tradisi leluhur, tetapi juga bentuk perlawanan atas krisis ekologi yang terjadi saat ini.
Dalam ritual itu, masyarakat tidak hanya berdoa meminta hujan. Mereka juga membersihkan kawasan mata air, memungut sampah, memperbaiki saluran kecil, dan menanam pohon di sekitar sumber air. Aktivitas itu dilakukan bersama-sama oleh warga dari berbagai dusun.
Di salah satu sumber mata air, beberapa pemuda terlihat menyingkirkan ranting dan lumpur yang menghambat aliran air. Di sisi lain, perempuan menyiapkan makanan untuk disantap bersama setelah ritual selesai.
Gotong royong seperti itu menjadi bagian penting dalam tradisi Nunas Nede. Bagi warga Kesik, menjaga air bukan tugas individu, melainkan tanggung jawab kolektif seluruh masyarakat.
Penelitian tentang ritual ini mencatat bahwa mata air dalam tradisi Nunas Nede dipandang sebagai simbol kehidupan yang harus dihormati dan dijaga keberlangsungannya. Kesadaran ekologis itu lahir jauh sebelum isu perubahan iklim jadi perhatian.
Masyarakat Kesik telah memahami bahwa kerusakan hutan dan hilangnya vegetasi di sekitar mata air akan berdampak langsung terhadap kehidupan pertanian mereka.
Karena itu, beberapa lokasi mata air di Desa Kesik masih warga pertahankan sebagai ruang yang tidak boleh rusak. Ada pohon-pohon besar yang terus tumbuh dan terlarang untuk ditebang.
Bagi masyarakat Kesik, ritual itu juga memperlihatkan bagaimana budaya dan ekologi saling terhubung. Ketika tradisi hilang, maka pengetahuan tentang cara menjaga alam perlahan ikut menghilang. Karena itu, mempertahankan Nunas Nede berarti mempertahankan masa depan desa mereka sendiri.
Cara menjaga air
Prosesi pengambilan air dari tujuh mata air menjadi bagian paling sakral dalam ritual Nunas Nede. Air dari masing-masing sumber warga ambil menggunakan wadah khusus, lalu mereka arak menuju lokasi ritual.
Sudah sejak lama, warga meyakini ketujuh mata air adalah sumber kehidupan. Sebagian mengaliri sawah, sebagian lagi menjadi sumber kebutuhan rumah tangga warga. Karena itulah, masyarakat memandang mata air bukan sekadar sumber air biasa, melainkan ruang kehidupan yang harus mereka jaga.
Dalam perjalanan menuju mata air, warga biasanya berhenti di beberapa titik untuk berdoa bersama. Selain itu, di beberapa lokasi, warga juga melakukan ritual nyawik, menandai area mata air menggunakan simbol-simbol adat sambil memanjatkan harapan agar sumber air tetap lestari.
Prosesi nyawik menjadi simbol penghormatan terhadap alam sekaligus bentuk pengingat agar masyarakat terus menjaga lingkungan sekitar mata air. Karena itu, setiap ritual tahunan selalu diikuti kegiatan penanaman pohon.
Amaq Marni mengatakan, leluhur mereka sejak dulu telah mengingatkan bahwa hilangnya pepohonan akan membuat mata air mati perlahan. “Kalau pohon habis ditebang, air juga ikut pergi. Itu pesan orang tua dulu yang selalu kami jaga,” katanya.
Warga menyadari bahwa keberadaan mata air tidak lagi bisa dianggap aman selamanya. Karena itu, ritual adat berkembang menjadi ruang edukasi lingkungan bagi generasi muda.
Anak-anak dan remaja desa mereka ajak untuk membersihkan mata air, membawa hasil bumi, hingga mendengar cerita para tetua tentang sejarah sumber air di desa mereka.
Muhamad Kadri mengatakan pelibatan generasi muda menjadi hal penting agar pengetahuan lokal tidak hilang. “Kalau anak muda tidak dikenalkan sejak sekarang, nanti mereka hanya tahu air keluar dari keran tanpa tahu bagaimana menjaganya.”
Dalam beberapa tahun terakhir, Nunas Nede kian populer dan dan menarik perhatian masyarakat luar desa. Namun warga berusaha menjaga agar ritual itu tak hanya hanya pertunjukan wisata yang makin kehilangan makna utamanya.
Amak Sati mengatakan dirinya selalu ikut ritual sejak kecil karena merasa kehidupan keluarganya sangat bergantung pada keberadaan air. “Kami ini hidup dari sawah. Kalau air tidak ada, kami tidak bisa tanam apa-apa,” katanya.
Dalam praktik sehari-hari, masyarakat Kesik memiliki berbagai aturan tidak tertulis untuk menjaga mata air. Terdapat larangan membuang sampah sembarangan, menebang pohon tertentu, hingga kewajiban membersihkan area sumber air secara berkala.
Tradisi itu menunjukkan bagaimana masyarakat adat membangun sistem perlindungan lingkungan berbasis nilai budaya dan spiritualitas.
Menjelang siang, prosesi ritual mencapai puncaknya di lokasi utama. Warga duduk melingkar menikmati hidangan hasil bumi yang mereka bawa bersama. Anak-anak berlarian di sekitar mata air. Sementara para tetua adat kembali memanjatkan doa.
Di tengah lantunan zikir dan suara gemericik air, ritual itu seolah menyampaikan satu pesan sederhana: manusia tidak pernah benar-benar hidup sendiri. Selama masyarakat Kesik masih berjalan menuju tujuh mata air setiap tahun, selama itu pula ingatan tentang hubungan manusia dan alam akan terus hidup di desa kecil di kaki Lombok Timur itu.
*****

title: South Africa: Enable Through Dance - Breaking Barriers for Dancers With Disabilities
content:
"It's about giving young people living with disabilities a chance to explore potential that they have not before"
To mark ten years of the Enable Through Dance programme, learners with disabilities took centre stage with professional dancers from the Moving Into Dance non-profit company at the Keorapetse William Kgositsile Theatre at the University of Johannesburg Arts Centre on the weekend.
The programme, established in 2016, works with over 160 learners from several schools and organisations across Johannesburg. They use dance and movement to give young people with disabilities opportunities for creative expression, while building their confidence and self-esteem.
Moving Into Dance, based in Newtown, was established in 1978 by Sylvia Glasser. As one of only a few mixed-race dance groups at the time, it used dance as cultural resistance against the apartheid regime.
Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines
The anniversary performance at the weekend was open to the public free of charge.
Nadia Virasamy, CEO of Moving Into Dance, said the programme started with the organisation having to reconsider its own understanding of dance and disability.
Virasamy said this was challenging for a professional dance company whose work had traditionally focused on particular ideas of physical ability and movement.
"It isn't about ability or disability, it's about inclusivity," she said. "It's about giving young people living with disabilities a chance to explore this potential that they have not before."
Moving Into Dance brings in specialists to work with the dancers and facilitators. The programme eventually became a weekly initiative in schools and organisations around Johannesburg.
The project offers more than simply teaching dance techniques, said Virasamy. She has seen young people become more confident and comfortable when interacting with people.
"There's no demarcation about who can do what within the space," she said. "It's everybody together embracing this beautiful art form we call dance."
One of the dancers, 29-year-old Tebogo Lelaletse, is from the North West and uses a wheelchair. He started dancing in 2019 with Unmute Cape Town before joining the Moving Into Dance company.
He said dance has given him a way to tell stories and express emotions without having to rely on speech.
"Sometimes I feel like when I'm speaking, everybody's muting you," he said. "So, it's better if you talk through movement."
Lelaletse also encouraged other people with disabilities to explore their talents in spite of their fears.
"Whatever gift we have, let's use it," he said.
Professional dancer Lesego Dihemo, who teaches learners at Johannesburg School for Autism, said she initially struggled because she had no experience of working with autistic learners.
Dihemo was trained through the Enable Through Dance programme and also did her own research about autism and seeking advice from teachers at the school.
She said the experience changed her as both a teacher and a dancer.
"When you are with the kids, you find the love, the laughter, you become free," she said. "Your creativity just opens up with them."
She said she has also developed a better understanding of what inclusive practice really means.

title: El legado de las artistas trans que pusieron la ciudad de Las Palmas en la vanguardia
content: El Archivo ‘Viejas Glorias’ recupera la memoria escénica del colectivo trans en Gran Canaria entre 1976 y 1998 y rescata su aportación artística a un panorama cultural que despertaba de cuarenta años de dictaduraNueva ola de desabastecimiento de medicamentos para personas trans: “No podemos ser conejillos de indias” Cuando Luis Lorite se embarcó en la creación del Archivo Viejas Glorias, lo hizo bajo el convencimiento de que el legado artístico de las artistas trans y travestis desde 1976 no solo debe ser rescatado, sino celebrado. Todo parte de la búsqueda de testimonios y testigos de lo que fue un día una ciudad abierta al mundo por su puerto, que salía de una dictadura cruel de 40 años y de un colectivo de mujeres que quería probar todas las formas de libertad a través de la canción, la danza y el humor con la generosidad de situar a la ciudad de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria en un circuito cultural de repertorios y propuestas que se estaban dando en las salas y teatros del panorama internacional. Cartel 'Hollywood travesti' en la sala Britania. Las Palmas de Gran Canaria. “Este proyecto surge de una vieja gloria, Margaret García”, cuenta a esta redacción el coordinador del archivo. “La conocí haciendo una campaña del Orgullo para el Gobierno de Canarias en el año 2024, donde ella representaba al colectivo trans. Me comentó que había sido artista en una sala de fiestas de Las Palmas hacía cincuenta años y que tenía el sueño de volverse a encontrar con su público, que ella creía que, de tener su misma edad, estaría entonces en centros de mayores”. La artista trans Margaret Archivo 'Viejas Glorias'. El destino quiso que Margaret falleciera en la misma semana que el Instituto de las Mujeres del Ministerio de Igualdad les concedió la financiación para el proyecto, convirtiéndolo, del todo, en un homenaje a su memoria. “Ya no nos hacía falta más confirmación”. La dimensión artística Para Lorite, que ha trabajado toda su vida en las artes escénicas, era crucial que este proyecto restituyera a las artistas trans una dimensión a veces secuestrada por la visión que de ellas se tiene como víctimas o supervivientes. Expandir la mirada y ver la aportación que legaron y la calidad de sus espectáculos para atrapar a un público estando más de diez años en cartel. Carla Antonelli. “Tenía la hipótesis, y la he confirmado, de que eran artistas, creadoras, intérpretes, que luego tuvieron mucho éxito. En la sala Britania, llenaron de domingo a martes durante más de una década, haciendo hasta dos pases y trayendo guaguas de turistas desde el Sur”. La valentía de ser ellas Decía el poeta griego Píndaro que ojalá todos los humanos lleguen a ser quienes realmente son. A veces se tarda toda una vida y otras veces no se llega a tiempo. Las viejas glorias tuvieron la valentía de apostarlo todo a la libertad y a ser quienes realmente fueron a un precio a veces muy alto, para ir cien pasos por delante de quienes en público las criticaban y en privado las envidiaban. “Representaban ese cambio de piel del país entero como nadie, con una mirada curiosa, que va más allá de lo artístico. Representaban qué se podía hacer con esa nueva libertad que estaba estrenando el país. La libertad en potencia después de cuarenta años de castración moral, mental y cultural. Esas mujeres cogieron esa libertad y la dinamitaron”. Un archivo en construcción, memoria de convivencia Aunque el trabajo de recopilación de Viejas Glorias, presentado esta semana en Gran Canaria, se ha centrado en el periodo comprendido entre 1976 y 1998, no pretende ser un relato cerrado sino seguir recopilando archivos, fotografías, programas, cartelería y continuando ese diálogo entre público y artistas. “Todas las fotografías que están en el proyecto y que se pueden ver en la página web reflejan a personas que están viviendo en su ciudad, moviéndose entre la gente. Por ejemplo, Sandy, que además de intérprete era costurera, que cosía para el carnaval, y en esa se eliminan los prejuicios”. Sandy, artista trans del barrio de Las Rehoyas y costurera. Luis Lorite invita a todas aquellas personas que quieran contribuir con material a hacerlo a través del formulario web del archivo. Esta redacción termina la entrevista preguntándole si el arte debe ser transformador: “Es la única razón para hacer arte”, sentencia.

title: Daughter brings her father’s cendol legacy home
content:
Old telephones, lamps and a retro radio fill its interior, while diners enjoy bowls of cendol and ABC outside beneath the raised house.
This is Warung Cendol Wak Paad, now run by second-generation owner Siti Zulaika Supaad, who’s keeping her family’s legacy alive.
Her father, Supaad Musran, began selling cendol in 1990, raising Zulaika and her six siblings with the income he earned. As each child grew older, they took turns minding the stall whenever their parents needed a break.
“I started helping out at the stall when I was in Standard Six and enjoyed it,” Zulaika told FMT Lifestyle.
Those hours nurtured her love for her father’s business and sparked her entrepreneurial spirit. She later sold cendol during school Canteen Days and at university.
The stall closed in 2004 when Supaad fell ill. Two of Zulaika’s sisters later sold cendol, but neither venture lasted. Still, the story of the family’s cendol business had another chapter waiting to be written.
Zulaika graduated in heritage studies during the pandemic, but struggled to find work and contemplated starting a business.
“I thought about my family’s business and asked my father whether he still remembered the cendol recipe,” recalled Zulaika, 29.
He did, and he encouraged her to go ahead, especially since former customers wanted him to revive the business. Some had enjoyed his cendol as schoolchildren and longed to taste it again.
In June 2021, Zulaika began selling cendol near her father’s former stall. His business never had a name, so she called hers “Warung Cendol Wak Paad” in his honour.
Zulaika, who is of Javanese heritage, explained that “Wak” means “uncle” in Javanese, while “Paad” is the name by which her father is affectionately known.
Zulaika stayed true to Supaad’s cendol and ABC recipes. Nothing pleased her more than hearing long-time customers say her cendol tastes just like her father’s.
As the business grew, Zulaika saw potential in the family’s old home, which was largely unused. Remembering how alive it once was, especially during Hari Raya, she longed to fill it with warmth again.
Some customers warned the house’s quiet location near a dead end would hurt the business – but Zulaika trusted her instincts.
After renovating the place, she opened in October 2021 and expanded the menu.
To create a nostalgic atmosphere, she travelled to Indonesia and Egypt for retro décor items. Others in the house are cherished family keepsakes – her father’s old ice shaver, her mother’s trays and a wooden bench that belonged to her late grandfather, Musran Surajak.
Fun fact: Zulaika’s roots in the area run deep: Musran established the street where her father first sold cendol and where her business now stands.
Indeed, the cendol does not disappoint, combining fresh santan with green cendol as well as palm sugar syrup and red beans prepared in-house. You can also opt for cendol with corn or glutinous rice.
For something richer, the decadent ABC Coklat comes crowned with roasted peanuts and chocolate sauce, while the creamy Jelly Cocktail Susu brims with a variety of fruits.
Savoury favourites include nasi lemak with fried chicken and house-made sambal as well as Penang laksa. The mee bandung is equally satisfying, with prawns, egg and more in a gravy.
Lighter bites include fruit rojak, a traditional Malay pancake called lempeng and crispy tempeh served with sambal kicap, a spicy soy dipping sauce.
Today, word has spread beyond Klang, drawing visitors from Kelantan and Johor. Even Singaporeans and Koreans have stopped by.
“I’m proud and happy that I am able to keep my family’s legacy alive,” she said.
“I hope customers will enjoy the cendol and the atmosphere I have created – as though they’re enjoying a bowl of cendol in a kampung or in their grandmother’s home,” she concluded.

title: PATRIMOINE - Le Morengy gagne du terrain
content: À Antsiranana, le Morengy attire les foules et dynamise l’activité locale. Cette pratique traditionnelle gagne ainsi en visibilité dans la région Diana.Les spectateurs sont restés jusqu’au bout, captivés par les affrontements entre les combattants, notamment le combat très attendu entre Kakabe Boucher et Zandry Bogossi.Le combat traditionnel Morengy s’affirme comme un véritable moteur d’attractivité dans la région Diana. Bien plus qu’un affrontement sportif, il s’impose progressivement comme un rendez-vous culturel capable de rassembler les communautés, d’attirer les visiteurs et de mettre en lumière l’identité du Nord de Madagascar. Dans la région Diana, cette pratique traditionnelle connaît un nouvel élan.À Antsiranana, aucun événement culturel ou sportif ne rivalise avec le Morengy pour drainer les foules. Dès l’annonce d’un combat, le public répond présent, confirmant l’emprise populaire de cette discipline sur la ville. Il ne se contente plus d’attirer les passionnés de combat. À chaque grand rendez-vous, il fait également circuler des personnes, des marchandises et de l’argent. Restauration, transport, commerce, artisanat, téléphonie, hébergement, billetterie et sponsoring : derrière le spectacle populaire se dessine une véritable chaîne de retombées économiques locales.Dans les chefs-lieux des districts comme dans les communes, les rings improvisés ne désemplissent pas. À l’approche d’un combat de Morengy, l’ambiance change. Les spectateurs affluent, les jeunes se mobilisent et les passionnés se retrouvent autour d’un spectacle qui puise directement dans les traditions locales.Mais le Morengy ne se résume pas aux coups échangés et à la confrontation physique. Il constitue également une véritable expression culturelle. Derrière chaque combat se trouvent des codes, une histoire, un savoir-faire transmis et une identité qui se perpétue de génération en génération.AttractivitéL’engouement autour des compétitions montre surtout la capacité du Morengy à attirer du monde. Les combats devien+++nent des occasions de rassemblement populaire, réunissant jeunes, familles, sportifs et curieux. Et même des hauts responsables régionaux.Pour la Région Diana, cette dynamique représente un potentiel d’attractivité à ne pas négliger. Un événement de Morengy bien organisé peut générer des déplacements, stimuler les petits commerces, mobiliser les acteurs culturels et sportifs et créer une animation autour des localités qui accueillent les compétitions. Le ring devient ainsi un espace de rencontre, mais aussi une vitrine du territoire.Cette popularité invite également à réfléchir à une meilleure structuration de la discipline. Organisation des compétitions, formation des combattants, encadrement des jeunes, sécurité, arbitrage, communication et valorisation culturelle constituent autant de leviers susceptibles d’accompagner le développement du Morengy, tout en préservant son authenticité et son identité traditionnelle.Le développement du Morengy peut donc également contribuer à promouvoir des valeurs telles que la discipline, le courage, le respect de l’adversaire et la maîtrise de soi, à condition que la pratique évolue dans un cadre sportif sécurisé et correctement encadré.L’enjeu est désormais de dépasser la simple logique du combat pour faire du Morengy un véritable produit culturel et événementiel du Nord. Associé à la musique, à la gastronomie locale, à l’artisanat et à d’autres expressions culturelles, un grand rendez-vous de Morengy pourrait devenir un événement capable d’attirer non seulement les populations locales, mais également des visiteurs venus d’autres régions et, à terme, des touristes intéressés par les traditions malgaches.Organiser un combat de Morengy représente toutefois un défi financier. Les dépenses sont nombreuses et la continuité des événements repose en grande partie sur la passion et le soutien des amateurs de la discipline. « Nous rencontrons parfois des difficultés financières, mais nous avons aussi des amis et des personnes qui nous soutiennent. C’est grâce à ces appuis que nous arrivons à continuer à organiser les combats. Il y a également les taxes et les frais administratifs, qui représentent une charge importante. Ils doivent être payés à l’avance avant de pouvoir obtenir l’autorisation d’organiser le combat. Pour un Morengy simple, sans artiste, il faut compter environ 400 000 ariary de dépenses. Avec un artiste, le coût peut atteindre 600 000 ariary », explique Iharitiana Ramiandrison, président des comités d’organisation de Morengy dans la région.Raheriniaina

title: Orkney island welcomes first baby in more than three decades
content:
Orkney island welcomes first baby in more than three decades
- Published
A baby has been born on Orkney's most northerly island for the first time in more than three decades.
Parents Jorge Suarez and Alice Traill Ford welcomed baby Duncan Wilder Thorstein Traill Suarez Ford in North Ronaldsay last week.
Islanders toasted the birth with a dram of whisky to celebrate the first newborn in the remote location since Thomas Brookman in August 1992.
The family, who split their time between Costa Rica and Orkney and travelled more than 5,000 miles for the birth, said Duncan was born in a much-loved place.
"North Ronaldsay has always been a very special place for me and I felt alive and free here every summer when I came up as a little girl," Alice told BBC Scotland News.
"My intuition was telling me this was the right place for us so we spoke to the NHS to see if it would be possible.
"We have this beautiful family home steeped in our history and ancestry so to be surrounded by that felt a very special introduction for him to come to Earth."
North Ronaldsay is Orkney's northernmost island and is only accessible from Kirkwall on the main island via a 20-minute plane journey or a ferry, which takes two hours and 40 minutes.
The island is famous for its seaweed-eating sheep, which are mostly confined to the shore by a 13-mile-long drystone wall that encircles the island.
Baby Duncan was born in Holland House, which was built by Alice's ancestors - the Traill family - who bought the island in 1727.
The house has been passed down through generations and is still owned by her family.
Alice's grandfather, Duncan, was the former Laird of North Ronaldsay and provided the inspiration for her son's name.
"I didn't know I was going to name him after Duncan when we arrived but I was sitting on the sofa and right in front of me was a collage of his pictures with my grandmother, so he has been very present with us," Alice said.
"He was an incredible man, very kind and really strong and I felt like there would be no better name than his to carry on and continue his legacy in the world."
Historically when the Laird was on the island, a flag was flown at Holland House to inform the residents.
So when baby Duncan was born at 04:05 on 15 September, Alice and Jorge followed the tradition to share the news.
"Over the years we have found a lot of magical four-leaf clovers here and have kept them in a book," Alice said.
"We stuck a four-leaf clover to a glass bottle, glued a Groatie Buckie to the lid then filled it with whisky and gave it to each of the islanders.
"We raised the flag and everybody opened their whisky and shared a dram - a celebratory drink - together."
A Groatie Buckie is a small, pale pink and white shell found on beaches across Orkney, which in local tradition brings good luck and fortune to the keeper.
The family will return to Costa Rica in November, where the couple run a school.
But Alice is certain her children will have the same opportunity to spend time in North Ronaldsay as she did growing up.
"Duncan will absolutely be back every year," she said.
"One of the things I want to give my children is the gift my mother gave us, bringing us to this island every summer, letting us run wild, explore the island and feel the connection to the community."

title: 烈士没留下照片，一群大学生却"画"出了他们的模样
content: 盛夏的皖中大地，骄阳似火。在安徽合肥，86岁的夏广英正在家中等待着一场迟到了82年的"见面"。 夏广英要"见"的人是她的父亲夏铁烈士。1944年，时任嘉山县洪山乡乡长的夏铁为掩护革命队伍突围，在战斗中牺牲，年仅34岁。彼时的夏广英只有4岁，战乱环境下，家中没有留存父亲照片，父亲的样貌仅依靠亲属口述想象，这成为老人长久的心结。 那天，当安徽师范大学（以下简称安徽师大）美术学院2023级学生李明玥携带着夏铁烈士画像来到夏广英家时，这位已经身患癌症的老人说"这辈子再也没有遗憾了"。 夏广英端详着父亲的画像。 李明玥是该校"红色青春守护人"志愿服务活动团队的成员，该团队的主要工作就是以素描复原烈士容貌，为烈士家属弥补未见亲人的遗憾。 "我终于见到你了" 李明玥画中的夏铁身着粗布短衫，兼具旧式教书先生的温和与革命者的坚毅。端详画像后，夏广英提出调整意见："家里长辈说，父亲的眉毛比较浓密，画像看着浅了些。" 李明玥当即取出绘画工具，对画像眉眼线条进行调整。修改完成后，夏广英反复抚摸画中人面部，低声说道："我永远不会忘记你，我的爸爸，我终于见到你了。" 那一刻，李明玥觉得，"我们是用画笔与时间赛跑，与不断消失的人和记忆赛跑。多画一张烈士画像，就能多促成一个家庭的重逢" 。 为完成这幅画像，她耗时一个半月，创作全程缺少烈士本人影像，只能参照烈属照片，剥离衰老特征，还原其30多岁时的样貌；军装、服饰、发型等细节逐一对照史料，多次将修改稿发给烈士家属，再根据反馈一遍遍调整。 "课本里的英烈大多只有文字评价，很难直观感受他们背后的家庭与人生。"李明玥说，创作过程中她始终担心细节偏差辜负老人的等待，"这不仅仅是一幅素描，更承载着一个女儿一生的等待与思念"。 烈士亲属一家和志愿者团队合影。 在安徽师大，李明玥并不是唯一一个给烈士画像的人。 据该校辅导员王伟介绍，"红色青春守护人"志愿服务活动于2021年启动。当年，王伟带领6名首批学生志愿者开展工作。目前，该团队已有400余名在校学生参与，累计完成对600余位烈士的容貌复原，志愿服务范围覆盖安徽、江西、浙江等地，并常态化前往烈士亲属住所、烈士陵园等地开展送画工作。 一支画笔的使命 王伟告诉《中国科学报》，为烈士画像并非单一的美术创作，而是一套包含史料考证、手绘创作、人工智能影像修复、实地走访、红色宣讲、绘本制作等在内的完整实践流程，学生全程参与各环节。 志愿者前往各地送画。 烈士画像的线索来源分为两类--由各地退役军人事务部门提供的烈士信息，以及一些烈属看到相关的公益事迹报道后主动联系。 "缺少烈士原始照片是普遍的难点。"2024年开始画像的该校学生潘宏宇对此深有体会。1943年春，新婚不久的河北青年王良参加解放军，并随着部队南下。妻子得知部队要经过隔壁村，便连夜缝制袜子送到丈夫手中，这也成了两人的永别。新中国成立后，妻子等来了一纸烈士证明书。此后，她再未改嫁。如今104岁的她想有一张与丈夫的结婚照。 了解到家属诉求后，潘宏宇花了一个多月，前后修改多版画像。他很清楚画像不能有一丝一毫的马虎，这既是对烈士的尊重，又是对烈属的负责。"表情严肃还是微笑？穿长衫还是短衫？戴的徽章什么样式......"他一边画一边思考。 最终，依据烈士弟弟的面部特征以及其遗孀的模糊记忆，潘宏宇绘制了夫妻二人的第一张新婚画像，完成了烈士妻子一辈子的心愿。 潘宏宇绘制的王良夫妻合照。 "我们现在20多岁，王良烈士牺牲时和我们差不多大。"潘宏宇说，"我们在学校安稳学习，他却奔赴战场再也没能回家。绘画过程中，我时常会想他当年作出抉择时的心境。" 作为项目启动时的6名首批志愿者之一，陈如意曾绘制过抗美援朝烈士王金生的画像。她告诉记者："校内人物写生时，我们面对的是模特，创作标准仅停留在造型准确层面。但绘制烈士画像时，除了要还原五官外形，还需要通过线条、神态体现革命者精神特质，绘画不再只是技巧练习。" 志愿者与烈属沟通画像细节。 交付画像只是实践的一环，团队依托美术专业拓展多项配套--组建10余人的红色宣讲团，先后走进部队、中小学、高校开展30余场爱国主义宣讲；成立绘本创作小组，完成《李家发革命故事绘本》《寻淮洲革命故事绘本》等12册红色绘本，印制5000册免费发放至乡村学校。 "铭记他们是我们的责任" 2022年，在为烈士画像项目启动一年后，王伟曾邀请青年志愿者分享画像经历，为新生上了一堂特别的入党启蒙教育课。那些烈士"回家"的故事在学生心中埋下一颗红色种子。每当群里发布"为烈士画像"活动通知，大家都抢着回复，手机很快便被一行行"我报名"刷屏。 "是因为有学分吗？"记者问。 王伟摇了摇头："活动没有学分、没有硬性考核要求，同学们都是发自内心地去做这件事情。" 2023年10月，为了给青年志愿者一个"家"，安徽师大专门成立了"红色青春守护人"工作室，由王伟担任负责人，并在学校大学生活动中心腾出一间画室。青年志愿者从此有了固定作画、交流和开展活动的场所。 工作室内，同学们正在画像。 短短5年时间，从6人志愿小组发展至400 余人常态化参与，为何如此多的学生都愿意参与其中？ "项目全程改变了教师单向布置任务的模式，将实践各环节主动权交给学生。"王伟说，"绘画中的各个环节都有学生参与。反复沟通打磨、线下送画、见证家属圆梦的经历，让学生产生成就感，觉得自己的画笔是有价值、有意义的，他们自然愿意参加。" 据王伟观察，长期以来，美术专业学生常常会被贴上"绘画脱离现实、专业价值有限"的标签。学生的作品仅限于课堂，难以让他们真正感受到美术的社会价值。而该项目将人像素描、插画设计、数字媒体、视觉设计等专业课程内容与红色实践巧妙结合，同步实现了学生专业能力提升与思想教育--课堂人像造型训练直接运用于烈士容貌复原；平面设计技能用于乡村红色文创、烈士陵园展板制作，插画能力用于红色绘本创作；数字方向学生负责人工智能彩色修复、红色主题短视频剪辑...... 此外，为了持续提升学生的获得感，"红色青春守护人"工作室还联合芜湖传媒中心推出了"小手拉大手"身边的榜样系列青春思政课，邀请志愿者分享志愿服务背后的故事，现已录制40余期节目。 安徽师大为"烈士画像"志愿服务宣讲会。 闻清晓是在一次讲座上听一位学姐分享她的志愿服务故事后，决定加入团队的。"我至今还记得那位学姐说：'为了和平，为了祖国，多少人再也看不到亲人的面孔，只剩下脑海中模糊的记忆。保家卫国是他们的使命，而铭记他们是我们的责任。'那一刻，我意识到我们的画笔是有用的，是可以让亲人跨越时空再次相聚的。"她说。 正是为了促成这份跨越时空的团聚，在安徽师大，这场跨越时空的青春对话仍在持续推进。 本文配图均为受访者供图。

title: Freediving helps Indonesia’s Bajau preserve traditions and marine life
content:
Mahari sits at the front of the boat, cigarette in hand, surveying the conditions of the waters off Poto Tano, a small fishing community on the island of Sumbawa, Indonesia. As ketua, the leader of this group of Bajau octopus fishers, Mahari decides which tool they will use today. He silently surveys the waters while the rest of the group sits back and waits for his cue.
The Bajau people are an Indigenous ethnic group spanning Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines. Traditionally living mostly on boats, Bajau people have harvested from the sea through traditional freediving for generations.
In Sumbawa, a recent ban on dives assisted by an air compressor, a dangerous diving technique that provides the diver with continuous air, means these traditional methods have become more valuable than ever. With the right skills, freediving can be gentler on both the environment and the body than more destructive modern practices.
Through expeditions like this one, Mahari and the other fishermen in his community work in cooperation with local NGOs to ensure this knowledge is passed to new generations.
‘Pocong time’
Depending on current and water visibility, Bajau fishers typically use one of two methods to catch octopus. If there is low visibility or a strong current, they will use a “shell” tool adorned with hooks, which they let go in the water and trail behind their boat. If there is better visibility and a weaker current, they enter the water to freedive and use the pocong.
“
Bajau people will always rely on the sea. Now that I have a family and children, I think a lot more about how our kids are going to be impacted.
Mahari, indigenous leader, Bajau Peoples
The pocong, the Indonesian word for “ghost,” is a fishing tool resembling a fake octopus made from wood and felt. Using the pocong, the Bajau dive to around 15–20 meters (50-65 feet) and dangle this decoy alongside the reef to lure an octopus.
When their prey responds curiously to this lure, the fishers either spear the live octopus or grab it by hand. While it may sound simple, this is actually a very skilled technique, as they cannot let the octopus touch the pocong. “They will immediately realise it’s fake and swim away,” says one of the fishermen told Mongabay. “Only 10 people in their community can use the pocong. You need strength and skill.”
On the boat, Mahari suddenly makes his pronouncement, “It’s Pocong time.”
The incredible skills and abilities of the Bajau freedivers are widely known and documented, earning them a global reputation as sea nomads and sparking studies in human physiology and genetics.
Mahari recalls some of his earliest memories in the ocean with a gleam in his eye, “As a Bajau, we know how to dive for as long as we can remember.” Another fisher, Nadir, tells Mongabay: “Bajau people can tell directions without GPS, but by reading the stars, the wind, the air, and the currents. One week after children are born, we bring them to the sea.”
In recent years, many Bajau fishers have felt the pull towards compressor diving as a more economically viable method of harvesting marine species. Often acting as the sole providers for their families, many feel pressure to bring home enough fish to support their households.
Compressor diving is a controversial and dangerous practice where divers breathe in surface air pumped by a compressor through a long hose, allowing them to stay underwater much longer and deeper than they would if freediving.
Extending their time underwater both increases their chances of finding valuable species and of returning home with a larger catch. “With compressor diving, you can stay underwater for much longer,” one of the fishers, Well, tells Mongabay. “If you get more octopus, you get more money. There’s a temptation. We’re human, right?”
But compressor diving systems are often improvised, with no safety checks. The risks and impacts of this form of diving include decompression sickness, air embolisms, paralysis and chronic disabilities, long-term mobility issues and heightened drowning risks. While freediving does have some known health risks, including injuries from pressure changes, they pale in comparison to the risks associated with diving with compressors.
Acknowledging these risks, the Jari Foundation has started to work in partnership with many Bajau fishermen to ease their transition away from compressor diving and towards traditional freediving practices.
Jari is a marine-based program focused on management, ecotourism and community development that currently works across the islands of Lombok and Sumbawa. Together with the local government and a small group of Bajau fishermen, Jari has established a community-based fishery group called PELITA [Persaudaraan Nelayan Gurita (Octopus Fishermen Brotherhood)], says Hani Nusantari, who runs Jari alongside her husband, Boen.
PELITA currently consists of around 40 octopus fishermen, many of whom previously relied on compressor diving. “Recognising the long-term impacts this practice was having on their health, they chose to return to traditional freediving methods while also becoming actively involved in marine conservation initiatives and ecotourism,” Hani says.
Literally translating to “light”, PELITA is named after the traditional oil lamp that once illuminated the homes of fishing families. “PELITA represents a guiding light for coastal communities, bringing people together to care for the sea, strengthen solidarity among fishers, and ensure that marine resources continue to support future generations,” Hani says.
Through PELITA, Hani says she hopes to strengthen fishers’ livelihoods by supporting a return to traditional practices and by combining traditional knowledge with conservation, fisheries management and alternative livelihood projects. This type of fisheries management is supported by more than just the male fishers of PELITA.
Hani initiated Women for Marine Conservation (WMC) in 2022 to strengthen community participation in conservation and fisheries management. Today, WMC members are also involved in fisheries data collection, tourism activities, environmental education and community organisation.
The compressor ban
Indonesia’s fishery laws do not explicitly mention compressors, but regulations that ban destructive and unsafe fishing gear and methods indirectly prohibit them. In 2020, the West Nusa Tenggara provincial government added a regulation that specifically stipulates a ban on compressor diving.
However, Jari’s Boen notes that the problem has not disappeared entirely: “The problem is that [some people] keep doing compressor diving at night when there is no surveillance. One night, we took our fishermen group out at night, and we found 50–60 compressor divers just in this area.”
All the PELITA fishermen have now stopped compressor diving. One of them, Wandra, says that many of his friends got sick, became paralysed, or even died because of compressor dives gone wrong. Fellow fisherman Well decided to stop after becoming paralysed for a month at a time, on three separate occasions. Mahari says he has been paralysed 30 times: “I would go to the chamber, get healthy, and then go to the compressor to get back.”
Compressor diving also has long-term physical impacts on freedivers’ abilities. “When they breathe with the compressor for a long time, it’s a challenge to return to freediving because they’re used to the compressor,” Hani says.
Despite the known risks, implementing the compressor diving ban has been complex, Boen says: “Some people were happy with the regulation, but for the Bajau people there were mixed emotions. Many families faced uncertainty because they depended heavily on marine resources for their livelihoods, so we had a stakeholder meeting.”
In December 2025, Jari proposed the addition of an article to place the Poto Tano village government in charge of governing its own marine resources, he says. “The problem is the Bajau are in the sea every day,” adds Mahari. “We suggest ecological management, so limits on catch and size. Everything is enough for everybody. The problem is when there are greedy people who take more than what they need.”
The fishers agree with conservation, Hani says, “It’s more a discussion about management approaches, where we propose sustainable use and local stewardship rather than unrestricted fishing.”
Rights-based fishery management
Boen and Mahari support the idea of traditional fisheries leading their own management under a rights-based fisheries management model practised in other countries such as Canada and Australia. “Our ideal situation is community-based fisheries led by communities and traditional ecological knowledge,” Boen says.
Traditional practices already support conservation, Wandra says, “We close two to three areas at a time for a few months to help the fishing grounds regenerate.” If the fishers catch an octopus that is too small, they will release it, Well adds. Compared with industrial fisheries, the tools, boats and catches of the Bajau people are also limited to ensure sustainable practices.
The article on village self-governance of marine resources was just recently approved, and JARI and PELITA are working to develop further village-level mechanisms and local regulations.
What does the future hold for the Bajau?
It is too early to say whether the community can sustain a shift away from compressor diving. In the meantime, Hani is passionate about ensuring traditional Bajau practices are not lost.
“The reality is that the majority of Poto Tano don’t know about their traditional culture,” Hani says. “The Bajau people have always had a strong storytelling culture, so we want to figure out how to pass down this knowledge in a way that makes sense to them.” There are nascent plans to create a Bajau museum in Poto Tano, she adds.
Kadir, another of the small number of fishermen skilled in using the pocong, says that “the younger generation has seen how others have been impacted by the compressor, so they don’t want to pursue it anymore.” Some youth, including Kadir’s son, are now involved in conservation, marine ecotourism and ecological monitoring.
“Bajau people will always rely on the sea,” Mahari says. “Now that I have a family and children, I think a lot more about how our kids are going to be impacted. There’s an interest in traditional technologies, but now there is also interest in gathering more data so that we can protect the reef better. Understanding trends over larger spatial areas would help us strengthen our management. My niece is now studying marine science.”
This story was published with permission from Mongabay.com.

title: Más allá de las aulas, los abuelos y sabios enseñan a los niños en la Amazonía
content:
Fecha de publicación:
Fecha de modificación:
Con el inicio del año lectivo Sierra-Amazonía 2026-2027, los escolares de las nacionalidades Waorani, Siekopaai y A’i Cofán regresaron a las aulas bajo un modelo único: los tejidos curriculares y proyectos educativos comunitarios. A través de ellos, los niños aprenden directamente de sus abuelos, abuelas, sabios y sabias, recorriendo la selva y rescatando los conocimientos que sostienen su identidad cultural. Los docentes son los guías y ejecutores de este modelo educativo.
El 10 de septiembre de 2026 se convirtió en un hito para los Waorani, Siekopaai y A’i Cofán. Ese día, las tres naciones de la Amazonía registraron sus proyectos educativos comunitarios y sus tejidos curriculares en la Secretaría de Educación Intercultural Bilingüe y Etnoeducación (Seibe) para preparar académicamente a los niños.
Este registro permite oficialmente a las tres nacionalidades implementar sus proyectos sin trabas en sus territorios a partir de septiembre, es decir, con el nuevo ciclo escolar que ya empezó en Ecuador.
Patricia Peñaherrera, líder de Educación Propia de Amazon Frontlines, explica que cada proyecto educativo necesita el registro oficial del Ministerio de Educación y de la Seibe. Sin ese reconocimiento, los niños de estas comunidades de la Amazonía no acceden a los derechos ni a los beneficios que corresponden a cualquier estudiante de Ecuador.
El proceso arrancó en 2019 con los Waorani, cuenta Peñaherra. La primera fase consistió en un diagnóstico: conversaciones con padres, madres, abuelos, jóvenes, docentes y funcionarios. El resultado fue un informe que se llamó ‘Los 100 problemas de la educación Waorani’. En resumen se detectó el poco funcionamiento de la educación y poco cumplimiento de los modelos rígidos, ninguna infraestructura ni validación de los conocimientos de niños y niñas, docentes sin capacitación, pérdida del idioma, pérdida de prácticas culturales y quiebre del vínculo espiritual con su territorio.
Tras el diagnóstico llegó una pregunta crucial: ¿qué proponen, qué quieren salvar? El pronunciamiento mayoritario de la nacionalidad Waorani fue: “queremos seguir siendo Waoranis, queremos pervivir, trascender. No queremos que nuestra nacionalidad se termine con la cuarta o quinta generación de Waoranis. Queremos que nuestros jóvenes sigan siendo wao, sigan hablando el wao terero, practicando la danza wao, tejiendo la chambira y practicando la siembra de sus alimentos y pescando en sus ríos y cazando sus animales”.
Pero también que los jóvenes adquieran conocimientos del mundo occidental: que sepan matemáticas, lectura, escritura, ciencias especiales, tecnología. “Queremos que se gradúen de bachilleres y también queremos que quiera estudiar en las universidades”.
Así marcaron su ruta y se elaboró la propuesta educativa durante dos largos años, dice Peñaherrera. En la tercera etapa decidieron entre que la propuesta fuera autónoma completamente y separada del sistema educativo nacional o mantenerse dentro del sistema de educación intercultural bilingüe. Ellos optaron por la segunda.
De ahí salió el tejido curricular: un documento que cruza los saberes propios con las materias oficiales bajo temas centrales, como “mi territorio” en el caso waorani. El proceso waorani tomó seis años, por la extensión de su territorio en Pastaza, Napo y Orellana.
Actualmente existen 64 centros educativos waorani, siete siekopaai y ocho A’i Cofán. El promedio de estudiantes es de 20 a 25 niños por centro en estas tres nacionalidades de la Amazonía. Asisten escolares de 3, 4 años, 14, 15 y hasta 16 años.
Solo hay tres escuelas pluridocentes, una por cada nación; las demás son unidocentes. De profesores, solo una parte pequeña es de nacionalidades, ya que el resto es kichwa, de otra nacionalidad y mestizos.
En este sistema de enseñanza tiene un elemento muy importante: La autoridad educativa pasó del Ministerio a la comunidad, a través de comisiones o consejos de educación propia. Ellas definen el monitoreo, la evaluación del aprendizaje y la participación de las familias. Cada comunidad tiene su comisión, pero en el caso de los Siekopaai, solo se conformó una comisión de 42 miembros.
Opi Nenquimo lleva siete años al frente de un proyecto que junta dos mundos en la selva de Pastaza. El presidente de la Organización Waorani de Pastaza cuenta que su pueblo construyó, junto a padres de familia y sabios de la comunidad, un tejido curricular que traslada el conocimiento ancestral al papel, sin dejar atrás la ciencia occidental.
Los abuelos funcionan como una biblioteca viva: la enseñanza tradicional se transmite de forma práctica, día a día. El proyecto no busca un regreso al pasado, sino una educación con dos mundos: waorani y occidental, destaca Nenquimo. “Los abuelos son una biblioteca ancestral”.
Hoy ese conocimiento convive con la escritura y el sistema educativo oficial. Su aplicación corre por cuenta del propio gobierno territorial. La organización provincial se unió con Nacionalidad Waorani del Ecuador (NAWE), el órgano de gobierno máximo, para capacitar a los profesores y así replicar en las escuelas.
En el territorio waorani de Pastaza, seis escuelas piloto arrancaron el proceso hace seis años, con cerca de 60 niños. Ahora la cobertura crecerá a 17 centros educativos, con 160 estudiantes en esa jurisdicción. A fines de septiembre comenzará el primer taller de capacitación en tejido curricular para los docentes de estos centros, antes de extender el modelo a las zonas de Napo y Orellana, los otros territorios de los wao.
Nenquimo explica que entre seis y 10 abuelos y abuelas sostienen la enseñanza en las escuelas pilotos de Pastaza. Uno explica cómo tallar una bodoquera o una lanza; otro transmite los cantos en wao o los rituales que acompañan un embarazo o un nacimiento. Cada niño aprende, además, a leer y escribir. “Si no hacemos esa transmisión, el conocimiento se muere”, advierte Nenquimo.
Las comunidades carecen de agua potable y servicios higiénicos para sus niños. El gobierno waorani construyó cuatro infraestructuras educativas y levanta una quinta, sin apoyo del Estado. Para Nenquimo, el territorio y la lengua se defienden desde el aula.
Nenquimo plantea que los jóvenes waorani estudien derecho, comunicación y otras carreras afines para volver a sus comunidades y asumir el gobierno territorial. Para él, el territorio amplio garantiza alimento, plantas medicinales y libertad para vivir en la selva.
Wilmer Piaguaje dirige la educación de la Nación Siekopai, un pueblo de apenas 825 habitantes en la provincia de Sucumbíos, entre los cantones Shushufindi y Cuyabeno.
Durante años, sus escuelas enseñaron con material ajeno a su cosmovisión, pensado por los kichwas de la Sierra, manifiesta. “La nacionalidad estaba a punto de perderse”, cuenta. Solo se leía y escribía en paikoca, la lengua propia; los demás saberes quedaban afuera.
Tras el diagnóstico de 2019 hubo un cambio de rumbo en los Siekopaai. De ahí nació el proyecto de educación comunitaria, con un tejido curricular construido desde los nueve mundos de la cosmovisión Siekopaai: el mundo del agua, el de la tierra, el subsuelo, la flora y fauna, los cielos. En el mundo del agua, por ejemplo, los niños no aprenden solo la fórmula del H2O, sino que conocen a la mujer y el hombre del agua, seres espirituales que habitan ese territorio.
Sin embargo, él aclara que no se han salido de la línea del modelo del Sistema de Educación Intercultural Bilingüe y más bien se han insertado estos saberes ancestrales para que los docentes puedan desarrollar sus clases con todos los temas y unidades de enseñanza y aprendizaje.
Tienen siete centros educativos, seis unidocentes y uno pluridocente, con 12 maestros propios de la nacionalidad y 3 externos, encargados de matemática, biología y español. El año pasado tuvieron 184 estudiantes y de este nuevo año escolar aún no hay datos.
Cuarenta y cinco personas, entre jóvenes, sabios y docentes, participaron en su construcción. “Es un trabajo por la pervivencia de la nación”, dice Piaguaje. El objetivo no cambia: que un joven Siekopaai resuelva una raíz cuadrada en cualquier universidad del país y jamás olvide de dónde viene.
La población Siekopaai es la más pequeña de las tres nacionalidades y por eso les dicen que la nacionalidad está en proceso de extinción y por desaparecer, cuenta Piaguaje. Sin embargo, cuenta que tienen familias en Perú, donde hay 1 200 siekopaai. A partir de la guerra de 1941 entre los dos países se dividieron, pero desde que se firmó la paz, en 1998, hubo los primeros acercamientos de familias que no se habían visto por más de 50 años. “Ahora sí tenemos más cerca la comunicación y hemos hecho el esfuerzo de contactarnos”.
Piaguaje se siente orgulloso de haber elaborado esta nueva forma de educar a los niños de la Amazonía. Así que recuerda que Siekopaai significa gente multicolor. Sieko es multicolor o de varios colores y paai es persona o gente, “pero ese pai no es una persona cualquiera, es como decir soy originario, nos da orgullo, más identidad”.
Wider Guaramag es de la comunidad cofán Sinangoe, en Sucumbíos, en el cantón Gonzalo Pizarro. Ahí viven 260 personas de las 3 000 que componen la nacionalidad A’i Cofán en Ecuador. El proyecto de educación propia nació en 2022, después de un diagnóstico que encendió las alarmas: se debilitaban las prácticas propias, el idioma y la conexión espiritual con la medicina tradicional.
“Nuestros antepasados enseñaban desde la práctica, desde la oralidad, desde el territorio”, cuenta Guaramag. La comunidad hizo 10 encuentros de revitalización con los abuelos: elaboración de canastos, de shigras y otras actividades ancestrales. De esa manera identificaron la metodología de enseñanza y de ahí salió el tejido curricular propio, con adaptaciones al modelo andino que llegaba desde la Sierra.
El objetivo es garantizar la transmisión de los conocimientos de su nacionalidad y que les permita pervivir en el tiempo como son y cómo heredaron de sus abuelos, enfatiza Guaramag.
Este modelo se aplica desde la práctica, la oralidad, caminando el territorio, recolectando en el territorio, tomando la medicina, por ejemplo. “Fuimos identificando todos estos puntos importantes para crear un proceso de educación propia”.
En clases, cuando toca hacer una olla de barro, el maestro no muestra el producto terminado. Los 49 estudiantes de la escuela, junto a los docentes y las abuelas sabias, caminan hasta el lugar donde se recolecta la arcilla. Aprenden los tipos de barro, cargan el material, regresan y lo mezclan con arena. Ahí entran las ciencias naturales, la geografía y hasta la matemática: cuando tejen la shigra, cuentan las fibras que extraen de la planta.
Para las artesanías, van a buscar el material y recolectar las semillas. “Nuestros abuelos nos guían a dónde están los árboles, las semillas, se recolecta, se regresa, se hace el proceso de lavado, secado y al final hacemos la perforación y empiezan los niños a hacer los diseños de artesanía”.
Incluso, el recreo se aprovecha para afianzar su identidad con el involucramiento de las familias. Cada día, un padre o una madre llega a la escuela con un refrigerio propio: chucula, una sopa, una comida tradicional. “Esto no lo hacíamos antes”, admite Guaramag.
Las clases se imparten en espacios vivenciales y de convivencia entre los niños y las familias. “Es una pedagogía basada en proyectos reales donde se tiene la mejor experiencia de aprendizaje, que no se olvida”, explica el líder educativo de Sinangoe.
Diez personas adultas de la comunidad sostienen el proceso, junto a una comisión de 15 personas entre docentes, abuelos y dirigentes. Para Guaramag, la amenaza no espera: “la globalización y la tecnología nos debilitan como pueblos indígenas”.
La educación intercultural en Ecuador
Son documentos educativos que cruzan los saberes ancestrales con las materias oficiales del sistema nacional de educación. Waorani, Siekopaai y A’i Cofán construyeron cada tejido bajo temas centrales propios, como “mi territorio” en el caso waorani o los nueve mundos de la cosmovisión Siekopaai. El propósito es que los niños aprendan matemáticas, lectura y ciencias sin perder su idioma ni sus prácticas culturales.
El 10 de septiembre de 2026, ante la Secretaría de Educación Intercultural Bilingüe y Etnoeducación (Seibe). Ese registro permite a las tres nacionalidades implementar sus proyectos sin trabas desde el ciclo escolar Sierra-Amazonía 2026-2027, que ya empezó.
Los waorani cuentan con 64 centros, los siekopaai con siete y los A’i Cofán con ocho. El promedio va de 20 a 25 estudiantes por centro, con escolares de entre 3 y 16 años. Solo hay tres escuelas pluridocentes, una por nacionalidad; el resto son unidocentes.
Comisiones o consejos de educación propia conformados por cada comunidad, no el Ministerio de Educación. Estos organismos supervisan el aprendizaje y la participación de las familias. Los Siekopaai, por ejemplo, conformaron una sola comisión de 42 miembros para toda la nacionalidad.
Falta de infraestructura, docentes sin capacitación, pérdida del idioma y quiebre del vínculo espiritual con el territorio. El diagnóstico se hizo en 2019 a través de conversaciones con padres, abuelos, jóvenes, docentes y funcionarios, y marcó el punto de partida para construir el tejido curricular waorani, un proceso que tomó seis años.

title: Connecting food systems at Portland Inaugural Indigenous food summit
content:
Lyric Aquino, Underscore Native News + Report for America and Nika Bartoo-Smith, Underscore Native News + ICT
For two full days earlier this month, community members from across Portland and beyond gathered to share knowledge and learn from one another during the inaugural Indigenous Food Summit.
Hosted by local Indigenous-led nonprofits, the summit came out of a labor of love and dedication to expanding access to first foods, land tending and food sovereignty.
“This gathering is not simply talking about the connected food systems, it’s practicing one,” said keynote speaker Nora Frank-Buckner, Nez Perce and Klamath. She helped organize the Native Grown and Gathered Food Expo in Seattle last year, which inspired organizers of this year’s Indigenous Food Summit.
“Our people have continued to carry the seeds, protect the knowledge, harvest the foods, and make place for one another,” she continued. “Our responsibility now is to make sure future generations inherit not only that knowledge, but also the land, the resources, the relationships, and power to act on it. Food sovereignty is how we remember who we are. It is how we take care of each other, and it is how we make sure future generations can set the table for themselves.”
As community members checked in at the Native American Student and Community Center at Portland State University on Sept. 9 and 10, they opened goodie bags that included a first foods cookbook compiled by the Native American Youth and Family Center, a hot sauce packet from Sakari Farms, a tea blend and smoked finishing salt. Over the course of the two days, just under 200 people attended.
Participants could choose from a wide range of workshops and sessions over the two-day summit, including cougar hide tanning, tea blending, wildfoods preparation, making natural cleaners, conversations about food in pregnancy and postpartum, and more.
Summit participants were invited to share meals that centered first foods and Indigenous chefs. Meals included wild rice and salmon or bison with a wojapi berry sauce, salmon chowder, elk stew and a three sisters salad.
On day two of the summit, a group of youth from the Siletz Valley Schools’ culinary program traveled to Portland and prepared four dishes to share before participating on a panel called “Nourishing Our Youth and Elders.” The four dishes included a cassava flour cracker with a honey huckleberry pudding; a butternut squash bisque with blackberry barbeque steelhead; a bison meatball with bluecorn polenta and huckleberry vinaigrette; and red heirloom popcorn tossed in duck fat with chili, lime and maple syrup.
“The hope for me doing stuff like this is just always that people know that they can participate in that reciprocity with our food systems and our medicines, and that they have every right to be in relationship with their prairies and their food forests and all of those wonderful beings that we get to coexist with,” said Emma Johnson, Cowlitz, Indigenous Traditional Ecological and Cultural Knowledge (ITECK) coordinator at Portland State University who helped organize the summit.
Johnson hopes that the summit becomes a regular occurrence, perhaps annual, along with supporting the potential for other similar summits across the region.
Tending to native and displaced plant relatives
For many, food sovereignty can feel hard to access in daily life, particularly for people living in urban areas, according to Johnson.
One of the goals with the Indigenous Food Summit was to make principles of food sovereignty feel more accessible to everyone.
“Everyone in this room carries something,” Frank-Buckner said during her keynote speech. “Some of you carry knowledge of plants or medicines. Some carry seeds. Some carry fishing knowledge, recipes or songs, language or stories. Some carry the responsibility of teaching our youth. Some know how to organize a market or a really awesome conference, write a policy, move resources, teach a class, build a business, or bring people together. Some are still discovering what has been placed in their hands. None of us carries the entire food system alone, and that is the point. Food sovereignty lives in the relationships among us.”
During the summit, participants were invited to take part in a series of hands-on workshops that centered around working with plant and animal relatives. While some congregated in the courtyard to learn about cougar hide tanning from Polima Joshevama, Hopi, and Amanda Freeman, Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde, others gathered around tables of plants.
In one room, Adrienne Sampson, Navajo, founder of Waterlilly Botanicals, led participants in a tea-blending session. She provided a variety of herbs such as mullein, blue mallow flower, nettles and peppermint. Each participant walked away with a stress relief blend, a respiratory lung support blend and an immune boosting blend.
“Making your own herbal blends or using herbs is good for food sovereignty,” Sampson said. “It’s giving you that ability to take your wellness in your own hands.”
At a different session, participants passed around a basket of freshly harvested chanterelle and lobster mushrooms, while hearing from presenter Leslie Lekos, founder of Wildroot Botanicals, who discussed how to harvest food in nature. She also identified medicinal qualities of different fungi and plants. Mushrooms are high in amino acids, while goldenrod is high in antioxidants, she said.
Lekos shared recipes with participants as well, like a wild rice and chanterelle pasta and a goldenrod cornbread.
While much of the summit focused on cultivating, harvesting, collecting and processing first foods, other topics included weeds and invasive species.
There were conversations about tending to and working with non-native plants — called displaced or misplaced plants by some — in ways that honor the land and are careful to avoid disturbing native species. For example, simply ripping out non-native blackberries can sometimes harm other native plants that may be coexisting with them. Some presenters pointed to simply continuing to harvest blackberries as invasive plant management work.
As summit participants left with bags of tea blends and recipes and bellies full of first food-inspired meals, organizers hoped they also left with a sense of connection to other land tenders, medicine makers and community members dedicated to incorporating ITECK principles of food sovereignty into their daily lives.
“To see so many people embracing Indigenous foods and reaching back to those roots and embracing these different practices and these different activities, it’s really beautiful to me,” said Marie Knight, Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs. “Because as Indigenous people, this was how we lived our life prior to colonialism, and we’ve had to adapt over centuries of changes. And to see us coming back to this, adapted to this modern world, and bringing those ideas back, this is really beautiful to me.”
Decolonizing Your Diet
The rich scent of curry powder and jollof seasoning wafted through the air as retired professional chef Darius Mani Yaw prepared coconut milk collard greens with spring onions and fresh ginger, freshly ground corn polenta with garlic confit, spring onions, and African jollof powder and salt-bed roasted salmon seasoned with African nettle powder for a classroom full of eager students.
Darius Mani Yaw, a postgraduate Indigenous traditional ecological and cultural knowledge researcher, hosted a workshop at the Indigenous Food Summit about decolonizing the diet through ITECK and Indigenous internationalism frameworks.
“We’re able to learn so much about one another through food, through history [and] how our foods came to be,” Darius Mani Yaw said.
Darius Mani Yaw, who is Occaneechi, Black Saponi, Freedman and Giriama, told workshop attendees that he uses ingredients that span multiple cultures and encouraged his students to weave together traditional first foods from tribal nations throughout Turtle Island — and the world.
“So many cultures around the globe have three sisters,” he said. “So why is it that we can see the three sisters but we’re not able to see other first foods across these arbitrary borders?”
In his teachings, Darius Mani Yaw encouraged workshop participants to look into the framework of the American food system and spark change by starting or participating in community grassroots efforts.
“We are going to settler colonialists and begging for scraps and for pennies on the dollar,” Darius Mani Yaw said. “We need to start taking community action and better supporting one another and understanding.”
For Darius Mani Yaw, this starts by making the conscious choice to eat fewer processed foods and more traditional foods while also making sure his neighbors and community have access to similar tools.
“We have to start eating differently, caring for ourselves differently, growing our food if we can, or at least being in community to grow our own food, and supporting one another with these [traditional] knowledges and whatnot,” he said.
A common theme throughout the summit was community, which Darius Mani Yaw has tried to embody in his life and career. A retired chef of over 20 years, Darius Mani Yaw has made more than 10,000 meals for those in need and spent time in houseless encampments bringing meals and resources to his community.
“If I have a freezer filled of salmon, but my neighbor is not eating, what’s the point of having a freezer filled of salmon or bison or game or whatever that may be,” he said.
When Darius Mani Yaw reflected on the food summit, he highlighted the importance of sharing information between Native nations in what he calls Indigenous internationalism. For him, that includes combining his Afro-Indigenous ancestry. He said he hopes events like the summit will inspire others to discuss political action regarding food sovereignty, identity and cultural and traditional Indigenous knowledges.
“This was open to the community, and many of us were sharing our Indigenous knowledges across arbitrary borders. Whether we’re Native or non-Native, no matter our tribal affiliation, our European affiliate, it didn’t matter,” he said. “And here we are coming together specifically in this matter, having a meal, having an identity [discussion] and a political discussion over a meal, making medicines, tanning hides, and being able to show this together and be within community. And really, this was not only a sign of action and resistance, but it’s a resurgence specifically.”
This story is co-published by Underscore Native News and ICT, a news partnership that covers Indigenous communities in the Pacific Northwest.
