title: Jóvenes indígenas k’iche’ interpretan el clima para salvar cultivos en Guatemala
content:
- Comunidades indígenas k’iche’ de Totonicapán, en Guatemala, combinan monitoreo climático y saberes ancestrales para adaptarse a heladas, sequías y cambios extremos de temperatura.
- La información climática compartida a través de audios, mensajes y redes sociales permite que las familias campesinas tomen decisiones que evitan pérdidas agrícolas.
- La iniciativa es parte de un proyecto mayor que incluye estaciones meteorológicas, viveros agroforestales y la conservación de los bosques y fuentes de agua en otros departamentos de Guatemala.
- En 2026, los indígenas k’iche’ de Totonicapán sembraron 500 árboles y planean plantar 2000 más en los bosques de siete comunidades.
Antonela Huinac recuerda las historias que su papá narraba sobre la vida en Tacajalve, una aldea de San Francisco El Alto, municipio del departamento de Totonicapán. “Él nos contaba que, entre 1985 y 1995, la comunidad no sufría mucho calor. No había plagas, todo era muy ‘natural’”, dice.
Pensar en calor parecía una utopía en Totonicapán pues se ubica en el altiplano, en el occidente de Guatemala, e históricamente los informes del Instituto Nacional de Sismología, Vulcanología, Meteorología e Hidrología (Insivumeh) lo identifican como la región con las temperaturas más bajas del país, donde su población, en su mayoría indígena k’iche’, vive de la agricultura, especialmente de granos como el maíz y el frijol.
Sus habitantes aseguran que cosechaban bastante durante el invierno, tanto que podían almacenar una porción para consumir en verano, cuando no había cosechas porque éstas dependían del ciclo de la lluvia.
Pero todo eso cambió. Desde hace unos diez años, estima la gente en Tacajalve, el clima ya no es el mismo. “Dicen que esta es tierra fría, pero ya no”, lamenta la joven lideresa comunitaria, Antonela Huinac. “A estas alturas de mayo [hace diez años] ya estaba lloviendo, pero vemos que el clima hoy en día es de mucho calor”, agrega. En tiempos de crisis climática no solo el calor se vuelve extremo, el frío también.
La aparición más frecuente e incierta de otros fenómenos como las heladas es una grave amenaza cuando la subsistencia está basada en la agricultura. Cuando la temperatura desciende tanto y de manera imprevista, puede acabar con cultivos enteros en las comunidades.
Es por eso que un grupo de 25 jóvenes, entre ellos 18 mujeres, se han convertido en promotores climáticos que comparten la información que se obtiene en las estaciones meteorológicas de la Asociación de Cooperación para el Desarrollo Rural de Occidente (CDRO). Los jóvenes interpretan los datos y generan boletines para las comunidades de Tacajalve, Chivarreto, Chuicruz, Chuipachec, Xejuyup, Juchanep y Paxtocá. Equipados con anemómetros y veletas, estos jóvenes interpretan información climática y la convierten en mensajes que ya han salvado cultivos de las heladas.
Monitorear un clima cambiante
A unos treinta kilómetros de Tacajalve se encuentra el Sendero Ecológico El Aprisco, un parque natural privado ubicado en las montañas de Totonicapán y manejado por CDRO —organización de base comunitaria que, desde hace 40 años, ha coordinado proyectos que buscan mejorar las condiciones de vida de más de 132 comunidades en el occidente de Guatemala—. Este refugio natural se utiliza como un espacio de sensibilización y educación ambiental para quienes lo visitan, especialmente niños y niñas.
El Aprisco es un bosque de 13 hectáreas conformado principalmente por pinos y cedros. La presencia de esta vegetación brinda una sensación de frescura, muy distinta a la de San Francisco El Alto y la cabecera municipal de Totonicapán. Durante el invierno, los trabajadores deben utilizar chaquetas que los protejan del frío, que ha alcanzado los -5 °C.
El parque está conformado por una serie de senderos. Al final de uno de ellos, y a un lado de la carretera, se encuentra una especie de jaula que protege un artefacto metálico con varios elementos que sobresalen, entre los cuales está un tubo de unos tres metros de alto y apenas unos 20 centímetros de diámetro. Se encuentra en un área libre y lejos de los árboles.
“Conozca de meteorología: las estaciones meteorológicas permiten predecir y analizar las condiciones meteorológicas y de los fenómenos atmosféricos como ciclones, huracanes, tormentas y sequía”, se lee en un cártel ubicado en la entrada.
Los objetos que sobresalen son un anemómetro, un objeto con tres medias esferas que giran y miden la velocidad del viento, y una veleta, una especie de flecha metálica que indica su dirección. No puede verse desde la superficie, pero debajo de la tierra hay un pluviómetro que registra la cantidad de lluvia que cae y permite determinar cuánta agua y humedad hay debajo de la tierra.
CDRO instaló esta estación meteorológica en 2018 como una herramienta para que los productores agrícolas puedan conocer los futuros eventos climáticos y prepararse para responder ante ellos. Es una de las cuatro que la organización tiene en el departamento de Totonicapán, a las que recientemente sumó otras cuatro en el área entre Cunén y Santa Cruz del Quiché, en el departamento de Quiché.
Alan Pérez, técnico de CDRO encargado del monitoreo climático, detalla que la estación del Sendero Ecológico El Aprisco “recolecta datos del ambiente para tener información más clara sobre los sucesos meteorológicos que pueden ocurrir en esa área”.
Luego, CDRO entrega estos datos a los promotores climáticos que han sido formados para interpretarlos. Con base en los hallazgos, ellos generan boletines con recomendaciones agrícolas y forestales.
El principal objetivo es que la información llegue a la mayor cantidad de personas. Algunos boletines se publican en redes sociales, como grupos de Facebook, se envían por mensajes de Whatsapp e incluso por mensajes de texto. Otros, con el permiso de los líderes comunitarios, se pegan en lugares clave de las comunidades como los centros de salud. Con apoyo de profesionales de radio, también se han realizado 33 spots en lenguas Ki’che’ y Kaqchikel. Todo esto ha permitido que la población tome decisiones informadas.
En una ocasión, los promotores climáticos lograron informar a una vecina de Santa María Chiquimula —otro municipio de Totonicapán— de la llegada de una helada la mañana siguiente. Que la información llegara a la mujer, productora de hortalizas, representó toda una hazaña, pero demostró que el esfuerzo por divulgar la información valía la pena.
La mujer no tenía un teléfono inteligente y era analfabeta, así que no tenía manera de leer la información en redes sociales o por WhatsApp. Los monitores tuvieron que recurrir al envío a través de SMS a la hija de la agricultora para que le leyera el mensaje y le diera las indicaciones: debía regar la plantación en la noche o en la madrugada y utilizar tapescos (tejidos planos hechos con caña) para cubrirla.
Y así lo hicieron. El brócoli y la coliflor sobrevivieron mientras las mismas hortalizas de su vecina —que no se enteró de la helada— se perdieron. “Esta es una experiencia que nos ha motivado a seguir trabajando porque sí es de utilidad. Es una cosa tan sencilla, pero que le cambia la vida a una familia”, asegura Antonia Xuyup, directora del Sistema Ambiental Comunitario de CDRO.
Entre certezas e incertidumbres
Aunque el monitoreo climático no puede predecir con certeza la llegada de una helada con muchos días de anticipación, sí permitió que los jóvenes identificaran la prevalencia de condiciones que podían favorecerlas. Monitorearon las temperaturas mínimas diarias, la entrada de masas de aire frío (generalmente del norte), la humedad, la nubosidad y el viento.
“Las noches despejadas y con poco o ningún viento favorecen una mayor pérdida de calor del suelo, por lo que, si además se esperan temperaturas cercanas o por debajo de 0 °C, aumenta el riesgo de helada durante la madrugada o al amanecer del día siguiente”, explica Xuyup.
Durante el último invierno —entre noviembre de 2025 y enero de 2026—, la aldea de Tacajalve enfrentó no solo una sino varias heladas fuertes. En las noches, la temperatura disminuyó y osciló entre los 4 y 6 °C.
Las mujeres del grupo de jóvenes promotores establecieron una rutina para responder a este fenómeno. Cada noche colocaban cobijas y chamarras para proteger las semillas de aliso que apenas germinaban. La hora en la que lo hacían dependía de su propia percepción de la temperatura del ambiente. En los días muy fríos lo hacían desde las seis de la tarde y, en los días que eran un poco más frescos, las cubrían después de la medianoche.
Las jóvenes volvían al invernadero a las 5 o 6 de la mañana del siguiente día y debían retirar las chamarras para que los rayos de sol alcanzaran a las semillas. De esta manera, garantizaron que las plantas experimentaran un desarrollo normal.
“Las comunidades pueden tirar rastrojo para cubrir las raíces de las plantas para que no mueran ni se pierda el cultivo”, resume Pérez.
Por su parte, Antonela Huinac reconoce que las heladas de hace unos meses fueron un gran reto para ellos, “pero las plantas se cuidaron de la mejor manera porque nos adaptamos”, celebra.
Aún con todos los logros que han tenido, los jóvenes promotores y los profesionales de CDRO tienen algo claro: el monitoreo climático no reemplaza los saberes ni el conocimiento ancestral de la población k’iche’. Más bien, se complementan. Es por eso que los boletines también incluyen datos relacionados a la fase lunar en la que se encuentran. Según una tesis de la Universidad del Valle de Guatemala (UVG), se observó que al cosechar durante la luna llena los granos presentan menos humedad y por lo tanto menor número de insectos y menor daño durante el almacenamiento.
“Esto es fundamental porque los abuelos y abuelas saben que no en cualquier momento se puede sembrar un árbol”, explica Xuyup.
Reforestación: una herramienta para enfrentar el cambio del clima
La historia del grupo de promotores climáticos empezó en 2024 con el verde de los árboles. Al notar que la temperatura y la sensación térmica aumentaban en Tacajalve, Antonela Huinac, junto a la pastoral juvenil de la iglesia católica a la que asiste, decidió unirse a una jornada de reforestación en San Antonio Sija, otra aldea de San Francisco El Alto.
El Grupo Intergubernamental de Expertos sobre el Cambio Climático (IPCC, por sus siglas en inglés), en su informe global de 2022, ya indicaba que la protección y restauración de bosques puede moderar el calor local mediante sombra y evapotranspiración. En ciudades, la evidencia sintetizada por el IPCC señala que aumentar la vegetación reduce el calor y los extremos térmicos, mientras que en áreas rurales también hay beneficios microclimáticos, pero se intersectan con otras variables como el tipo de paisaje y el agua disponible.
Aunque la ciencia ya había hablado de esto, en Tacajalve se dieron cuenta que los árboles jugaban un papel central en la ecuación climática acudiendo al dato empírico. En la zona donde la carretera atraviesa la comunidad, el sol pega con fuerza y “se siente la diferencia porque allí no hay árboles que refresquen”, dice Huinac. Ella y sus jóvenes compañeros empezaron a preguntarse: “¿Cómo podemos ayudar a nuestra madre tierra, a nuestra naturaleza?”.
Decidieron pasar de las palabras a la acción, buscaron posibles donantes de árboles y fue así como dieron con CDRO.
En mayo de 2024, la organización les dio 150 cipreses (Cupressus) y 150 árboles de pino blanco (Pinus chiapensis), especies nativas en Guatemala. Realizaron la jornada de siembra el día 24 de ese mes. CDRO también les impartió talleres sobre reforestación y el cuidado de ciertas especies de plantas.
Al finalizar el proceso y luego de ver el interés de los jóvenes, CDRO les ofreció instalar un vivero en su aldea. Ellos aceptaron y consiguieron un terreno —que la familia de Antonela Huinac prestó— donde construyeron esa “sala cuna de árboles”. En especial las mujeres del grupo se encargaron, con palas y picos, de nivelar el suelo que se ubicaba en una pendiente y, actualmente, son quienes garantizan el cuidado de las semillas y plántulas que posteriormente se convierten en árboles para reforestar.
En 2026, ellas y grupos organizados de la comunidad, como los comités de agua potable, ya han sembrado 500 plántulas de aliso (Alnus acuminata) que fueron cuidadas en el vivero. Además, junto con las autoridades comunitarias, han planificado plantar 2000 más a partir de septiembre, cuando esperan que llegue la lluvia.
Huinac ha asumido el liderazgo de la iniciativa de reforestación y motiva a sus compañeras a seguir en el proceso, al tiempo que trabaja desde su casa en el oficio de corte y confección de ropa.
La información climática no debería ser un lujo
Raquel Sigüenza, representante de la Unión Internacional para la Conservación de la Naturaleza (UICN) en Guatemala, considera que el monitoreo climático reduce la vulnerabilidad de las comunidades al sustituir la incertidumbre por información climática local y oportuna. Esto permite, según la experta, que las inversiones sean sostenibles a los efectos extremos del cambio climático. Es por eso que la organización internacional, a través de su proyecto Altiplano Resiliente, apoya la labor de CDRO con sus estaciones de monitoreo meteorológico.
“El enfoque de la UICN no se centra sólo en establecer sistemas de monitoreo que arrojen datos técnicos, también se enfoca en asegurar que esa información llegue a actores locales para quienes históricamente la información climática no es accesible, ayudando de esta manera a reducir la brecha de acceso a la información climática. Es una forma de justicia climática”, explica Sigüenza. “La información climática ya no es un lujo al alcance de pocos”.
La UICN no solo apoya en Guatemala a la iniciativa de monitoreo climático de CDRO y los jóvenes promotores. También acompaña otros proyectos relacionados con la adaptación de prácticas agroforestales con las que han llegado a 132 000 personas pertenecientes a los pueblos indígenas k’iche’, Kaqchikel y Mam. Especialmente a mujeres, jóvenes y hogares monoparentales femeninos.
En medio de los esfuerzos, Sigüenza reconoce que el monitoreo climático ha enfrentado dificultades en la región. Las principales están relacionadas con capacidades técnicas y operativas limitadas en los municipios y organizaciones comunitarias, barreras culturales reflejadas en resistencia a nuevas prácticas de restauración y brechas de género.
Las dificultades mencionadas por Sigüenza se viven también a escala mundial. Actualmente, la gran mayoría de las redes comunitarias operan gracias a asignaciones temporales de fondos de la cooperación internacional o proyectos de ONG que, al expirar, dejan a las comunidades sin presupuesto para reponer equipos dañados, comprar sensores o mantener activas las plataformas de comunicación.
Además, en cuanto a brecha de género, según datos de la Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Alimentación y la Agricultura (FAO, por sus siglas en inglés), si las mujeres agricultoras tuvieran el mismo acceso que los hombres a recursos productivos, sus rendimientos podrían aumentar entre 20 % y 30 %.
Aún así, tanto UICN como CDRO y los jóvenes promotores consideran que el monitoreo climático es una iniciativa que debe continuar porque sí ha tenido un impacto positivo en reducir la pérdida de cosechas. “Vale la pena porque con este tipo de pérdidas las familias quedan muy dañadas, no solo en la parte productiva, sino emocional y psicológica”, finaliza Xuyup.
*Este reportaje es una alianza periodística entre Agencia Ocote y Mongabay Latam.

title: Bringing Aotea back to life through a te ao Māori lens
content:
The fight against feral cats on Aotea Great Barrier Island
Ko au te taiao, ko te taiao ko au.
I am the nature, and nature is me.
For the people behind an iwi-led conservation project on Aotea Great Barrier Island, that relationship sits at the heart of the mahi.
Tū Mai Taonga is a Ngāti Rehua Ngātiwai ki Aotea-led conservation project working to remove introduced predators and restore balance to the whenua.
They are undertaking one of the largest feral cat eradication operations in the world.
Project lead Makere Jenner told RNZ the kaupapa was about protecting native species and healing whānau.
"While we're doing a feral cat eradication to restore the whenua, we also are restoring and healing ourselves. That's a holistic te ao Māori way to do things."
Jenner said being able to bring people home was an important part of restoring the whenua.
"The Tū Mai Taonga project has provided jobs that allow whānau to be able to return home to Aotea who have had to live on the mainland for work and other reasons.
"To be able to come home, reconnect with the marae, reconnect with whānau, reconnect with culture, te reo Māori, and also gives them the opportunity to heal the land with their own hands, is really magical."
For trapper and team lead Lyrik Murray, the mahi had also provided a way to reconnect with a part of her identity.
"For me personally, I didn't grow up with that, Māori, like our culture was beaten out of our family literally, you know, so to work for like an iwi led project and reconnect with that kind of mahi is pretty important."
New Zealand added feral cats to the official Predator Free 2050 target species list for national eradication in 2025.
Tū Mai Taonga was currently working from north to south of the island, setting up hundreds of cage traps and cameras across the ngahere.
The first phase of the kaupapa involved cutting around 90 kilometres of tracks through Te Paparahi, a 3414-hectare rugged forest block located at the northern end of Aotea.
Once the number of feral cats was brought down in one zone, the trapping network moved into the next.
The island was estimated to have around 2500 feral cats, while data from the northern area suggested that now, fewer than 15 remained.
Jenner said the decision to remove the introduced predators came from an understanding that people were part of the environment too.
"We see ourselves as part of te taiao, as part of the environment, we are protecting, restoring and sustaining the natural environment, so that the environment is able to sustain us."
And that meant taking responsibility for the damage humans had caused.
"It's not the cat's fault that it's here causing damage in an environment, it's our fault. We brought cats here, people brought cats here and so from a te ao Māori perspective, we are a part of the environment and so sometimes we cause damage but we also need to take every opportunity we can to be able to make things right."
Aotea had specialised ecosystems and was home to native species including takoketai, or black petrel, niho taniwha, the chevron skink, and the kākā.
Jenner said those taonga species could not withstand the pressure of feral cats.
"It's important for us to be able to try to make a way to restore balance for them and to make a way for our taonga species to survive."
The human side of eradication
Restoring that balance also meant confronting the difficult reality of killing the animals that threatened it.
For some of the project's trappers, that could be confronting.
Trapper Phoebe Ngawaka remembered her first kill.
"I went and dug a hole and then asked for [my team lead] to bring the feral over, so she did and then I buried it and planted a little tree on top, had me a little karakia ... but it was traumatic, I wasn't happy about it and it's still the only feral that I've caught."
But Ngawaka said the reason behind the mahi was to create a future where native species could safely return to the ngahere.
"It'd be really cool to have our area set up so that it's safe for those natives to come back, like the kōkako, maybe one day the kiwi, and until then, until all the cats are out of the ngahere, then we can't really have them back."
Jenner said the project's trappers were trained to approach the animals with respect.
"We teach our crew when they're onboarded to be respectful of the fact that that is a living thing. We humanely kill, we don't cause undue distress."
Some people have questioned why the feral cats could not be rehomed, but Jenner said that was not feasible given the numbers involved and the difficulty of domesticating feral cats.
Keeping Aotea's pets safe through manaakitanga
While the project targets feral cats, it also recognises the importance of companion cats to Aotea whānau.
Aotearoa New Zealand is one of the world's biggest domestic cat owners, with around 40 percent of homes owning at least one cat.
Unwanted pets made their way into becoming what's referred to as stray cats - the cats which lived close to humans often surviving on scraps.
Feral cats were the truly wild cats, generations removed from their domestic roots and having had no human interaction. It's these cats even the SPCA accepts should be killed due to the risk they pose to wildlife.
Through the project's de-sex drive and Safe Cat programme, free microchipping and desexing was available on Aotea, while pet owners could register their cats in the island's "Cat-alogue".
Collars and ear-tipping could help identify pets, while a "cat taxi" took animals to the vet and brought them home.
Auckland Council conservation advisor Annamarie Clough said keeping pets safe was an important part of the programme.
"Feral cat control is important, but on the other hand, we recognise the importance that companion cats play in households, so we really want to keep them safe while we're undertaking feral cat control."
Seventh-generation Aotea resident Judy Hale has four cats. She used the free desexing service, saying she could not have otherwise afforded the procedure and travel costs.
Petrol and diesel at the time of RNZ's visit was over $4.44 a litre.
"I was very lucky that we had this available for us, you know, because there's no way as a pensioner that I could have afforded to have had my cat spayed, so it would have been more kittens.
"And gone are the days you could get rid of them yourselves."
This intitative was an example of how the island's approach was looking after the people and pets who called Aotea home, while protecting the wider taiao, she said.
For future generations
Te toto o te tangata he kai, te oranga o te tangata he whenua.
While food provides the blood in our veins, our health and wellbeing are drawn from the land.
Jenner said success would not only be measured by how many cats were removed, but by whether future generations grew up knowing abundance as normal.
"My generation has grown up, with the northern bush on Aotea particularly, being absolutely silent, ghostly silent, sadly silent," she said emotionally.
"Particularly sad for the generation before me, who got to experience the remnants of abundance up there. And that generation, my mum's generation, witnessed that peter away at almost nothing.
"Our ambition is for our tamariki, for our future generations, for their normal to be that abundance that two generations ago had."
With the work now well underway in the north, the next phase of Tū Mai Taonga will see the trapping network expand further south.

title: This man draws visitors to Vietnam’s Dong Van with viral traditional dances
content:
Sung Manh Hung, 34, also known as Hung Ha Giang, has become a familiar name to people who love Dong Van Ancient Town in former Ha Giang Province, now part of Tuyen Quang Province.
Three years ago, Hung’s first videos featuring traditional Hmong dances went viral, bringing more visitors to Dong Van eager to meet him and experience local culture.
Without making an appointment, visitors can gather at 8:00 pm at the community activity area in Dong Van Ancient Town to join Hung in singing and dancing.
It is also where the dances and flute music of the Hmong people in Dong Van have reached audiences around the world.
Recalling the situation three years ago, Hung said Dong Van Ancient Town had no community activities at the time, and visitors mainly came to walk around and admire the old town.
As someone who enjoys community activities, Hung came up with the idea of creating a space where people could connect with one another and express a spirit of solidarity and love for Vietnam.
“Every place has its own distinctive features. Dong Van is home to many ethnic minority groups, and each has its own cultural beauty,” Hung said.
“That is why I want visitors who come here not only to admire scenic spots and national-level heritage sites, but also to immerse themselves in the cultural spaces of ethnic minority communities.”
Hung performs traditional Hmong dances while adapting them so that visitors of all backgrounds can join in.
“I was lucky that when I built my channel, digital platforms directed my videos to people in many countries,” Hung said.
“Many international visitors called me directly and said they wanted to come to Dong Van to have fun and explore the area.
“Many told me, ‘Wow, I didn’t think that such a remote place in Vietnam could have such a fun activity.’
"They also shared in short interviews on my page that anyone who has not been to Ha Giang should visit it at least once in their lifetime because the place is wonderful."
According to Hung, community cultural activities can take place anywhere because Vietnamese people have a strong sense of patriotism.
When revolutionary songs or songs praising the country are played, everyone can come together and move to the same rhythm.
And Dong Van has indeed changed after three years. More visitors are coming and staying longer instead of simply passing through.
Speaking to Tuoi Tre, Pham Duc Nam, chairman of the Dong Van Commune People’s Committee, said Hung has helped spread local culture to visitors, particularly international tourists.
To date, Dong Van has recorded visitors from 124 countries.
Each visitor can in turn help promote Dong Van to more international travelers through their own social media accounts.
Today, Hung's team of community entertainers in Dong Van Ancient Town has 10 members, most of them from ethnic minority communities.
The first criterion is that they must be local, while the second is to give priority to young people from low-income households.
Previously, young people had few opportunities to earn a living from their own culture, and many had to leave Dong Van to find jobs at companies and support their families.
As more visitors arrive and demand for local cultural experiences grows, local residents have also become more aware of the importance of preserving their cultural heritage.

title: Kaushik Kappagantulu’s Greenhouse in a Box Is Aiding India’s Farmers
content:
Kaushik Kappagantulu’s grandmother raised eight kids and 20 grandkids, including him, mostly by herself in the bustling Indian city of Hyderabad. An educated woman, she taught Kappagantulu that if you work hard, you will succeed. But after graduating from engineering college and doing a volunteer program teaching homeless kids, Kappagantulu realized this was not the case for everyone. “In rural India, most of the people work really hard, but because of a lack of access to different things, their hard work does not convert into success,” he tells TIME.
This revelation prompted Kappagantulu to dedicate himself to uplifting others. For six years he worked with school dropouts, helping them access jobs through vocational training. “Every single one of those kids was from a farming family and they were coming to us because farming was failing,” he says.
Sensing a systemic problem that needed addressing, Kappagantulu pivoted to agriculture. In 2015, he launched an agri-tech enterprise called Kheyti, which means farming in Hindi. The goal was to help the more than 100 million smallholder farmers who produce the bulk of India’s staple foods like rice, wheat, and pulses. And one of the biggest challenges facing farmers today is the changing climate.
In India, the combination of extreme heat, unseasonable rain, and depleting groundwater is making it difficult for farmers to grow during the summer season from March to June. During a heatwave this April, sensors installed by Kheyti recorded ground temperatures on multiple farms hitting 125 degrees Fahrenheit. “Climate change is wiping out their hard work,” says Kappagantulu, adding that the average Indian farmer earns about $1,000 a year. “It is not even enough for them to make ends meet,” he says.
Kheyti’s solution was a low-cost modular “greenhouse-in-a-box.” These net houses are designed to be smaller than conventional greenhouses, suitable for the one-acre farmer. They have shade cloth on top, which reduces internal temperatures by about 9 degrees Fahrenheit, and drip irrigation. Each greenhouse is also paired with an AI-powered tool that offers farmers advice on things like choosing the best crops and managing pests. This model works: Farmers reduce their crop losses by 58% while using 67% less water and 70% less fertilizer. Farmers using Kheyti’s structures also increased their net income, earning three times what non-Kheti farmers did on the same amount of land. And thanks to Kheyti’s partnerships with local governments, subsidies and low-cost loans mean the greenhouses are relatively affordable, each costing between $200 to $300. “We have to be the bridge that makes high tech agriculture accessible to the poorest farmer,” Kappagantulu says.
The greenhouse-in-a-box concept won the Earthshot Prize in 2022. It’s been growing ever since, with Kheyti now working with roughly 7,000 farmers across eight Indian states. Kappagantulu aims to double this over the next 12 months with the support of the Indian government, which has recommended states partner with the company.
Kappagantulu hopes to take the greenhouses global in the next three years and has a pipeline of other products, including flexible solar panels that can be installed on top of the greenhouses. His aim is to help one million farmers build secure, climate-smart livelihoods by 2033. But he knows he can’t do it alone. “Long-term change in the climate sector for agriculture doesn’t happen through one solution or one organization,” he says, “but through forming coalitions.”

title: Cross-border project explores growing up after GFA
content:
A cross-border project examining what peace means to the generation that grew up after the Good Friday Agreement in 1998 will culminate in a theatrical performance that will be streamed live tomorrow, the UN's International Day of Peace.
Thirty young people aged 18-25 from North and South, who lived together during the summer, will perform 'Project Lighthouse,’ in the Hawk’s Well Theatre in Sligo.
The Hawk’s Well Director Kieran Griffiths said the project examines "what conflict means to a generation that inherited peace," while "exploring difference and hoping to celebrate it".
The production is a partnership between the Hawk’s Well Theatre, the Millennium Forum in Derry and the John and Pat Hume Foundation, supported by the Special EU Programmes Body.
The project participants, some of whom had no theatrical experience, were selected after they responded to advertisements, in a production guided by artists Abby Oliveira and Bob Kelly.
Mr Kelly describes the production as "a tasting board" of the young people’s discussions, using an open-mic format that expands into dance, movement and abstract theatre.
"What we’re hoping the audience will experience isn't so much a cohesive dramatic arc, but that they have had an encounter with these very interesting young people," he said.'
Grace Doherty from Derry City said the production "was great craic from day one," adding that it was a real success in terms of collaboration.
"Personally, for me, peace means that everyone, regardless of creed, race, religion, whatever, can just live and exist in the world without fear," she said.
Ms Doherty said participants, such as herself, were "very aware of the privilege" and "the safety" that the Good Friday Agreement brought, noting it was "talked about a lot".
She alluded to what the group believes is required for society to move forward as a key point of their discussions.
"A big issue that's been discussed is the rates of violence against women in the north, as well as the male suicide epidemic that the north is grappling with…
"So, there's a balance of being aware of the privilege that we have, while also being aware of what's needed moving forward," Ms Doherty said.
Luke O’Grady from Derry city, who has a background in writing, said he had never experienced theatre and found that he enjoyed "acting and loved improvisation."
"My understanding of peace after taking part hasn't really changed for me, but that's not a bad thing. I've always been quite an open person.
"The dialogue in the group was fantastic. I thought we all got on well, very quickly. It helped that the Sligo people had to stay in Derry; we were seeing each other every day."
Participant Kaylee Finnegan from Limavady, who composed a solo piece for the production, said "peace means collaboration".
Patrick Donlan from Ballintrillick in Co Sligo said he really enjoyed this project and hopes the group can remain in contact.
"Being up there really changes your perspective. It's a recent history. It's not something long gone, and it's something that still needs to be learned about," he said.
Evan Ennis from Dromahair in Co Leitrim said the group wrote their scenes together and will be on stage together, throughout the production.
"It’s so important to have that dialog, not just talking about differences, but being able to create, and highlight how similar we are and how brilliant it is that we can all come together."
Oleksandra Pidopryhora from Ukraine, who lives in Sligo said it was an amazing opportunity, to learn more about Irish history, and to discuss Ukraine’s situation as well.
"This is so great to see how people found this peace, after the troubles and this hard history and I wish that one day our people in Ukraine will live the same way in a peaceful country."
‘Project Lighthouse’ can be viewed online on The Hawk’s Well website tomorrow morning, however, online registration is required.
The production is also the subject of a fly-on-the-wall documentary, which will be included in a digital resource for schools, and it will inform another project, currently in development.
The White Dove, which will be staged at the Hawk’s Well Theatre and the Millennium Forum in 2029, will complete a trilogy of ‘The White Handkerchief’ and ‘Hume: Beyond Belief.’
Chief Executive of the Millennium Forum David McLaughlin said the cross-border initiative is a fantastic example of what can be achieved with a shared ambition.
"It demonstrates how collaboration across the island can strengthen the arts, create meaningful opportunities for the next generation and showcase the creativity and stories of this region on an international stage," he said.

title: First Nations netballers driving change, bringing cultural safety
content:
Netball's First Nations Tournament part of creating culturally safe spaces
While netball may be Australian girls' and women's top participation team sport, it has long fallen short of producing — or at least nurturing — elite Indigenous talent.
Just three Indigenous Australian women have represented the Diamonds: Marcia Ella-Duncan, Sharon Finnan-White and, after a 22-year gap, Donnell Wallam.
In 2024, Wallam left Australia for New Zealand, taking a swipe at her former club, the Firebirds, on the way out.
At the time, she wrote that the New Zealand clubs' "respect for inclusion and culture" was a key factor in her decision to leave, while she eventually returned to the Sunshine Coast Lightning this year.
Netball Australia was not idly watching.
As accusations of a 'toxic culture' at the Firebirds were aired, the governing body launched an investigation and kickstarted a series of measures to enshrine 'cultural safety' for First Nations athletes in the sport.
This included the introduction of Australia's inaugural First Nations team, the Black Swans, following the appointment of Ali Tucker-Munro, Netball Australia's General Manager First Nations and former Diamonds squad member.
Tucker-Munro was also influential in establishing the First Nations Tournament, a yearly national championship currently being held in Melbourne, and the Spirit Series, which launched in 2026 and saw the Black Swans go undefeated against Australia's Pacific neighbours.
Speaking from the State Netball and Hockey Centre, Tucker-Munro, alongside players Gabby Coffey and Scarlet Jauncey, said the measures had begun to address the lack of visible role models for First Nations netballers, with more work to be done.
Embraced in Alice Springs
Twenty-six-year-old Coffey, representing the Northern Territory, is one of several First Nations netballers who have been stuck at the cusp of national competition.
The defender spent four years as a Melbourne Vixens training partner before eventually making the decision to move to the UK to further her netball career.
She represented Birmingham over two seasons, and has since returned to Alice Springs.
Coffey had seen the writing on the wall at the Vixens.
"I knew there wasn't much movement in their defensive end, and the same with a lot of defensive ends around Australia," Coffey told ABC Sport.
While she has not given up on a professional career, she is also at peace with the idea that her role may be to support other First Nations athletes with their sporting aspirations.
The Wiradjuri woman grew up in Alice Springs, away from mob and country, but remembers being embraced by the community in Arrente.
"When you grow up on other Indigenous land and tell people you're Indigenous, they pull you into their culture, so [my family and I] were super lucky and blessed to grow up in the centre of Australia where arguably their Indigenous culture is very sacred and traditional," she said.
Determined to pursue netball, she was advised by coach Gillian Lee to move down south, and remembers the transition to Melbourne as a difficult one.
"It was really hard being away from home," Coffey said.
"I was really lucky with the team I entered [the Vixens] and the support I did have, but it's not the same for everyone. There's a lot of girls who do get those opportunities to move and then don't last because there's just not that support in place."
Hailing from the Northern Territory, Coffey said, was an additional barrier.
"Even with competitions like these, we don't get together until we're here, and we're training away from each other, so it can be quite a challenge."
Visible Indigenous role models key
Asked what more could be done to help First Nations netballers make it to the elite level, Coffey said role models were key.
"If you can't see it, you can't be it," she said, pointing out that there are only two Indigenous players currently in Super Netball.
Coffey said her own experience of spending multiple years as a train-on player, without breaking into the elite environment, showed how difficult it was to make it into a professional team in Australia.
"We get a number of internationals [coming to Super Netball], which I think makes the game better and more exciting, and I don't think [that] should be restricted," she said.
"But I do think there should be more focus on bringing Indigenous girls into the elite level."
She pointed to Netball Australia's plans to introduce two new teams into the competition, saying this would open further list spots.
A New Zealand team, she added, may take pressure away from the Australian players vying for contracts.
Scarlet Jauncey has spent the last year as a training partner for the West Coast Fever, pinching herself to line up on names like Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard at training.
A Yaruwu woman from Rubibi/Broome in Western Australia, Jauncey agreed with Coffey that cutting international talent was not a solution.
"We're happy to be playing against the best in the world, that's what we want," the defender said.
Like many of her teammates, Jauncey grew up idolising Wallam.
"I think it just gives us something to strive towards, knowing that we can be in that space," she said.
In 2025, Jauncey captained the Black Swans, in turn becoming a role model to other First Nations players.
"It was the best tournament I've played in, the best teams I've been with," she said.
"I think just being able to come to First Nations tournaments and having that connection with each other has been really great."
Coffey agreed, saying the experience had given her "goosebumps".
"I think it gives not only myself, but a lot of players so much power and push to keep going and play at the highest level," she said.
Cultural safety means listening to community
Tucker-Munro smiles when hearing the players' responses to playing for the Black Swans.
It has been one of her signature initiatives, alongside the First Nations Tournament and Spirit Series.
"These tournaments are aspirational in terms of trying to inspire the next generation of our kids — who we know love sport and netball in particular — to trial for their respective state and territory," she said.
"It's about the kids that are here this week wanting to aspire to take that next step into the big leagues in terms of Super Netball and Australian representation as well."
Tucker-Munro acknowledged that while it was important to bring First Nations netballers into elite environments, those environments had to be culturally safe.
"First Nations people come into these spaces with our culture and community on our back, as well as cheering us on, so you want to do them proud," she said.
"It's also a tough journey, especially for the kids who have to relocate, so it's about thinking strategically about how we can support them."
Since her appointment, the code has put in place a First Nations Cultural Council, and last year ran a cultural safety review in collaboration with community.
The review considered the perspectives of the wider netball workforce, including coaches and umpires as well as athletes
Tucker-Munro conceded there are "multi-faceted" barriers to having more elite Indigenous netballers, including financial constraints and geographical barriers to access.
"For too long our voice has been very silent," Tucker-Munro said.
"We're not a homogenous people, so it's really important that we make sure we're hearing the voices of many.
"One thing we're really big on in our community is not to do things for us or to us, you've got to do it with us.
"There's real intent and good will to actually drive some of this change across the sporting landscape of netball in Australia."

title: THE CONVERSATION: What happened when a South African school switched from English to bilingual science tests
content:
South African no-fee primary schools use African languages as well as English for teaching and testing. Before 2025, children started learning in their home language in the first three years and then switched to English in Grade 4 (aged 10 and 11). Now, bilingual education is extending gradually into the upper primary grades.
South Africa’s public basic education system serves roughly 12.7 million learners. 80% of these learn through a language that is not their home language.
I am an education researcher with a special interest in language across the curriculum in multilingual contexts. In a recent case study of a bilingual science learning intervention in a Cape Town school, I wanted to know how effective it was to teach and test in more than one language, and what parents thought of the approach. Past studies hadn’t made it clear whether parents usually supported it.
The study found that teaching and testing science topics in the children’s home language and English produced much better results than using English only, and that parents were in favour of it.
The results suggest that bilingual classroom teaching and assessment could be used more widely, and it’s important to make sure parents understand why.
Better test results using two languages
The study took place in a school in Khayelitsha, in the Western Cape. The no-fee school attracts learners from a wide area because it is well run. At the time of the study, the school language policy was English medium in all subjects in Grade 4, including science. The principal, however, agreed to try the bilingual approach in science for the study.
We gave 168 Grade 4 learners a bilingual science textbook in English and isiXhosa, their home language. The same teacher taught four classes bilingually, and learners used both languages in writing in their exercise books. One class was given a bilingual test while the others wrote the conventional English-only test.
The findings showed that children were more engaged in their learning in class compared with similar aged children who were learning in English only. In our study children contributed more to class discussion and wrote more in their exercise books.
In addition, those who wrote the bilingual test, with all questions written in isiXhosa and English, scored an 86% pass rate. Those who wrote the English-only test scored a 51% pass rate.
What parents said
The parents of the children in the study said during a feedback session after the test was written that they were very happy with the programme. They commented on how the bilingual textbook connected them with their child’s learning at home. Parents said their children taught them about science while at home – making links between the world around them and the concepts they were learning at school.
One parent said:
My child came back home more interested in things happening around us.
Another mentioned their own ability to get more involved in their child’s schoolwork when using their own language:
Sometimes a parent may be busy cooking, so when they ask a question you are able to answer even if you didn’t see the question.
Similarly, a parent said:
I went through the pages and read for myself without calling my child and asking what it said.
Parents also described how using more than one language was common in their neighbourhoods. Their children were multilingual and translated for one another when something was not understood. Therefore, the bilingual model of language use at school was closer to language use at home.
One parent noted that they had high hopes for their child continuing with science as a career one day because of this strong start. Parents also wanted to know if mother tongue based bilingual education would be rolled out across the country and in all grades.
None of the parents expressed a concern about their children losing out on English.
Debates on language in the classroom
This last point is important because the dominance of English in society leads to a popular belief that the earlier children learn through English only, the better equipped they will be for the world of higher education and the workplace later on. Teachers report feeling a pressure from parents to avoid code-switching from English into an African language.
In reality, research shows that English-only education contributes to the low achievement of South African children, especially in subjects such as mathematics and science.
When parents have been surveyed on their opinions about language in education, they have usually been given an unenviable choice between monolingual English or monolingual African language instruction.
Furthermore, parents have had little to no exposure to strong models of bilingual education in English and an African language to draw on in their responses. Often the only association black South Africans have with home language teaching is with Bantu Education, the inferior system that the apartheid state designed for black children between 1953 and 1979.
Bilingual programmes can succeed
The bilingual science study demonstrates that when a bilingual programme is well resourced with teaching, assessment and bilingual learning materials it can produce excellent results.
Furthermore, when parents are well informed about bilingual learning, they support it. Parents can appreciate the positive impact of children’s full participation in their learning, both for school and for life outside school. DM
